ASRS:1783341.n: Saw a lightsport looking plane out of periphery of my vision while punching in a button or two on GPS on my panel. Immediately pushed forward and rolled away in steep descending turn to the left, as I was already positioned level and about 100 feet left of a head-on alignment with the other aircraft. I was heads down for less than 6 seconds estimated by time of noticing other aircraft due to relative movement in my field of view that would not have been apparent further out in distance and time from the near-miss. Immediate recognition of need to deviate to left (rather than right) was made along with recognition that a collision would not result due to the immediate evasive action taken. The other aircraft did not take any evasive action and is therefore assumed to have been unaware of my presence. I looked towards aircraft as I rolled and kept eyes on aircraft as it passed by me towards my 5 o clock position while I was rolled in a 70 degree left bank. I then recovered to level flight and continued to climb to 6,300 pattern altitude at my destination airport. I had ADS-B out from a modern solid state transponder unit as well as ADS-B in capability, but I was not referencing ADS-B in on any device screen at the time of the near-miss. The situation may have been avoided in the difficult to see case of a head on convergence had I had my ipad or phone connected to my ADS-B over wifi and a method for monitoring the ADS-B situation with auditory alerts in my headset so that an alert of impending collision would have taken my attention away from a cockpit task and diverted my eyes outside to search for a collision waiting to happen. I was lucky that my field of vision included enough of the view in front of me in my periphery to permit my vision to inform me of the near-miss by the time the aircraft was less than 1,000 feet in front of me. Closure rate was estimated to be 170-190 knots taking both of our speeds into account, with 100 foot lateral separation and less than 30 feet vertical separation before evasive action was taken about 2 miles north of Boulder reservoir, coming southbound from Longmont, CO.
ASRS:1783341.s: A pilot climbing to 6,300 feet near Boulder Reservoir executed a steep left turn to avoid a head-on near-miss with a lightsport aircraft while distracted by GPS inputs. The pilot attributed the incident to being heads-down for six seconds and noted that ADS-B auditory alerts might have provided earlier warning.

ASRS:1783348.n: It has been hard to fly during the pandemic, and the aircraft had been in for annual inspection, so I had not flown for two months. I went out for practice. I chose the back-course approach at ZZZ, as it can be challenging. Also, during recurrent training in Month, we had noticed some odd autopilot behavior when flying this approach. My aircraft has Garmin avionics but these are mated to an older analogue autopilot.By the time I was told to switch to ZZZ1 Approach, I was still at 12,000 feet and quite close to ZZZZZ intersection on the approach. When I gave my request for the approach, the controller gave me vectors to circle back to rejoin the course while descending to 4000 feet. She then cleared me for the approach. I believed she said 'Maintain 4000 until established...', but in our later discussion she said her instruction was 'Maintain 4000 to ZZZZZ.' I believe I read back the former. In any case, when back on extended approach course, but a short distance before ZZZZZ, I began to descend further. The chart showed 3000 feet for the segment between ZZZZZ and ZZZZZ1, which is the FAF and 5.8NM from ZZZZZ. My GPS displayed an altitude of 3100 at ZZZZZ, which I believe is its indication of a safe altitude. So, I had set altitude capture for 3100 feet and was descending. The controller alerted me that she had expected 4000 feet to ZZZZZ. While we were discussing this, the autopilot failed to capture and the descent continued to 2900 feet. The controller told me to switch to tower.On my first attempt to call tower at ZZZ, I had not hit the switch correctly and was still with ZZZ1 approach. At the same time, I noticed the autopilot taking me off course for the approach and interrupted it while calling the tower. We were in the descent within the FAF by this time. The tower controller told me I was low for the course and left of course, and he asked if I was flying the approach visually instead of using the Back Course. Due to the autopilot issue, I was by that time flying visually. It was a clear VFR day, and at no time was I in close proximity to terrain or other aircraft. The problem arose for several reasons. The pilot (me) was rusty and needed practice. It was a mistake to do the more challenging BC approach as the first one. (After this event, I did the missed approach as planned at ZZZ and did two fine approaches at ZZZ1 and ZZZ2.) Also, I believe there anomalies with my avionics set-up and back-course approaches, and I should not have been trying to troubleshoot that as a single pilot, especially being a bit out of practice. Another contributor was my misunderstanding of the controller's instruction, along with using the 3000 foot altitude indicated on the chart for that segment ZZZZZ to ZZZZZ1) and the 3100 foot altitude indicated as the target for ZZZZZ on my GPS for the altitude I was trying to attain. All of these issues increased workload, which is better handled by an in-practice pilot (which is why I had gone out to practice). A final recommendation from this experience is that I will avoid flying BC approaches with my autopilot until I can do a flight with a competent pilot and avionics technician aboard. The BC approaches are quite rare, and almost all have GPS overlays nowadays. So, they are not really a high priority, I actually chosen this one to be challenging and give me practice monitoring the autopilot and taking over if it acted strangely. But given the altitude misunderstanding, resulting discussion, and then the strange autopilot behavior, it was a bit choppy. I flew the airplane in a safe manner throughout (there was no terrain issue along my path), but my adherence to published instructed and published altitudes on the approach was poor.
ASRS:1783348.s: A pilot flying a Garmin-equipped aircraft on a back-course approach descended below the cleared 4,000 feet due to misunderstood ATC instructions, autopilot capture failure, and confusion over chart versus GPS altitudes. The pilot attributed the incident to being out of practice, avionics anomalies, and high workload, though no terrain or traffic conflict occurred.

ASRS:1783353.n: Cleared for takeoff, power was applied, and aircraft veered left and departed the pavement coming to rest in the grass next to the parallel turf runway. Main runway was temporarily closed, and alternate intersecting runway put into use. Once responding airport vehicles released the aircraft to taxi back to parking, aircraft taxied on closed turf runway prior to stopping at main (closed) concrete runway and calling Ground for taxi instructions. It would probably have been preferable for aircraft to call for taxi instructions prior to any movement. Signage could possibly be added as reminder that turf operations should have taxi instructions as well.
ASRS:1783353.s: The pilot reported that after takeoff clearance, the aircraft veered left off the pavement onto grass, closing the main runway. The aircraft later taxied on the closed turf runway without prior Ground contact, prompting a recommendation for signage requiring taxi instructions for turf operations.

ASRS:1783359.n: While at FL410 in cruise flight. We experienced a loud 'bang' from the #2 (right) engine followed by increasing ITT (Interstage Turbine Temperture) and engine vibration. We advised ATC of our situation and requested a lower altitude. During our descent, the smell of jet fuel was entering the cabin and cockpit. At that point, we notified ATC, did a precautionary engine shutdown and planned our diversion. ZZZ [airport] was located 50 miles to our right. The airfield had all the resources we would need. We accomplished all checklists and landed uneventfully. At the time of the event, the weather was Clear VFR at FL410. We had three (3) passengers on board and no baggage.
ASRS:1783359.s: The crew of a three-passenger flight at FL410 experienced a loud bang, high ITT, and vibration in the #2 engine, followed by a fuel smell. They performed a precautionary shutdown, diverted to ZZZ, and landed uneventfully.

ASRS:1783361.n: Normal takeoff roll. After gear up and 400ft. flaps up. I noticed the aircraft would not nose trim down as the flaps were going from 10 to 0 as I tried to maintain 10deg to 12deg climb angle. The aircraft was trying to pitch up and it took increasingly excessive force on the yolk pushing forward to try to keep the airplane under 15deg nose up pitch. The trim switch on the yoke was ineffective.I was not using the auto pilot but pressed the autopilot disconnect switch thinking I had an electrical jammed trim motor. I then went to turn off the main trim switch in order to use to manual trim wheel and the trim wheel seemed frozen. We could turn the wheel but it took a lot of effort to get minor movements. At the same time we were getting FGC 1 and FGC 2 CAS messages. I went back to two hands on the yoke and asked for assistance from the non flying pilot. We noticed that we had a flight guidance computer 1 and flight guidance computer2 failure. At the same time the flight guidance panel went blank and the flight director disappear from the PFD. We had no heading reference and no pitch reference. The auto throttles were also not controlling the speed and when selecting Auto throttles 'off' they still appeared engaged but only 'holding' not moving. We were just trying to hold a basic pitch angle and heading and trying to level off. We were now still climbing through 2,500 ft. and ATC. cleared us up to 4,000 ft. we had a hard time controlling the airplane in the pitch mode. It wanted to climb! All of this happened within a few short minutes of flight.I had two hands on the yolk when NAME asked me if he could take the yoke and once he felt the yoke he agreed there was something serious with the aircraft and we notified ATC that we had flight control issues. We were able to adjusted the throttles to maintain pitch and we figured it was best if NAME controlled the yoke and I controlled the throttles adjusting power and I tried to trim the trim wheel. By NAME flying the plane I was able to try to regain some flight director functions. I pulled FGC1 and FGC 2 circuit breakers let them stay unpowered for a few seconds and reengage them and attempt to determine what systems were working and which failure we actually had. Resetting the circuit breakers brought back the heading indicator and the flight director. We switched the FD command to the Right side. We advised ATC we did not want to climb into the clouds we needed to stay VFR. ATC assisted us with radar vectors to final to Runway XX atZZZ1My thoughts are the pitch motor servo or pitch windings failed or became frozen thus causing the flight guidance computer 1 to not be able to get a valid signal from the pitch feedback then it switched over to flight guidance 2 that also was not able to see a valid signal from the pitch and disengaged. When the flight guidance panel did not have a valid signal from either FGC it therefore lost heading, auto throttles, vertical and lateral modes. The primary flight controls all worked (elevator ailerons and rudder all seem to work properly and the flaps could go up and down normally. The landing gear function was also normal. I believe this was a pitch trim issue which triggered a flight guidance issue and made the aircraft extremely uncontrollable. By splitting the pilot duties and using crew coordination we were able to safely land the aircraft.
ASRS:1783361.s: During climb after takeoff, the flight crew encountered a frozen pitch trim system and dual flight guidance computer failures that caused uncontrollable pitch-up tendencies and loss of flight director references. The pilots manually controlled the aircraft using split duties and circuit breaker resets to restore instruments, then safely landed under ATC radar vectors.

ASRS:1783364.n: Was doing a training flight for a rusty pilot returning to flight. Wind was about 270/17 [kts.] G24. We were taxiing from parking to Runway XX. Pilot seemed to be fine on the taxi. I was looking down trying to fix some static on my headset by readjusting the plugs. The aircraft rotated suddenly to the right and off the taxiway into the grass. I took control and taxied back onto the taxiway. No further issues. We ended up not flying due to the strong crosswind.My analysis was that the pilot was overpowered by a strong gust from the right that was strong enough to rotate the plane about 30 degrees to the right. The pilot hit full left rudder but did not apply brakes or try and counter with brakes due to his lack of experience. My fault as I should not have been heads down. He just got hit by a very strong gust and didn't react properly. The taxi back onto the taxiway was uneventful but I was a bit more observant!
ASRS:1783364.s: During a training taxi, a strong gust rotated the aircraft 30 degrees off the taxiway because the inexperienced pilot failed to apply brakes. The instructor, distracted by headset issues, took control to return to the taxiway, and the flight was cancelled due to the crosswind.

ASRS:1783375.n: On approach to ZZZ from the NW (northwest) after a practice mission to ZZZ1, the ZZZ controller instructed me to 'remain below 2,000 [ft.] and stay west of [the] lake.' I had never flown this route before. I reduced altitude to 1,200 feet, to get close to pattern altitude of 1,039 feet as I approached the airport. My route took me over a small rise in terrain that was higher than I realized. I flew over the rise at approximately 500 feet AGL. Previously I have only flown to the east of this rise.In future I will fly higher or around this rise in order to maintain 1,000 feet clearance.
ASRS:1783375.s: A pilot on approach to ZZZ from the northwest flew over an unexpected terrain rise at approximately 500 feet AGL while complying with a clearance to remain below 2,000 feet. The pilot attributed the low altitude to unfamiliarity with the route and plans to fly higher or around the rise in the future to maintain 1,000 feet clearance.

ASRS:1783389.n: There was a pair of arrivals staggered by about 0.5-0.75 miles, with the Runway 28 Right arrival preceding Runway 28 Left arrival. There was a solid 16-32 knots crosswind from the north depending on what altitude they were at. Runway 28 Left glide slope is 2.85 degrees while Runway 28 Right is 3.00 degrees. In this very rare set of circumstances, the left arrival is getting a rough ride form the right arrival. Aircraft X [the first E175] was cleared to land Runway 28 Right and Aircraft Y [the second E175] was cleared to land Runway 28 Left. Aircraft Y was about 2.3 mile final when they advised going around. I gave them runway heading and 3,000. I advised them of traffic that departed north and stopped climbing in their southbound turn, an A320, and got visual separation transferred to the pilot. I then coordinated the go around and was asked the reason. I said I assumed unstable approach but was not sure. The aircraft was coming up on level flight and so I confirmed the reason. The pilot said they were hit by wake turbulence. I shipped them to Departure, then coordinated with their coordinator the reason. We logged it in the Tower log, but did not write an MOR (mandatory occurrence report). When the airplane came back around and landed, I inquired about the event. They said that the airplane yawed to the right and then began rolling to the left so they went around. That sounds very unsettling to me, however they made it out to fly another approach. No recommendations, it sounds like the pilots did what they were trained to do to save the ship.
ASRS:1783389.s: An E175 on final for Runway 28 Left encountered wake turbulence from a preceding E175 landing on Runway 28 Right in crosswind conditions. The aircraft yawed right and rolled left, prompting the crew to execute a go-around and successfully land on a subsequent approach.

ASRS:1783416.n: Aircraft X had to return to ZZZ for an electrical problem. On the ground after landing, I learned from the flight attendants that there had been a problem with a passenger. They initially described it as a medical issue, saying prior to departure the CSR had struggled to evaluate if he was fit to fly and eventually decided he was. I was told he was the last passenger to board. There were issues with him not wearing his mask properly and several crew members had asked him to cover his nose. He was seated in the wrong seat prior to departure. At one point he was coughing/hacking severely to the point where other passengers began to react with concern. On the return back to ZZZ, two flight attendants said he was unresponsive when they asked him to put his seat and tray table upright. They said they had to resort to physically shaking him before he responded, They asked him if he knew his name and where he was going and he either would not or could not provide this information, but eventually just said he was 'going home.'When he was pointed out to me in the terminal prior to the 'second' flight, on a new aircraft, and his mask was down below his nose. The flight attendants were very concerned and did not want him on our flight because he would not obey crew member instructions. I agreed the situation would likely not improve once airborne and did not want to risk yet another diversion if that it indeed turned out to be the case and therefore told Customer Service not to board the passenger.I told one CSR he would not be allowed on the flight. As we prepared the new aircraft for departure I was confronted by yet another CSR Supervisor who again tried to talk me into taking him. 'We're out of options. There are no more flights out. He's crying. He's very nice. He just wants to go home.' I was moved, but the unruly passengers are always nice to the agents when they're on the ground trying to make up for bad behavior and I had to remember that every Flight Attendant in the back, to a person, had an issue with this passenger and did not feel comfortable taking him. I stood my ground. The FAA adopted a Zero Tolerance policy earlier this month. I am disappointed in our lack of training and or communication of FAA regulations to pertinent front-line employees.
ASRS:1783416.s: The pilot refused to board a passenger on a new aircraft at ZZZ after the previous flight diverted due to an electrical issue and the passenger's unresponsive, non-compliant behavior. The decision was made because flight attendants reported the passenger could not follow instructions, posing a safety risk under FAA Zero Tolerance policies.

ASRS:1783417.n: I was the Captain on Aircraft X (ZZZ-ZZZZ) on date. I just wanted to give some details regarding ZZZZ's refusal to allow us to enter the country without a negative COVID test, and to give a well-deserved kudos to those who helped us.Upon arrival in ZZZZ, we were walking towards the customs area when we were approached by a man from the 'health department.' He asked us for our COVID-19 test results, which (according to our information) were not required for crews in ZZZZ. When we told him that we didn't have a test result, he said we could not proceed further, as a negative COVID test was a requirement for entry into Country.Two airline employees arrived to assist us - the Station Manager X and another employee Person Y. Both were outstanding and went above and beyond to try to help us. They spent considerable time attempting to explain to the health department official that crews were exempt from the COVID requirement. This did not matter to the official, who insisted that 'All passengers must have a negative COVID test prior to entry.' Manager X explained that we were crew, not passengers, and therefore were subject to the crew exemption. He stated that he understood that there was an exemption, but he refused to change his position and stated that we couldn't proceed.Several calls were made by Manager X, attempting to get someone to explain to the health department official that we were exempt. Someone then called the official on his cell phone, resulting in a somewhat spirited conversation. After the call, the official decided that if we'd had a COVID test in the last 14 days we would be allowed to enter. When we said we hadn't, he said if we'd had the vaccine, he would let us in, but of course we hadn't had that either. Manager X pulled us aside and said that this official was simply trying to make a name for himself, and she again apologized, even though it was clearly not her fault. It occurred to us later that perhaps he was fishing for a bribe, but while that's very common in small GA airplanes, I've never had that happen as part of an airline crew. Unfortunately, I was not able to get the name of the health official.By this point, we had the Flight Operations Manager involved, and he was working on getting us seats on the plane back to ZZZ as it was clear we weren't going to be allowed into ZZZZ. Manager X and Person Y were both doing an outstanding job of keeping us informed since neither the F/O nor I spoke [the foreign language].We proceeded back to the gate while Flight Operations Manager got our seats worked out and worked with dispatch to make sure the outbound crew didn't leave without us. As we were leaving, the health department official made one last offer - we could proceed, but he would 'Send a doctor to your hotel room to give you a COVID 19 quick test.' A quick discussion with my FO, confirmed my thoughts that this was a bad idea. Needless to say, we declined his offer. When we arrived at the airplane, FO was physically standing at the bottom of the stairs to make sure that they wouldn't close the door before we arrived.While it was a frustrating endeavor, we couldn't have navigated this successfully without Flight Operations Manager, Station Manager X, Person Y, Dispatch and the outbound crew of Aircraft Y. The crew desk was on the ball as well as I received a couple of pairing change alerts as we walked to the gate. My FO, did an outstanding job, especially considering it was his first trip after OE.
ASRS:1783417.s: The Captain and First Officer of Aircraft X were denied entry into Country ZZZZ by a health official who incorrectly demanded a negative COVID-19 test despite crew exemptions. With assistance from airline staff, the crew returned to the gate and departed for ZZZ after declining an offer for an on-site test.

ASRS:1783422.n: As we turned on to the lead in line at gate X, we noticed self-park guidance indicated STOP in red letters. We stopped. We noticed two ramp service agents on both wing tips and a marshaller under the unit. We decided that we were expected to taxi down the lead in line with marshaller hand signal guidance and ignore the self-park guidance STOP signal. We parked without incident. On debriefing we (me and the FO) both agreed that taxiing down the lead in line with a marshaller issuing hand signals in the face of a self-park guidance STOP indication is a normalization of deviance that has crept into the culture at ZZZ and should not be accepted at company.During the debriefing the FO encouraged me to consider setting the parking brake, shutting down the engines and politely and professionally request a tow in. It should not come to that.It is lazy and sloppy. It is, of or pertaining to, an organization that because of COVID, layoffs, displacements, cash burn, disappointments, you name it, has taken their eye off the ball. It goes against the pilot culture of never accepting RED. e.g. flight deck indications, Runway Status lights, VASI/PAPI, Runway Stop Bars, REIL, PWS, yet on this occasion, I'm just expected, in the course of normal operations, to taxi to [gate] X at ZZZ with a self-park guidance red STOP indication.This is the second report on such an occurrence at ZZZ.
ASRS:1783422.s: The Captain and First Officer ignored a red self-park STOP signal at gate X at ZZZ, following marshaller hand signals instead to park without incident. They identified this as a normalization of deviance caused by organizational complacency, noting it contradicts the safety culture of never accepting red indications.

ASRS:1783426.n: Ops normal from pushback to takeoff roll. I was flying pilot, [the] Captain non-flying pilot. Power was set and autothrottles and FMAs all had normal indications. At approximately 60 knots there was a loud bang and the jet swerved to the right. I steered the jet back to centerline with rudder and the Captain initiated the abort. We stopped quickly on the runway and told ATC we'd aborted and instructed the passengers to remain seated. After quickly assessing the risk, and talking with the Lead Flight Attendant, Captain determined it was safe to taxi clear of Runway XX and we stopped on the parallel taxiway. We requested assistance from [the] Fire Department to look at the landing gear to ensure we hadn't blown a tire or had smoke/fire coming off the brakes. After getting the all-clear, we coordinated with Operations/Tech Ops to return to Gate X. We closely monitored brake temp indications during the taxi back and saw that they were all decreasing in normal fashion as expected. We were met by many company personnel at the gate and Maintenance was able to quickly determine we had an Engine Number 2 compressor stall during takeoff roll. Passengers deplaned in normal fashion through Door 1L, and the flight crew was then escorted up to ZZZ Flight Ops to discuss our readiness and ability to continue flying the trip. Captain and I then proceeded to fly as scheduled. During takeoff roll, heard a loud bang and aircraft swerved to the right. Executed rejected takeoff procedure. Exited runway. Personnel inspected aircraft externally. No visible damage and no fires were detected. Returned to gate. Maintenance data showed engine stall on Number 2 Engine. My compliments to the First Officer and Flight Attendants for their professionalism during this unexpected event.
ASRS:1783426.s: The flight crew aborted takeoff at 60 knots after a loud bang and right swerve caused by an Engine 2 compressor stall. The aircraft was inspected with no damage found, returned to the gate, and the crew continued the scheduled flight.

ASRS:1783443.n: Ramp called to unlock flight will add ballast. Flight did not have 15 bags minimum to secure DG (Dangerous Goods). Unlocked flight waiting for cargo to add DG Quick Pak. Once ballast was added (by ramp) I locked the flight. DG can go thru the locks therefore I was not notified when the DG was added. At departure and ramp finals I realized ballast is loaded with 14 bags and Quick Pak but Quick Pak did not indicate as DG. Cargo Specialist [Name] confirmed DG radioactive. Invalid flight but it did not go thru ACARS as invalid all this happened with 4 minutes of from OUT.
ASRS:1783443.s: Ramp and a Cargo Specialist loaded radioactive Dangerous Goods and ballast on a flight with only 14 bags, violating the 15-bag minimum requirement. The flight departed four minutes after OUT with an invalid load that failed to trigger an ACARS alert.

ASRS:1783446.n: Descent and approach were briefed with expectation of [Runway] XXL at ZZZ. ATC advised during descent to expect Runway XYR. ATC was advised that we were a 747-8 and a request for [Runway] XXL was made. ATC advised that Runway XXL was not available unless operationally required. Runway change checklist was performed and performance obtained for [Runway] XYR. Captain briefed that a right turn [off] [Runway] XYR was not allowed except for Taxiway E. However we did not expect to make this exit so he briefed a left turn at [Taxiway] K or roll to the end. Arrival and landing were normal, after slowing through 60 kts. we were past [Taxiway] E and the Captain stated that he would be exiting left on [Taxiway] K. As we began our left turn toward the high speed taxiway I noticed a line of lights on the ground marking the taxiway closed. These were very dim and low to the ground. Very hard to see. I said very affirmatively, STOP, STOP Barrier. The Captain [stopped] the aircraft and then corrected taxi course. The aircraft did encroach on the first few feet of Taxiway K but not far enough that he couldn't correct back onto the runway. On our rollout ATC did issue an invalid taxi clearance that was a distraction. The taxi clearance was corrected after our [query] and the remainder of the taxi was uneventful. Post flight review of NOTAMS (Notice to Airman) and ATIS (Automated Terminal Information Service) revealed that the taxiway was NOTAM closed and was missed on our part. The poor lighting of the taxiway closure barrier was a large factor in us not seeing it sooner. Prior to top of descent we briefed and prepared to fly the ILS (Instrument Landing System) approach to Runway XXL at ZZZ. Our airport briefing guide does say that arrivals between XA:00 and XB:00 should expect Runway XYR for landing, but goes on to state that 747-8 aircraft should expect XXL. Upon check in with ZZZ Approach, we were told to expect [Runway] XYR. I reminded the controller of our aircraft type and queried whether [Runway] XXL was available. We were told that due to noise abatement procedures at that time of day that we could only use [Runway] XXL if it was due to operational necessity. After a quick discussion with the Captain, we decided that due to our light gross weight, we could accept [Runway] XYR. We quickly reprogrammed the FMS (Flight Management System) and briefed the new approach, to include the many 747-8 taxi restrictions and the fact that taxi to parking was likely to be somewhat complex. We decided that a left turn off the runway on Taxiway Kilo was the most likely scenario. While we did these things quickly, I felt that we had covered all of our bases and did not feel rushed or that the workload was too high. What both the Captain and I missed however, was the fact that [Taxiway] Kilo was closed. We had both reviewed the NOTAMs (Notice To Airmen) and ATIS (Automated Terminal Information Service), but since we were planning on landing on [Runway] 8L, I believe we both simply failed to register the Taxiway Kilo closure, as it did not apply to our original taxi plan. The approach and landing were uneventful and both the Captain and I were focused on identifying Taxiway Kilo in order to vacate the runway. At no point during our approach or rollout did Tower relay any instructions on how we could expect to vacate the runway. As we began to make the turn for [Runway] Kilo, the IRO (International Relief Officer) forcefully stated 'Stop! Stop'. He had managed to pick up the extremely dimly lit barricades that marked the closure. The Captain managed to get the airplane stopped before we were committed to Taxiway Kilo. Around the time we stopped, Tower transmitted that [Taxiway] Kilo was, in fact closed, and that we could expect to make a right turn off the runway at Taxiway Charlie. This was an invalid clearance, as the -8 is restricted from using that portion of [Taxiway] Charlie. As we were about to query Tower, I believe he realized our aircraft type and issued a clearance to taxi clear of the runway at the end. The rest of the taxi was uneventful. I think there are several take-aways from this incident. First, the IRO was worth his weight in gold this morning. Had he not spoken out in a timely and forceful manner, I think there was a very good chance we would have impacted the barriers or at the very least been unable to continue our taxi. The IRO was the last link in the error chain and that link held strong. Second, I think both ZZZ Approach and the Tower Controller were both unaccustomed to a 747-8 arriving at that time of morning. Landing on [Runway] 4R presents a number of taxi challenges to a -8, and perhaps the best practice may be for -8 crews to declare 'operational necessity' and request [Runways] 8L or 8R unless there are other extenuating circumstances. In the event we must land on [Runway] 4R, a simple 'plan to vacate the runway at X' from Tower would be extremely helpful. Finally, while I do believe the way our situation evolved created somewhat of a setup regarding the closure of Taxiway Kilo, the information was in fact available in the NOTAMs and via ATIS. I overlooked that information largely due to an incorrect expectation bias. I am aware of my ultimate responsibility to digest that information and will make an effort in the future to pay more attention to the 'Plan B' options in addition to the expected one.
ASRS:1783446.s: A 747-8 crew missed a NOTAM closing Taxiway Kilo due to expectation bias after switching runways, nearly entering the dimly lit barrier. The International Relief Officer called "Stop," preventing a collision, while ATC issued an invalid clearance before correcting the taxi instructions.

ASRS:1783453.n: Landing [Runway] XXL on final, aircraft in front of us reported a 10 knot loss. The FO was pilot flying at the time and over corrected for the wind, causing us to descend below glideslope very quickly on short final. As soon as I was calling go-around the GS aural warning came on. The FO executed a go-around. Because of the difficult wind conditions and seeing we were already at 2,100-2,200 LBS, I decided that I would land the second attempt as I did not want to get into a fuel situation. We were in agreement with this. On short final for the second attempt, with me as pilot flying, at about 150 feet, we had the wind-shear caution alert and proceeded to execute our second go-around. ATC gave us instructions to set up for [Runway] XXR but due to fuel concerns I said 'Unable' and declared min fuel. Also, I added that if we did have to take any delays we would be declaring emergency fuel. ATC set us up immediately for a close pattern for [Runway] XXL. On this attempt, I stayed slightly high as the wind shear seem to be the worse right at the tree line at about 150 feet. On this third attempt, we landed successfully and taxied back to the gate.Unstable approach recognized by me and a wind shear caution message for the second attempt.Inexperienced FO who had only flown once since May 2020 and challenging weather conditions with wind shear.Two go-arounds and declared min-fuel.Have pilots who have been out a while receive more recurrent training. It was evident due to lack of recency the FO was struggling with the conditions that day. Also, be vigilant on [Runway] XXL as I have had issues on windy days before where the tree line ends and the field begins. With the second attempt we had a 15 knot increase with the wind shear caution message. I was the Pilot Flying. The Wind shear changes in combination with the amount of time since I've been flying in the airplane were contributing factors. There were changes of +/- 15kts and on short approach I went slightly below glide slope and then the Wind shear happened which caused the Glideslope aural warning to sound. The Captain called for a Go-Around which we executed. Once we were at a safe altitude and being vectored back for another approach the we exchanged controls and the Captain became the Pilot Flying. As we were coming in on short approach the Wind shear Aural Caution message sounded so we executed a second go-around. ATC told us that they were going to vector us around for Runway XXR, but were now low on fuel and declared min fuel. They instead kept us close pattern for Runway XXL and we landed safely. Upon landing we had 1,450 LBS of fuel. We taxied to the gate with no issues.Glideslope Aural Warning System on first attempt and Wind shear warning system on second attempt.Wind shear affecting experience level.Go-Around executed twice.Keep crews more recent on flying or more time in simulator if it's been a while.
ASRS:1783453.s: The First Officer and Captain experienced two go-arounds on Runway XXL due to wind shear and an unstable approach caused by the FO's lack of recency. The Captain declared minimum fuel, landed successfully on the third attempt, and recommended increased recurrent training for pilots returning from extended breaks.

ASRS:1783480.n: Aircraft X, ZZZ1-ZZZ did a block-turn-back for maintenance and transload. Due to delay, flight ended up arriving in ZZZ when Tower was closed. I knew ZZZ Tower was closing due to staffing/COVID cleaning and because of the block-turn-back, I simply forgot to add Non-Tower Ops worksheet.Airport towers are constantly closing early due to COVID cleaning or staffing and just need to pay attention to them. Suggest going ahead and sending crew via email Non-Tower Ops Worksheet just in case of delay.
ASRS:1783480.s: The pilot of Aircraft X (ZZZ1-ZZZ) arrived at ZZZ after a maintenance block-turn-back while the tower was closed due to staffing and COVID cleaning. The pilot forgot to add the Non-Tower Ops worksheet because of the delay and suggested emailing the worksheet to crews proactively.

ASRS:1783481.n: Received request from ZZZ hub to apply dry ice supplemental procedures after crew had signed release and headed to aircraft but before they had initialized ACARS. Approved the request with intent to notify crew and amend release once they were on the aircraft. During this time frame, got busy with other releases and departing flights with payload increases, alternate changes, etc. Forgot to get back to [Aircraft X] until after aircraft was airborne and on the way to ZZZ1.This event was caused due to simply had too much going on at one time. I had even put a flag on the flight as a reminder but still got tied up. Dispatcher suggests reducing the domestic flight desk workload.
ASRS:1783481.s: A dispatcher approved a dry ice request for Aircraft X but forgot to amend the release before the aircraft departed for ZZZ1 due to high workload. The dispatcher attributed the oversight to being overwhelmed with other tasks despite setting a reminder and suggested reducing domestic desk workload.

ASRS:1783497.n: At the start of our flight there were thru passengers, one of which was a family of 4. Their small child was not wearing her mask correctly, so I ask that they use the child mask that the previous crew left for them. They were compliant and not a problem. During boarding, another family of 4 boarded with a child that had his own seat and was clearly not under 2. He had no mask at all, I told the Mom that he needed to have a mask on before boarding the plane. She said she told the Gate Agent that he was under 2. I let her board and called down the agent who said that even though he had a purchased seat there was no way other than to take her word for it. During the flight his sister came up and spoke to us about her vacation and told us that she had a baby brother who is 3. This being the same kid that was questioned. My problem with us not having a policy to check for birth dates is that it essentially creates a problem with compliance. How can I be expected to enforce the mask policy to the family that was honest about their child's age while the family that lies does not have to comply. If this was done when the ticket was purchased, then it makes it fair for everyone.
ASRS:1783497.s: Cabin crew reported a boarding incident where a family claimed their 3-year-old child was under 2 to avoid wearing a mask despite having a purchased seat. The crew allowed boarding based on the gate agent's inability to verify age, highlighting a lack of policy to check birth dates that creates unfair enforcement of mask compliance.

ASRS:1783505.n: I was the least involved crew member. Passenger X was assigned to seat XX2 but upgraded herself to YY6, an exit row seat next to her friend. The A [FA] gave her a mask when she boarded because she only had a scarf. Passenger X had food in front of her for much of the flight so that she wouldn't have to wear a mask. I picked up her food trash about 1 1/2 hours into flight and advised Passenger X that she needed to wear a mask. Fellow FAs had told her that she needed to wear a mask previously while not eating. She stated, 'I won't' very clearly.Suggestion - Have a National Policy on mask wearing and ban passengers that fail to comply. This passenger told my coworkers that she didn't intend to fly our airline again. A coordinated policy might have more teeth, and since these passengers are failing to comply with crew member instructions, consider a permanent ban.
ASRS:1783505.s: A flight attendant reported that a passenger refused to wear a mask while seated in an exit row, citing food consumption as an excuse despite prior crew instructions. The passenger explicitly stated she would not comply, prompting the crew member to suggest a national policy and permanent bans for non-compliant travelers.

ASRS:1783520.n: We departed ZZZ en route to ZZZ1. Captain and myself, First Officer, noticed a light harmonic droning noise during climb out but no vibration. About 30 minutes after takeoff while in cruise at FL370 the LH Gen Master Caution illuminated. We ran the QRH and reset the LH generator. At this time the generator did not come back online. We then decided to reduce the electrical load on the remaining generator. The QRH indicated to land as soon as practical. With one hour and 20 minutes left in flight we elected to continue to our destination with the remaining generator.At this time we informed Dispatch. Along our route of flight we determined which airports were suitable for landing in the event we lost our right generator. This proved to be beneficial due to the events that happened down the road. About 40 minutes after the LH generator failed the LH engine rolled back. N1 fell back to almost idle and the ITT dropped immediately as well as fuel flow. We then advised ATC of our engine problem and determined ZZZ2 was suitable and asked ATC for radar vectors direct to ZZZ2.Captain pulled back the power lever on the LH engine at which time we noticed the engine spooled back up but was fluctuating erratically. We started our descent since we were only about 65 nm from the airport. During the descent the engine seemed to stabilize. The droning noise became louder and strangely seemed to come from the front of the aircraft. No noticeable vibration though. Descending into the pattern at ZZZ2 the droning noise become pretty loud and we felt a thump in the fuselage. The thump we latter determined to be a bird strike on the RH wing. (No damage to wing). Conditions on the field were night VFR and the runway was dry. With the loud noise that appeared to come from the front of the aircraft Captain decided during landing to hold the nose off as long as possible. We landed with no issues and no structural damage. We then taxied off the runway and were met with the Airport Fire Department. Priority handling was not requested, but fire was staged as a precautionary measure. As we were taxiing to Company, a repair station on the field, Captain gently pushed up the LH throttle at which time we both noticed it had spooled down by itself. He then went to idle cut-off. Being that Fire was following behind the aircraft a firefighter advised us that he saw a very large puff of smoke from the back of the LH engine when it died. Employees from Company were waiting on the ramp also saw the same plume of smoke. Upon the walk around inspection we found no evidence of structural damage to the engine or any damage where the bird struck had occurred on the right hand wing. The fan blades turned easily. We did observe underneath the LH engine cowl large black streaks from the starter generator cooling exit.
ASRS:1783520.s: The flight crew experienced a left generator failure followed by a left engine rollback and loud droning noise during cruise and descent. After landing safely at an alternate airport, the left engine spooled down with a smoke plume, revealing starter generator cooling exit streaks but no structural damage.

ASRS:1783528.n: I departed ZZZ at ZA:10 local on an IFR flight plan to ZZZ1 in [a rented aircraft]. A preflight inspection at ZZZ revealed no items of concern, and the brakes responded as expected when I tested them upon first movement from the tie down spot and throughout my taxi. The weather was VMC for the duration of the flight, and the weather I picked up on the ZZZ1 ATIS 15 minutes prior to arrival was winds 320@7kts, 9SM visibility, sky clear. I informed ZZZ Approach I would take the visual approach to Runway XX, at which point they cleared me for the visual approach and handed me off to ZZZ1 Tower. Tower requested me to continue on course to fly a left base for Runway XX and report three miles west of the field. Upon my reporting three miles west of the field, they cleared me to land runway XX. Upon nearing the extended centerline, I turned 90 degrees left and aligned myself on an approximately three mile final for Runway XX while at approximately 1,200 feet MSL and 90 KIAS. I completed my final approach and before-landing checks, including pumping the brakes to check for pressure, and crossed the runway threshold at approximately 65 KIAS with 30 degrees of flaps. Immediately upon touching down, the aircraft yawed violently to the left. I applied full right rudder deflection, which somewhat arrested the left yawing and increased the radius of the turn. However, the left main wheel by that time had entered the grass adjoining the runway, further aggravating left yaw. The aircraft continued to rotate about the left wheel until it came to a stop facing approximately due east approximately 75 feet from the west edge of the runway. After ensuring there was no immediate danger of fire or structural damage, I checked the main gear tires out the windows to see if one had blown, but they appeared to be OK. I advised Tower I would try to taxi back to the runway and proceed to the ramp. Upon applying throttle, the aircraft pivoted about its pitch axis into a slight nose-down attitude, which ceased upon decreasing throttle. I tried twice more to increase throttle to induce forward movement, but the aircraft continued to pitch forward when throttle was increased and pitch backward when throttle was decreased. At that point, I informed Tower I would need a tug. An airport crew came with a tug and attached a towbar to the aircraft. Upon attempting to pull the aircraft forward, the tug was not able to move it and subsequently became stuck in the ground. The airport crew then tried using a pickup truck to pull the tug while the tug pulled the aircraft, but the pickup truck became stuck. A 4wd pickup truck came and was able to remove the tug and the first pickup truck back to the runway. The airport crew used a shovel to dig the front wheel of the aircraft out of the ground, as it had become stuck during the previous attempts to taxi back onto the runway. They then attached the towbar to the 4wd pickup truck and were able to get the aircraft moving and onto the runway. I was then able to taxi the aircraft to the ramp under its own power, but noticed it had difficulty tracking in a straight line without additional brake inputs. Upon reaching the ramp, I did a quick inspection of the brake assemblies and discovered a metal-on-metal scraping noise when moving the aircraft back and forth by hand and no movement of the calipers when the toe brakes were actuated. At this point, I felt it was unsafe to continue operating the aircraft and arranged for a mechanic to inspect it the following morning. I called the owner, and he told me, 'that is why you shouldn't take that airplane places on a [weekend] afternoon - no one is around to fix it.' The mechanic inspected the brakes and found that the caliper slider pins were void of lubricant and rusted frozen, one brake lining was missing its rivets due to them rusting away, and several fasteners were loose. He replaced the linings on both slides, lubricated the assemblies, and torqued all the fasteners. I visually inspected the brakes, tested them on the ramp and during runup, and was satisfied that the aircraft was safe to operate. I departed ZZZ1 and had an uneventful IFR flight and landing back at ZZZ.In the future, I will add more thorough visual inspection of the brake assemblies to my preflight inspections, along with checking to make sure the calipers move when the brakes are actuated. I will also land prepared for a problem such as stuck brake, blown tire, or FOD and be more ready to immediately lift back off if safe to do so.
ASRS:1783528.s: The pilot of a rented aircraft experienced a violent left yaw and runway excursion upon landing at ZZZ1 due to frozen, unlubricated brake caliper slider pins. The aircraft became stuck in the grass and required a tug and 4WD truck for recovery before a mechanic repaired the rusted brake assembly.

ASRS:1783561.n: After starting the engine and during our pre-taxi check at ZZZ Airport, the student pilot and I performed a brake check. The student occupied the pilot seat, and myself in the co-pilot seat. We both confirmed positive brake pressure in each pedal. We contacted Ground Control and received taxi clearance to taxi to runway XX via taxiway A. During the taxi from the FBO ramp to taxiway A, we had positive brake pressure. As we approached the end of taxiway A for runway XX, we started to maneuver the aircraft to the left so that we could make a 180-degree turn into the wind in order to perform an engine run-up. As we started to go left, the student pilot stated that he did not have pressure on the right brake. I took control of the aircraft and confirmed that I did not have pressure or authority in the right brake. I applied full right rudder for nose wheel steering and full right brake and the airplane continued straight ahead. At this time I determined the plane was going to depart the taxiway surface, and promptly pulled the mixture to idle cut-off to stop the engine running. I believe that this was the safest thing that I could do to ensure the safety of my student and myself. After that, the airplane departed the taxiway and the left main landing gear came into contact with a taxiway light.
ASRS:1783561.s: During taxi at ZZZ Airport, a student pilot and instructor experienced a total loss of right brake pressure while maneuvering for a run-up. The instructor shut down the engine to stop the aircraft, but it still departed the taxiway, causing the left main gear to strike a taxiway light.

ASRS:1783567.n: I was working the Operational Supervisor Desk when a controller told me there was an aircraft that had not [requested priority handling], but was trying to figure out a technical difficulty. The aircraft [requested priority handling] with an engine malfunction, and requested to land at [a] Naval Air Base immediately. There was a layer of clouds over the field. The airport lies within a Restricted Area that was hot. We had already coordinated direct to the airport with the Military Radar Unit for the [priority situation]. The pilot asked what the MVA was in the area he was at because he needed to get down to land and was on top of a cloud. The controller issued the MVA. I instructed the controller to issue the aircraft a short range IFR clearance to get him down. I made the decision as a safety of flight due to [a priority] situation. There was a disagreement as to if it was legal. Our LOA (Letter of Agreement) on controlling in the Restricted Area Complex allows us to issue short range clearances when aircraft in the complex encounters IMC conditions.
ASRS:1783567.s: An Operational Supervisor issued a short-range IFR clearance to an aircraft with an engine malfunction requesting priority landing at a Naval Air Base within a hot Restricted Area. The decision was made for safety of flight to descend through clouds, despite a disagreement regarding its legality, citing an LOA allowing such clearances in IMC.

ASRS:1783569.n: Aircraft X checked on and I climbed the aircraft to 23,000 feet, and gave them normal speed leaving 13,000 feet. A little bit later, Aircraft X and an aircraft on another frequency of mine transmitted at the same time. I responded to the other aircraft first, and when I went to look at Aircraft Xs data block, they were squawking XXXX. They requested to level at 12,000 feet and fly a 360 heading. I immediately assigned it to them. I called Departure, requested control and told them they were a priority handling. I went back to Aircraft X and they requested a 090 heading. I assigned that to them, notified my Controller in Charge, and began to collect the information. I asked for the nature of their situation, which they told me there was high vibration in their left engine.I also gathered that they wanted to return. It was difficult to understand the pilot due to a language barrier, but finally I understood how many souls on board there were and that there was more than 10 hours of fuel remaining. I then called Departure to forward the information and ask them for a heading and altitude I could turn the aircraft to. They gave me a 160 heading and 12,000 feet, as well as a frequency. After going back to the pilot, I called Departure back to ensure he was radar contact with them. Departure said yes, and asked if he needed to hold. I told them I had not asked. I then shipped the aircraft to TRACON. By the time the aircraft had turned back and I had shipped the aircraft, the aircraft did fly through and leave the southern tip of an adjacent Approach's airspace. However, I did not have a chance to call them as I was busy coordinating with the other TRACON and trying to get information from the pilot. I also never cleared the aircraft back to its departure airport. I simply turned the aircraft to a 160 heading and shipped the aircraft to Departure.I don't believe there was much I could do to prevent this situation. If I had the chance, I could have called TRACON, but in this scenario I didn't have any time to call due to the high workload.
ASRS:1783569.s: An air traffic controller managed Aircraft X, which reported high left engine vibration and requested a return while climbing to 23,000 feet. Due to high workload and a language barrier, the controller transferred the aircraft to Departure without issuing a clearance back to the departure airport, resulting in the aircraft inadvertently leaving adjacent airspace.

ASRS:1783578.n: On flight XX, ZZZ to ZZZZ FO pre- loaded FMC with arrival ZZZZZ XA with Runway XXR. Before descent checklist (6 hours) later briefed STAR and arrival into ZZZZ for both XXL and XXR. ZZZZ ATIS stated both XXL and XXR were in use. Obtained landing data for both runways. Approaching ZZZZZ we got vectors to ZZZZZ1 with expect XXL. On descent ATIS was calling for gusty winds on final from moderate to severe broken clouds at 2,500 feet. We talked about the winds and before we got to ZZZZ1 we got vectors and a decent to XXL we talked about the winds and forgot to change the FMC to XXL. On vectors to XXL with the approach mode armed we intercepted the LOC to XXR. We still were not aware of the error until the controller told us we were lined up for XXR and wanted to give us a heading of 160. We knew traffic was very light so asked if we could continue to XXR and was cleared to continue and land XXR. Landed without incident. Upon returning to the flight deck from break, I was briefed on the ZZZZZ XA arrival and ILS XXL approach. ZZZZ ATIS broadcast that both XXL and XXR were in use. Runway data for both XXL and XXR were had been obtained earlier. Prior to descent we completed the descent checklist. At the FMC's, radios, item on the descent checklist, I intended to check the FMC to verify the approach and checked the item complete, but was interrupted by a radio call and never completed it. I did not catch the error that the FMC had ILS XXR programmed instead of ILS XXL, which had been briefed and anticipated. On the descent we were cleared the ZZZZZ XA Arrival to ILS XXL. Having briefed the ILS XXL, and believing we had ILS XXL programmed, no changes were made to the FMC. We did not catch the error until receiving radar vectors to the final approach. We were given a base leg and shortly after a vector to intercept. The turn to final seemed late and the aircraft but captured and lined up on the centerline. At that point, ATC gave us a 'right turn to 160' and then stated we were lined up for XXR and that we had been cleared for ILS XXL. He said there was no traffic for XXR and asked if we wanted to continue. We were at least 4 miles from the FAF so we accepted the approach clearance. We were able to review the approach noting the LOC identifier, changing the minimums and reviewed the Missed Approach procedure prior to descent on the GS. A stable approach was flown from the FAF to the runway for landing and was uneventful, as was the rollout and taxi-in.On the ATIS, gusty winds were noted and moderate, possibly greater, turbulence mentioned. This was a topic of discussion during the briefing and after. We briefed the cabin crew to have the cabin secured early and to take their seats as soon as possible after the chimes for the sterile cockpit notification. The aircraft was slowed early and we had begun configuring early as well so as to be stable early. The discussion was possibly an additional distraction during the briefing and Descent checklist.While we were able to comfortably get set up for the approach that was incorrectly loaded in and able to fly a stable approach, we should have asked for vectors to a new approach in order to properly brief prior to the initiation of the approach phase. We were lucky there was no traffic conflicts as there was little if any traffic due to time of day and the current state of airline traffic due to COVID.
ASRS:1783578.s: The First Officer on flight XX failed to update the FMC from Runway XXR to the cleared Runway XXL due to distraction during the descent checklist. ATC intercepted the error during vectors, cleared the crew to continue the XXR approach, and the aircraft landed safely without incident.

ASRS:1783607.n: Zone X room number Y, separate two tables to avoid any contact with each other while employee is taking their break, CSR states table were better when there was one by the wall and the other one by the window preventing no contact with another person. Plastic shield should still be used on both tables.
ASRS:1783607.s: A CSR reported that two break tables in Zone X room Y should be separated by a wall and window to prevent employee contact, while retaining plastic shields on both tables.

ASRS:1783619.n: Fumes on flight ZZZ-ZZZ1. This report is to highlight the procedures used to resolve fume events. It isn't to report the fume event. In summary, after the flight and cabin crew smelled fumes during flight and after landing, Maintenance worked to resolve the problem. After performing various procedures, Maintenance said the problem was fixed three separate times. Each time, the flight and cabin crew pointed out that the fumes were still present. Even so, a manager from another department was brought in to see if she smelled any fumes-she did not. So, as the maintenance policy allows, the aircraft was returned to service, overruling six professional and very experienced flight and cabin crewmembers' specific and detailed descriptions of the characteristics of the still present fumes' smell, the locations in the flight deck and cabin where the fumes were detected and the air supply vent locations from which the fumes were emanating. Approximately an hour later, a flight crew reassigned to ferry the aircraft to ZZZ2 started the #1 Engine, smelled the fumes and refused the aircraft. The fume event began during descent below at 5,000 ft., at 15 miles from ZZZ1 airport when I noticed musty smelling fumes on the flight deck coming from the eyeball vents on both the overhead and instrument panels. I recognized the smell from previous experience (along with information supplied by both Air Carrier and the Pilots Association), as being from petroleum based fluid being heated and entering the air conditioning system. Being close to the ground and landing, I wanted to find a solution quickly so I closed the flight deck vents to see if there was any change. There was not, so I reopened them thinking that if the fumes were transient that air flow might move the fumes through and off of the flight deck. I also started to feel slightly nauseated so I donned my O2 mask. After donning my O2 mask the nauseated feeling subsided somewhat. Landing was made without incident. At taxi speed I opened my window, turned off the air conditioning packs and taxied to the gate. I then spoke with the flight attendants to see if any of them had smelled the fumes. The flight attendant at Door 3L said that shortly before landing some passengers asked him about a smell in the area. Once they had pointed it out, he said he had then smelled the fumes. No other flight attendants reported smelling the fumes at their jumpseat locations during flight. I wrote up the fumes in the AML (Aircraft Maintenance Logs), then completed and submitted a smoke, odor, fume form. When Maintenance arrived I described the smell of the fumes to them. None of the mechanics with whom I spoke (four I believe), smelled the fumes. From then until when the flight was cancelled at XA:00, one mechanic (of the four), acknowledged that he smelled the fumes 'slightly' and only one time. During this time, Maintenance completed procedure(s) three separate times and after each time said that they didn't smell the fumes and wanted to sign off the AML. Each time, my flight and cabin crew pointed out the smell of the fumes in the cabin and flight deck, so Maintenance continued their procedures. At some point after those three attempts to resolve the problem, one mechanic told me that the aircraft was going to be there until at least XB:00 that day. Soon after that, a manager from another department was asked to walk through the cabin and see if she smelled the fumes. After a bit I checked my schedule and saw that we were reassigned to take that same aircraft back to ZZZ at XC:00 on [Date]. That was consistent with the last I heard from the mechanic who said the aircraft was going to be there until at least XB:00 that night. Around XD:00, I saw that another crew had been reassigned to fly our aircraft to ZZZ2 at XE:00. I texted the Captain on that flight to be sure he was aware of the seriousness of the problem. He replied, stating that after they had started the #1 Engine, the fumes returned. He did not accept the aircraft. I then called [Pilots Association] Safety for some guidance. I am concerned because, despite all the procedures in place to determine whether the source of the fumes is eliminated, the methods to determine whether the fumes are present or remain:1. Expose maintenance personnel and possibly other people to the fumes and their potential harmful effects (isn't that what we're trying to avoid?).2. Allow using the olfactory senses of random individuals that, (a) may not be able to detect the smell of the fumes, (b) have never smelled the fumes and/or, (c) have no knowledge of the seriousness of the smoke, odor and fume events and their potential and documented health threats.3. Allow the complaints and input of those that do smell the fumes to be ignored or overruled by any randomly chosen person that does not smell them. It seems that the goal should be that if just one person still smells the fumes, the problem isn't solved and the aircraft won't be released to flight status.
ASRS:1783619.s: Flight and cabin crew detected petroleum-based fumes during descent below 5,000 ft. on flight ZZZ-ZZZ1, but maintenance overruled their reports and returned the aircraft to service. A subsequent ferry crew refused the aircraft after smelling fumes upon starting engine #1, confirming the issue remained unresolved.

ASRS:1783631.n: On departure from ZZZ, nose wheel door indicated unlocked/open on instrument panel and overhead following gear retractions. Captain selected 230 kts on FCP and we continued climb while requesting a lower than planned level off alt. We executed QRH procedures and determined we did not have fuel quantities required based on QRH multiple. Coordinated with ATC for return to ZZZ while coordinating with Dispatch. Recovered uneventfully at ZZZ.[Cause was] Aircraft system failure. The nose landing gear door indicated open on both indication panels after gear retraction. We complied with the ECAM and QRH. Based on the increased fuel requirement of the malfunction, we no longer had the required fuel to continue to ZZZ1. We communicated with Dispatch via ACARS and decided to return to ZZZ. [Cause was] Aircraft malfunction.
ASRS:1783631.s: The crew experienced a nose landing gear door open indication after gear retraction on departure from ZZZ. Following QRH procedures, they determined insufficient fuel for the original destination and returned to ZZZ due to the aircraft system failure.

ASRS:1783644.n: Airborne at XA:32z. Crew received FTX GEAR DISAGREE MSG. GR DOORS WONT CLOSE. Recycled the gear, still had indication. Broken actuator.
ASRS:1783644.s: The flight crew encountered a gear disagreement message and open gear doors while airborne at 32,000 feet. Recycling the gear failed to resolve the issue, which the crew attributed to a broken actuator.

ASRS:1783646.n: Block turn back for possible leak in steering tube.
ASRS:1783646.s: The crew blocked the aircraft's turn back due to a suspected leak in the steering tube. No further details regarding the specific phase of flight or outcome were provided in the narrative.

ASRS:1783697.n: We were on the ZZZZZ arrival at about 15,000 ft. MSL to ZZZ to cross ZZZZZ at 8,000 [ft.] MSL when the left engine flamed out (failed). We subsequently [advised ATC] and ran the checklist. We had all favorable conditions to restart the engine. The engine airborne restart was successful and we landed at ZZZ without incident.[Company] Mobile Service is in process of repairs. A faulty engine run/stop switch is suspect.
ASRS:1783697.s: The flight crew experienced a left engine flameout at 15,000 ft MSL while on the ZZZZZ arrival to ZZZ. A successful airborne restart was achieved, and the aircraft landed without incident, with a faulty engine run/stop switch suspected as the cause.

ASRS:1783698.n: I took the plane out to practice maneuvers etc. and was out for about an hour and a half. There were a lot of planes in the area when I returned from the north and was asked to fly down the east side of the valley to enter a right downwind for Runway XX and to report midfield. I repeated the instruction and entered the right downwind for Runway XX. As I was about to report at mid-field, the controller stated that he saw me and cleared me to land on Runway XX. A couple of minutes later, I believe he also stated that a plane was holding short for takeoff until I landed.I passed around the back of the landmark, made the right turn to the runway heading and saw the runway. I then finished my landing checklist and proceeded to land on what I thought was Runway XX. Just as I was about two feet off the runway a second or so before the wheels touched, I heard the tower say to 'go-around' just as my wheels touched the ground. This was immediately followed by the tower stating-- [aircraft call sign] cleared to land Runway XX.I have no one to blame, nor any condition to blame for my mistake--I was shocked beyond belief that I had landed on the wrong runway and as many times as I've heard other pilots talk about it happening to them, I honestly thought it would never happen to me, as I have not had a single incident in 10 years of flying. I have only one possible answer for my error and that is the 'confirmation bias' I've read about and heard discussed in the FAA courses and webinars I've taken.I take full responsibility for my error. To say I'm embarrassed is an understatement, but one good thing has come of this: I'm now acutely aware of the reality of confirmation bias from this first-hand experience and will definitely be intensely focused on confirming and reconfirming my runway prior to landing forever more.
ASRS:1783698.s: A pilot practicing maneuvers landed on the wrong runway despite ATC clearing them for Runway XX and reporting a holding aircraft. The pilot attributes the error to confirmation bias, noting they touched down just as the tower ordered a go-around before re-clearing the correct runway.

ASRS:1783713.n: I had the idea in my head from somewhere in my training about what medicals were due for what type of operation. And if you are not confronted with it you don't really look into it. You feel you know the answer. In the course of running my business I got a database to track currencies, compliance, inspections and flight and engine times. While I was loading the database and setting up alerts and warnings I noticed that I may have, in the past, been flying commercially on a third class for a couple of short periods. I am not sure since I do not have all my old medicals to check. And by the past I am talking about 4 to 5 years ago. Remembering exactly what happened is difficult. Because of this incident I am super vigilant now about medicals, although because of COVID, I had to use an extension on my last medical. My database now warns me when I am getting close to my medical due date. I have gotten the idea out of my head that I can let a second class turn into a third class.
ASRS:1783713.s: A pilot realized they may have previously flown commercially on an expired third-class medical certificate four to five years ago due to a lack of tracking. The pilot now uses a database to monitor medical due dates and has corrected the misconception that a second-class medical can lapse into a third-class.

ASRS:1783723.n: We had planned on doing a touch and go at 33V on Runway 22. After we had touched down we raised the flaps and began to add power. While we were rolling at about 65 mph, a pickup truck with a snow plow on the front of it pulled out onto the runway, and started coming down Runway 4 head at us. I didn't believe we had enough room to stop, so I kept the throttle in for full power and tried to get airborne so we could side step the runway. The airplane was not able to break ground effect due to the high density altitude. The vehicle drove off the side of the runway and we were able to continue down the runway for takeoff. We had made standard radio calls on the CTAF frequency.
ASRS:1783723.s: A pilot conducting a touch-and-go at 33V on Runway 22 encountered a snowplow truck entering the runway head-on at 65 mph. The aircraft failed to lift off due to high density altitude, but the truck exited the runway, allowing the pilot to continue the takeoff.

ASRS:1783731.n: Flaps failed at about zero degrees on retraction after takeoff. Could not extend, retract, or reset. Crew returned to ZZZ safely for a zero flap landing at ZZZ without any further interruption to the flight.
ASRS:1783731.s: The crew experienced a flap system failure at zero degrees during retraction after takeoff, preventing extension, retraction, or reset. They returned to ZZZ and completed a safe zero-flap landing without further interruption.

ASRS:1783734.n: Corporate flight to ZZZ [Airport]. Approximately one hour from arrival airport we had multiple route changes. Final route change was ZZZ [VOR] VXXX ZZZ1 [VOR] ZZZ [Airport]. Had difficulty programing Proline Fusion with new route so I built each intersection on VXXX and reconfirmed route.Given a descent to 7,000 ft. by TRACON arrival. We had discussed and programed RNAV (GPS) Y Runway XX. We didn't ask TRACON for the approach we planned. TRACON cleared us direct to ZZZZZ [Intersection] for the ILS Runway XX. I had reviewed the ILS and knew ZZZZZ Intersection wan on the approach. I had the ILS programed in the number two Navigation unit under the number two FMS RNAV.I gave Captain a heading left to intercept the ILS as I had raw data up. Captain was not set up for the ILS and tried to load frequency and inbound course. Now we are high. I pointed the airport our to Captain. Captain had set up on his ILS navigation display 065 inbound.Speed was 250 kts. I told Captain to slow down. ATC asked if we were too high on approach. Captain advised we could make the field. Switched to Tower. I saw we were too high in altitude and speed to make a stable approach. I advised the Tower that we would like a visual approach with a right down wind for Runway XX. Captain was in agreement. Twice more I advised Captain to slow down. I put my hand over his hand and pulled throttles to idle. Captain brought throttle back up. I believe we were at 3,000 to 4,000 feet descending. Tower instructed us to make a right down wind to Runway XX. Again, I advised we are way too fast. Captain started his right turn. Tower advised us about an aircraft ahead of us. I am not positive, but I thought Tower said to climb to 4,000 feet. I did hear tower state pattern altitude was 2,000 feet. We picked up aircraft visually coming right to left as we were making the right turn to downwind. We received a RA but had visual sighting. I think the aircraft was about 1,000 feet horizontal and about 200 vertical feet above us. I advised Captain twice I had the aircraft. He handed me the aircraft and I slowed the aircraft and started to configure the plane for landing. Once configured for landing I gave aircraft back to Captain. I took aircraft back a second time when I did not think he was quite aware of where we were in relation to Runway XX. We were advised of VFR aircraft and cleared to land. Captain was preoccupied looking for VFR traffic. I brought aircraft around to final on the PAPI. Gave the aircraft back to Captain and asked if he was OK to land aircraft. Normal landing.I have been a Captain for a Major airline and told pilot and mechanic I wished to have debrief to address the errors we made with loss of situational awareness and getting behind on the aircraft.The proline fusion avionics system I believe has bugs to be worked out. Almost all numerical fonts are the same size. with all the color enhanced background if you do not know specifically where to look nothing stands out. None of the National flight training facilities have a simulator that has the Fusion avionics system. Flight Safety ZZZ2 has a stand-alone practice system that has no real time capability. We are pretty much self-taught to use the Fusion Proline Avionics system. To change an approach with the Fusion system also take time to set up an instrument approach means if you are in Navigation FMS mode you need to go to heading select. go to the VOR/ILS. set up the frequency and inbound course. then go back to FMS/NAV mode. I believe Captain made his error in the heat of the moment by putting the reverse course inbound with the tail of the VOR/ILS needle.My errors where I knew we were getting behind the aircraft and thought I could talk the Captain through what we needed to do verses taking the aircraft sooner.I have learned in Corporate flying that standardization in aircraft management means there is no standardization if you work for a small fight department. Especially as a contract pilot. This was without a doubt the most difficult flight I have had in many years. Pilots have great attitudes and always seek to learn and improve. I certainly learned but wish to not learn by making and compounding errors.
ASRS:1783734.s: The First Officer and Captain of a corporate flight experienced loss of situational awareness and an unstable approach due to Proline Fusion avionics programming difficulties and Captain errors. The First Officer took control twice to manage speed and traffic, resulting in a normal landing after a debrief on standardization and system limitations.

ASRS:1783735.n: This flight started the night prior when my normal First Officer had flown someone a few days earlier who contracted COVID-19. That night, I was left trying to find a new First Officer for the next morning's flight at XA:00am. I found an FO who has not flown in a while. Our flight to ZZZ was uneventful. On climbout from ZZZ the Tower Controller had issued a speed of 230 kts and a climb to and maintain 10,000 feet. I asked the FO to run the climb checklist. While doing so, the Controller issued us instructions. My FO was caught off guard and looked at me as if to say, 'I didn't hear that.' I thought I heard and understood the instructions to be 'Normal speed and climb 12,000 feet and I read back 'Normal speed, climb 12,000 Aircraft X'. I then began to climb. This put me into conflict with Aircraft Y that was in the downwind for ZZZ, I never got a TCAS or TA/RA alert from my TCAS system.I know that after the instruction to proceed with normal speed, there was another instruction after that statement. I just cannot remember what it was. The crew change and heavy workload contributed to the misunderstanding. I do not know what could have been done differently to avoid this in the future. I do wonder why ATC would have pilots turn left towards another aircraft even if they were planning to keep the aircraft separated by 2,000 feet. I have flown this departure from ZZZ many times in the past and the point where we were issued normal speed was completely normal from past experience. I really wish that ATC would issue a climb straight ahead until the departing aircraft is no longer in a position to potentially interfere with other aircraft."
ASRS:1783735.s: The Captain and a replacement First Officer misunderstood ATC climb instructions during departure from ZZZ, causing a conflict with an aircraft on downwind. The pilot attributed the error to crew changes and high workload, noting no TCAS alert occurred despite the proximity.

ASRS:1783745.n: I went out to assist with a engine run for a fellow employee who was changing a scavenge oil transmitter. When I arrived to the [Aircraft] he said he had everything ready and just need to do a engine run to see if the message stayed away. I proceeded to run the engine at idle for 5 minutes and the impending clog light never came on. During the run all engine parameters were completely normal and nothing noteworthy was noticed. I shut down the engine and let him know that no message appeared. My coworker forgot to install the O-rings on the transmitter and inflight the oil quantity went to zero. The plane had to make a diversion into ZZZ1.
ASRS:1783745.s: A mechanic assisted a colleague with an engine run to test a new scavenge oil transmitter, observing normal parameters. The colleague later forgot to install O-rings, causing oil quantity to drop to zero in flight and forcing a diversion to ZZZ1.

ASRS:1783749.n: There was a recent change with how our the Military Operating Area (MOA) has been handled in conjunction with ZZZ1. For the years past the MOA has been handled as an autonomous airspace which Center cleared [aircraft] in and out of. The decision has been made to have the ZZZ1 control the aircraft in and out of this airspace by designating a new control area. This week was the first time [new control area] has been in operation since its development and we expected issues, and encountered numerous airspace violations and automation issues throughout the day.
