The event I am reporting was only one of the numerous issues I encountered during this 1.5 hour session, and there will be numerous reports regarding this airspace from other controllers.The situation that caused the most alarm was [Aircraft X, Aircraft Y] which is a flight of 2. We received a call from [new control area] giving us the 5 minute notice that [Aircraft X, Aircraft Y] is ready to leave the airspace. This is the procedure that is published in the Letter of Agreement and following this call [new control area] will initiate an automated radar hand-off. For [Aircraft X, Aircraft Y], there was no hand-off initiated and [Aircraft X, Aircraft Y] called Center stating they were at 25,000 ft. descending to 13,000 ft. I look in the airspace and search the 5 limited targets and do not see [Aircraft X, Aircraft Y]'s beacon code. I then notice a beacon code 5 to 10 miles outside the airspace at 25,000 ft. which is heading back to ZZZ1 and towards some ZZZ arrivals. I quickly pair the data blocks and establish communication with [Aircraft X, Aircraft Y]. Thankfully this time the traffic into ZZZ was far enough away that this was not an immediate issue. This area [Aircraft X, Aircraft Y] was in is a very heavy area for military traffic, ZZZ arrivals, ZZZ Departures, ZZZZ1 Arrivals, ZZZZ2 Departures, and ZZZZ3 Departures. If this issue happens again during a busier session this could very well end in a TCAS/RA event or even worse due to the speed of the exiting [aircraft] speeds. Either better training on the procedures for the ZZZ1 Controllers and the [aircraft] fighter squadron, or amendments to the [new control area] procedures.
ASRS:1783749.s: An air traffic controller reported that two military aircraft exited a new control area without an automated radar hand-off, causing them to fly outside the designated airspace. The controller manually established contact with the aircraft at 25,000 feet, attributing the incident to automation failures and inadequate training on new procedures.

ASRS:1783773.n: Here is the cut and paste from my IOR (Internal Occurrence Report)....I don't know if we swapped aircraft due to my statement to the mechanic and Dispatch that I would refuse the aircraft or not ...but last time this happened the CPO said I needed to file an IOR....so here it is. Also...there is no flight info on this flight when my previous flights pops up on the main menu for IOR and [Reporting Program].We returned to the gate due to an ELAC (ELevator Aileron Computer) 2 fault ECAM. Maintenance said they would defer it and send us with one ELAC. I told the mechanic that if they did that I would refuse the aircraft on account of the potential flight control degradation if the remaining ELAC failed. I informed Dispatch of the situation and we ended up with a new aircraft. I don't know if this was a result of my input or not, so I'm submitting this IOR just in case.
ASRS:1783773.s: The pilot refused to depart with a deferred ELAC 2 fault due to concerns over flight control degradation if the remaining computer failed. After notifying maintenance and Dispatch, the crew was swapped to a new aircraft before departure.

ASRS:1783784.n: Show up to gate X to work a flight and a coworker wasn't wearing a mask the whole shift also another coworker was wearing his mask on his neck. While the Supervisor watched 12 feet away. We signal him about the problem and he ignored it.
ASRS:1783784.s: Crew members reported that two coworkers failed to wear masks properly during a shift at gate X, with one supervisor ignoring their signals from 12 feet away. The incident involved non-compliance with mask protocols while the supervisor observed but took no action.

ASRS:1783788.n: [Consulting Team] was on [Aircraft X] to ZZZ1. It was a miss communication with the team. They did not properly review flight CARD, the aircraft was being loaded with other employees. When I arrived and did not verify all Dangerous Goods cargo was loaded also [Consulting Team] prevention team did not show up or help in anyway when they showed up it was 5 to 10 minuets before departure and they did not verify that dangerous goods were on board the aircraft. These teams were put here to help and verify and locate freight mail and other items and fail to do so.
ASRS:1783788.s: The Consulting Team failed to verify Dangerous Goods loading on Aircraft X before departure to ZZZ1 due to poor communication and not reviewing the flight card. Their late arrival five to ten minutes prior to departure resulted in unverified cargo, as they did not fulfill their role to locate and check freight.

ASRS:1783812.n: Please reference ZZZ [airport], ZZZZZ 4 RNAV SID. We were assigned the ZZZZZ 4 RNAV SID and departed Runway XXR at ZZZ. After checking in with Departure Control the FO (pilot flying) called for the After TO Checklist. This is when several things happened at once. Before finishing the checklist the Departure Controller told us to climb to 10,000 feet and said we were clear ZZZZZ1 [Intersection] then ZZZZZ2 [Intersection]. At the same time we received an ECAM alert for a #1 Pressure Regulator Fault. By the time I set the altitude in the FCP, read back the clearance, re-visited and completed the after TO checklist and trying to diagnose what the ECAM was telling me we were over ZZZZZ1 [Intersection] and the aircraft was starting to turn to the next point on the SID which was ZZZZZ3 [Intersection]. The FO put turned the auto pilot on and placed the aircraft in heading mode and started a turn to ZZZZZ2 [Intersection]. We got the aircraft navigating to ZZZZZ2 [Intersection] but apparently it was not quick enough for the controller. He chimed in and gave us a heading for ZZZZZ2 [Intersection]. We told him we were in the turn and navigating to ZZZZZ2 [Intersection] at that time. Probably not a big deal. No conflict with other aircraft or terrain. No airspeed or altitude violations. Just a lot of things happening at once during a busy phase of flight. The result was we were a few seconds late to make our turn when our departure instructions were changed from what was given to us on the PDC.We complied with the ATC instructions as soon as we could. It was a busy phase of flight and we were task saturated at the time. Getting an ECAM message for a pressurization fault was an added distraction. I have been off work for almost a month due to COVID leave and this was my second trip since returning. I was a little slow to respond but I've been off work almost X weeks and I'm still shaking off the cobwebs.Not pointing fingers, but a change to our SID would have been nice to know BEFORE we took off so we could expect, brief, and build the change into the FMS. When taking off on [Runway] XXR via the ZZZZZ 4 RNAV SID you are over the first point, ZZZZZ1 [Intersection], seconds after TO. Having a change to the SID when approaching ZZZZZ1 [Intersection] only gave us a few seconds to react. Trying to read back and amend the departure clearance in the FMS, clean up the airplane, finish the after takeoff checklist, and diagnose an ECAM caution made for a lot of balls to juggle.
ASRS:1783812.s: The crew departed ZZZ on the ZZZZZ 4 RNAV SID but faced task saturation due to a simultaneous #1 Pressure Regulator ECAM fault and a last-minute ATC clearance change. This distraction caused a slight delay in turning to the new waypoint, though no conflicts or violations occurred.

ASRS:1783816.n: [Company] Duty Officer informed CA (Captain) and FO (First Officer) (me) via company email that after block-in of a revenue flight from ZZZ-ZZZ1 that ZZZ1 offload crew discovered [Aircraft X] had unmanifested ADG in position 12L. The container at 12L was labeled as IBX (International Box Volume), but actually contained 321 pieces of flammable gas (this info provided via Duty Officer in same company email). It was my understanding based on standardized DG (Dangerous Goods) procedures pre-flight that [Aircraft X] did not have any DG loaded.The cause of Hazmat violation was improper tracking of DG materials. DG unmanifested in non-DG labeled container.I suggest more vigilance and thoroughness when handling, tracking, and loading DG.
ASRS:1783816.s: The Captain and First Officer were informed post-block-in that unmanifested flammable gas was loaded in a non-DG labeled container at position 12L on Aircraft X. The reporter attributed this Hazmat violation to improper tracking of dangerous goods materials.

ASRS:1783828.n: Coming to ZZZ on the ILS [Runway] XXR, we were continually slowed by ATC for spacing of traffic ahead and behind. At about 1,200 MSL on glide path still IMC Tower told us to go-around. I was PF and hit GA button and advanced power levers. We went through missed approach procedure, but as flight guidance was attempting to be set the aircraft was also capturing the level off of 2,000 MSL so took a little longer to complete. Meanwhile we were a little late on turning to 195 heading. ATC queried us as we were in the turn. We had also climbed to 2,180 feet before stopping and returning back to 2,000 immediately. After we got settled ATC vectored us back to ILS with no further issues. ATC told us they had to send us around because aircraft on final for parallel Runway XXL behind us had gotten .99 miles from us. Spacing needed to stay a min of 1 mile.I should have paid more attention to altitude and started turn to 195 even if flight guidance wasn't quite set yet. Also pulled back power sooner or not add as much to avoid going through altitude. During our arrival into ZZZ, when told to run base (heading approximately toward ZZZZZ [Intersection]), we were slowed to 170 KIAS. We were maintaining 4,000 feet throughout base turn and intercept turn onto final. Once established on final (approximately 20 NM from ZZZZZ1 [Intersection]) we were slowed further to 160 KIAS, with traffic approximately 4 NM in front of us. Once we intercepted the glideslope, we maintained approximately 1,000 feet above the preceding traffic, but gained to within 3 NM distance. Meanwhile, ATC vectored a airline flight onto final for [Runway] XXL close behind us.I told the First Officer (PF) to potentially fly a half-dot high on the glide slope to avoid any potential wake from the preceding aircraft. Once we reached approximately 10 NM from ZZZZZ1 [Intersection] we were slowed further to 150 KIAS.As we continued down the approach, the TCAS showed us to be approximately 2.5 NM from the preceding traffic, with the traffic behind us close in trail (unable to tell the specific distance). At approximately 600 AGL, ZZZ Tower issued a Go-Around, with nonstandard missed approach instructions (Right turn heading 195, climb and maintain 2,000). The First Officer initiated the Go-Around and the Captain (PM) proceeded to re-program the Flight Guidance.Due to the light passenger load, the subsequent climb rate caused the Flight Guidance to immediately switch from a Climb indication to an Altitude Capturing indication, which caught the Captain off-guard, and he tried to re-configure the Flight Guidance back to a Climb indication. The Flight Guidance again sequenced to an Altitude Capture indication. At this point, the Captain (PM) noticed the aircraft was off course to the left approximately 35 degrees and was rapidly approaching 2,000 feet. The Captain brought this to the attention of the First Officer while also simultaneously acknowledging ATC stating 'Turn right heading 195.' The Captain also prompted the First Officer to reduce the power setting, as the airspeed was approaching maximum flap speeds. The missed approach up to leveling off at 2,000 feet was all hand-flown (i.e. not with the autopilot).Once the aircraft was established on the appropriate heading, altitude, and configuration, ZZZ Approach vectored the flight around for a second attempt at the ILS 16R, which occurred without further incident. In researching the First Officer's seniority, he has been here less than X years (Date). After debriefing the flight, he stated that that was his first Missed Approach / Go-Around in the actual aircraft EVER.Since we had been slowed down significantly early during the approach, we knew we could expect to be sandwiched in between other aircraft. However, we did not know that ATC needed only 1 mile separation between aircraft on parallel ILS approaches (told to us by ATC during our second attempt). There was no mention of spacing requirements on our first approach.Due to 'COVID loads;' the aircraft type climb rates are very good, requiring steeper than normal attitudes so as to not exceed flap speeds. This factor, combined with the First Officer's relative inexperience with missed approaches, caused a momentary loss of situational awareness by the First Officer.This required the CA to not only re-configure the flight guidance for a missed approach, but also ensure the First Officer did not over speed the flaps, communicate with ATC, and ensure the aircraft was following appropriate flight guidance (which was a non-standard missed approach).Also contributing to the loss in situational awareness was the altitude at which ATC issued the Go-Around: 600 AGL. This caused a significant startle factor in both the Captain and First Officer. Had ATC mentioned anything about a potential missed approach, we would have been much more prepared.Last-minute ATC-issued Go Around instructions (below 1,000 AFE), caused by inadequate spacing with simultaneous parallel approach aircraft.RECOMMENDATIONS:1. ATC NEEDS to let crews know 'be ready for a missed approach' if there is potential for a spacing issue. We were given our Go-Around instructions at 600 AGL. This is a very high-risk area to issue a Go-Around, when spacing throughout the entire approach was tight. Some sort of notification to us would have primed for a potential Missed Approach and therefore could have avoided any loss of situational awareness and subsequent heading / altitude deviation.2. STOP ISSUING NON-STANDARD MISSED APPROACH INSTRUCTIONS. The ILS [Runway] XXR's Standard Missed Approach instructions are to fly runway heading to 900 feet, then climb on heading 195 to intercept the ZZZ 210 degree radial, maintain 2,000 feet. This is VERY similar to what we were assigned (heading 195, climb to 2,000 feet). However, when we're given nonstandard missed approach instructions, not only do we have to interpret what it is ATC actually told us, but also program that into the Flight Guidance. This programming is CONTRADICTORY to what our normal Flight Guidance programming procedures are. Had ATC simply said 'fly the published missed approach;' that could've aided in our appropriate handling of the aircraft.LESSONS LEARNED:Don't trust ZZZ ATC to not screw up. If spacing looks tight, brief a missed approach, even if it's done on the Final Approach Course. Also, do not trust your fellow crew member to fly a perfect Missed Approach. Watch them like a hawk for course, airspeed, and altitude management, and IMMEDIATELY speak up if there is even a minor deviation.
ASRS:1783828.s: During an ILS approach to Runway XXR at ZZZ, ATC issued a late go-around at 600 AGL due to insufficient spacing with parallel traffic. The First Officer's inexperience and non-standard missed approach instructions caused a momentary loss of situational awareness, resulting in altitude and heading deviations before the crew stabilized and vectored for a second approach.

ASRS:1783846.n: Tower was very busy with a single Controller working Ground and Tower. On initial climbout we wanted to confirm our initial altitude but had a difficult time getting in contact with ATC. While this was occurring, I missed PIC call for autothrottles, and he did not recognize that I had failed to engage them. We momentarily exceeded 250 knots below 1,000 feet, accelerating to ~290 knots. After clarifying with ATC we both noticed the speed, PIC noticed speed and made adjustments to pitch and power and then I engaged autotrottles. Flight continued normally.Recency of experience due to COVID-19, early morning fatigue may have played a role.
ASRS:1783846.s: During initial climbout, the crew missed engaging autothrottles while struggling to contact a single controller handling Ground and Tower, causing the aircraft to accelerate to 290 knots below 1,000 feet. The pilot-in-command corrected pitch and power after noticing the speed, and the flight continued normally, with fatigue and recency of experience cited as contributing factors.

ASRS:1783856.n: A passenger wore a mask that looked like it had holes in it, he was irate when I told him it was not allowed onboard. He had a kid with him and to make things easier I grabbed him a mask from the galley. When I got to his seat he had another face covering but I still offered him the mask. He took it but and threw in the seat back pocket. He told his kid he didn't wanna make a fuss, it wasn't necessarily a non-compliance but it is definitely worth reporting my point of view.
ASRS:1783856.s: A cabin crew member reported a passenger wearing a defective mask who became irate when informed it was prohibited. Although the crew offered a replacement, the passenger discarded it and told his child he did not want to make a fuss.

ASRS:1783872.n: We landed on Taxiway 1 at ZZZ in front of the FBO hangar. We then began to hover taxi to parking at approximately a 3 foot skid height above the ground. A tug pulling a cargo container was approaching from the south traveling north on the service road. As I neared the service road to cross it, the tug just kept traveling towards us and refused to stop. I had to abruptly stop my taxi and let the tug proceed but, in the process, he passed directly in front of the helicopter and underneath the rotor disk. I reported this incident to my manager and county airport personnel. This is the 5th incident with personnel in the same location within the last 3 months. The others were all very similar. Basically, the tug drivers refuse to give way to moving aircraft.
ASRS:1783872.s: A helicopter pilot hover-taxied at 3 feet on Taxiway 1 at ZZZ when a tug driver refused to stop on the service road. The tug passed directly under the rotor disk, forcing an abrupt stop, which the pilot reported as the fifth similar incident in three months caused by drivers failing to yield.

ASRS:1783879.n: The problem arose when I went to log the flight and found out that I was not current. Contributing factors (beside my inattention) could be that with COVID, both in general and having had it, I have not flown the amount that I normally would. However, I should have been more alert to my 'currency.' I file IFR for every trip whether VMC or IFR and so I filed IFR, again without checking for currency. For corrective actions I have set dates in my calendar quarterly to make sure I am on track for currency.Concerning my medical currency, I have two years 'under my belt' with Basic Med. I went in for my annual physical and gave the forms to my doctor. However, when it was discovered that I was not under Basic Med, I called the Doctor's office and his response was that he remembers the conversation but not filling out any forms. He had done my last Basic Med so I left it in his hands to complete. I understand that it was/is my responsibility to follow up on this, but I did not. Again, I have placed a reminder in my calendar both to renew my Basic Med in two years and then a week later to follow up with my doctor.
ASRS:1783879.s: The pilot discovered they were not current for flight logging and Basic Med due to inattention and a doctor's failure to complete forms. The pilot attributed the lapse to reduced flying during the pandemic and implemented calendar reminders to ensure future currency compliance.

ASRS:1783883.n: I was instructing on a training flight, and departed from ZZZ, while climbing out and making a crosswind departure to the east. The student was flying while I was making radio calls. Upon reaching approximately 2,300 feet MSL, I caught a plane performing a steep left turn bank towards us. I took flight controls from the student and descended around 500 feet approximately 1,000 feet AGL to avoid the other traffic. I made radio calls on CTAF at the local airport and the other aircraft was not on frequency. I proceeded to warn an aircraft behind us on CTAF performing a low approach with a departure to the east as well about an aircraft performing unpredictable maneuvers on the departure end at a low altitude. Once on the ground we were able to review the flight data and track logs of the other aircraft. My assumption is the other aircraft was unaware of their proximity to the airport and performing steep turns. Another contributing factor could have been the difference in altimeter settings between the two local airports and change from departure of approximately .11 in/hg. The maneuvers were being performed outside the local practice area box. Panel mounted ADS-B-In could have assisted with our situational awareness of the aircraft location. We had a portable receiver but did not have an tablet out as we were practicing crosswind landings so we had no traffic advisory until after corrective action. Once corrective action was taken, and tablet was consulted, we still had traffic above and turning towards us from the opposite side. We maintained a low altitude until well clear of the aircraft. Which leads me to believe he was unaware of us and their proximity to other aircraft and airport.
ASRS:1783883.s: During a training climb from ZZZ, an instructor took controls to descend 500 feet to avoid a student pilot's aircraft performing steep turns near 2,300 feet MSL. The reporter attributes the conflict to the other pilot's lack of situational awareness and altimeter setting differences, noting that ADS-B-In could have provided earlier traffic advisories.

ASRS:1783885.n: In being given instruction to taxi from Ramp 1 to Runway 7R, the instructions were to enter Delta taxiway to [Taxiway] D4 then to C3 and hold short. Taxiway Delta is a newly constructed taxiway with a vehicle roadway just prior to Taxiway Delta. In executing the turn, the vehicle access road was mistaken for Taxiway Delta. Immediately upon realizing this error, I contacted DVT Ground Control and advised them of the situation. I was given the choice of remaining where I was and be re-positioned by ground personnel or taxi around to the north side of the airport via the vehicle access road and proceed normally from the north runway (Runway 7L). While I was deciding, the Ground Controller stated that aircraft had been previously towed on this very road in the past. Bearing this in mind, I chose to taxi around the vehicle access road, ultimately discovering it to be too narrow and resulting to the necessity of ground personnel having to dismantle all the remaining signs, so as to allow me to complete this route and arrive at the [Runway] 7L run-up area, after which I was given instructions to proceed normally to the hangar area on the south field, which occurred without further incident.It should be noted that in reviewing this incident, that the vehicle access road and Taxiway Delta are immediately adjacent to each other and if additional signage were present to further clarify this potential hazard, it would be an important addition to improve safe taxi at this airport.
ASRS:1783885.s: The pilot mistakenly entered a vehicle access road instead of the newly constructed Taxiway Delta while taxiing to Runway 7R. The road was too narrow for the aircraft, requiring ground personnel to dismantle signs to allow the pilot to reach Runway 7L and return to the hangar.

ASRS:1783900.n: I was sitting front seat, doing my tail wheel training in the Citabria practicing touch and goes. I was practicing my second ever short field landing in this aircraft and as I was applying breaking to the aircraft I heard my instructor telling me to press harder on the brakes, as we were nearing the end of the landing. I then applied brakes to the point of the tail wheel rising up and then the propeller struck the runway. We were practicing short field landings for training. After landing the student started applying brakes very lightly. I prompted the student to increase braking action and the student suddenly applied aggressive braking action. The tail began to rise and I applied full aft elevator to help slow the rise but was unable to prevent the prop from striking the runway. From the time aggressive brakes were applied until the prop struck the ground was less than .5 seconds. I had previously briefed with the student what the appropriate short field landing and braking action should look like on the ground and in flight just before the demonstration. I then demonstrated how the maneuver was to be performed before allowing the student to execute the maneuver. Total distance covered from the time the prop impacted the runway was only approximately 5 feet. After the aircraft came to a stop I shut everything down besides the radio, made a radio call to traffic in the area to temporarily close the runway and then had the student monitor the radios while I contacted airport management to notam the runway closed and get assistance with the aircraft. A preliminary inspection revealed damage to the prop, spinner, and lower cowling. No injuries were incurred and not further damage is known at this time.
ASRS:1783900.s: A student pilot and instructor in a Citabria suffered propeller, spinner, and cowling damage during a short field landing training touch-and-go. The incident occurred when the student applied aggressive braking, causing the tail to rise and the propeller to strike the runway within 0.5 seconds.

ASRS:1783902.n: After filing IFR, I got an email (Foreflight) stating 'Expected Route Received' of 'BFI TAOMA J5 SUMMA J54 BKE BYI BEARR5 ZZZ. BFI clearance delivery gave me a verbal clearance of NRVNA1 TAOMA fly 135, climb via SID. The SID has a climb limit of 2,000 feet. Tower cleared me for takeoff and (I believe)135 heading. After takeoff, I checked in with Seattle Departure and a few seconds later, they asked me what my heading was. I replied 135 then direct NRVNA which is what the SID says. They asked me again and now I was SURE I was not doing what I was supposed to be doing. They gave me a 30deg LEFT turn followed shortly by a climb, so I believe I flew farther to the west than what they expected of me. I am still confused by what I would term a sort of 'hybrid' clearance. Was I cleared to fly the NRVNA SID or was I supposed to maintain 135 deg heading until further notice. It was the combination of 'fly 135' and 'climb via SID' that seemed contradictory. I should have been more forceful in querying the controller, but the freq was very busy. A simple solution, in my opinion, would have been for Tower to say 'Fly 135, climb and maintain 2,000 feet, cleared for takeoff'. Then it would have been clear to me that the NRVNA SID was not expected right after takeoff.
ASRS:1783902.s: The pilot reported confusion during departure from BFI after receiving a clearance to "fly 135" and "climb via SID," which they interpreted as contradictory. This ambiguity caused the pilot to fly west of the expected route until Seattle Departure issued a corrective left turn and climb.

ASRS:1783903.n: During ground roll, prior to rotation, a bird flew in front of us and impacted the left wing. Resulting in a dent to the left leading edge. We immediately informed tower and turned on to a taxiway.
ASRS:1783903.s: During ground roll prior to rotation, a bird struck the left wing, causing a dent to the leading edge. The crew immediately informed the tower and diverted to a taxiway.

ASRS:1783926.n: I sat down next to the controller working SDWR (west) radar to assist them with a few coordinations. The sector wasn't busy but coordinations with approach (for handoffs) and ATCT (for opposite direction arrivals) would have added to the complexity. I noticed that an IFR Aircraft X talking to SEE ATCT was turning away from the airport and the final approach course northeast to a higher MVA. The aircrafts lowest indicated altitude was 2,400 ft. and the MVA in the area is 4,200 ft. and 3;300ft. I quickly called SEE to see if the pilot was okay. They responded that she was having issues and they were correcting her. The weather was broken at 3,300 ft. with few clouds at 2;400ft. The tower called me back asking if we could take the aircraft back. I asked if the aircraft was VFR or IFR. They stated IFR and I had them issue her a 270 heading and a climb to 6,000 ft. By the time the tower switched her back to us, the aircraft was westbound safely above the MVA.Since she needed special handling, I asked SDMR (Miramar) radar to work the aircraft back in and she landed safely. I truthfully never considered this to be a pilot deviation. And since the tower was talking to her at the low altitude, I knew they were handling the low altitude alert, getting her back on course and trying to see if she could cancel IFR. Only when the tower advised me she was IFR and needed to come back to us, did I consider her a special priority case. But also with my years of experience, I assumed she was a low hour IFR pilot that needed special handling.I didn't tell the OM immediately about the event because she was with the tower when she was at a low altitude and I knew they were handling the situation and would be filling out the appropriate paperwork on their end. Only a little bit later did I think, I should probably have the OM watch the replay and if anything, it may be declared an priority handling. The OM advised me it should have been a pilot deviation, but I still don't understand why a disoriented pilot would get a brasher. In the future, I won't assume the classification of an event, I'll ask the OM for their guidance.
ASRS:1783926.s: An IFR pilot descended to 2,400 ft below the 4,200 ft MVA while turning away from the airport, prompting the tower to request radar assistance. The controller issued a heading and climb to 6,000 ft, allowing the aircraft to land safely, though the event was later classified as a pilot deviation.

ASRS:1783930.n: [Aircraft X] was being vectored for an ILS approach into BFI RWY (Runway) 14R by the Arrival West (1W), Arrival East (1E), Boeing Arrival (1D), and Paine (1P) sectors combined. As [Aircraft X] was being vectored traffic was issued for two VFR aircraft on 1200 codes transitioning both north and south through the localizer for Runway 14R. Due to this traffic I left [Aircraft X] at 3,000 ft. and obtained a point-out with SEA Final (1F). Despite this altitude, [Aircraft X] responded to a TCAS RA and, in an effort to protect the sea final approach course, I turned [Aircraft X] right to a heading 220. As [Aircraft X] turned southbound I observed a C172, [Aircraft Y], being vectored for the ILS Runway 20 approach into PWT. I turned [Aircraft X] further right to a northwest heading, and measured the distance between [Aircraft X] and [Aircraft Y]. I observed approximately 3.3 miles between the two and since I had already issued the turn, I judged that sufficient separation and attempted to continue working to not fall further behind. [Aircraft X] turned slower than anticipated and caused a separation error between themselves and [Aircraft Y]. The root of this issue is the continual constant conflict between IFR jets into BFI and VFR aircraft transitioning through the localizer in both north and south flow. It is a well-known, persistent issue that has been thoroughly reported for several years. Several solutions have been proposed, but none have been adapted.The only fix for this issue is a restructuring of the Seattle Class B airspace to protect the finals in both directions at BFI. I have personally submitted redesigns for this issue that both protect BFI, and in doing so protect SEA, and allow VFR operations in and out of BFI, and are not unduly hindering to the general aviation community. If safety is truly the priority of the FAA and the Seattle region, changes will be initiated immediately. I understand the process for airspace changes take time, however, the changes will never take place if the process is not started. When the inevitable aircraft incident finally occurs, I hope that no one dies and I am not on position. [Aircraft Y] was on vector, at 2,500 ft., to ILS Runway 20 approach at PWT. [Aircraft X], controlled by W Sector, was on final to Runway 14R at BFI and experienced a TCAS RA with an uncontrolled VFR aircraft. The W Controller was already at a high level of complexity and volume as sectors were combined. The BFI Runway 14R final is in close proximity to PWT 20 mile final and is also underneath the Runway 16 finals at SEA. With limited options [Aircraft X] was turned to the southwest towards [Aircraft Y] with only 500 ft. between them. There are many factors that lead to this situation. These include airport proximities, sector overload, traffic complexity. There is also the issue of lack of controlled and protected airspace in and out of BFI. This is an issue controllers have been bringing to local management for years. The workforce is metaphorically beating our heads against a wall as we are asking for help and are given zero assistance in return. The final to BFI is underneath the SEA finals so we are forced to descend large, fast turbojet aircraft out of Class Bravo airspace into a very high VFR traffic area. This leads numerous TCAS situations. Many suggestions have been brought up through established reporting procedures so I will not waste my time typing them out again. The feeling of a lack of support for change is disheartening. There needs to be change made into airspace and procedures for aircraft landing at BFI, and this should be done for both arrival directions at BFI.
ASRS:1783930.s: An air traffic controller vectored Aircraft X for a BFI ILS approach while managing combined sectors and VFR traffic. A TCAS RA forced a turn that reduced separation to 500 feet with Aircraft Y, an outcome the controller attributes to sector overload and unprotected airspace near BFI.

ASRS:1783971.n: Aircraft X was taxing out via Spot XX with ATC ground control. The Aircraft X flight deviated from the taxi line and taxied onto the X pad to join Taxiway G. During this time period Company Y had deicing truck(s) on the X pad and reported a near miss.
ASRS:1783971.s: Aircraft X deviated from the taxi line while taxiing out via Spot XX and entered the X pad where Company Y deicing trucks were operating. This incursion resulted in a reported near miss with the deicing equipment.

ASRS:1783972.n: A person came to work and his wife had COVID. He was among several of coworkers in a Kiosk. I went with co-worker Y to Manager's office and explained the situation because we were in the Kiosk with him. We asked if the Kiosk could be cleaned right away before anyone else entered. She said she sent the Supervisor to wipe things down and that the cleaning service would clean/spray it tonight. Co-worker Y said the Supervisor did not wipe it down. This is a potential risk of spreading COVID to many people at work and their families. I gave co-worker Y my own personal can of LYSOL spray to use in the KIOSK.
ASRS:1783972.s: A crew member reported a coworker with a COVID-positive spouse entered a kiosk, prompting a request for immediate cleaning. Although management claimed a supervisor wiped surfaces, the crew member disputed this and personally sprayed the area with Lysol to mitigate infection risk.

ASRS:1783995.n: On climb out of ZZZ [airport] we received an ACARS message from Dispatch saying that the TRACON was closing and that we should ask ATC if we could do Tower enroute to get into ZZZ1 [airport]. It also said if we couldn't return to ZZZ. We were still climbing on the SID out of ZZZ and I was still running the after Takeoff checklist. I finished the checklist up and consulted the FO. We were both confused by this message. I went ahead and asked ZZZ Departure if they knew anything about it. They did not know anything then handed us off to ZZZ Center. I checked in with ZZZ [Center]. I responded to Dispatch asking which facility it was that was closing. They replied with ZZZ1 TRACON and that it was to be closed from XA:30 to XB:30z. After getting this response. I asked ZZZ Center if they had any information on it. They checked with their managers and didn't know anything about TRACON in ZZZ1 shutting down. I messaged Dispatch saying that we wanted to continue and see how things progress since ZZZ [Center] said they didn't know anything. The reply we received was a strong negative. Dispatch wanted us to turn back to ZZZ [airport] right away. At this point in the flight, we were half way to ZZZ1 [airport]. We were estimated to arrive in the ZZZ1 [airport] area around XB:00z and had enough fuel onboard the aircraft to hold for a while before having to go to an alternate that we would have added. ZZZ2 [airport] was close and had good weather. Dispatch didn't give us any time to explore other alternatives, so we complied with their demand to return to ZZZ [airport]. The entire time, my FO and I were trying to figure out why we were returning to the airport. The workload was high on the return. The risk for making mistakes was pretty high on both our parts. Thankfully, ZZZ [airport] wasn't busy and was able to cut down a lot of our workload by giving us a descent and direct a fix on the approach. Once on the ground I was able to call Dispatch and talk. They closed the TRACON for COVID cleaning and only gave about 20 minute notice. It sounded like the dispatcher knee jerk reacted to it and wanted us on the ground as soon as possible. That's why she didn't want us to continue. I complied because it was a safe course of action to return and because I couldn't get Dispatch to agree to continue. So this was the safest course of action that was mutually agreeable.Suggest going over delay options inflight with dispatch and to not make the decisions for the flight crew. Dispatch should seek the advice of other dispatchers and most importantly of the crew to come up with many options and narrow it down the best one in a non-time critical situation as this. Freaking out and demanding an air return is not a normal way to run an operation. Dispatch should be made aware that there are many options available to crews to stay in the air longer while saving fuel. We could have easily slowed down and held until TRACON opened again or we could have diverted to ZZZ2 [airport] and picked up some more fuel if we needed to. Both would have been faster options of keeping the operations going while being safe. After departing ZZZ we received an ACARS message from Dispatch informing us that ZZZ1 TRACON would be closed upon our arrival. Shortly after we received another message instructing us to return to ZZZ.We received an ACARS message from Dispatch.The flight return to ZZZ per Dispatch request due to ZZZ1 TRACON closed prior to us landing.We returned to ZZZ and the Captain contacted Dispatch after returning to the gate.Suggestion - If possible, comply with Dispatch instructions. Coordinate with Dispatch for clarification via ACARS or after returning to the gate.
ASRS:1783995.s: The flight crew received a Dispatch ACARS message during climbout from ZZZ stating the ZZZ1 TRACON was closing for COVID cleaning, prompting an immediate return to ZZZ. The crew complied with the demand despite having fuel to hold or divert, citing high workload and a lack of alternative options presented by Dispatch.

ASRS:1784041.n: I recently completed the B737 Max training. I found the training to be good but do have concern for the Airspeed unreliable when the stick shaker is going continually. The loudness contributes to a continued distraction and ability to clearly communicate. This all for an erroneous warning. The ability is there to disable the erroneous stick shaker via pulling the offending circuit breaker. This is somewhat analogous to not silencing the fire bell until the fire is out and you're on the ground. Additionally, with the distraction, auto throttles off while running the QRH, the opportunity presents itself for masking a real stick shaker if in low speed event. Would you recognize the other stick shaker going off if the pilot monitoring was not on the controls? One additional step in the QRH after identifying the erroneous side would take a significant distraction out of the equation. Other than the initial stick shaker and identifying the erroneous airspeed indication, I feel the continuous stick shaker is the greatest threat in this situation. By taking away the erroneous stick shaker distraction you can eliminate one of the 'holes in the cheese'.
ASRS:1784041.s: A B737 Max pilot reported that continuous stick shaker activation during erroneous airspeed warnings creates dangerous distractions and communication difficulties. The pilot suggested adding a QRH step to disable the erroneous shaker via circuit breaker to prevent masking real low-speed events.

ASRS:1784065.n: At the gate we had a passenger board without permission from gate agent, then we had a non-compliant passenger not wearing a mask. That was mitigated when gate agent came and explained to the elderly passenger that masks must be worn. On taxi out Captain and First Officer were discussing mitigation strategies if that event were to re-occurrence on taxi and failed to run pre-takeoff checklist. Cause - Distraction by pre-flight events with gate agent and non-compliance of the passenger.Remain focused on task at hand. Not replay scenarios until the debrief phase of flight.
ASRS:1784065.s: The flight crew failed to run the pre-takeoff checklist during taxi out due to distraction from a non-compliant passenger and gate agent interaction. The cause was identified as discussing mitigation strategies for the event instead of focusing on the immediate task.

ASRS:1784079.n: Revenue leg with X passengers. Second in Command was Pilot Flying, I was Pilot Monitoring. Upon reaching 16,500 feet I determined the cruise power setting, and we ran the cruise checklist. The fuel was balanced and normal, neither myself nor the Second in Command recall seeing an unusual imbalance or a fuel pump light on. Once the checklist was complete, I touched base with the passengers. We were approximately 40 minutes from our destination at this time and talking to Center. As I reached down to grab the can to start paperwork, I noticed that both fuel pumps were illuminated. I noticed them both turn on, turn off, then immediately turn back on. This gave me cause for concern as the only condition that would have both pumps on in-flight suggest low fuel pressure. I pointed this to the Second in Command and began running the checklist.I first went to the fuel pumps page, which stated 'Condition: Left Fuel Pump is operating. If indication cycles on and off every 10 seconds: Carry out Low Fuel Pressure Emergency Checklist'. I ran the checklist, which called for a reduction in power and to turn the fuel pumps on. I instructed the Second in Command to set approximately 15 psi torque, which he did. The checklist next called for a monitor of the balance. At this time neither the Second in Command or myself noticed an imbalance, so we continued with the pumps on. The checklist calls for a descent to warmer air, as ice crystals may cause the fuel filter to be blocked. I made a gut decision that ice was unlikely to be the culprit, as the outside air temperature was +6 and we had only just leveled off at the coldest temperature we had encountered. The next step of the checklist called for the pumps to be returned to auto. I did this and noticed the pump lights remained illuminated and continued to cycle. I returned the switches to ON and reached the end of the checklist which called for an immediate landing.I notified Center, stated we would be diverting to a nearer report and squawked XXXX. The Second in Command and I performed the descent and approach checklists concurrently. I then briefed the passengers that we had a mechanical issue and were going to make a precautionary landing. I guided the Second in Command to stay high on the approach to guarantee a landing in the event of an engine failure, and once a landing was assured we put the gear and flaps out to bleed energy and increase our rate of descent. The before landing checklist was completed and the landing was nominal. Upon shutdown I noted that there was a 4 or 5 segment fuel tank imbalance, right tank heavy. The fuel filter bypass was in its normal shut position, indicating fuel had been passing through the filter normally for the flight.I genuinely feel the Second in Command and myself handled the situation as safely as possible given the circumstances. There was no rushing, no skipped items, clear and concise cockpit communication, strict adherence to Standard Operating Procedures, good airmanship, and excellent teamwork. This event highlights the strengths of the training department.
ASRS:1784079.s: The Pilot Monitoring and Second in Command experienced cycling fuel pump lights indicating low pressure during cruise at 16,500 feet. They followed the emergency checklist, diverted for a precautionary landing, and landed safely with a minor fuel imbalance.

ASRS:1784085.n: While conducting a FAR 91 reposition flight from ZZZZ to ZZZ, we were cleared to maintain a cruising altitude of Flight Level 260. Approximately three hours into our cruise, the Central Advisory and Warning System (CAWS) triggered a master caution and the LH FUEL PUMP and RH FUEL PUMP green indicator lights illuminated. About 10 seconds later they extinguished, only for another master caution to sound and the same lights to return, indicating a low fuel pressure situation. We ran the emergency procedure checklist for low fuel pressure. After completing the low fuel pressure checklist, we were unable to rectify the low fuel pressure condition and [advised] ZZZ Center. Per the low fuel pressure checklist, we diverted to the nearest suitable airfield. ZZZZ1 was the nearest suitable airfield. Center informed us that all nearby airports, including ZZZZ1, were closed at sunset and personnel were being contacted by ZZZZ Approach to turn the lights on at ZZZZ1. We conducted the RNAV RWY XX Approach to a visual landing at ZZZZ1 and parked the aircraft without further incident. The aircraft was then grounded. Lack of guidance in emergency checklist on time frame for both rate of descent to warmer air, as well as restoring boost pump switches to AUTO after descent to warmer air.
ASRS:1784085.s: During a FAR 91 cruise at FL260, the crew experienced low fuel pressure triggering CAWS master cautions and pump lights. After failing to rectify the issue, they diverted to ZZZZ1 for a visual landing, grounding the aircraft due to checklist guidance gaps regarding descent timing and pump switch restoration.

ASRS:1784088.n: I was scheduled to fly out of ZZZZ to ZZZZ1. While in cruise, I noticed the rudder pedals on the pilot side didn't mobilize as they should when pressed on to engage the brakes. I asked my SIC to perform the same checks on his side and he noted the pedals felt operational. We decided to continue our flight to ZZZZ1 and land taking into consideration that we might not have brake pressure and would have to perform a go-around and diversion to a longer runway. Rain had just ended in our destination and the runway was slightly wet. After touchdown, I try to engage the brakes to verify their status. Brakes started engaging on and off while we rolled on the runway. We decided to go-around. Before diverting to ZZZZ2 we acknowledge the fact that the runway was slightly wet and decided to try landing again. This second landing was firmer than the first one, I, as pilot flying, applied the brakes once more and this time around, no braking action was noticed therefore we decided to perform a go-around and divert to ZZZZ2. After touching down in ZZZZ2, brakes didn't engage appropriately, they were intermittent. After shutting down at the main ramp in ZZZZ2, deplaning and sending the passengers to a lounge, I talked to our mechanic on the phone and we both noted the brake fluid was lower than usual. The company flew another aircraft with a mechanic which happens to be also a pilot. He inspected the brakes visually and noted that the system looks fine. With that assessment, we accepted a ferry permit to fly back to base ZZZZ without passengers, for proper maintenance action. After touchdown in ZZZZ RWY XX and noting the fact that my 'now' SIC is a mechanic, I pushed on the rudder pedals to engage the brakes and try to assess what the issue was. This prompted no braking action. I communicated this to my SIC/Mechanic, and I increased pressure on the rudder pedals trying to note a response from the system with no luck. Eventually, after I kept applying pressure to the rudder pedals, the left and right main gear tires deflated disabling our aircraft in the runway. After this happened, we notified ATC (ZZZZ Tower) and shut down on the runway.
ASRS:1784088.s: The pilot reported intermittent brake failure during cruise and landing at ZZZZ1 and ZZZZ2, attributed to low brake fluid. During a subsequent ferry flight to ZZZZ, applying pressure to the rudder pedals caused main gear tire deflation, disabling the aircraft on the runway.

ASRS:1784113.n: Departed ZZZ on IFR flight to ZZZ1 as first leg of a reposition. Deice systems were inspected on the ground and tested prior to departure with no apparent failures. Boots and prop heat were activated upon entering icing conditions in cruise and both failed within a few minutes. OAT was within boot operation limits. Ran appropriate checklists and were unable to clear the failures. We elected to divert initially selecting ZZZ2. In the descent to ZZZ2 we discovered that our EFBs (electronic flight bags) did not have any approach procedures for the area downloaded. ZZZ2 showed VFR conditions so we attempted a visual approach but were unable to find the airport beacon light. ATC issued delay vectors while we worked on a new plan. It appeared that ice accumulation had stopped and that the layer of rime ice accumulated in cruise had been removed, but the OAT was still below freezing and we were still encountering precipitation and clouds. At this point we [advised ATC] and opted to land at ZZZ3. Upon nearing ZZZ3 It became clear that a visual approach was not going to be possible so we copied the RNAV RWY XX Approach at ZZZ3 from ATC and successfully completed the approach. After shutdown we discovered a layer of clear ice on the wings behind the boots that had not been visible in flight. Deice equipment tested on ground prior to departure with no issue. During cruise, light ice was encountered, and plane was configured appropriately. De-ice boot message appeared, and was troubleshooted, but could not be rectified. Propeller deice failed shortly after, was troubleshooted, and could not be rectified. ATC was notified to coordinate descent out of icing conditions. Conditions persisted in descent, and decision was made to divert as altitude in positive temperatures could not be established. Vectors were given for ZZZ2, but airport lights could not be confirmed as on in marginal conditions. New vectors were given for approach into ZZZ3. Approach assisted in vectors onto course as EFB issue (unable to pull up approach plate) prevented standard ID of approach. Landing was safely achieved and flight was terminated and calls were made to Dispatch, Director of operations, and Maintenance. Crew believed aircraft to be free of ice on approach descent through visual inspection. Upon landing, patches of clear ice were found on the top of each wing behind the boots. Boots were clear of ice on approach and upon landing.
ASRS:1784113.s: The crew diverted a repositioning flight after deice boots and propeller heat failed in cruise icing, compounded by EFB approach plate unavailability. They landed safely at ZZZ3 after discovering hidden clear ice behind the boots post-landing, despite visual inspections suggesting the aircraft was ice-free.

ASRS:1784120.n: Upon landing on Runway XX in ZZZ the aircraft struck a deer shortly after touchdown. The approach to runway 6 was normal, fully configured, flown at Vref +10. Shortly after touchdown the deer ran into the prop while the aircraft was traveling around 70kts. The time from initially observing the deer to impact was about one second. The engine started vibrating immediately after impact and the PF (Pilot Flying) shut down the engine on the rollout. The airplane came to a stop 500 ft. from the end of the runway. Upon stopping we did a normal shutdown. No injuries onboard and the aircrafts propeller and engine were damaged. Upon landing at ZZZ, aircraft suffered a deer strike on roll out. The runway XX landing was fully configured flap 40 landing. Approach speed was carrot + 10 knots due to runway length. Deer spotted at the moment of impact in the right landing light cone. Sound of impact was followed by immediate engine vibration. Estimate impact speed at 70 knots during beta application for stop. Shut down engine on the roll out estimate 45 knots to minimize further damage and blade separation. Came to a stop approximately 500 ft. from the end of the runway. Preformed normal aircraft unloading. No injuries on board and damage was limited to aircraft prop and engine.
ASRS:1784120.s: The pilot flying landed a fully configured aircraft on Runway XX at ZZZ and struck a deer at 70 knots shortly after touchdown. The impact caused immediate engine vibration, prompting an engine shutdown on rollout; the aircraft stopped 500 feet from the runway end with damage limited to the propeller and engine and no injuries.

ASRS:1784132.n: On [Date], we were scheduled to fly [Aircraft X] out of ZZZZ to ZZZZ1 at XA:00 local time. While en cruise, my Captain noticed the rudder pedals on the pilot side didn't mobilize as they should when pressed on. My Captain requested for me to step on the rudder pedals to see if I could notice any anomalies with the brakes on the Pilot Monitoring side. I did not notice anything unusual about the rudder pedals. We then proceeded to set up for the approach at ZZZZ1. We did a approach and landed on the runway and on the rollout I noticed that we were not slowing down like we should, the plane seemed to stutter (as if the brakes were engaging and then disengaging) The Captain then performed a go around. After the go around we both agree that we are in a position to safely try again. This time we come in a little bit slower and once again on the roll out my Captain was pressing the brakes and we were not decelerating as normal. After the second go around we both agree our best option is to divert to ZZZZ2 where there is a significantly longer runway. We land at ZZZZ2 without incident and deplane the passengers.
ASRS:1784132.s: The crew of Aircraft X experienced rudder pedal anomalies en route and ineffective braking with stuttering deceleration during two landing attempts at ZZZZ1. After performing two go-arounds, they diverted to ZZZZ2 for a safe landing on a longer runway.

ASRS:1784152.n: After making the turn at ZZZZZ intersection at FL300, we had a bleed 1 leak caution message. We ran the QRH and isolated system 1 and after a few minutes the message returned forcing us to continue the checklist through the descent portion. As we were waiting the three minutes before the descent, I initiated contact with AIRINC to reach dispatch as our ACARS had just lost coms most likely to it transitioning from one frequency to another. However with the need for a descent arising we lost communication with AIRINC before establishing any plan with dispatch. We requested priority handling with ZZZ Center and initiated a turn towards ZZZ as the thought of continuing towards ZZZZ or ZZZZ1 was the longest stretch of open water on the route and worst case scenario we were 60-80 miles north of the coast and ZZZZ2 was the closest [authorized] airport around if we had to continue the checklist and shut down the engine. As we got closer to ZZZZ2 while still 130 miles from ZZZ we were able to get an ACARS connection and get dispatch caught up on the situation. They did not realize how bad the situation was and thought we were closer to ZZZZ and ZZZZ1 than we actually were. As the aircraft was stable and the bleed temp of system 1 was around 50C, the system still held almost 70psi throughout the flight indicating one of the valves was still open and not properly closed, we confirmed with dispatch that it was safe to continue beyond ZZZ to ZZZ1 for an uneventful landing. Throughout the communication black out center was very professional and extremely helpful. I hope our thanks and appreciation for their work can be passed on to the controllers working with us. Prior to ZZZZZ1 [fix], flight sent an ACARS message stating a Bleed Leak. Flight followed the QRH and three minutes later the message returned requiring a diversion to nearest suitable. There was quite a bit confusion going on because the flight also attempted to contact us via ARINC. The ARINC call failed, and the flight seemed to be in an ACARS dead spot as well. A few minutes later, I received multiple ACARS messages stating the flight was diverting to ZZZ. Per the flight's location, ZZZZ1 seemed like the closer, more suitable option and would've had the flight avoid going EOW (Extended Over Water) at 10,000 [with priority handling]. After running numbers for ZZZZ1, flight informed me over ACARS that ZZZ or ZZZ1 was closer. Although [our equipment] showed the flight over ZZZZ1, in reality the flight was 250 nm to the east, indeed much closer to ZZZ or ZZZ1. With that information, we decided ZZZ1 was a more suitable airport. In addition to runway length, ZZZ ops informed us that pax would not be allowed off the aircraft due to customs issues. Flight landed and blocked in.While I was certainly caught off guard and should've opened the QRH a few minutes faster, I was seriously hampered by our lack of equipment accuracy, ACARS dead spots, and ARINC being unable to raise the flight. It's hard to have an accurate, timely discussion over ACARS when both sides of the situation are working quickly on fixing the problems. If this were being done via remote dispatching, I do not wish to imagine the consequences. In the future, I will remind myself to remain calm and follow step-by-step actions to reach a quicker, less confusing end.
ASRS:1784152.s: The flight crew encountered a Bleed 1 leak at FL300, triggering a diversion decision complicated by ACARS and ARINC communication failures. Despite initial confusion regarding aircraft position and airport suitability, the crew diverted to ZZZ1 for a safe landing after confirming system stability.

ASRS:1784173.n: We flew to ZZZ on aircraft X. We then were scheduled to fly same aircraft from ZZZ to ZZZ1 with a new flight attendant crew. When the flight attendants did their pre-flight, I was notified that the emergency equipment in the AFT bins were in the incorrect bins. They were in the opposite bins as depicted in the 737 diagram and the flight attendant manual. Apparently they were installed that way back in month when the modification was complete. The stickers that were on the bins depicting what emergency equipment was correct but the emergency equipment was on the incorrect side. I called dispatch who connected me to maintenance and they said couldn't find any diagram that would place emergency equipment where it was. ZZZ maintenance agreed that emergency equipment was installed incorrectly. The aircraft was taken out of service.The equipment was installed wrong. In is my understanding this airplane flew around since April like this. More emphasis on flight attendants checking proper locations of emergency equipment.More checks to make sure when there is an interior modification that it's installed correctly Upon arrival a ZZZ, we received a new cabin crew for the flight to ZZZ1. ZZZ to ZZZ1 was to be the flight deck crew's second flight using the same aircraft. During the pre-flight, the aft cabin crew called the flight deck and advised us that the emergency equipment that is stowed in the two most aft overhead compartments were not located in their proper location. TO fully understand, I also went aft to see for myself. The FA showed me in her manual, the proper location and orientation of the equipment. I went back to the flight deck, verified the same information in the aircraft operating handbook. I advised the Captain of the discrepancy. Maintenance was called. This discrepancy was found on the second leg of the day, while utilizing the same aircraft. The location of the equipment was inverted in its actual location vs. the location as stated in the manuals.Cabin crew may have not been facing forward in the cabin when pre-flighting the emergency equipment. While the equipment was stowed in an overhead bin correctly, with the proper associated placards, the actual location of the equipment did not match the location stated in the manual. As an example Oxygen is to be in the port side overhead. Its actual location was starboard. It is possible that during a pre-flight that a crew member facing aft will simply associate that the oxygen is 'on my left side' This aircraft also had new overheads and added capacity within the last year. During that change, the equipment may have been installed incorrectly. Cabin crew may need to have greater situational awareness as to the actual right and left side of the aircraft, regardless of their orientation within the cabin.
ASRS:1784173.s: Flight deck and cabin crew discovered emergency equipment in the aft overhead bins was installed on the opposite side of the aircraft compared to manuals during a pre-flight check on a Boeing 737. Maintenance confirmed the error, likely from a recent interior modification, and the aircraft was taken out of service.

ASRS:1784182.n: We were taxiing from the landing runway to the gate and turning right onto Taxiway 1 from 2 when the airplane started sliding in the wrong direction (to the left), the Captain had the tiller going right however, the airplane still was going left so he applied the brakes and momentarily activated the right thrust reverser in an attempt to quickly stop the forward momentum of the airplane before sliding off the taxiway. He was able to get the airplane completely stopped while still on the taxiway with no further issues.We believe the taxiway was more slick than expected due to the wet conditions of the field.In the future, we think even slower taxi speeds would help, even though we were taxing at a good safe and slow speed at the time of the occurrence. Also, we would probably elect not to shutdown the number 1 engine in the future to help eliminate any chance of asymmetric thrust on wet taxiways.
ASRS:1784182.s: During taxi on a wet field, the aircraft slid left despite right tiller input, prompting the Captain to apply brakes and briefly activate the right thrust reverser to stop safely on the taxiway. The crew attributed the incident to unexpectedly slick conditions and asymmetric thrust from a shutdown engine.

ASRS:1784184.n: During my leg while cruising at FL350 to from ZZZ to ZZZ1 with the autopilot engaged. multiple caution messages popped out, suggesting some electrical issue with the #2 IDG/BUS. there was not a lot of communication in between the pilots but the Captain grabbed the Quick Reference Handbook and began working, So I decided to keep flying and work the radios. I kept monitoring the Captains body actions because I know that moving the wrong electrical switch could lead to further electrical issues. During the troubleshoot I confirmed that he could touch the Integrated Drive Generator 2. when he mentioned he was going to turn on the APU I reacted and say no, he asked me Why I did not want APU, so I advised that we were above the maximum altitude for APU start, so he understood and agreed to wait. advised descending, to which he agreed. I requested 29,000 ft. from ATC, and descended to 29,000 ft. When I suggested we were at an altitude where we could, he asked me to turn on the APU. When attempted to start APU about 4 screens went black momentarily and the autopilot and auto throttles disconnected. I announced I had the flight controls, and the throttles. The Captain re-engaged the autopilot without asking me but voiced it over and I monitored the correct engagement. Given the autopilot was responding correctly I decided to leave it engaged and monitor it. Given the APU caused appeared to cause the distruption for the APU I did not attempt turning it on again. Captain kept working Quick Reference Handbook, and coordinated with Dispatch and flight attendants. Captain decided to do the approach and landing, we briefed and landing at ZZZ1 without incident. No request for priority handling was declared.Multiple electrical failures.While we seemed to reach each other fairly well, I feel like the threat was treated like a no-time threat rather than a time threat. However, the outcome was positive.
ASRS:1784184.s: The First Officer and Captain managed multiple electrical failures and IDG issues while cruising at FL350. After descending to 29,000 ft, an APU start attempt caused screen blackouts and autopilot disconnect, but the crew landed safely at ZZZ1 without incident.

ASRS:1784222.n: Arrival process and COVID screening under new ZZZZ guidelines contribute to extreme fatigue, physiological and psychological concerns. The entire process takes more than several hours. The arrival screeners are unprepared for each flight adding time to the process. The crew is sequestered within the airport during the process without access to toilet, food, or water. Cell phone contact with the company or union is prohibited during the testing phase. The threat of a possible positive test result and subsequent 14 day quarantine in an unknown government facility causes great psychological stress to the crew member.
ASRS:1784222.s: Crew members reported extreme fatigue and psychological stress during arrival processing under new ZZZZ guidelines. The lengthy, unprepared screening process sequestered the crew without basic amenities while prohibiting contact with the company or union.

ASRS:1784233.n: Parking at stand X in MZBZ, we taxied into the parking spot. The Marshaller was giving guidance and was very slow with the stop signal. I was unsure of the command and proceeded to move forward, but quickly realized I was past the stop mark. I brought the plane to a stop and set the brake. The ramp agent informed me that a ground worker approached the aircraft and was almost run over. I told the managing agent the aircraft never came to a stop intermittently and did not stop until I brought it to a stop and set the brakes.
ASRS:1784233.s: The pilot reported that while parking at MZBZ, they misinterpreted a slow marshaller stop signal and overshot the mark, nearly striking a ground worker. The pilot attributed the incident to the delayed signal and clarified that the aircraft did not stop intermittently before the brakes were finally set.

ASRS:1784237.n: While approaching to land in ROA Runway 24 we were being vector by ATC for a straight in approach. At 4,000 feet in level flight. The aircraft was approximately 3.0 NM southeast of the final approach fix of HIBAN. ATC issued us a turn 'To a heading of 290 to intercept the GPS course. Cleared for the GPS Y Runway 24 approach.' Shortly afterwards the aircraft GPWS system activated with 'TERRIN TERRAIN PULL-UP.' Pilot flying disconnect the autopilot and climbed to approximately 4,700 feet. Then turn to the assigned heading and intercepted the GPS course and continued the decent to land into ROA. On the approach flight crew verified altitude and position and told what had occurred. ATC verified that the aircraft was at the appropriate altitude and position. They also added that their minimum vector altitude in the area that the aircraft was at was 4,000 feet. The flight continued the approach and landed safely on Runway 24.Still unsure on what the cause of the GPWS.
ASRS:1784237.s: During a GPS approach to Runway 24 at ROA, the flight crew received a GPWS terrain warning at 4,000 feet while being vectored by ATC. The pilot disconnected the autopilot and climbed to 4,700 feet before intercepting the course and landing safely, though the specific cause of the warning remained undetermined.

ASRS:1784245.n: Prior to initiating descent to ZZZZ1, the flight crew contacted ZZZZ Center and advised that we were unable to accept RNP-1 (Required Navigation Performance) arrival procedures. At this point, Center instructed the flight crew to fly an RNP-1 arrival despite having been informed of the incapability and the flight crew reiterated the fact they were unable to accept the arrival. Instead, the flight crew requested to fly direct to ZZZZZ waypoint for the start of the RNP RWY (Runway) XX approach. However, Center ignored this request and instructed the flight crew to fly direct to ZZZZ1 VOR and expect the VOR-A approach (Jeppesen Plate [Page]). When the crew once again requested to fly direct to ZZZZZ for the RNP RWY XX, Center repeated the instruction to fly direct to ZZZZ1 and expect the VOR-A approach without further acknowledgement or explanation of denial. The flight crew speculated that Center's refusal to assign the RNP approach was due to misinterpretation of the flight crew's inability to accept the RNP arrival, and efforts to clarify this case were also ignored by Center. The Captain (Pilot Monitoring) selected the VOR-A approach in the MCDU (Multi-Purpose Control Display Unit) and verified the route information while the First Officer (Pilot Flying) briefed the approach plate. At this time, both crew members observed what appeared to be inconsistencies between the MCDU approach database and the Jeppesen approach chart, specifically that the waypoint on Chart X did not match the waypoint shown in the MCDU routing, nor did the MCDU approach procedure indicate the required procedure turn under routing [FLP page] or Procedure Turn Info page [NAV - Page 2 - Patterns - Procedure Turn]. As the workload for the flight crew increased due to the inconsistency between chart and MCDU database, Center's refusal to assign a more effective approach, continuing descent towards mountainous terrain, and multiple segmented and non-standard clearances from Center that threatened to interrupt critical flight deck operations (notably the approach briefing), the flight crew elected to fly the VOR-A approach under raw data (green needles). All elements of the planned approach thus far mentioned became void after the flight crew received the hand-off to Approach Control who instructed them to fly direct to the airfield and complete a visual left-hand traffic pattern from overhead the runway.This flight crew highly recommends that an investigation be conducted into inconsistencies observed between the Jeppesen approach plate for the ZZZZ1 VOR-A Approach [Chart] and the MCDU database for the EJET fleet, namely the incorrectly labeled waypoint identified as ZZZZZ1 on the chart. This flight crew also highly recommends that effective communications be made between [Company] Flight Operations and the [Country] Air Traffic Control agency to ensure better understanding of which procedures [Company] flights are able to conduct and which procedures they are not, specifically the differences between RNP-1 'Arrivals' and RNP Approaches.
ASRS:1784245.s: The flight crew and ZZZZ Center experienced communication breakdowns regarding RNP-1 arrival capabilities, leading to conflicting clearances and observed discrepancies between the Jeppesen VOR-A chart and the MCDU database. The crew elected to fly the approach using raw data due to these inconsistencies and increased workload before receiving a visual traffic pattern clearance from Approach Control.

ASRS:1784258.n: After I briefed the A Flight Attendant, she asked if I would be wearing a mask whenever they came in the cockpit for a lavatory break. I informed her as per our protocol I am not required and for operational safety reasons I do not wear my mask in the cockpit. She then informed me that they would not enter to give us a break unless I wore a mask. I then initiated calls to Dispatch and Operations to inform them of this problem. I understand their concerns and respect their decision. Yet, I do not understand why they would take issue with cockpit members facing forward and unmasked when they are continuously exposed to passengers in the cabin who have their mask off while eating or drinking as well as children who are not required to have a mask.On a recent flight my First Officer and I had a hard time understanding the ATC Controller due to the muffled sound because they were wearing a mask. It is also difficult understanding a First Officer who is wearing a mask in the loud cockpit environment. Safety of flight is my priority followed by mission and passengers. I regret the inconvenience this brought to passengers and company alike but this difference in protocol needs to be resolved without imposing non safety operational constraints on the cockpit. I realize this is a novel disease and the information from the CDC and NIH [National Institutes of Health] is at times confusing and conflicting but believe that we should not take information to extremes and compromise operational safety.Lack of cohesive policy between Cockpit and Flight Attendant protocols that plays between personal concerns over operational safety. I also feel misinformation or agenda also play a role on differences regarding relative issues.Keep the current Pilot protocol which works well and imposes minimal restrictions regarding operational safety. Clarify Flight Attendant protocols so they do not conflict with the cockpit. To each individual this pandemic is relative and emotional. Any preconceived or personal perception cannot be satisfied by one fits all protocols, so I believe individuals overly concerned should be required to get the vaccine. I will at the earliest opportunity get vaccinated for myself, family and coworkers.
ASRS:1784258.s: A pilot reported that flight attendants refused to enter the cockpit for a break unless he wore a mask, conflicting with his operational safety protocol. The pilot attributed this incident to a lack of cohesive policy between cockpit and cabin crew regarding mask usage during the pandemic.

ASRS:1784263.n: Bleeds off TO. After starting engines, I turned off APU switch - IAW Normal after start flow. I should have left APU switch on IAW OM XXX.6 (Bleeds off/APU on TO). We did, however, carefully configure bleeds/packs IAW OM XXX.6. We did not subsequently catch that APU switch was off before takeoff. After departure, First Officer reconfigured bleeds/packs IAW with XXX.6 and continued normal flight to ZZZ.This was the 4th line trip I've flown at airline since April 2020. A lack of recency flying into ZZZZ1 and a reliance on the muscle memory/normal after start flows contributed to my error in turning the APU off prematurely. Both the First Officer and I were very aware of the bleeds/packs configuration as we had previously emphasized this TO briefing item at the gate prior to departure. Ultimately, by accurately following the pre-briefed OM 120.6 to reintroduce bleeds/packs after TO we trapped my error and the threat was mitigated.We received ACARS msg and SELCAL warning bleeds/packs off on climbout as First Officer was restoring the bleeds/packs per OM XXX.6. The SELCAL was a helpful reminder/backup to the crew.
ASRS:1784263.s: The Captain prematurely turned off the APU after engine start due to reliance on muscle memory, violating the required "Bleeds off/APU on" procedure. The First Officer corrected the bleed and pack configuration during climbout after an ACARS and SELCAL warning, mitigating the threat.

ASRS:1784272.n: We were entering the terminal area with given heading descending from 11,000 feet down to 4,000 feet from the South west of the airport for RNAV 28. Passing through 5,000 feet we called the 'airport insight' and received the clearance for the visual approach for Runway 28. By the time we were abeam the airport flap 1 was down and altitude was 2,400 feet descending to 2,200 feet which was final approach segment altitude. Even though I was fully aware of the presence of obstacle (1,687 feet) on the path of our downwind I was confident that 500 feet margin and few thousand feet right of the course would give us good margin for safety. As we were getting close to the tower crane 'terrain' aural message came and after 2-3 second later 'terrain! pull up!' message came. I applied immediate max power and established pitch between 15-20. The message lasted few seconds and we climbed about 2,700 feet. After the conflict was resolved I intercepted the final course and follow the PAPI to the runway as normal operation.When we have received the visual clearance about 20 miles away I bugged the altitude down to 2,200 feet assuming within the 10 mile radius to the airport there cannot be anything that can pose threat to our path. Even though I was aware of the Tower, I didn't mention it during my briefing and considered it a big threat. When the Captain brought me an attention about the Tower once we were getting closer to it and asking me to turn inside the final approach point I delayed his suggestion wanting to intercept the final course outside the FAP. I could have been clear to ask him his intention or worries as we are nearing the obstacle and get the concurrence from both of us that 500 feet is enough or not.1. Better understanding of EGPWS logic could have given me the conservative altitude margins. 2. Detailed briefing, I could have planned better plan by flying higher or going around the tower instead of over flying it. 3. Rushing, I could have gone further out and fly higher to intercept instead of tightening my base turn to join right at the FAP.
ASRS:1784272.s: The First Officer descended below the obstacle clearance margin during a visual approach to Runway 28, triggering a terrain warning. The crew executed a go-around after the First Officer delayed the Captain's suggestion to turn earlier, attributing the event to rushing and inadequate briefing.

ASRS:1784281.n: The above pairing or trip is built with a tag after an all-night flight and I feel it is not safe for the employees and passengers. We check in at XA:X5 for an all-night flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1. After arriving in ZZZ1 exhausted from working all night the crew has to sit 3 hours at a hub where it would be easy to crew the next flight from ZZZ1 to ZZZ2 with a fresh crew that has slept. Instead a crew that has been up all night has to board and work a 2 hour flight. This I feel is not safe or healthy for the employees and lowers our immunity making us more apt to catch COVID, or some other sickness also not safe for passengers traveling with a crew that is exhausted.
ASRS:1784281.s: The pilot reported that a crew pairing scheduled an all-night flight followed by a 2-hour sector after only a 3-hour layover. The reporter stated this schedule is unsafe for employees and passengers due to crew exhaustion and increased susceptibility to illness.

ASRS:1784334.n: I was switched from ZHU Center to Kingsville Approach and I requested direct to the IAF CELIV for the COPTER RNAV 22 into the Alice Hospital. Kingsville Approach stated that they could not clear me for the approach, because they did not have the procedures, yet in the past we have had other controllers clear us.
