This has been an on-going issue with this particular facility. The approaches are certified and have been established for this hospital for some time. A short time later Kingsville came back and told me to maintain altitude until reaching CELIV and established, switch to advisory and report IFR (Instrument Flight Rules) cancellation on the frequency, or call their number when I'm on the ground. In hindsight, I'm not sure if they were finally able to locate their copy of the procedure, and I may have confused their last set of instructions as the clearance. When I contacted Kingsville TRACON by phone to coordinate my departure from the hospital, I was given the designated Obstacle Departure Procedure (ODP) for that particular location, adding further confusion, because there must be a copy of the procedure.
ASRS:1784334.s: A pilot flying a helicopter into Alice Hospital was initially denied a COPTER RNAV 22 clearance by Kingsville Approach due to missing procedures, despite the approach being certified. The controller later instructed the pilot to maintain altitude and cancel IFR, while a subsequent phone call provided an Obstacle Departure Procedure, highlighting ongoing facility confusion.

ASRS:1784342.n: I was on the ground at JNX with my student pilot getting ready for a soft field takeoff. The pattern was very congested with 5 aircraft in the pattern in various places. An aircraft had just landed, and there were a few other aircraft on downwind. A downwind aircraft stated that they were extending their downwind for departing traffic. I told my student that after the landing aircraft had exited the runway to be ready for immediate departure. The exiting aircraft called clear at this point and I told my student to make the radio call and take us out. As we were taxing out the aircraft that had said they were extending downwind was now on a 1.5 mile final. I told the student to accelerate and a radio call over the CTAF said go-around. I took the controls from my student to avoid a confliction with the aircraft going around. The aircraft going around side stepped to the right to avoid conflict. At no time was a G1000 traffic advisory issued, and no aircraft came close to contact. The overpopulated pattern with 4 aircraft doing stop and goes and my aircraft trying to find a spot to get out was a contributing factor to this issue. After the aircraft sidestepped, they immediately departed the pattern, and we continued our takeoff and entered left closed traffic to continue landing practice. Myself and a student who is currently working toward his CFI certificate went out for a training flight. After an hour of practicing maneuvers we approached JNX to practice takeoffs and landings. During our final approach into landing on Runway 21 at JNX my student made a call to let the other traffic in the pattern know of our position and our intentions, shortly after this call another plane pulled out on to the runway in frontof us. We made the decision to go-around and commenced a turn to the west so not to be on a collision course with the downwind traffic. We then proceeded to climb and leave the area.
ASRS:1784342.s: A CFI and student at JNX faced a congested pattern while preparing for a soft field takeoff. A downwind aircraft extended its leg and executed a go-around, forcing the instructor to take control to avoid conflict, though no traffic advisory was issued and no contact occurred.

ASRS:1784352.n: The last time I flew this aircraft before today was [Date] a flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1. The airplane was flawless.Memory items leaving the runway, pitch trim 2.1 [units], speed brake retracted, flaps up all accomplished.The airplane remained in the hangar except for a Jeppesen update and insertion of new 32GIG SD cards pursuant to Honda Service Bulletin 420-42-015.The insertion of the SD cards are nowhere near the trim hat on either yoke and the standby trim was never activated.Today was my first flight since that date and when I pre-flighted the cockpit I noticed that instead of 2.1 the pitch trim was full nose up about 13 units at the bottom of its travel.I re-trimmed to 2.1 and to the best of my recollection the roll and yaw trim were where they should have been.There was no reason that I knew for any of the trims to have been moved and the aircraft was locked at all times.Takeoff was normal but as I climbed out and engaged the autopilot the airplane suddenly rolled right and the AP (Autopilot) disconnected.I counteracted the roll and trimmed left wing down.I was able to regain control but when queried by ATC (Air Traffic Control) I agreed to [request priority handling] and asked for an immediate return to the airport.ATC gave vectors to final and the landing was uneventful.I contacted Honda and was told that this had been reported twice before but they had ascribed it to a child in the right seat. I fly single pilot and I have no children in the right seat or anyone else usually.I explained the circumstances and Honda agreed to contact a Honda maintenance provider to have them check the trim system. I will also follow up with Honda engineering because there is not a chance in the world that I inadvertently put full nose up trim in my airplane or full right wing down roll trim. In fact the Honda Jet uses very little trim at all in all configurations. There is no pre-flight procedure or other that I am aware of where a pilot would roll trim full nose up or full right wing down.I have learned that if one trim is out of whack, make certain all the others haven't been reset out of limits by any problem in the airplane before takeoff. I also learned that electronic airplanes have glitches even the factory doesn't understand. That isn't comforting.
ASRS:1784352.s: The single-pilot Honda Jet experienced an autopilot disconnect and sudden right roll during climb-out due to pitch and roll trims found full nose-up and right-wing-down after hangar maintenance. The pilot regained control, returned to the airport, and reported the unexplained trim shift to Honda, suspecting an electronic glitch.

ASRS:1784356.n: I departed ZZZ East ramp in [a] R22 with a private pilot student for pre-solo training at ZZZ1. We practiced emergency procedures en-route. After listening to ZZZ1 ASOS we determined to set up to enter the traffic pattern for Runway XX. 8 miles west from ZZZ1 we announced our location on CTAF and identified there were two airplanes in the pattern. We entered a 45 degree left downwind for Runway XX at ZZZ1 at 1,100 ft. and 75 kts. We announced and turned left base for Runway XX at 900 ft. and 60 kts. during which I could see Aircraft Y in a close left downwind. We announced turning final and turned final on Runway XX rolling out at 300 ft. AGL (900 ft. MSL) and 60 kts. I instructed the student to perform a normal approach to the approach end of Runway XX and terminate to a 3 ft. hover directly over the numbers (just as would be required during solo or a check ride). The student initiated his normal approach at the normal 10 degree angle required. I then heard Aircraft Y announce he was on final for Runway XX and had the helicopter in sight. I assumed the airplane had misjudged his spacing in the traffic pattern would either adjust his airspeed, perform turns for spacing, or go around. This is not uncommon and simple courtesy to the lower aircraft. On short final for Runway XX I looked out the left rear of the helicopter and could see Aircraft Y on short final right behind us. Aircraft Y asked me my intentions on CTAF. I replied that I intended to complete a landing to a hover at the approach end of Runway XX and then conduct a normal takeoff. Three things were on my mind. First, an aircraft on final and at a lower altitude always has the right of way. Second, I wanted the student to have the opportunity to conduct a normal approach to a hover just as he will be required to do during upcoming solo flight and his PPL checkride. Third, I need to access the student's ability to terminate the landing to a stationary hover. I asked Aircraft Y if he intended to 'go around' as it was clear either we would have to rush off the runaway, before completing the landing, or Aircraft Y could go-around. Aircraft X immediately replied with a complaint over CTAF stating that 'you little black helicopters are hogging the runways here and as a local pilot I can tell you that we are sick of you'. Just as I decelerated to a 3 ft. hover over the numbers for Runway XX I heard the sound of an airplane at high rpm overhead. I looked up to see Aircraft X directly over my helicopter about 20-30 ft. As he overflew me, he stated, 'he intended to report me to the FAA' and requested my name. I provided my tail number for his use as I did not want to provide my name over CTAF. I then contacted Aircraft Y over CTAF and requested that he not over fly my aircraft (for fear of collision) and that I will work with him to gain proper spacing in the pattern. Aircraft Y insulted me over CTAF and challenged me to a physical altercation. I instructed the student hover taxi to the parallel taxiway for Runway XX. I then noticed a pickup truck [surveying] our helicopter. I instructed the student to land on a nearby taxiway intersection near parking and go to idle. I exited the helicopter and approach the truck. I greeted the driver of the white truck with a handshake, introduced myself, and asked if there was an issue. I was told by the driver that they are reporting me to the FAA and they are just 'sick of our little helicopters that are difficult to see and tie up the runways for airplanes.' I sympathized with the driver but told him this is a public airport and that we have a right to conduct flight training here just as much as anyone, provided we all adhere to the rules. Furthermore, I told him that the airplane made an error in spacing by turning downwind, base, and final too quickly and essentially attempted to push me off the runway while conducting a landing. I told the driver that I am sorry this happened, but I feel the airplane did not adhere to Part 91 Right of Way rules to a lower aircraft on final. I gave the driver my number and told him I'd be more than happy to work with him on any future issues. We shook hands and went separate ways. I returned to the helicopter and returned directly to ZZZ. My chief concern with this incident is that the airplane should not have rushed or crowded another aircraft on final approach. A change in speed, turns for spacing, or a go-around were all options for the airplane pilot. Furthermore, executed a go around directly over and in close proximity to another aircraft is dangerous. What if I had directed the student to execute a go around or immediate takeoff (because we were being rushed on final and had climbed up into the airplane. As a military aviator and civilian helicopter and airplane pilot of over XX years I had always striven to fly with the utmost safety and friendliness. I preach this to my students, and I hope that all Aviators practice this as well. My goal is simply to encourage friendly, smart, and safe flying by all pilots at both ZZZ and ZZZ1.
ASRS:1784356.s: A helicopter instructor and student conducting pre-solo training at ZZZ1 encountered a fixed-wing aircraft (Aircraft Y) that failed to maintain spacing on final approach for Runway XX. The airplane pilot overflew the hovering helicopter at 20–30 feet, issued threats, and was joined by a ground vehicle driver who also threatened FAA reporting due to runway congestion concerns.

ASRS:1784361.n: Personal training flight. Weather clear. Wind 05 at 120. Had flown east about 10 miles to the training area East of Morse Lake. I was flying at 2,600 feet. Cleared area. Flew S turns, turns around point, when I saw a plan approach on ADS-B (I was using a Dynon ADS-B receiver and wifi to my cell) Airplane approached close to me from the East. I noticed, since the plane's symbol turned orange - meaning it was 'close' I continued my training. The plane approached closer, and his symbol turned red. I looked to my left where he should have been viewable, but was unable to make contact. I turned away, to the right, and during my turn noticed a Aircraft Y above me, about 300 feet. I ID'd the plane on my ADS-B (Aircraft Y). I immediately pulled power and lowered to 2,100 feet. I turned course to Morse Lake, and the Aircraft Y followed me, above approximately 300 feet. I was able to see it, since my plane has a 'greenhouse' roof, and I was able to simply look up. The ADS-B signal was now one single red dot on my screen. The plane followed me right/left across Morse Lake.... We had NO Prior agreement to fly in formation. I had no way to contact this plane during my flight. The operator of Aircraft Y was obviously following my plane. My opinion, they were playing a weird cat and mouse. This behavior is contrary to proper airmanship. My major concern in writing this report is the fact such an act is now very easy. Any plane equipped with ADS-B can easily follow/shadow another --- and keep the signal on top of another. I have concerns this may be a new way for pilots to play cat and mouse - it is a very dangerous maneuver and against the FAR's separation guide.
ASRS:1784361.s: During a personal training flight at 2,600 feet, the pilot observed Aircraft Y approaching within 300 feet vertically and following them across Morse Lake without prior agreement. The pilot descended to 2,100 feet to avoid the aircraft, attributing the incident to dangerous "cat and mouse" behavior facilitated by ADS-B tracking.

ASRS:1784362.n: We had departed ZZZ1 to the south, when Tower was shut down due to COVID-19, VFR to pick up IFR clearance over ZZZ2. After passing under the [ZZZ] Class B to clear it, we contacted ATC. After giving us the clearance, the Controller gave the Captain a phone number to call (which he did later after landing), and advised of a report, that we had strayed into [ZZZ] Class B airspace. ZZZ airport Tower was closed for to Coronavirus. [ZZZ is] a busy airport with mixed high speed and low speed aircraft.I departed VFR to pick up IFR clearance over ZZZ2 for arrival into ZZZ3.ATC, as always was very busy in that congested area and it took several attempts to make contact with ZZZ Approach.Very busy in cockpit looking for traffic, etc. May have clipped Class B airspace.ZZZ Approach advised, I may have entered Class B airspace and to copy phone a phone number.I replied: thank you, what altitude and heading would you like? The Controlled replied: 'continue, there is no traffic and then handed us off to ZZZ Center.I followed up with a phone call and thanked them for the wonderful service and protection they provide.I have been flying there for years. I have thousands of hours in general aviation and XX years flying airliners.The controllers do an unbelievable job working with an airspace system that does not work. The way it is designed doesn't work for the controllers or the pilots. At times the controllers are at max effort to keep up with the congested radio traffic.I am sure just they have their distractions with the maximum workload and have their own mistakes to sort out.That airspace configuration needs a good look at for something that works better for high speed aircraft. Get them out up and out of the way as fast as possible.It's a poor system to have jet aircraft level off at 1600 feet right after takeoff for normal operation under IFR conditions. In the cockpit of a jet aircraft you are very busy during this time.There needs to be change even if it slows down the current operations.
ASRS:1784362.s: A pilot departing VFR to pick up an IFR clearance over ZZZ2 may have inadvertently entered [ZZZ] Class B airspace due to high cockpit workload and congested radio traffic. ATC advised the pilot of the potential incursion, provided a contact number for a report, and handed off the flight to ZZZ Center without further action.

ASRS:1784364.n: Holding short of Runway XX at ZZZ, our aircraft was given a departure clearance void time of 60 seconds from ZZZ Center. We initiated an immediate departure on Runway XX. After climbing via the obstacle departure procedure, we proceeded enroute and contacted ZZZ Center again. We then heard another aircraft call back to ZZZ Center, and stated they were forced to initiate a go-around as they were on final approach to Runway XX. It is my guess that our departure is what caused that aircraft to go-around. I however, do not recall seeing the aircraft on final approach, or hearing a radio call that the aircraft was on final approach. Conditions were VFR at the airport, but IFR traffic load was heavy. I do not recall ATC advising us of the aircraft on final approach. It again is responsibility of us as a crew to ensure the approach/runway was clear for takeoff. If this incident was caused by our departure, we should have more clearly made sure it was safe for takeoff, and will do so in the future.
ASRS:1784364.s: The pilot departed Runway XX at ZZZ under a 60-second void time clearance while VFR conditions prevailed. The crew suspects their departure caused another aircraft to execute a go-around on final approach, noting they did not see the aircraft or receive an ATC advisory regarding the runway occupancy.

ASRS:1784367.n: I was conducting a training flight with a student and entered the pattern at PWT on the 45 for a full stop landing on Runway 20, making all radio calls in the pattern. As I was on short final (100 ft. AGL), the aircraft holding short makes a radio call that he is 'taking the active [Runway] 20'. He did not move his aircraft and continued holding short as I crossed the threshold, at which point I assumed he saw me as I passed right in front of his windshield in my roundout. I could not make any radio calls within those few seconds due to other traffic making calls in the pattern. As I am completing my landing roll to exit on taxiway A3, I hear a plane takeoff right on top of me. I asked on CTAF if he took off while I was still on the runway, to which 3 different aircraft concurred that he did. After a few minutes, as I'm departing the airspace, the aircraft in the pattern (along with myself) were discussing the events that transpired over radio. At that point, the pilot in question keyed up saying 'I'm still on frequency guys, what's the problem?'. I told him that he took off while I was still on the runway, to which he replied 'yeah, what's the problem with that?'. Another pilot noted that immediately after lift-off, he executed a steep right turn and exited the airspace at low level. In my professional opinion, the actions of the PIC of Aircraft X is a textbook example of a reckless operation, and a clear demonstration of several different hazardous attitudes. He obviously showed no remorse for his actions, believing that they were considered 'normal' things to do. There was absolutely nothing I could have done to prevent this from happening, because it is clearly all happening from the other guy's end. If I had to execute a go-around, it would almost definitely have resulted in a midair collision. The only way to prevent something like this from happening again is remedial training for this guy, or even a reevaluation of his certificate, because the way he operates his aircraft is clearly without regard for anyone's safety.
ASRS:1784367.s: During a training flight landing on Runway 20 at PWT, the reporter was on the runway when another pilot took off from the same runway despite holding short. The departing pilot executed a steep low-level turn and displayed no remorse, creating a situation where a go-around would likely have caused a midair collision.

ASRS:1784371.n: During heavy traffic with inbound and outbound traffic Aircraft X was on short final. Aircraft Y was in line with several other aircraft for a [Runway] 28 departure. Aircraft X was calling position inbound for [Runway] 28. When Aircraft Y was number one in line to depart, the aircraft advanced on to the Runway 28 without any radio traffic and departed. This caused Aircraft X to go missed to avoid a collision. Aircraft Y never responded to any radio traffic. Event happened at Yampa Valley Colorado. Contributing factors were a weather pause for both incoming and outgoing traffic. As we were trying to take off Denver Center was trying to sequence arrivals and departures. The aircraft in front of us was cleared to take off by Denver Center. We were asked if we could take off and be airborne within 90 seconds due to an inbound aircraft. We had an aircraft in sight and believed that to be the aircraft which we were cleared in front of. Contributing factor was Pilot in command was on ATC frequency but not on CTAF frequency. First officer was on both frequencies, but VFR aircraft was not transmitting position in pattern. As we took the runway and began our takeoff roll, chatter on the CTAF frequency alerted us to the traffic conflict. First Officer began giving vectors to Pilot Flying to avoid possible conflict. Due to being on takeoff roll we did not have visual on conflict aircraft. After getting airborne and getting in a safe flight configuration we took a slight left turn to displace ourselves from the TCAS information. We did not receive an RA likely because we were too low.Situational Awareness of Pilot Flying was increased dramatically once on both frequencies. Both pilots were under the impression clearance to depart was given with the aircraft we had in view to be the called traffic.
ASRS:1784371.s: Aircraft Y departed Runway 28 without radio communication while Aircraft X was on short final, forcing Aircraft X to execute a missed approach. The conflict resulted from the Pilot in Command monitoring only the ATC frequency, misinterpreting clearance, and failing to hear CTAF traffic alerts during the takeoff roll.

ASRS:1784379.n: We had completed the pre-flight check of the aircraft and pulled it from the hangar at ZZZ Airport to the alley way between hangars.We had completed the pre-start checklist items, picked up the ATIS and our clearance to transit out of the SFRA (Special Flight Rules Area).The aircraft started normally. There was a single backfire after or as the engine started but not too uncommon. The throttle was retarded following normal procedures.Shortly after engine start the cockpit began to fill with an acrid smelling smoke from under the left side of the panel. The engine was immediately shutdown and we exited the plane. All electrical (master/alternator/ignition) was shut off.Co-pilot grabbed the fire extinguisher as we exited. After exiting the Tower was called. The Tower called the on-field fire company. Response time was about <5 min as the on-field company was sent to the wrong side of the field.We opened the engine cowling to see if we could identify a source and possible extinguish. No fire was evident in the engine compartment. The fire departments had not yet arrived.The prop began a very slow rotation as if the engine was trying to crank.We went to check to verify that the Master Switch was off. It was.Smoke from the panel was much heavier. Appeared to mostly originate from the pilot side.Close evaluation showed flames from top of the left side-wall upholstery.We used the fire extinguisher to extinguish the flames along the sidewall. The amount of extinguishing agent or time for a full discharge seemed less than expected (perhaps 30 seconds).Fuel valve was moved to Off.A person called indicating that the Emergency Locator Transmitter had activated. We began a search for the beacon to deactivate. Determined that it is behind the panel in the back of the passenger area behind the stretcher. Requires panel removal.Fire department from ZZZ arrives.They verify that there is no excess heat in area where the flames were extinguished or other locations.The mechanic we used at [Company] arrived and began assisting with assessment and possible causes and removal of the ELT.Fire departments determined that no action on their part was needed and departed. On the scene perhaps 30 minutes.No immediate cause was noted the A&P from [Company].We returned the plane to the hangar. We called [Company1] to see if they could determine any immediate cause. We were trying to decide if we needed to use [Company1] vs [Company2].The technician from [Company1] saw no immediate issues.We disconnected the ground side of the battery, wrapped and secured to make certain no contact could occur that might provide a power source.We left the airplane doors open or ajar to allow for ventilation and secured the hangar.The plan at this point was to have the aircraft moved to [Company2]. We pulled the aircraft out of the hangar, shut the hangar doors and climbed into the cockpit for the start. We completed the normal procedures checklist setting the parking brake, received our SFRA (Special Flight Rules Area) clearance and shut down the avionics for start and noted the time as XA:X0 pm. The engine was primed with the auxiliary fuel pump, mixture was set to full rich and throttle to full open. The ignition was turned to start and as the engine began to turn over it ignited, and the throttle was retarded to slow the RPM to approximately 1000 RPM. As the RPM was beginning to stabilize, there was a backfire explosion and almost simultaneously smoke began pouring out from the defroster duct? at the left side of the wind screen and from underneath the dash panel by the PIC (Pilot-in-Command)'s rudder pedals. The smoke intensified filling the cockpit and the door was opened to relieve the smoke. Since the smoke was continuing, the mixture was pulled, the ignition was turned off removing the key and the battery and alternator switches turned off. Co-pilot exited the aircraft to determine a cause of the smoke and as he was investigating, I pulled the fire extinguisher from behind the co-pilots seat. I then exited the aircraft while he continued to walk around the nose of the aircraft looking for any source of fire. None was noted and the smoke was ventilating and dissipating. I called the tower on my cell phone to notify them of our situation and asked for fire assistance. I told Tower we were [at] the hangars on the east side just south of the terminal building at hangar. Tower took immediate action to alert the airport firetruck and ZZZ City Fire Dept. We did not see any evidence of a fuel fire or flames exiting the engine compartment although we did notice that the propeller began to rotate slowly for a few terms before stopping completely. The engine compartment was opened and there was no evidence of any fuel or oil leaks or any fire or smoke damage to the engine compartment. We went back behind the right wing and looking through the cockpit door, co-pilot noticed flames between the sidewall and left rudder pedal. He activated the fire extinguisher and sprayed the area of the flame, extinguishing it.While waiting for the fire equipment to arrive, I called Maintenance to ask them to have a mechanic come over and evaluate the situation. Fortunately, their lead was on the way to the east side and he arrived to look at the aircraft. Shortly thereafter the Airport Operations Director was first to arrive on scene and supervised the arrival of the fire equipment. The airport team was first ARFF (Airport Rescue and Fire Fighting) unit on the scene and were very professional in evaluating the situation so that no unnecessary action was taken. The smoke gradually dissipated and the aircraft was checked for residual hot spots, none of which were found. The fire equipment returned to their stations and the aircraft was hangared until it could be moved to the local maintenance facility.
ASRS:1784379.s: Pilots experienced two separate engine start incidents at ZZZ Airport where backfires caused smoke and flames in the left cockpit sidewall and defroster ducts. Fire crews and mechanics responded to extinguish the fires, but no immediate cause was identified despite the ELT activating and the propeller rotating after shutdown.

ASRS:1784380.n: I was on top of scattered clouds at 5,500 ft. arriving at HAF from the south. Weather reports from the airport all indicated the airport was VFR. As I approached the IF for the approach I had to decide between coordinating a pop up approach with Approach Control or descending through a large opening in the cloud layer and flying up the beach. I chose to remain VFR and fly up the coast due to the fact that it was getting dark and I had no idea how long it would take Approach Control to coordinate an approach. I descended uneventfully below the clouds and proceeded to the airport at between 1,000 and 1,500 ft. over hills that vary from 100 ft. to 300 ft. high. Apparently there is some drone operator who operates off a hill that gets upset when aircraft fly over at low altitude. He called me right after I had landed. He told me he 'I can not enforce this but I am requesting that we not fly over his drone operation'. I never saw a drone and am not sure if he was operating one at the time. Talking to other pilots it appears he calls every pilot he sees fly over at 1,500 ft. or below. I typically fly higher but on days when the ceilings are 1,500 to 2,000 ft. it is unavoidable to fly low. I am concerned about the drone operator calling pilots and possibly influencing their decisions when sacrificing safety of flight of the aircraft vs. inconvenience of the drone operator.
ASRS:1784380.s: A pilot arriving at HAF in VFR conditions descended below scattered clouds to 1,000–1,500 ft over hills to avoid delays. After landing, a drone operator called to complain about the low altitude flight, though the pilot saw no drone and expressed concern that such calls could negatively influence pilot safety decisions.

ASRS:1784382.n: During this incident I was on a checkride and we ran a partial panel VOR Runway X approach with a circle to Runway XY. This is normally a Class D airspace but the Tower at ZZZ is currently closed due to COVID and this has presented some challenges to the arriving and departing process given we share the airport with airline operations. We made it to the left downwind for XY and there was a carrier aircraft holding short of XY getting ready to take the runway and they requested over CTAF for us to extend our downwind so they could takeoff. We extended our downwind about a mile or so and decided to turn base. About the time we were turning base there was another carrier that called a 10 mile final for XY. With the position report given, we were under the impression we had the appropriate spacing for us to get on the ground and off the runway before they reached the field. We continued and turned in for final and the carrier taking off was on the roll. I made position reports and heard nothing back that would indicate an issue. When we were on short final carrier made a 6 mile final call. I then made a position call for short final and we were within a half mile of landing. About the time I was roughly 100 feet over the runway threshold, the carrier aircraft called and stated, 'Aircraft on short final, we are going around and will be flying above you.' We landed safely and had to extend our ground roll down the runway to exit because another carrier aircraft was taxiing to Runway XY via Taxiway A and we had to taxi beyond where they were. That concludes the incident. I do not know how accurate the position reports were from carrier or their speed but there didn't appear to be an issue on spacing and if they knew they were catching us that fast they could have let us know and I would have executed a go-around. This was not a near-miss event and we never saw the aircraft near us on ADS-B radar or receive any traffic notification. It seems to be more lack of communication in a non-towered environment with busy airspace as a root cause. I think they were well aware of our location in front of them and didn't speak up to let us know how quick they were catching us. I feel like there should be some additional measures in place when a tower is closed at an airport like this with heavier volume and many different types and sizes of aircraft operating. Sharing an airport between GA and airline ops in a non-towered environment is setting the stage for incidents like this to happen and truly presents some added challenges and hazards.
ASRS:1784382.s: During a checkride partial panel VOR approach at a non-towered airport with a closed tower, a carrier aircraft on final called a go-around while the pilot was 100 feet over the threshold. The reporter attributes the incident to poor communication and lack of traffic awareness in a busy mixed-use environment, though the landing was completed safely.

ASRS:1784385.n: Upon reaching 10,000 [ft.] we ran our 10,000 [ft.] climb checklist, we noted that the pressurization system was not functioning normally and indicated approximately 7,000 [ft.] cabin altitude. We verified all the bleed air system were in the correct position. Shortly after that time we noted that there was smoke/fumes in the cabin. We [advised ATC] and began to turn back to ZZZ and initiate a descent. We ran the Cockpit Smoke Fire Fumes checklist. We intercepted and flew the ILS into Runway 09 at ZZZ and landed without incident.
ASRS:1784385.s: The flight crew encountered a pressurization failure and cabin smoke at 10,000 feet, resulting in a 7,000-foot cabin altitude. They diverted to ZZZ, executed the smoke checklist, and landed safely on Runway 09 via ILS.

ASRS:1784388.n: For information, this Cirrus SR22T has about only 40 total hours frame/engine. After a normal pre-flight, normal start up, taxi, takeoff and climb without any issue or indication of trouble, About 9-10 minutes after departing ZZZ, and just leveling at 7,500 feet, I set the engine parameters to cruise settings. Looking at my PFD information I noticed I was 15 NM from ZZZ at this time. Suddenly I heard a 'thump' noise coming out of the engine, immediately followed by a loss of power of about 25%-30%. I immediately initiated a 180 degree turn towards ZZZ. After the turn, I confirmed oil indications were in the green, I switched fuel tank, I engage [the] high boost fuel pump, but nothing changed as far as engine power, RPM kept dropping slowing. I contacted ZZZ and informed the controller that I was experiencing engine troubles and returning to ZZZ. Control clear me for VFR decent and handed me over to ZZZ Tower. I could maintain altitude but I had a constant low rate of decent of 300 feet-400 feet. I decided to stay as high as I could until short final into ZZZ. Because I was coming directly from the north I planned on a short approach. I tried to move the throttle to full power but wasn't getting any change in rpm. At that time I decided that if I wasn't going to be able to maintain altitude to make it to the runway, as I reach the shoreline, I would activate the BRS/CAPS (Cirrus Airframe Parachute System) of the Cirrus. I had enough altitude though and made it to base, heard another thumping noise from the engine, landed safely. Tower told me while taxiing that there was a lot of smoke coming out of the bottom of the pane, the Fire Department Captain of the CFR (crash fire rescue) crew who was following me during taxi came up on the radio and told me smoke was increasing and advised to stop the engine immediately. I had reached the FBO ramp at that point. There was lots of oil dripping from all the front of the aircraft and after first quick observation with the manager of the maintenance facility in ZZZ we noticed pieces of the turbo lodged at the top of the right exhaust pipe. At this point, Cirrus Aircraft has taken over the process to find out what happened with this Continental TSIO-550K. They have informed us that the right side turbo shaft sheared off and pieces went through the engine and oil system. The engine is supposed to be sent to Continental for further analysis.
ASRS:1784388.s: The pilot of a low-time Cirrus SR22T experienced a sudden engine power loss and thumping noise at 7,500 feet due to a sheared turbo shaft. After returning to ZZZ with a controlled descent, the aircraft landed safely, though post-landing inspection revealed oil leaks and turbo debris lodged in the exhaust.

ASRS:1784392.n: I flew into ACT to see our son. This was a night flight and upon entering the ACT airspace it was very difficult to see the runway lighting. The runway lights were very dim and indistinguishable from surrounding city lights. When I asked the tower to turn up the runway lights, the Tower Controller stated they haven't been able to control the runway lights for 9 months due to a lightning strike. They have filed numerous maintenance requests, but none have been acted upon. This is unacceptable and a safety of flight issue. I request the runway lights be fixed as soon as possible to allow the tower and pilots to control the lighting intensity.
ASRS:1784392.s: A pilot reported difficulty distinguishing dim runway lights from city lights during a night arrival at ACT. The tower controller stated lightning damage nine months ago disabled light intensity control, and despite multiple maintenance requests, the issue remains unresolved.

ASRS:1784398.n: Enroute at 2,000 feet when I received a message on GPS and EFIS saying RNAV signal is lost, ADS-B is lost. iPad does not show correct location. No problem because VMC and not going anywhere. No navigation and no traffic. I called Approach Control to ask if they knew of any GPS outages. They said they hadn't and nobody else was having a problem. After landing, about 20 minutes later the system was back to normal. Another pilot had the same experience. Called Approach Control again on the landline and they advised that they had gotten several reports but they had no prior record of it and they should have been advised that Navy was doing testing offshore. There were no local NOTAMs and when I went back to look, there was a NOTAM for the outage lasting for about a week at various times for Center. Send [a] NOTAM to all Approach Controls that underlie testing area and also to local airports so that flights that never touch overlying airspace are aware of possible outage. They should also be sent to EFB providers so they can include it in their system. Had this occurred in IMC it would have spiked the workload considerably and only VHF navigation would have worked.
ASRS:1784398.s: A pilot en route at 2,000 feet experienced simultaneous RNAV, ADS-B, and EFB GPS outages caused by unnotified Navy offshore testing. The pilot landed safely in VMC, but the incident highlighted a lack of local NOTAMs and the potential for increased workload in IMC.

ASRS:1784399.n: I was approaching L52 from the north/west to enter a left downwind for Runway 29. As I was crossing the shoreline at 1,000 AGL (one mile out) and decelerating, my passenger and I spotted two powered gliders crossing the departure end of 29 at approximately 900 feet AGL.They seemed to be transitioning from the southern part of the dunes to the norther part of the dunes through the upwind part of the traffic pattern. I veered the aircraft slightly more to the south to avoid them when I spotted another powered glider transitioning from the south to the north by intersection the downwind leg of the left pattern to 29. He was coming directly toward my aircraft in the opposite direction of traffic pattern. I then had to veer slightly to the left (north/east) to avoid that vehicle. I then landed without incident on 29.When parked at transient space we witnessed another powered glider takeoff from the tarmac and join the other gliders. They continued to overfly the airport at pattern altitude and not seem to adhere by any observable pattern.
ASRS:1784399.s: A pilot approaching Runway 29 at 1,000 feet AGL veered to avoid three powered gliders operating outside the traffic pattern, including one flying opposite to traffic. The pilot landed safely but observed the gliders continuing to overfly the airport without adhering to standard pattern procedures.

ASRS:1784407.n: I departed ZZZ about XA:38 via a right downwind departure to the southwest and direct to ZZZ1. I climbed to 4500 ft. and began experiencing intermittent moderate turbulence, so I began a gradual descent. I was still on the ZZZ Tower frequency (although out of the class D) and Tower advised of traffic about 11 o'clock and same altitude. I advised I was descending. I had traffic on TCAS and saw traffic at about my 10 o'clock, 700 ft. above and probably 3000 ft. horizontally, and told ZZZ Tower that I had traffic in-sight. It appeared to be an experimental aircraft. I then switched ZZZ2 Approach for flight following and picked up flight following about 15 [miles] north of ZZZ1. I was told to enter a right downwind for Runway XX and then told to maintain 2000 ft., which I did (actually closer to 2100 ft.), and was told to overfly a Cessna who was slower and would follow me in and that I was number 2 following a Learjet on final. I saw the Cessna. ZZZ1 Tower spun the Cessna to the left as I overflew him by 500 ft. as instructed. I reported the Lear in-sight and was then cleared to land behind the Learjet and started my approach. I landed on Runway XX behind the Learjet at about XA:54 and taxied to my tie-down.
ASRS:1784407.s: The pilot departed ZZZ, descended due to turbulence, and received traffic advisories from Tower before switching to Approach. The pilot landed on Runway XX behind a Learjet after overflying a Cessna by 500 feet as instructed.

ASRS:1784424.n: I released Aircraft X for departure from BFI in a south flow. Aircraft X reported climbing to 2,000 ft. on the NIRVANA1 SID. I radar identified Aircraft X and climbed them to 6,000 ft.. As Aircraft X was climbing through 1,800 ft. I noticed that Aircraft X appeared to be making a right turn towards the SEA VOR and not following the NIRVANA SID. I instructed Aircraft X to 'turn left immediately, left turn heading 130.' At this point, Aircraft X was starting to converge with Aircraft Y who was on final approach into SEA descending through 1,100 ft. on the ILS Approach to Runway 16R. Aircraft X was about 1.5 miles laterally separated and 700 ft. vertically separated from Aircraft Y and converging. I observed Aircraft X achieve vertical separation from Aircraft Y, then saw the turn to heading 130 start occurring. I gave Aircraft X the Brasher statement. The pilot of Aircraft X stated that it 'looks like the activation for the autopilot for the NIRVANA1 did not take place.'I honestly don't know how to fix this problem, but it is a recurring, systemic issue. This is not my first event with almost identical circumstances, and many of my co-workers have had very similar events. Attempts have already been made to alter the SID, or issue an initial heading for aircraft departing BFI, but these events still occur. The typical issue is that pilots are filing SEA.J5 and though BFI is issuing the NIRVANA1 SID and a Preferred Departure Route that would join J5 from TAOMA or SUMMA, pilot error including unchecked autopilot actions that result in a turn to SEA VOR will immediately cause convergence at the same altitude as aircraft inbound to SEA within the final approach fix, as well as any aircraft departing SEA during that time. There is very little and very subtle warning, and immediate action is necessary to recover separation and end the rapidly worsening danger of the situation. I believe in most cases it is a result of an individualized pilot deviation, and I don't know how to end those completely. The only other solution I can think of would be to completely remove/decommission the SEA VOR.
ASRS:1784424.s: An air traffic controller intervened when Aircraft X deviated from the NIRVANA1 SID at BFI, turning toward the SEA VOR and converging with Aircraft Y on final approach to SEA. The pilot attributed the deviation to a failed autopilot activation, while the controller identified this as a recurring systemic issue involving pilot error and route design.

ASRS:1784426.n: It was toward [the] end of the rush, I was working the low side and had all of my aircraft slowing to 170 kts. Controller Y plugged in for a relief briefing after working as the main arrival coordinator. As I was going through the position relief checklist Controller Y noticed something was off. At first I thought Controller Y was looking at the spacing on final, which was perfect. But then I saw Aircraft X on a 180 heading racing towards the Runway XL final. My first reaction was to turn Aircraft X right to a 330 heading but then Controller Y suggested a left turn to continue eastbound away from final. I issued a left turn 090 and then a climb to 050 to get above the traffic on final approach.It was clear that Aircraft X took the left turn to 180. Aircraft Y had turn to a 180 heading at his appropriate time.If it wasn't for the fast acting from Controller Y the issue could have worsen.In this new world of 'COVID Traffic' pilots need to do a better job of listening to control instructions especially when the volume is high.
ASRS:1784426.s: The low-side controller and relief Controller Y managed Aircraft X, which incorrectly turned 180 degrees toward Runway XL final during high traffic. Controller Y identified the error and directed a left turn to 090 and climb to 5,000 feet, preventing a conflict caused by the pilot's failure to follow instructions.

ASRS:1784449.n: The minimum cleanup altitudes for Runways 32L and R on the Jeppesen OMA (Omaha) Simple Special EFP chart differ by one foot as compared to the flap retraction altitudes for the same runways on the OMA Takeoff and Landing Report generated (date) at (time), [Report Number] for [Aircraft X].Shouldn't the Jeppesen chart minimum cleanup altitudes and TLR flap retraction altitudes agree?
ASRS:1784449.s: A pilot reported a one-foot discrepancy between Jeppesen OMA chart minimum cleanup altitudes and TLR flap retraction altitudes for Runways 32L and R. The pilot questioned why these two sources did not agree for Aircraft X.

ASRS:1784451.n: On climb out, after pressing the ATTEND CALL button as part of my flow, the A Flight Attendant immediately called the flight deck and complained of a loud squeal coming from the main door (L1) and that they could 'see daylight' coming from the door seal. I could hear the squeal in the background on the interphone. I looked on the overhead panel and verified that there was NO door light illuminated, I then went to verify pressurization and noticed that the cabin altitude was approaching 9,500 ft. I immediately instructed the First Officer to level off and then called ATC and reported a 'pressurization issue' and requested 10,000 ft.. We did not get a CABIN ALTITUDE WARNING at any point. I then requested to return to ZZZ and they gave us a further descent to 5,000 ft. and direct to the field. I made a PA and let the Passengers know that we were returning to ZZZ because of a pressurization issue and that we would be on the ground in ten minutes. I never requested priority handling because I didn't feel like it was necessary because we had already received an immediate descent clearance, but ATC declared one for us and had the trucks standing by on arrival. We had just enough time to run all of the checklists and get our landing data. The arrival and landing was uneventful. I called the Flight Attendants and asked how everyone was. The A and B Flight Attendants said they felt a 'little dizzy' but they said all Passengers seemed fine and there didn't seem to be any issues. Before opening the main door on arrival I inspected the seal and on the aft part of the door from top to bottom I could indeed see daylight and could run my hand in between the seal and door frame from top to bottom. Loss of pressurization in the climb, due to forward entry door not sealed properly due to malfunction. Climbing through 10,000 ft. and beginning the Climb Checklist, the Flight Crew received a chime from the Cabin Crew that the forward entry door was squealing loud and air rushing through the front area enough causing the Flight Attendant's hair to be circulating with the flow of air. No indication of the event on the flight deck. Cabin pressurization reached 9,500 ft. The aircraft reached a peak altitude just over 12,000 ft. before descent. Returned to ZZZ uneventful. ATC themselves gave us priority handling for our return to ZZZ. Upon landing and at the gate, all Passengers were removed and no indications of any medical distress.
ASRS:1784451.s: During climb, the flight crew experienced a pressurization loss to 9,500 ft cabin altitude caused by an unsealed forward entry door (L1) with no flight deck warning. The aircraft descended to 5,000 ft and returned to ZZZ uneventfully, with crew reporting mild dizziness but no passenger distress.

ASRS:1784467.n: The Ground Crew had finished pushing our flight from the gate. I cleared the Ground Crew off and was then shown the bypass pin and wireless headset bag per normal procedures. We started #2 for a single engine taxi. Upon rolling, the aircraft started veering left with no nose wheel steering. I made a quick and unexpected stop which occurred during the flight attendant demo. (No one was injured but it did get the attention of the flight attendants). I realized that the Ground Crew probably failed to ensure the towing lever was in in the normal position after removing the bypass pin which would have enabled the hydraulic nose wheel steering. I called OPS and they sent a ramp person out to lower the lever. The nose wheel steering then worked normally. I suggest the following: ensure the Ground Crew at all stations verify the towing lever is in the normal position after removing the bypass pin and that a warning is added in section X.2 of the AOM that proper nose wheel steering operation should be verified as the aircraft taxis forward. I recommend that the AOM is revised in section Y-1 to read: 'fuel verified, final is clear'. This ensures that the proper fuel on board is verified at the last possible moment before taxiing onto the runway instead of at the beginning of the Before Takeoff Checklist so unexpected delays would not cause a takeoff below the min fuel requirement.
ASRS:1784467.s: During single-engine taxi, the aircraft veered left with no nose wheel steering because the Ground Crew likely failed to return the towing lever to the normal position after removing the bypass pin. The pilot stopped the aircraft, and steering was restored after a ramp technician lowered the lever.

ASRS:1784530.n: In ZZZ we attempted to start number two engine using APU air and it spooled up abnormally slowly, and I noticed that the EGT seemed to lag. At 45% N2 the start stagnated and decayed until a 2.5% N2 decrease and Engine Fail indication on the ECAM. We stopped the start, then following guidance in our paperwork, we started number one (which also stagnated a little bit but then started normally) and then attempted a second start on number two using cross-bleed from the number one engine. We allowed the engine to spool up to 25.7% N2, then added fuel. At starter cutout, the engine hung again, dropping to about 43.2% N2 and hanging there before slowly spooling up to about 43.8% N2 when it timed out for the start and Engine Fail was indicated on ECAM again. Our Quick Reference Handbook said we could attempt a second start after the first hung start, but that maintenance action was required if the second start failed. At that point we requested a tug and BTB to our parking space. This is where Maintenance Control got involved. At first they suggested that we defer the APU bleed, however it was obvious to me that the air was not the problem (we used a separate source for each start), so I told him the APU bleed deferral was not sufficient. Then he suggested that a problem with the Integrated Drive Generator might be causing the hung start and suggested we defer that, and I agreed it could be tried. As part of the maintenance action during start the Inetgrated Drive Generator was disconnected and deferred, and the Airworthiness Release in the log book was signed off, then we continued getting the jet started and were on our way. During the flight the APU was running as required by the deferral, and at 36,000 ft. it automatically shut down. I attempted to start the APU, and on the second try, it started. I requested and descended to a lower altitude of 30,000 ft. and the APU operated normally for the rest of the flight. If I had not been able to start it, I would have had to advise ATC and divert. I wrote up the APU under a P code for momentary or transitory malfunction. In ZZZ1, maintenance checked the APU for any failure codes, did the repetitive inspection for oil quantity for the Integrated Drive Generator deferral, and signed off the APU. The FO (First Officer) and I discussed the situation and agreed that the APU was not malfunctioning and may have had a momentary problem with operating at high altitude. We accepted the jet for the leg to ZZZ2. With a fresh Airworthiness Release in the log book, we started the number one engine first, then started number two using cross-bleed at the request of maintenance. The number two engine came close to exceeding time limits, but did eventually spool up. We were filed for 33,000 ft., and at that altitude the APU did the same thing--it shut down--and we were able to get it started again on the second try. We requested and descended to 29,000 ft. for the remainder of the flight. Again, the APU operated normally from there on, and again, I wrote it up with a P code for the shut down. I also made a comment in the logbook about the number two engine start, even though our flight paperwork said that comments for a successful start were not needed. There I made a note that the EGT from fuel introduction to the point where the start stagnated, then started to spool up, seemed abnormally low and was at least 50 degrees cooler at 45% N2 than the other engine. The stagnated start was evident from fuel introduction until after started cutout when it became apparent that the engine was not ready to continue the start on its own. The Integrated Drive Generator has nothing to do with the EGT during start. I suspect something else is going on here, perhaps a Electronic Engine Control problem with the fuel mixture at high altitude, or a sensor malfunction. On further reflection, I feel that the deferral of the Integrated Drive Generator was inappropriate for the problem we had, and I should not have accepted it. It created a problem where we could have been forced to request priority handling and divert. It is likely that whatever is wrong with our engine starts does not pose a safety of flight risk once we get the engine going, so it makes no sense to do a deferral that could compromise safety. Until this is figured out, the guidance needs to be specific and it needs to go out to everyone in the maintenance and crew pipelines and it should be operations friendly. My recommendation is that everything in the fuel system be checked in case it is causing the starting problem for cold engines at high altitude. I think that the bleed system is less likely to be the issue because of the low EGT I saw during all four start attempts on that engine. I also recommend that maintenance be able to attempt at least one more start before the aircraft is taken out of service, and that crew get more guidance concerning the problem. 'Maintenance action' is not enough to let a Captain know what to expect or what to accept. I also have felt for a long time that our systems manual has been scrubbed of a lot of detail about systems with which we do not directly interact, so we are less able to make informed decisions and instead have to rely on experience. That will not always save us from making the wrong call. Everyone in this situation acted in good faith, and I am not writing this report to cast any doubt on anyone. I only want to point out a safety issue that we can avoid in the future.
ASRS:1784530.s: The crew experienced repeated hung starts on engine two at ZZZ, leading to an inappropriate Integrated Drive Generator deferral and subsequent APU shutdowns at high altitude. The pilot suspects a fuel system or sensor issue rather than the deferred component, noting that the deferral created unnecessary diversion risks.

ASRS:1784535.n: During the climb out on the SID, ATC instructed us to maintain 4,000 ft. for traffic. During the cruise at 4,000 ft. Pilot Flying requested autopilot to be engaged. After clearing the traffic we received ATC instruction to continue climb to 16,000 ft. Pilot Flying used VS mode and added power to start the climb, few seconds later we heard a loud bang and all ENG 2 parameters started to roll back with ENG 2 OUT EICAS message and other messages related to the ENG failure. At the same time Pilot Flying disconnected the autopilot and hand flew the airplane while requesting from the Pilot Monitoring to [advise ATC]. Pilot Flying requested ENG 2 OUT QRH and we started going through the items. We decided not to start the engine again due to the loud bang we heard. Pilot Flying requested the autopilot to be engaged after we received an ATC clearance to maintain 5,000 ft. Captain called the Flight Attendant using the call button and gave her the report. Planned and briefed ILS XXR weather were overcast 600 and IMC condition during the whole event. After making sure that everything is complete and we are not overweight as we had only 20 passengers on board, we advised ATC that we are ready to start the approach. Pilot Flying hand flew the [Runway] XXR approach and made a successful landing, requested taxiing to the gate and fire trucks were following the plane all the way to the gate. At the gate, the Captain made an announcement apologizing and explaining to the passengers the situation and they were so understandable. Maintenance came on board and a maintenance logbook write up was complete. [We] departed ZZZ bound for ZZZ1. We departed from [Runway] XYL on the ZZZZZ 3 departure with an assigned heading of 110 after takeoff. ATC instructed us to maintain 4,000 ft. for traffic, which we noted on our respective TCAS pages. ATC gave us clearance up to 16,000 [ft.]and the Captain smoothly applied climb thrust and began a climb. Shortly after that, a loud audible pop was heard outside my window and the Engine 2 EICAS message illuminated and Eng 2 indications began dropping. That Captain quickly identified the dead engine and told me to notify ATC. We notified ATC and ran through our checklist. We were instructed to level at 5,000 [ft.] and turn North HDG 360. I loaded XXR approach in the FMS and I went back to the checklist to finish up for our single engine approach. We were vectored to the final approach course for ILS XXR. I received runway speeds and we adjusted per the QRH. The Captain flew a flawless ILS and landing to Runway XXR. We safely exited the runway and taxied with no further incident.
ASRS:1784535.s: During climb to 16,000 ft, the crew experienced a loud bang and Engine 2 failure, triggering EICAS messages. The Captain hand-flew a single-engine ILS approach to Runway XXR, landing safely with fire trucks escorting the aircraft to the gate.

ASRS:1784538.n: Normal takeoff, level off at 10,000 feet. Clearance to 17,000 feet, at 10,500 feet Right Engine Flameout caution message. Reference QRH, two items. Thrust lever confirm and idle and engine instruments monitor auto relight. The caution message did go away although N2 was below 40%. After approximately 45 seconds I advanced the thrust levers slightly to monitor auto relight. While all this was going on the flight attendant called the flight deck, I did answer and told her we were returning to ZZZ. Also talking to ATC and getting vectors and a decent. The First Officer did a great job, after running the checklist and setting up the cockpit for the return, I also had him call OPS, and let the folks know we were returning. I did fail to mention to test the flight attendants. Normal landing and taxi in. Around 10,500 feet we had a Right Engine Flame Out with auto relight. Performed checklists and returned back to the field.
ASRS:1784538.s: The pilot reported a right engine flameout at 10,500 feet during climb, triggering an auto relight and return to ZZZ. After completing checklists and coordinating with ATC and cabin crew, the aircraft executed a normal landing and taxi.

ASRS:1784540.n: On climb out after 5 min. for approximately 15 min. FA (Flight Attendants) 3 and 4 reported smelling sweet glue like odor that went away in about 15 min. About 35 min. into flight FA 3 reported a headache and FA 4 reported headache and nausea. FA 2 reported the smell was faint but did smell it but felt OK. FA 1 and flight deck did not smell odor. The odor was noted from Row 10 to aft of aircraft. The FA 4 reported feeling worse at 35 min. into flight so we elected to return to ZZZ. 1 passenger in 13A reported slight irritation in nose and slight headache. On return to ZZZ as a [prioritized] aircraft on descent through 10,000 ft. flight deck and cabin noticed a distinct odor like Elmer's Glue. Uneventful landing with flight deck on O2 and cabin use of 4 portable O2 bottles. FA 4 went to hospital remaining crew felt fine and continued on new aircraft to ZZZ1 as rescheduled.The probable cause was possible oil leak but no indications in flight deck.Dependent on maintenance findings.
ASRS:1784540.s: Flight attendants and one passenger smelled a sweet odor and experienced symptoms during climb and cruise, prompting a return to ZZZ. The crew used oxygen on descent and landed safely; the probable cause was a suspected oil leak with no flight deck indications.

ASRS:1784542.n: After takeoff during initial climb out we received a ACARS message. The message informed us of dangerous goods being carried and to expect a NOTOC (Notification to Captain) prior to gate departure.Reporter suggests it would be preferable to have a system in place that would ensure a NOTOC was presented to the flight crew prior to closing the boarding door.
ASRS:1784542.s: The flight crew received an ACARS message after takeoff during initial climb indicating dangerous goods were on board and a NOTOC was expected prior to departure. The reporter suggests implementing a system to ensure the NOTOC is presented before closing the boarding door.

ASRS:1784560.n: Upon landing at their destination of ZZZZ1 and looking at the W/B (Weight and Balance) for the next flight ZZZZ1-ZZZZ2, I noticed the W/B had Dry Ice loaded in the lower forward compartment. I checked the W/B for the ZZZZ-ZZZZ1 leg, and ZZZZ had loaded Dry Ice in the lower forward compartment and did not notify me, thus no 0.4% overburn had been applied. Flight crew did not say anything to me as well. Dispatcher suggested better ramp training for them to be aware of need to inform Dispatcher if Dry Ice will be loaded in lower compartments of 777. Also, suggest programming [Software] to trigger an FPS ball alert to the Dispatcher anytime Dry Ice gets loaded in a lower compartment of a 777. I made this suggestion previously to [Name] in an email sent on [Date].
ASRS:1784560.s: A dispatcher discovered dry ice was loaded in the lower forward compartment of a 777 without notification from the ground crew or flight crew, resulting in a missing 0.4% overburn calculation. The dispatcher recommended improved ramp training and software alerts to prevent future occurrences.

ASRS:1784579.n: I believe complacency played a role in this error. I am always checking and double checking my work but unfortunately I missed an important piece of information on the Center of Gravity (CG) and Passenger Count (PC) data. Next time I will slow down and thoroughly check my work without rushing and recognize my complacency.We arrived to our aircraft in the morning to perform our duties for the first leg out of two for the day. Boarding was complete and I received the cargo sheet and CG/PC Data from the gate agent. As I plugged the numbers in for departure I noticed the passenger count seemed low. Thinking that it was due to the slow season and COVID I continued to run the numbers for our takeoff data. With the low passenger count I figured we were going to also need a ZFW reset from the dispatcher. I confirmed with the Captain and went ahead and contacted Dispatch with our new ZFW and confirmation of our CG. New numbers were sent back and we took off uneventfully.While in cruise the Captain requested a lavatory break. Upon his returned, he voiced his concern with the passenger count from what he saw in the cabin while checking our CG/PC. That is when we realized that the incorrect CG/PC was given to us. As we were starting our decent, the Captain transferred the controls to me while he referenced the COM and tables to calculate our correct weight along with the landing data and Vapp. As a precaution we also added few knots to the Vapp. The Captain completed the tasks and I confirmed that all the information was correct and within safe parameters for a safe landing. We had sufficient runway and the field was VMC at the time of landing. The landing was uneventfully and we continued to the gate.
ASRS:1784579.s: The flight crew missed incorrect Center of Gravity and passenger count data due to complacency during pre-flight planning. They recalculated weight and landing data during descent, added speed to Vapp, and executed a safe, uneventful landing.

ASRS:1784583.n: The crew conducted a Maintenance Test Flight, to test the repairs made on the Right Engine Fire Loop. During the climb phase of the flight while passing FL380, the crew observed the R/H Fire T-Handle illuminate flashing associated with a flashing Master Warning indication. As the crew was expecting this possible indication during the flight, the on board Mechanic was notified to observe the indications. Immediately afterwards the crew began to perform the memory items of the QRH ENGINE FIRE Checklist in an effort to extinguish the illuminated/flashing T-handle. After performing all memory items followed by the QRH checklist, the Engine Fire T-Handle continued to flash. The PIC (Pilot in Command) asked the on board Mechanic to observe if there was any indication of engine fire outside the window to which he confirmed there was not. ITT Engine indications also confirmed that there was no indication of an actual engine fire. As the aircraft was now single engine, the crew [requested priority handling] with ATC and elected to return to ZZZ. The aircraft landed safely and without incident. No suggestions at this time.
ASRS:1784583.s: During a maintenance test flight for a right engine fire loop repair, the crew experienced a false right engine fire warning at FL380. After confirming no actual fire via visual and ITT checks, they returned to ZZZ and landed safely.

ASRS:1784603.n: While on initial climb out, myself and the medical crew noticed a burning smell coming from the back of the cabin. I turned off all the blowers and A/C (Air Conditioning) thinking as these might have been the cause, continuing to fly for some more time, it was evident that the smell hadn't gone away. I made the decision to turn back to ZZZ and swap planes. We did not need to dump fuel, and landed under max landing weight.
ASRS:1784603.s: The pilot and medical crew detected a burning smell in the cabin during initial climb. The pilot turned off blowers and A/C, but the odor persisted, prompting a return to ZZZ for an aircraft swap and landing at maximum weight without fuel dumping.

ASRS:1784615.n: Around 40 minutes outside of ZZZ, while in cruise flight at FL360, the LO HYD light illuminated. The hydraulic pressure gauge confirmed that the pressure was below normal. We monitored the gauge and realized it was losing pressure. As a crew we prepared for the possibility of a complete hydraulic failure. We prepared the cabin and medical crew for a possible [forced] landing. TRACON was informed of our hydraulic system failure and assisted us in our descent. Once on approach to Runway XXR we tried to lower the gear with no success. At this point the hydraulic pressure gauge indicated zero pressure. We then performed the Hydraulic System Failure/Alternate Gear Extension procedure which blew the gear down and 3 green, 2 red lights confirmed the gear was down. At this time we [received priority handling] with ZZZ Tower. After the auxiliary hydraulic pump was energized we were able to lower the flaps to 20 degrees and adjusted our target speed accordingly. On touch down to Runway XXR, First Officer released the parachute and we felt the drag for 1-2 seconds before the chute separated from the aircraft. I was then able to use the thrust reversers and also had regular breaking. We then exited the runway and made it to the ramp under our own power. Upon inspection of the aircraft we found hydraulic fluid on the left flap, left main gear wheel well and on the left side if the [empennage]. During the initial preflight, the hydraulic reservoir had fluid to the top of the sight glass and the indicating ball was at the top. I did not visually recheck the fluid level after that but during post-flight and preflight walk arounds before and after each leg there was no indication of a hydraulic leak. About 40 minutes from landing at ZZZ, the Low Hydraulic Caution light illuminated, and the gauge was showing under 1,000 psi. The PF (Pilot Flying) and I reviewed the QRH Yellow Tabs 10 and 13 a couple of times to ensure we understood what was going to happen and found the related circuit breakers. We discussed our time schedule and decided that we would [have priority handling] if we needed to blow the gear down. We did inform Center and Approach of our issue and they were vectoring us to give us time to descend and slow down for the gear extension. We informed the medical crew of the situation and told them to ensure that all the gear in back was stowed and secured tightly. We followed the QRH and when the gear failed to fully extended, we followed through and blew the gear down. After which we [received priority handling] with the ZZZ Tower and was cleared to land on Runway XXR. We turned on the electric pump on short final per the QRH and once the main gear touched down, we deployed the drag chute, thrust reversers, spoilers, and found we had normal hydraulic braking but stayed ready to use the emergency air brakes if needed. We turned off the runway and advised the tower that we were dropping the drag chute, but it had already detached right after deployment. We taxied back to the FBO and inspected the aircraft. Hydraulic fluid was present on the left flap upper and lower surfaces, and the underbelly of the plane from the gear doors back being heavier on the left side of the aircraft. The drag chute was found on the runway around the point of touchdown and deployment on the center line. I am not sure what caused the low pressure so it is hard to say if anything could have prevented it.
ASRS:1784615.s: The flight crew experienced a low hydraulic pressure failure at FL360 while en route to ZZZ, requiring alternate gear extension and priority handling. Post-landing inspection revealed hydraulic fluid leaks on the left flap and empennage, though the cause of the pressure loss remained undetermined.

ASRS:1784634.n: We departed ZZZ part 91 to relocate Aircraft X to ZZZ1. Few minutes after crossing ZZZZZ intersection at FL370 in contact with ZZZ Center, I notice a red fire light blinking on left engine accompanied with both red master working lights. No indication of engine stall, no vibration felt, no lost of power notice.Within 5 seconds I retarded to idle the left throttle, 3 seconds later the 'ENG FIRE PULL' Handle light extinguish making me believe that was only bleed air leak in the sensing loop, but 7 seconds later, the 'T' handle again starting flashing indicating fire.I pulled the thrust lever in cutoff position, I pulled the 'T' handle and once the two arm lights where illuminated, I pressed left one first, seconds later when I realized that the fire light was continued flashing, I pressed the second fire extinguishers light to the same engine.Unfortunately, the 'ENG FIRE PULL' handle was still flashing, taking the decision to turn left to the closest airport.We were flying the [airway] eastbound at 85 nm from ZZZ, only 3 airports where closest before ZZZ, but no rescue services most likely or not enough runway available for our landing configuration (gear down, max flaps 20 deg).Since the checklist says 'land as soon as possible' and bad weather was in front of us, while my copilot was advising ATC I started my left turn while descending, circumnavigating the weather (during my 90 deg turn, I looked behind my left shoulder to see if a white or black smoke trail was left behind, but I couldn't see nothing), and after clear of mountains I continued descending to 5,000 feet where I preferred to maintain a low altitude and close to the shoreline if a ditching was necessary.During our diversion we had time to talk to the Controller where we answered every question he asked.Every question was answered at the moment and once we were established on the localizer about 20 nm out, the fire light extinguish. While on my final descent I asked the tower that the ground equipment if possible, to be waiting on the left side of the runway since I was requesting a visual confirmation if actual fire was still on the left side or not.After landing I stopped the airplane and I requested again a visual confirmation and the answer was 'they are on the way.' At that moment with the right engine running, I asked my copilot to open the upper main door since I never felt or saw fire and to have his visual confirmation from him.My intentions were to taxi the airplane out of the runway if no danger or fire existed.As soon as my First Officer opened the door, he gave me the visual that NO FIRE WAS ON LEFT ENGINE and I talked to the Tower that my intentions was to move the airplane out of there to the ramp. The Tower responded to not move since the fire truck was already in my left side. When I saw to my left, I saw a fireman with his hose in position so, I turned off the right engine shutting down everything and jumping out of the airplane. By the time I was stepping out, the fireman started to spray the left engine and I thought that finally a real fire was there.Few seconds later all the fireman started to spray with soapy water the hole airplane, from the cockpit, fuselage, wings and the two engines from the front side and from behind (right engine was only from behind).As soon as I see all that I started to ask the fireman if they saw actually fire, but no fireman spoke Spanish or English. I tried to speak with 5 of them but was a loss of time.By the time they finish spraying the airplane, people from different departments approached the airplane and as soon as I found one who could speak English I asked him to translate the only question I've been asking.'Did anybody see fire?''Can someone say if actually a fire was on either engine?'And the answer was 'No fire was detected by anyone.'After that, we proceeded to tow the airplane out of the runway. While following our route of flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 we leveled at 37,000 feet before entering ZZZ [Center] airspace just before the fix ZZZZZ. As we passed that fix, ZZZ Center switched us to ZZZ2 Center and before first contact was made, we had an indication of fire on the left engine.The Captain proceeded with the memory items procedure. He put the left power to idle and we were waiting for that light to extinguish, it did, but in about 8-10 seconds it started flashing again, giving the indication that fire might still be present. Then the Captain continued with the procedure of cutting out the engine to secure it and pull the T-Handle of the left engine, continued by pressing the ARM button of one of the fire extinguishers.The flashing light indicating the possibility of fire in the left engine continued, so the Captain pressed the second ARM button. In both intents to extinguish the light with the fire extinguishers the flashing light of the T-Handle never shut off. So the PIC decided to call on the requested checklist out of the planes QRH and initiated [expedited] descent. I, as the First Office went through the procedures on tab 5 'Engine Fire Shutdown' section of the QRH. I went through all the checklist out loud and twice to confirm everything requested was performed. Then followed the checklist to the single engine landing procedure on tab 14 abnormal checklist, and went through it twice and out loud.While the descent was performed, I advised ATC and asked for vectors to the closest airport, which in this case the only appropriate airport and closest was ZZZ1. The Controller first indicated to fly to a fix which I could not understand and when I asked about 2 times to spell it or give us vectors, he then instructed to fly to the ZZZ VOR. I immediately set the FMS and GPS to the VOR and ZZZ1 airport. The Captain continued VFR descent and decided to cross the mountains as soon as possible so that we can continue descending and get closer to the ground and shore and make a straight in into ZZZ1.While the descent was being performed the left fire, light continued to flash. The Captain took communications while I was setting the procedures into ZZZ1 on the GPS and FMS. In about 3 miles short of the airport. We noticed the light stopped flashing. The Captain requested the Tower to let the rescue and firefighters know that they were needed in our left side once we landed, they confirmed that they were ready and waiting for us. Once we landed and the airplane came to a complete stop I got out if my seat and opened the left exit door to verify if there was any fire present at the moment, I communicated to the Captain that NO fire was visible from the front of the engine and then he instructed for me to get out. As soon as I got out, he was still in communication with the Tower, he shut the right engine as instructed by the Controller and exited the airplane.Once we stepped away from the airplane the firefighters started spraying the left engine immediately through the front and back of the nacelle, and seconds after, another group of firefighters started spraying the right engine. I personally told the captain that if they were spraying is because probably, they saw fire but when I noticed them spraying the right engine too then we thought it was their protocol to follow.Once they stopped spraying the captain asked if they saw fire to several of the Firefighters but they could not understand what we were asking, it was not until a ground handler or someone that understood English approached the airplane and we asked him to ask them if someone saw fire, they answered that No fire was visible. We then proceeded to tow the aircraft out of the runway.Personally, I believe this could be a glitch on the system of the aircraft. I am not a mechanic so it's hard for me to say what might have caused the aircraft to give that indication of fire on the engine. We treated the indication as a real fire so the airplane couldbe secure and everyone on board too. I don't know if this could be a maintenance issue or if it has happened before. My suggestion is just to continue to give the progressive and preventive maintenance to the aircraft as they are required and for the pilots to continue to communicate with maintenance any issues given big or small as no matter how small it may seem it could lead to other problems in the long run.
