Definitely the airplanes have their years so the more they are used for the missions they are going to require more and more maintenance.
ASRS:1784634.s: Pilots of Aircraft X reported a false left engine fire warning at FL370, prompting an emergency descent and diversion to ZZZ1. Although fire crews sprayed the aircraft upon landing, no fire was detected, leading the crew to suspect a system glitch or maintenance issue.

ASRS:1784664.n: During initial climb out (400 or 500 ft.) we heard a call from Medical saying that 'something's burning'. I looked behind and noticed the cabin was beginning to fill with a smokey hazy layer. The temperature in the airplane had increased and now the smoke was reaching the cockpit. I reset both bleed air valves in case we had a stuck valve, but this did not change anything. I told FO (First Officer) to turn off all fans in case that is the cause. I looked back again and I could visible see the smoke rising out of the rear right wall panel. We stopped the climb at 2,500 ft., [advised ATC] and I made the decision to return back to ZZZ. I assumed control of the airplane and radios while FO completed checklist and set us up on the approach and calculated the weight of the airplane. He advised me that we were currently 500 lbs. overweight, I made the decision to still continue to the airport as I did not know the cause of the smoke and did not want to waste any time burning off extra fuel. We ultimately made a safe left base visual approach and landed 300 lbs. overweight. We were able to taxi into the ramp and shutdown and safely exited the airplane. We followed checklist and [Company] SOP.
ASRS:1784664.s: During initial climb, the crew encountered smoke and heat in the cabin originating from a rear right wall panel. After resetting bleed valves and turning off fans failed to clear the smoke, the pilot returned to ZZZ and landed 300 lbs overweight to ensure a safe shutdown.

ASRS:1784672.n: On a flight to LAX, after being cleared for the approach for Runway 25L around 9 DME our aircraft was snapped hard to the right due to wake turbulence from a preceding MD11. Continuous turbulence, crew climbed above glide path & a dot off of localizer to the right primarily due to the direction the wake snapped us. A B-737 was on the approach for [Runway] 25R. They were in sight the entire time. Crew corrected back on course. Crew stayed high on glide slope, at 100 ft. some turbulence was encountered. There was no wind during the entire approach. On approach (estimate 2500 ft. MSL) above clouds we encountered wake turbulence from a 'heavy' aircraft landing ahead of us. Aircraft was properly configured for landing and on profile. Wings rocked left and then right by 15 degrees or so, but rapidly. I recall that we exited the turbulence in a right bank and held a course perhaps 5 to 10 degrees right of course as we both acknowledged verbally what had happened. I called Tower and advised them we had experienced wake turbulence. ATC responded by asking our intentions and I responded that we were deviating right. ATC responded not to deviate right. Both PF (Pilot Flying) and I saw an aircraft to our right, presumably on parallel approach. We maintained visual separation from it and the PF returned to the LOC centerline, now maintaining a profile slightly higher than GS. We continued the approach and landed without further incident. Our flight up to this point had been characterized by light to moderate turbulence along the majority of our route, resulting in many altitude changes in attempt to find smoother air for our passengers. The flight itself was fatiguing.I have to admit that I was anticipating the end of the flight and was not properly considering contingencies for wake turbulence. Proper SA (Situational Awareness) would have led me to help the PF out by suggesting that he climb, or deviate left rather than right. I also think that we as a crew need to include wake turbulence in any approach briefing at airports where heavies are operating, and where parallel approaches are in progress.
ASRS:1784672.s: The flight crew encountered wake turbulence from a preceding MD-11 during the LAX Runway 25L approach, causing a hard right snap and deviation. The crew corrected course, maintained visual separation from a parallel B-737, and landed safely, though the pilot attributed the initial deviation to poor situational awareness.

ASRS:1784688.n: At [Gate] at ZZZ, the First Officer said he saw [Package] near the aircraft, I had just received the cargo load report, so I asked the tug driver over the headset if [Package] was loaded onto the aircraft, he said he would double check and asked someone. He got back to us with that there was no [Package] onboard. I also specifically asked about the presence of dry ice (Dangerous Goods), and the answer I got was that there was not. So neither of those were marked on the cargo load sheet, and neither were onboard according the verbal response I received. I assumed it was coming off our aircraft from the previous flight or destined for another flight. The First Officer during the post flight at [Gate1] at ZZZ1 saw [Package] in our cargo compartment waiting to be unloaded. I do not know if there was any dry ice with it.
ASRS:1784688.s: The Captain and First Officer at ZZZ received verbal confirmation that a specific package and dry ice were not loaded, despite the package being seen near the aircraft. Post-flight at ZZZ1, the First Officer discovered the package in the cargo compartment, indicating a discrepancy between the load report and actual cargo.

ASRS:1784690.n: I was notified of my reserve assignment at XA:00 by Crew Scheduling. They stated when they called me to pack a bag because I might not be home as the airplane we were to repo back to ZZZ was still broken. They assigned me a XB:00 showtime on the phone. I however noticed later my show time was modified to XC:00. Either way I arrived at the airport and sat down at the gate that was on my schedule. The First Officer texted me and stated the hotel van was just pulling up. At XC:00 when no gate agent was around the gate area at [Gate] I called my Dispatcher at [the] desk. I asked if he could get someone to let us down to the plane. After placing me on hold he stated we would be originating from the maintenance hangar. He asked the maintenance department where we needed to go to be picked up. They stated [Gate1]. He then started to fill me in that we would be hauling two mechanics, their tools and few other miscellaneous items. We met the maintenance personnel at [Gate1] and was transported to the airplane near the maintenance hangar. Upon arriving we noticed a 5 gallon bucket of Skydrol hydraulic fluid in front of the airplane along with what appeared to be a hydraulic pump and some hoses that were located in an open top box. The maintenance personnel stated that Maintenance Control okayed this being transported onboard the airplane. The FO (First Officer) went up to the flight deck and stowed her bags. I called the pilot on duty to get some direction on this 5 gallon container and was also hoping he could put me in touch with the hazardous materials specialist. The pilot on duty tracked him down and he okayed it based on being less than 5 gallons and it was in a sealed container. The box with the pump, hoses and other miscellaneous items was also OK. I question that now based on the [Operations Manual]. The last bullet point is my question. While I was inspecting the cabin's emergency equipment the FO notified me that the maintenance personnel stated that there was a substantial amount of items loaded in the forward cargo bay accumulating to about 300 lbs. I asked if they had a CLR or if the items happened to get weighed as they went on. The answer was they did not and someone was going to come out with a scale to unload and weigh the items. I called the pilot on duty to confirm needing this information on a CLR. FOM 12.6.11 Note D. The maintenance personnel did provide a paper CLR after unloading and reloading the cargo bay. During this time the 5 gallons of Skydrol was brought into the cabin and placed between two first class seats. The box with the pump also was. I called the scheduling and asked to speak to the manager on duty. I was connected. After explaining the situation to him he stated he would call me back. The maintenance personnel placed the Skydrol in a first class seat and placed a seatbelt around the container. Sometime after this they place an orange ratchet strap around this bucket also. After some time Scheduling Duty Officer [SDO] called me back. At this time Maintenance removed the Skydrol and the pump from the aircraft and stated we would be going without it. He stated they would remove it and place it below and secure it. He instructed us not to leave if it was placed below and not secured. At some point after this call with SDO crew scheduling called me questioning where I was at and why we have not departed yet. I explained to them we were on the airplane and attempting to safely depart after everything was in order. I called the Dispatcher and inquired about a new release because our release was timing out. We decided to add fuel to the airplane at that time because the APU has been running for along time now. While waiting for the fuel truck to arrive the maintenance personnel drove back up to the plane and loaded the Skydrol and the pump into the forward cargo bay. I went to look at how these items were secured. They were just sitting in boxes and not secured. I took a few pictures to send to SDO and the maintenance personnel asked me if this was OK. I stated I was told it had to be secured and that I was send this pictures to my manager. The maintenance personnel stated they would remove it from the plane and we could depart. The items were removed. While waiting for the fuel truck we also inquired with scheduling on what hotel we would be staying at in ZZZ1. They stated that we would be flying back because the 14 hours from our reserve availability period only was restricted to passenger flying and since this was Part 91 flying we were good for 16 hours. We were told we would have to call off if we didn't want to work the flight back. The fuel truck arrived and we departed soon after. The remainder of the flight was uneventful. We concluded the flight in ZZZ1 at XD:00. We were sent to the hotel and was scheduled for a min rest overnight. We called when we reached the hotel and had the show time adjusted to allow us 10 hours.
ASRS:1784690.s: The Captain reported that maintenance personnel loaded unsecured Skydrol and equipment into the cabin and cargo hold of a Part 91 ferry flight. After the crew intervened to ensure proper securing and documentation, the items were removed, and the flight departed uneventfully to ZZZ1.

ASRS:1784716.n: I was given the SID and cleared to FL150. During the initial climb, I had a Trim Runaway and I tried resetting the autopilot but it happened again. In terms of my GPS issues it was not responding to my inputs. So by me dealing with that and I got behind the aircraft and violated my altitude and heading. On the climb on the departure I believe I had asked ATC for Direct to Destination but I was given a heading instead. On the trim runaway it pitches the nose of the aircraft down, so I had to disconnect the autopilot etc. And long with trying to handle the trim runaway and disconnecting the autopilot and I made the deviations. Also, while being vectored to ZZZ, Center notified me that the weather had dropped there and there were airplanes holding so at that point I decided to go to ZZZ1. However, I was being vectored around a bit, so at that point I decided to land at ZZZ2 as it was right of me about 10 miles. So as to obtain fuel, as I had to take off with minimum fuel as possible in order to meet the climb gradients. My apologies. I should have notified ATC of my Trim issue and GPS issues sooner. This was my first time flying into ZZZ3. In terms of learning from this incident - I should have had another Pilot with me instead of Single Pilot operation into a challenging airport such as ZZZ3.
ASRS:1784716.s: A single pilot experienced a trim runaway and GPS failure during initial climb after departure, causing altitude and heading deviations while handling the emergency. The pilot subsequently diverted to an alternate airport due to weather and fuel constraints, acknowledging that earlier notification of the issues and a second crew member would have improved safety.

ASRS:1784740.n: On taxi out to Runway 34 at BGM airport there was blowing snow bringing the visibility down to almost 0. The only taxiway sign for taxiway L (Lima) was obscured. The yellow directional markings on ground were covered with snow. We missed the taxiway and slid off ramp just west of taxiway Lima(L). No injuries but substantial damage to nose gear. Began taxi from ramp between Taxiways M and L. While taxiing parallel to Bravo PF (pilot flying) called for taxi checklist. PM (pilot monitoring) head was down for a brief period while doing taxi checks. When PM looked up he told PF that something looked wrong about the aircraft position. Almost immediately the aircraft entered the grass on the east side of Lima. PF attempted to continue through grass to Bravo and the Aircraft dropped into a snow obscured swale and came to a stop. Aircraft secured and evacuated. 2 crew and 2 passengers on board. No injuries.
ASRS:1784740.s: A crew of two and two passengers on a taxiing aircraft at BGM airport slid off the ramp and into a snow-obscured swale due to blowing snow, obscured signage, and ground markings. The incident caused substantial nose gear damage but resulted in no injuries.

ASRS:1784744.n: While in initial climb through 5,000 ft. my passenger detected smoke in the cockpit. I confirmed the smoke in the cockpit. I did not know the exact source. We were 6 miles north of ZZZ. I [advised] ATC. They offered me runway XXR at ZZZ and I acknowledged. I shut down my electrical system and was unable to communicate with ATC after that transmission. I landed safely and taxied to the ramp.
ASRS:1784744.s: During initial climb through 5,000 ft, the pilot detected smoke in the cockpit and advised ATC while 6 miles north of ZZZ. After shutting down the electrical system, communication was lost, but the pilot landed safely and taxied to the ramp.

ASRS:1784748.n: Flying C172 on an IFR flight from ZZZ to ZZZ. Was flying a RNAV approach to ZZZ. Soon after hand off to ZZZ Approach, I disconnected the autopilot when the aircraft was at about 4,000 feet AGL. At that time ATC advised to turn left to 220 heading to intercept initial approach fix. Right after disconnecting the auto pilot, the aircraft banked left steeply to about 60 degrees roll and started descending while the ATC keep advising to turn left and cleared me for the RNAV approach. The conditions were IMC and aircraft was hard to control. It took a few minutes to get the aircraft under control. The ATC workload obviously increased while not knowing the exact situation and even doubted at one point if the pilot (me) was IFR rated and current. Once I was finally able to get the aircraft stabilized, I informed ATC that I was having trouble with the controls and apologized. The flight ended safely after all at ZZZ. The probable cause was having an iPad mounted on the yoke. Will never mount the iPad on the yoke again.
ASRS:1784748.s: A C172 pilot flying an IFR RNAV approach in IMC lost control after disconnecting the autopilot at 4,000 feet AGL, causing a steep 60-degree bank and descent. The incident was caused by an iPad mounted on the yoke interfering with controls, though the flight ended safely after stabilization.

ASRS:1784767.n: I wish to report a near mid-air collision. We were operating Aircraft X, ZZZ-ZZZ1, on a 737-900ER. The FO (First Officer) was the PF (Pilot Flying). I was the PM (Pilot Monitoring). Our IFR clearance was [SID]. Upon takeoff clearance from Runway XXR, we were given a heading of 290 with a initial climb limit of 3,000 [feet]. We received no notification of any traffic that we should be looking for upon takeoff clearance or during our initial climbout. As we were climbing out and cleaning up the aircraft, we received a TA at out 1 to 2 o'clock and high. I stopped my PM duties to search for source of the TA. As I searched, we got the altitude alert for the level off. I found the aircraft. He was not moving in relationship to our direction of travel. I told the PF to stop his climb. As I was saying that, we received the RA. The PF lowered the nose the slow the climb, as he was doing that the TCAS annunciated 'monitor vertical speed.' I glanced at the MFD to see the aircraft was only +200 feet above us. I was still on the 5 mile range and the symbol was inside the 2.5 mile tick mark at our 1 o'clock. The PF executed the RA escape maneuver to comply with the RA. I then told ZZZ Departure that I had the GA aircraft in sight, as we still hadn't been given any traffic alerts. The TCAS announced 'clear of conflict' and we resumed the climb uneventfully. Aircraft X, ZZZ-ZZZ1 I was the PF (Pilot Flying). Our clearance was [SID]...off Runway XXR heading of 290 with a initial climb limit of 3,000 [feet]. We received a TA at about 2,200 [feet]. There was an aircraft approximately 2,500 feet. No notification from ATC about the traffic. TCAS told us monitor our vertical speed which I did. I performed an RA escape maneuver and TCAS said clear of conflict. We notified approach about the traffic and TCAS RA. It seemed as if there was something going on at ZZZ or surrounding airport with an emergency at the time...rest of the trip was without incident.
ASRS:1784767.s: Pilots of a 737-900ER experienced a near mid-air collision during initial climb after receiving no traffic advisories from ATC. A TCAS Resolution Advisory was triggered by a general aviation aircraft 200 feet above, prompting an escape maneuver that resolved the conflict.

ASRS:1784768.n: For the ILS Runway 04R at ZZZ, performance numbers were run for a Flaps 30 landing with a good stopping margin at Autobrakes 3. ATIS winds were calling approximately 070/13 - no gusts. Upon switching to Tower at ZZZZZ on the localizer course and tracking the glideslope, Tower cleared us to land with winds now gusting to 20. As PF (Pilot Flying), I elected to add 4 knots to the Vtarget and as an added Safety measure at ZZZ, I selected Autobrakes MAX to compensate for a slightly increased approach speed. The PM (Pilot Monitoring) attempted to quickly re-run the performance data, but the gusts were not yet accounted for in the METAR. Rather than going heads down any longer inside 1,000 feet AGL, we agreed a 4-5 knot addition to VTarget and using Autobrakes MAX would be more than sufficient to account for the gust factor.At approximately 500 feet AGL, we received a GPWS Too Low Flaps Alert. The PM immediately called for the go-around and it was initiated. A quick scan of the flap handle and I realized that I had neglected to call for Flaps 30 from a Flaps 15 setting, and the Before Landing Checklist was not run. We were quickly vectored around for another uneventful ILS. The minor distraction of adding a gust factor and changing the Autobrakes setting sent me out of a normal approach configuration sequence and we ended up both missing the final flap setting and subsequent checklist.With the normal ZZZ procedure of not contacting (and often not switching to) Tower until reaching the fix at about a 5-mile final, it's possible for us to miss out on cues to changing weather on the ground. We were number 3 or 4 in a sequence of landings on 04R. Had we switched to Tower five or more miles sooner, we may have caught the gusting winds earlier and had more time to type in the adjusted winds and send away for the performance numbers prior to 1,000 feet AGL. This was another series of events combined with mild fatigue that led to poor task prioritization on our parts. The short version is that we got 'Too Low, Flaps' at 500 feet because we were at Flaps 15. We went around. Planned winds were 070/7. Tower winds were 070/12G20. I re-ran the performance landing numbers at 1,500 feet, but did not override the METAR and got back the numbers for 070/7. The PF (Pilot Flying) chose to add 5 knots to VTarget and we agreed to go from Medium to Max braking and continue.There is no guidance I am aware of as to when we would be required to re-run our landing numbers. I should not have tried to re-run the landing numbers at that point. That would have eliminated the distraction that led to not selecting our planned final flaps or running the Before Landing Checklist.
ASRS:1784768.s: The flight crew missed the Flaps 30 setting and Before Landing Checklist during an ILS approach to Runway 04R due to distraction from adjusting for gusty winds. This resulted in a GPWS "Too Low Flaps" alert at 500 feet AGL, prompting a go-around.

ASRS:1784771.n: Over last few days, there is indication that certain aviation companies are looking into making the COVID vaccine mandatory for their employees. I strongly believe that this is a potential security risk, due to the fact that if an individual is forced to do something against their will, they might fight back. In the aviation industry, as history has shown so well, there is a strong possibility that airplane safety might be compromised, especially by individuals that have direct access to the unsecured aircraft, such as gate agents, operations personnel, mechanics, and ground handlers.Due to the significant safety concerns, I strongly urge the FAA to prohibit mandatory vaccinations.
ASRS:1784771.s: The reporter, concerned about potential security risks, argues that mandatory COVID-19 vaccinations for aviation employees could lead to safety compromises by disgruntled staff with access to unsecured aircraft. They urge the FAA to prohibit such mandates to prevent individuals from fighting back against forced compliance.

ASRS:1784779.n: With about 4 hours to go before landing, I had just emerged from the crew rest bunk when Lead Flight Attendant asked me if I could have the flight deck crew wear a face mask when a Flight Attendant was in the cockpit in flight. I told her no for the safety of flight reasons. I did not add anything further.I personally was not going to wear a face mask in the cockpit since I would be in the cockpit for the rest of the flight. I am required by the FAA on my medical 'Must wear corrective lenses, possess glasses for near/intermediate vision.' Since my glasses fog up every time I wear any type of face mask I know that wearing a mask at my flight deck seat is a safety of flight issue. About two hours later when the Lead came to in to give us a restroom break we, First Officer and I, offered her an N95 mask to wear for her safety and set it on the pedestal for her. She did not put it on and chose to wear what appeared to be a non-N95 certified black cloth mask.
ASRS:1784779.s: During cruise, a pilot refused the Lead Flight Attendant's request for flight deck crew to wear face masks, citing safety concerns regarding fogged corrective lenses. The crew later offered the Lead an N95 mask, which she declined in favor of a non-certified cloth mask.

ASRS:1784792.n: While in line for takeoff on Taxiway for XXR, we received a notification from the flight attendants that the cabin was filling up with smoke which was coupled with a foul odor akin to burning rubber. We smelled the odor at the same time the flight attendants notified us of the smoke. I asked them if it was thick enough to block view of the back of the aircraft and if they thought we needed to evacuate right away. They answered no to both questions. I then told them that we would be moving to a cargo ramp to run a QRH and if they thought at any point we would need to evacuate while moving to call me back and we would stop immediately. I also informed them that the next time we stopped would be the last time we would move without calling them and that once stopped, if they felt the need to evacuate, they were to do it. We taxied to the cargo ramp just south of taxiway after alerting ATC that we were [requesting priority handling] and would be pulling off to the side to run a QRH and to have the fire trucks standby. We ran the entirety of the smoke fire fumes QRH, which had us deactivate the PACs (Air Conditioning Packs) and close the bleed valves. We elected to not drop pass O2 or go on O2 ourselves as we were not having any adverse reactions, but just dealing with an unpleasant smell in the flight deck. We called the flight attendants at this time and asked about the passengers' condition and they stated that everyone was fine. The smoke slowly dissipated throughout the rest of the event. At this point, we decided to go back to the gate as the smoke was no longer producing from the vents and the passengers were not complaining about any issues when asked. We cancelled [priority handling] but requested that crash rescue follow us to the gate. Once arriving at the gate with the aircraft shut down and the flight deck door open and main cabin door, we had one woman reportedly having bronchitis coughing to a large extent. She was the first off. I was not aware she had an adverse reaction until pulling into the gate. We deplaned everyone as quickly as possible and had Maintenance confirm that PAC 2 was the culprit. To my knowledge, all passengers refused medical attention. We later got another aircraft and had all passengers board.The probable cause was something happened with the Right PAC as we were single engine no APU taxiing to XXR with Engine 2 running.
ASRS:1784792.s: The flight crew and cabin crew experienced smoke and a burning rubber odor while taxiing for takeoff on a single-engine taxi with Engine 2 running. Maintenance identified the Right Air Conditioning Pack as the cause after the crew executed the smoke QRH, diverted to a cargo ramp, and returned to the gate for deplaning.

ASRS:1784801.n: TCAS RA on arrival into ZZZ [airport]. Assigned descent to 7,000 feet and vectors to final by ZZZ Approach. We reached 7,000 feet and noted approach was extremely busy where the Controller was being stepped on seemingly more than half of her transmissions. While level at 7,000 feet the TCAS noted a proximate target converging from 1 o'clock, 400 feet below. We attempted to contact Approach but there was zero opportunity to get a word in due to the sheer amount of communication on frequency. I advised the Captain PF to 'get ready' while we attempted to locate the aircraft visually. A few seconds later the TCAS noted traffic and ordered a very shallow climb. I announced to ZZZ Approach that we were responding to an RA, but I believe I was blocked, the frequency still jammed with constant communication. A very short time later the controller issued traffic to us and I again advised 'Climbing on RA.' Controller replied 'Roger' I believe and the event was over shortly after. We returned to 7,000 feet and were vectored for the visual, but the controller still had to vector us around multiple VFR targets on our way to the runway. Most significantly we were cleared for the visual approach, but were restricted to flying and intercepting between 5 and 7 NM from the airport due to area traffic. This caused a perceived limitation that pilots are not used to. The CA/PF then overflew the Localizer slightly attempting to maintain these limitations. The aircraft was clearly stable by 1000 feet and we continued in to land, but this was following an incident due to the same cause.Cause was due to the intense level of traffic in ZZZ Approach's airspace. I spoke with a contact at ZZZ [Approach] later who noted the Controller had 15 active aircraft not including the VFR targets attempting to get clearance from the closed airspace, Practice IFR traffic, and VFR flight following requests. The Controller was doing an excellent job and maintained a very professional demeanor throughout. There was just no reasonable way for Controller to maintain communications with the volume of aircraft. I am not sure, but this could have been a result of reduced staffing due to COVID. Maybe there was an East and West ZZZ [Approach] sector available, but no staffing to accommodate. My suggestions would be to either split ZZZ Approach or to draw a new arrival for ZZZ airport to reduce the amount of communications and possible routes needed for the controllers.
ASRS:1784801.s: During arrival into ZZZ, the crew received a TCAS RA while level at 7,000 feet due to a converging target. The incident was caused by excessive traffic volume and frequency congestion, which prevented timely communication with the controller managing 15 active aircraft.

ASRS:1784811.n: Flew ZONNA1 arrival to TUS. I was PF (Pilot Flying) and did the arrival briefing prior to descent which included terrain hazards and the MSA. Both pilots had terrain selected. Approach control gave us a clearance to turn right to 270 and descend to 10,000' for sequencing. Soon after this clearance we entered IMC. Passing north and abeam Mt Lemmon at about 10,300', we got an EGPWS TERRAIN PULL UP warning. I executed the EGPWS Recovery Action. Almost immediately we went VMC. After passing the MSA of 10,700 and visually verifying terrain clearance, I resumed normal flight, leveled at 11,000' and informed ATC that we had responded to a GPWS terrain warning. They acknowledged and gave us a descent to 9000'. Remainder of flight was uneventful.Either the Terrain system gave us a false alert or we were given a clearance to descend below the radar minimum altitude. We never got any indication on the Terrain display. STAR page showed us north of Mt Lemmon and the terrain depicted around it. While we had good terrain awareness, I should have queried Approach about an IMC descent below the Sector MSA.I recommend a Radar Minimum Altitudes chart be included in the Jeppesen pages for TUS.
ASRS:1784811.s: The Pilot Flying received a GPWS terrain warning while descending to 10,000' in IMC during the ZONNA1 arrival to TUS. The crew executed a recovery, and the pilot attributed the event to either a false alert or a clearance below the Minimum Sector Altitude.

ASRS:1784836.n: ATC turned us onto the approach while still at 4,000. Told us to 'maintain 3,000 till established cleared ILS [Runway] XXL. FO (First Officer) put in 3,000 in the altitude selector and I acknowledged it. Once established, instead of selecting 2,700 feet for the FAF altitude he rolled the altitude selector to 3,300 and started a slow descent. Stated he was going to just control the altitude himself. I thought that was strange, but let him do it figuring it was just a technique he liked to do.As we approached 2,700 feet, he was still descending at ~700 FPM, so I realized he was going to blow through the altitude. I told him he needed to stop descending and return to the FAF altitude until we intercepted the GS. The first time I said this he seemed confused and didn't really do much. I said more sternly that we needed to climb back to the proper altitude. This time he initiated a climb back to the proper altitude and we were still stabilized and fully configured by 1,000 feet AGL. ATC did issue us a low altitude alert as we were climbing back to the proper altitude and we got a single 'Glideslope' callout from the aircraft.The cause was the FO's improper use of the altitude selector and VS (Vertical Speed) mode. Contributing was me allowing him to do the method he did instead of asking him to just put the FAF altitude in the altitude selector till GS intercept.I should have insisted that the FO put the FAF altitude in the altitude selector, especially in IMC. I also told him afterword's that he could have just stayed at 3,000 once established and intercepted the GS from there since at that point we were already close to GS intercept. Cleared ILS [Runway] XXL, we were given an intercept heading and told to maintain 3,000 feet. The Controller kept us close and fairly high before clearing us for the approach. We were at 4,000 feet when cleared. Captain was PM (Pilot Monitoring), First Officer was PF (Pilot Flying). Once established, PF started down with vertical speed to capture glide slope by 2,700 feet at ZZZZZ. PF moved altitude knob up to 3,300 feet from 3,000 feet instead of to 2,700 feet causing us to go below published altitude by almost 500 feet. Was immediately corrected and aircraft was stabilized. Given a close proximity intercept, task saturation was high with intercepting, radio communications, and configuring aircraft. Should have cross checked better and stated intentions more clearly (PF to PM).If crew starts to feel rushed or task saturation is high, ask for longer final or a more stable intercept from ATC. Never let cross checking suffer due to task saturation, should always come first. PM should state approach intention more clearly while getting established. Don't have tunnel vision (Example Focusing on getting configured and not having correct altitude set).
ASRS:1784836.s: During an ILS approach in IMC, the First Officer incorrectly set the altitude selector to 3,300 feet instead of 2,700 feet, causing a descent below the published altitude. The Captain corrected the error after a low altitude alert, attributing the incident to improper mode selection and task saturation.

ASRS:1784841.n: Operating flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1. After landing on Runway XX, exited on Taxiway A and turned left on Taxiway C, and believing that Tower had actually cleared us to taxi to the gate, we started to slowly taxi, when Tower called us and asked that we call Ground. We called Ground and he stated 'You started to taxi without calling us, and crossed Runway XX, which is an active runway'. We had barely started to taxi on C. We had read the NOTAMs, and in fact, Runway XX was 'NOTAMed CLOSED', so it could not be an 'Active' at all. Regardless, we asked Ground for taxi clearance to the gate, and received clearance to the gate via 'C.' We did not want to argue with the Ground Controller, but we do know that Runway XX is Closed at ZZZ1, so it's not Active in any way. We asked the Ground Controller if we should 'expect any paperwork', and he said 'no'. I do not believe we did anything wrong, but it's better to be safe and proactive, and learn from our possible mistakes.We had flown into ZZZ1 previously (a few days before) and due to controller shortages or consolidation of ATC positions (During COVID-19 times), the Tower normally gives us the taxi instruction after we cleared the landing runway. This time, we cleared the runway and thought we had heard the Tower tell us to 'taxi to the gate' (as they have been doing recently). We started to slowly taxi on Taxiway C and that's when Tower asked us to 'call ground for taxi;' something they had not done in the past 3-6 times we had landed there recently. So, probably I was expecting the same ATC procedures to happen, but regardless, in the future, will come to a stop on the taxiway and not move until further taxi clearance is received.I would suggest to avoid being complacent, and instead of expecting the same type of ATC handling from small airports as we may be getting every day during COVID-19 (combined controller positions, where there is perhaps combined Tower and Ground, or even Approach/Tower/Ground Controller), and instead treat it just like a busy airport.
ASRS:1784841.s: The flight crew inadvertently began taxiing on Taxiway C at ZZZ1 without Ground clearance, believing Tower had authorized gate movement based on recent combined-controller procedures. Ground controllers reported the crew crossed active Runway XX, though the crew noted the runway was NOTAMed closed and no paperwork was issued.

ASRS:1784887.n: Aircraft X was assigned to the hangar midnight crew for the 'A' check. The first contact that technicians had with the aircraft occurred at approximately XA00 local time. Avionics technicians, including myself, began the night with completing operational checks within the aircraft in preparation for the rest of the crew to perform their assigned tasks. Later technicians began to migrate in and out of the flight deck, cabin, galleys, lavs, etc., to their assigned tasks. All technicians were in compliance with the mask policy.Approximately 4 hours later, the Lead Technician and Supervisor alerted everyone on board that the aircraft had not gone through its disinfecting process which usually occurs at the gate upon arrival. The aircraft was cleared and the Lead performed the disinfecting procedures.Concerns were raised from this event. The potential of an infected passenger being on board and the potential of technicians being exposed to COVID.The protocol for traveling to ZZZ is to have a COVID test within an XX hour period of departure time. However, once you are tested there are no guarantees that the individual will quarantine or shelter in place prior to boarding the aircraft for departure. The cleaners finally arrived for the disinfecting process at midnight. I asked the supervisor what the protocol is for an event such as this and he was unaware of one in place.This aircraft originated from ZZZ1.
ASRS:1784887.s: Avionics technicians working on Aircraft X during an 'A' check discovered the aircraft had not been disinfected after arriving from ZZZ1. The Lead Technician performed disinfection procedures, raising concerns about potential COVID-19 exposure due to the lack of a defined protocol for such events.

ASRS:1784889.n: I returned to work after a 3 month absence. I am still qualified on the module. I was assigned as the trainer to Mechanic Y. I was training him on the stator case assembly. I demonstrated how to tighten each vane segment foot bolts. The procedure that I was taught, and which had been in use as long as I can remember, was to slide the case and vane assembly, so that approximately one third of it overhung the table surface. Then the bolts were tightened from below with a ratchet with a socket and long extension, repositioning the case and vane assembly as necessary until all bolts were tightened. At the time of the incident, I was not in the work area, having gone to the restroom.Support the case with a hoist and sling before tightening the bolts. This should be added to the job card. One week after return from 3 months off and being the first time working on this unit as a trainee.On Graveyard shift I was working on the module and order # XXXX. I was tightening the bolts of the vanes. The bolts are tighten from the bottom while the case sits on the table. To access the bolts part of the case is moved slightly beyond the edge of the table. I was sitting in a chair with rollers while I was tightening the bolts. The chair moved, the wrench and its extension did come off the bolt head causing the case to slide off the table and fall to the floor approximately 30 inches.There was no visible damage to the case because it fell directly on my arm and that cushioned the fall. Inspection will be called to inspect the unit.I would add to the job card to support the case with a hoist before tightening the bolts. Or developing a fixture that would allow to reach the bolts from the bottom without having to move part of the case off the edge of the table.
ASRS:1784889.s: A trainee mechanic and trainer were involved in a stator case assembly incident during the graveyard shift. The case fell 30 inches when the trainee's rolling chair moved, causing the wrench to slip; the trainer's arm cushioned the fall, preventing visible damage to the unit.

ASRS:1784890.n: I was performing a functional test of the stall protection computer. On step XX, the task tells you to put the aircraft in the weight off wheels configuration. On the first page of the task for putting the aircraft in the weight off wheel configuration you are told to pull and tag Circuit Breakers (CB): CB P-1, A12, A13, A14, G14, & CB P-1 lower U7. On the second page to pull and tag CB P-1 lower T7, T8, T9, CB P2, N6, H8, CB P2 lower S1, V5 and CB P-5, B10.I pulled the circuit breaker on the first page but failed to pull the circuit breakers on the second page of the task. On the next step on the functional test of the stall protection computer you are told to set the air data test set to 90 kts and the altitude to 18,000 feet. During this step is when we noticed smoke coming from the left pitot probe. I ran out to check the pitot probe and saw that I melted the pitot probe test head to the pitot probe. I quickly removed heat from the pitot probe.To pay more attention to the Aircraft Maintenance Manual and to double check all the correct circuit breakers are pulled. While performing a functional check of stall protection system we were required to put aircraft in weight off wheels and put aircraft at 18,000 feet and 90 kts using pitot static test set. During the test, the test head on the LH (Left Hand) pitot static probe was melted to the probe.While performing the test I looked up and saw smoke coming from LH side of nose.My partner found the task in the AMM (Aircraft Maintenance Manual) and pulled breakers but failed to read far enough down and only pulled the breakers for the RH pitot static probe. Causing the heat to still be on to the LH probe.We quickly removed heat from probe.Pay more attention to AMM task and I should have double checked the CBs my partner pulled.
ASRS:1784890.s: During a stall protection computer functional test, a mechanic failed to pull all required circuit breakers, leaving heat on the left pitot probe. This caused the test head to melt to the probe and produce smoke when the test set was configured for 18,000 feet and 90 knots.

ASRS:1784899.n: While descending into LRU airport, I heard ATC call to another aircraft (Aircraft Y) that was also inbound. I was arriving from the west, and Aircraft Y from the north, North West area. I could see him on ADS-B. While Aircraft Y was behind me, he was much faster, however ABQ (Albuquerque) center had him climb and then hold as I continued my descent. Leveling off at my assigned altitude, I was still unable to see the airfield, despite the field reports of better weather. I was, however, still several miles away. At about the same time, Aircraft Y called in, cancelling his IFR stating that he had the airport in sight. ATC cancelled his IFR as he stated he was now in VMC. I then asked ATC for a report from the Aircraft Y, as he was able to see the field and I was not, despite me being at a lower altitude. (I asked hoping I would break out of the clouds soon, or find an area where I could, such as where Aircraft Y came from). Quickly after, I did get the airport insight below me and was able to descend VFR. I also cancelled my IFR at that time.Being almost over the airport, I extended away from it and then I called entering the Left downwind for runway 26. (The winds at the time were reported as being 240 at 22 - 27, making runway 22 or 26 the best options.) I then called a base turn, and then final. At that time I also heard Aircraft Y call in for the RNAV for runway 12. Being as he cancelled IFR with no mention of practicing approaches, I anticipated his landing before me, with no conflict. As I came on short final for runway 26, I heard Aircraft Y call out that he was going missed from 12, which would then be intersecting my landing path. At that moment I looked up and saw Aircraft Y just ahead and to my right, above me, but very close. I would estimate within 200-300 feet. Already being close to the ground, no evasion action could have been taken. I landed and taxied into the ramp. Shortly after, Aircraft Y landed on a different runway and parked as well. I called the center to report the incident and express my concern and safety issue that had occurred.
ASRS:1784899.s: While descending into LRU, the pilot observed Aircraft Y executing a missed approach from Runway 12, which intersected the pilot's final approach to Runway 26. Aircraft Y passed within 200–300 feet above and to the right of the pilot's aircraft, leaving no time for evasive action before landing.

ASRS:1784901.n: I was cleared to transition underneath JFK's Class B Airspace, along the shoreline below 500 feet. while flying a westerly heading, I encountered wake turbulence from a plane landing on Runway 04R. Roughly 30 seconds before the encounter, I was cleared to climb, not leaving me adequate time to climb above the turbulence. The wake we experienced was stronger than expected. It shook our plane and dislodged the battery onboard my aircraft. I first noticed the acidic smell and shortly after observed smoke in the cockpit. I decided that I would need to land the plane immediately at JFK. After contacting Kennedy Tower, I got clearance to land on [Runway] 13R. Once acknowledging my clearance, I informed the Tower that I was shutting down my battery to prevent the fire from expanding and that we may lose further communication. We made a safe return to the airport and I stopped the plane on Taxiway P. I shut the motor down and deplaned my passengers. [Ground personnel] put out the fire and towed the plane to the FBO. Both myself and my passengers were evaluated by medical staff and were thankfully unscathed.
ASRS:1784901.s: The pilot encountered unexpected wake turbulence while transitioning below 500 feet near JFK, which dislodged the battery and caused smoke. The pilot executed an immediate landing on Runway 13R, shut down the battery, and evacuated safely after ground personnel extinguished the fire.

ASRS:1784902.n: With a pre-checkride PPL (Private Pilot License) student, we were discussing pre-takeoff briefings and engine out after takeoff procedures. For our flight that day, I decided it would be good practical experience to get the student thinking about emergency landing options after an engine failure on takeoff. I believed it would be beneficial to see in reality what the landing options would look like with engine loss shortly after takeoff.The student performed a normal takeoff. Shortly after handoff from Tower Controller to Departure Controller (estimated 550 [feet.] AGL), I reduced the throttle to idle and instructed the student to pitch for best glide. I asked the student where an attempted landing might be possible based on our altitude and glide. I then asked if a 180 degree turn back to the departure runway seemed possible. After asking these two questions, I pushed the throttle back to full power and resumed normal climb. We continued to discuss procedures for engine failure on takeoff.Shortly after this, I noticed that our heading had deviated from the assigned runway heading by about 40 degrees to the south. Before I was able to correct, the Departure Controller assigned us an on-course heading. A few minutes later, Departure Controller asked if we had experienced an issue or needed assistance. I did not think much of it at the time and responded that we didn't need assistance.I later learned (from a phone call from Tower Controller to the flight school) that the Tower Controller had heard the engine power reduction and had seen the turn, and assumed an engine failure. I am not fully aware of what was experienced on the Tower Controller's end, but it is clear that my decision to practice an engine out procedure on takeoff caused a distraction to the Tower Controller that may have ended up impacting safety.Additionally, the fact that I did not notice the aircraft had turned 40 degrees to the south indicates that practicing that maneuver caused me to become more distracted that I had realized, or expected to be.Remedy:-Notify or request to Tower/ATC of my intention to practice any sort of maneuvers/procedures that are out of the ordinary from what is expected.-Be more aware of the probability of distraction while practicing any sort of maneuver during a high workload phase of flight.-Consider making engine out on takeoff procedures a ground instruction maneuver rather than in-flight.Human performance/Judgement:Ultimately, I made a bad judgement call by practicing an unusual/unexpected maneuver in controlled airspace. I did not expect or anticipate any disruption to the tower procedures, but I should have been more aware and given more thought to how my maneuvers would affect ATC.
ASRS:1784902.s: A flight instructor and PPL student simulated an engine failure at 550 feet AGL during takeoff in controlled airspace without notifying ATC. The maneuver caused the instructor to lose situational awareness regarding a 40-degree heading deviation and led the Tower Controller to mistakenly assume an actual emergency.

ASRS:1784925.n: I was working the entire area combined. The evening west departure push was going on along with other aircraft throughout the airspace. I was pretty busy on a small scale and multiple frequencies.I descended Aircraft X to 16,000 and verified he had the weather at ZZZ [airport] and what approach he wanted. I cleared him for the LOC/DME [Runway] XX at ZZZ [airport]. I started to hand the aircraft off to ZZZ [Approach] and took it back thinking ZZZ [Approach] had gone home for the evening and we had the airspace. Another Controller had sat down to help but didn't yet get a briefing. ZZZ [Approach] called to give up the airspace and I just went 'Crap.'Apparently Aircraft X had gone over to Approach on his own and the controller had been watching him.I made a mistake thinking it was later than it was and that ZZZ Approach had gone home for the night.Since the COVID started everything has been off. We are combine sectors too much and too early. The scale and number of frequencies we are required to work is not helpful. We get a lot of EA [Excused Absence] and are just not as proficient as we use to be. I would like to see sectors de combined more often or not combined as early. There are a few that push to combine and we just accept it and work through it. It is really not safe or comfortable to work. Mistakes are being made.
ASRS:1784925.s: An air traffic controller descended Aircraft X to 16,000 feet and cleared it for a LOC/DME approach at ZZZ airport. The controller mistakenly believed Approach had gone home and attempted to retain the aircraft, but the pilot had already transferred to Approach, an error attributed to sector combining and reduced proficiency.

ASRS:1784937.n: We taxied into ZZZ, Gate X, with both engines running. After shut down the F/O (First Officer) started to operate the AC (Air Conditioning) packs off the APU bleed. Immediately after the switch we smelled fumes and a slight haze/smoke was noticed the AC, we believed the source to be the packs so we shut down both packs and APU bleed and the fumes and haze started to dissipate. The jet way was already pulling up so after discussing with my F/A's (Flight Attendants) and F/O we decided a normal deplaning would be best.I made a PA and informed the passengers there was not an [urgent situation], and to deplane normally. After the aircraft was secure and checklist completed I asked Ramp to do a walk around then come to flight deck to inform me on anything suspicious that was discovered. I followed up with a walk around to look at packs for any noticeable damage or smell. The right pack had a hint of the suspicious smell left. We did not [request priority handling] because we believe we had identified and isolated the issue and at no time were flames observed just smell and slight smoke.
ASRS:1784937.s: The crew experienced fumes and slight smoke from the air conditioning packs after switching to APU bleed at the gate. They isolated the issue by shutting down the packs and APU, allowing for a normal deplaning with no flames observed.

ASRS:1784943.n: As I was leaving the flight deck approximately 6.5 hours into the flight for my break the Captain informed me the Purser had spoken to him about mask usage on the flight deck. Upon returning from my break I was informed there was further conversation with the flight attendants. Not much detail was discussed as we began the preparation for descent into ZZZ. I never spoke to any FAs about the issue nor did they speak to me about it.I am aware the Captain chose not to wear a mask for safety of flight reasons concerning his glasses while on the flight deck.
ASRS:1784943.s: A First Officer reported that the Captain declined to wear a mask on the flight deck due to safety concerns regarding his glasses, prompting a discussion between the Captain and the Purser. The First Officer was not involved in the conversation, and no further details were shared before the crew prepared for descent into ZZZ.

ASRS:1784952.n: I was deadheading on Aircraft X. I identified myself to the A Flight Attendant (FA) (as I always do) as a safety and security asset.The flight was nearly full. During boarding a man who I later learned was Mr. X approached my seat. He was wearing a camo gaiter around his neck which was partially covering his mouth but was not covering his nose. As he approached, I identified myself as a crew member and politely asked him to pull his mask up over his nose. He complied but said that I should pinch my mask tight over my nose. I didn't quite hear what he said so I queried him. He said, 'You should pinch down on your nose to close the gap at the top of your mask.' My mask was an NP95 which had no gaps anywhere around my face. It was my sense that the man was being sarcastic and antagonistic. I said nothing further to him.I advised the FA A what happened before we pushed back. She told me that the man had boarded without his face covered and was told to cover his face. Thus he had pulled his face covering off his face between the time he boarded (when he was told to put it on) and the time he approached me, which was no more than thirty seconds. He clearly had no intention of complying with the mask policy. FA A asked me to brief the Captain about the incident and asked if I would talk to the CSR agent whom she wanted to speak with Mr. X. I agreed. Before departure I walked into the jet bridge and spoke with FA A and the CSR. I briefly explained what I observed and what he said to me then I went back onto the airplane and took my seat. A short time later I observed Mr. X walk back down the aisle past me.Sometime during the flight FA A advised me that Mr. X had been [violating other regulations]. She advised me that Mr. X demanded to know the crews names (including mine) but that she did not give him any names. She was clearly concerned about this and I could see how his actions were distracting to the flight crew and were thus interfering with their duties. She told me that she was going to have CS meet the aircraft and asked me to stay as a witness. FA A as well as the rest of the inflight crew were nothing but polite and professional the entire flight, when I observed her dealing with Mr. X or otherwise.After leaving the aircraft I was standing in the jet bridge and spoke with a CS Supervisor. Mr. X walked by me and said in an aggressive and hostile tone, 'I want your name.' I told him that I could not give it to him and that I could not speak with him about this matter. He again demanded my name and moved closer to me. I backed up. He then raised his camera and said, 'I'm taking your picture.' I stated, 'Do not take my picture.' He said, I'm taking your picture.' I quickly turned around and walked around the jet bridge corner toward the aircraft door. I do not know if he took my photograph or not but felt that his forcing his camera in my face was one of belligerence, hostility, and aggression. I felt threatened. All of this simply because he was asked to properly wear his mask. After the CSR Supervisor and Mr. X walked into the terminal, I remained in the jet bridge as I did not want to encounter Mr. X again.When the CSR Supervisor walked back onto the jet bridge, I explained to her that I could not have my photograph taken and suggested that if he loitered around the terminal waiting for me that she please call law enforcement. I asked her if she felt he was being hostile and or belligerent. She agreed that he was. After some time, Mr. X left the area, and I departed the terminal.Based on his behavior and actions I would strongly urge that Mr. X is not allowed to fly on our airline in the future.
ASRS:1784952.s: A deadheading crew member on Aircraft X reported that passenger Mr. X became hostile after being asked to properly wear a mask, demanding the crew member's name and threatening to photograph them in the jet bridge. The crew member felt threatened by this aggressive behavior and recommended banning the passenger from future flights.

ASRS:1784953.n: The Lead Flight Attendant had apparently talked to the Captain or First Officer about masks. They said something to me about it after my break along the lines that she was upset and combative. I was surprised, as I wore my mask (a KN95 on the ground and a solid multi-layer cloth one in the air) all times outside of the flight deck and in the flight deck if a Flight Attendant was present. Additionally, the other First Officer did as well. The Captain wears glasses that fog easily with a mask on. He wore a mask on the ground, he did not airborne because it would greatly interfere with his duties both because he wouldn't be able to see and could not communicate. This was our 4th leg together and we had no issues with masks among ourselves or other flight attendants. Additionally, both the Captain and other First Officer already had COVID which they had gotten from people they knew at home, not in the workplace. Before our next rest room break I got out a new unused N95 mask for the Flight Attendant that would be in the flight deck while I was in the bathroom. When I called back and ask for the break she ordered me that the pilot remaining in the flight deck should wear the crew oxygen mask. I said that was not something that we did anymore-the practice stopped months ago because of COVID. I offered her the N95 for extra protection because the Captain can't wear a mask and do his job. She refused it. Instead continuing to wear what appeared to be a single layer stretchy black cloth mask. Additionally the flight attendant blocking the cart was wearing a KN95 but the Lead FA did not send her into the flight deck. I found the flight attendant to not be willing to exercise self-help and any wearing of an N95 and apparent multiple complaints to be a distraction from my flight duties. This was not good for crew CRM. While the single pilot on the flight deck, I was distracted from monitoring the airplane by her distress and complaints.
ASRS:1784953.s: A First Officer reported that a Lead Flight Attendant became combative over mask policies during a flight, refusing an offered N95 and demanding the sole pilot wear a crew oxygen mask. The pilot stated this distraction impaired monitoring duties and degraded crew resource management.

ASRS:1784955.n: We were met at the hotel by the van to be transported to ZZZZ [airport]. The driver wasn't wearing a mask when he loaded the bags. He finished loading and sat down in his seat without a mask. I said something to the effect of, 'You aren't wearing a mask?' He didn't really say anything. After a few seconds, I said, 'Since you aren't wearing a mask, we will need fresh air.' I assumed that after seeing the 4 pilots with masks on and me saying something, he would put his mask on. He never did.Instead, he started fumbling with the AC controls. I told him that without a mask, we would need the front windows opened in order to ensure ventilation in the van. He eventually complied. We then drove 30 minutes to ZZZZ with the windows open with the OAT ~ 34 degrees. We were freezing cold.We were all upset, cold, and potentially distracted for our flight. This is a safety of flight issue. We used our CRM skills to identify this threat and deal with it. But, the bottom line is that we shouldn't have had to deal with this easily avoidable threat in the first place.
ASRS:1784955.s: Four pilots reported a ground transport driver refused to wear a mask, forcing them to open van windows for ventilation in 34-degree weather. The resulting cold and distraction were identified as a safety of flight threat that required Crew Resource Management to mitigate.

ASRS:1784970.n: It wasn't supposed to be a very long leg or a long day. The plan was to fly from ZZZ to ZZZ1, grab a quick snack and go to ZZZ2 for the overnight and good food. But, that wasn't what happened. Snow flurries forced us into unplanned deicing. Bad alternates required reworking and refueling. In the middle of deicing, a sudden snow squall sent visibility plummeting and negating any holdover times. New takeoff alternates then had to be amended onto the paperwork, and re-validating required new paperwork. To describe our departure out of ZZZ as a struggle would be an understatement. But, ever so slowly and methodically, we did eventually depart to ZZZ1. It was on arrival that we were notified that our overnight had changed and to contact scheduling on the ground. So, you can imagine that when we landed in ZZZ1, we were mentally bruised, hungry, tired, and on edge. The landing was normal, as was the taxi to our planned gate. What confused us is what we saw upon turning to face south, looking at [Gate X]. There was nothing. No rampers, or wands or even lights. It was a completely empty and dark. I set the parking brake and asked my FO (First Officer) to send another in range report and commented that we should probably call ZZZ1 OPS and see if they had changed our gate. FO dutifully called OPS on the number two radio so I dialed the north ramp frequency into radio one to monitor. At that exact moment the ACARS message returned as my FO was repeating what OPS had just said, gate change to [Gate Y]! I released the parking brake and began a slow turn to the right when I realized I wasn't at an outstation in the middle of nowhere or on an uncontrolled ramp. I had lost all situational awareness and was in the middle of ZZZ1 moving without permission! I immediately stopped the aircraft and called North Ramp with the gate change. He replied yea there was a gate change and 'did i just do a 180?' I don't recall saying much before he asked 'and are you still moving???' I immediately replied we were not moving. At that point I was told I should never, ever do that and that he had numerous aircraft with beacons on trying to push. I should have apologized right then but instead fumbled though the gate change and having the pushing aircraft in sight. I still can't believe I would make such stupid mistake. I can't believe I didn't apologize. I was just beat up and wanting desperately to just take a five minute brake. Instead I let my guard and awareness down which led me to make a very stupid move.
ASRS:1784970.s: The fatigued flight crew at ZZZ1 lost situational awareness after a gate change notification and moved the aircraft without clearance while the First Officer contacted operations. The pilot stopped the aircraft after being alerted by North Ramp that they were moving in an active area with other aircraft pushing back.

ASRS:1784973.n: I was cleared on the RNAV departure to maintain 3,000 feet. When loading the departure an additional fix not noted on the chart was loaded in. I reloaded the departure to ensure I had the proper transition and the fix appeared again. This fix is not on the RNAV departure. I later realized that this is how the G1000 creates additional heading legs, but at the time I did not realize this and so I deleted the extraneous fix to have the flight plan reflect the proper departure. After reaching 1,000 feet the departure states to turn left heading 295, which I had briefed. I began turning right and was adjusting the heading bug and noted it was taking a long time to reach 295 before I realized that I was turning the wrong direction. I corrected and initiated the turn back to the left heading 295. I was about 20 to 30 degrees off from the heading when ATC called and asked if I was VFR or IFR. I responded with that I was IFR and turning left to 295.There are a few contributing factors that lead to my error. First was my general lack of recency with the G1000. In the last 120 days I had amassed a total of only 6.7 hours in the aircraft. Additionally I only have a total of 24 hours in the aircraft since my check-ride last summer. This lack of familiarity, currency and comfort in the aircraft contributed to the error. After passing 1,000 feet the G1000 was showing a magenta line to the right which is probably partially why I turned the wrong direction. An additional contributing factor was that I was operating single pilot IFR in icing conditions with little experience in the aircraft. This was a Part 91 flight and the 100 hour rule for commuter passenger operations did not apply. While the General Operations Manual has a dual qualification policy it does not adequately address low time pilots. When a pilot is only qualified in one aircraft type they are afforded an opportunity immediately after completing their check-ride and Operational Experience to gain significant flight time and consolidate their knowledge and skills in the aircraft over the course of a few months. In my scenario I have accumulated only 9 hours since the completion of Operational Experience. I am in full compliance with the policy and have been active in ensuring I fly the aircraft within the 90 days and make an effort to coordinate a flight when I haven't flown in over 30 days. As is evidenced by my low hours recently this does not afford a pilot new in the aircraft any significant flight time, nor the ability to consolidate their knowledge. While all aircraft are of the general purpose multi-engine variety this aircraft is the only Technically Advanced Aircraft (TAA) in the fleet. This adds a significant amount of complexity to it's operation.I would suggest that when a pilot is qualified on any aircraft we afford them the necessary time and hours to consolidate their knowledge and skills. Part 121 recognizes this issue and has the requirement for consolidation of knowledge and skills in new type aircraft. While again our aircraft are of the same type I feel with dramatic difference in this aircraft particularly, being a TAA, there should be a similar effort. Under Part 121 a pilot would be required to obtain 100 hours within 120 days of becoming qualified in the aircraft. I think we should model a policy to have similar protections. Consolidation was identified in a joint government/industry task force in 1993 to be of concern. One primary reason was 'in recent years manufacturers have introduced a greater number of new aircraft containing more equipment and systems variations within type. Pilots must not only learn different aircraft handling characteristics but they must also be able to work with a variety of aircraft equipment such as automated flight control and flight management systems.' (Federal Register Vol 60 No 81). As this aircraft aligns closely with the concerns listed here that resulted in the regulatory change (advanced aircraft systems)I think a policy to ensure a similar amount of experience is obtained in each aircraft a pilot is qualified in. This would not be to change the dual qualification policy, however, it would most often be triggered and impact pilots who are dual qualified. If a pilot were unable to accomplish the consolidation of knowledge and skills then I think it would be best to enter them into a recurrent training program. As a direct result of this deviation and review of my recent experience I have requested a training event from the flight training department to ensure that I have the requisite proficiency and after that I will make a concerted effort to add shifts to ensure I can achieve my consolidation of knowledge and skills.
ASRS:1784973.s: A single-pilot IFR flight in a Technically Advanced Aircraft deviated from a cleared RNAV departure by turning right instead of left to heading 295 after 1,000 feet. The pilot attributed the error to low recency with the G1000 system, which displayed a misleading magenta line, and initiated corrective action after ATC queried the flight status.

ASRS:1784981.n: We departed on time for a XX minute flight. Climbing through 10,000 feet I chimed the flight attendants and we continued our climb to 21,000 feet. Center was telling me to expect bad rides all the way to our destination. So when we leveled off at 21,000 feet. I made an announcement stating that the ride was going to be rough and that I would keep the seat belt sign of the entire flight. I also asked the flight attendants to remain seated for the duration of the flight as well or so I thought. The ride was not good. Continuous light occasionally moderate turbulence. The arrival is challenging on a good day and today was no exception. We were dealing with a complex arrival, turbulence, icing and multiple changes to speed and altitude. We were cleared to descend via the arrival with no speed restrictions with about a 90 knot tailwind.We would be early. Around the time that we started our descent I noticed that someone was trying to use the door code to gain access to the cockpit. I immediately declined it and made sure door was locked. The Pilot Flying and I both thought that was strange so I tried calling back to a Flight Attendant to see what was going on. That was the first indication something was wrong. When I turned on the speaker for the cabin I could hear an audible cycling noise. When I tried to chime the flight attendants I couldn't hear the chime and I could not hear any voices on the interphone. I tried to make a quick announcement but nothing was coming out back in the cabin. As the Pilot Flying and I were extremely busy managing the descent and approach we heard a knock at the door and could faintly hear a voice. Pilot Flying turned around and saw a note on the ground that said INTERPHONE INOP.I wanted to get up and grab the note to try and write something back but we were too busy. A few minutes passed. The cockpit door lock code was entered again and I denied it a second time. I tried to yell as loud as I could that we got the message. I think they must have heard that time because they stopped knocking on the door. We landed and began our taxi to the gate. After clearing the active runways I had Pilot Flying call maintenance and inform them that our Cabin Interphone and Public Address system was inoperative. We taxied to the gate and shutdown. After the shutdown checklist was complete and before the forward door was opened I got up to check on the A Flight Attendant and see if everything was OK. He was visibly upset. After the passengers got off the other two Flight Attendant's joined us up in first class to discuss what had happened. A Flight Attendant said that it was the scariest flight of his life. He said that after we had hit a rough patch of turbulence the cabin lights in the plane started to cycle on and off. They were still doing it after I went back to talk to them. He then had tried to call me to see if everything was OK but couldn't reach me. He thought that maybe we had lost pressurization and that we might have been incapacitated. He tried the door code to maybe get a peek inside to see if we were OK. He left a note under the door in hopes that we would grab it and write back. Only after the last time that he tried the door lock and I denied it did he hear me yell through the door. The other two flight attendants were also upset that they couldn't communicate with me. I spent at least 15 minutes with them trying to explain why I couldn't respond to them even though I wanted to.Trying to unlock the cockpit door without my authorization put me on high alert. This is not something I expected. If this had been a different flight with more time I would have taken their note and responded to it and sent it back. That would have been the best way. I tried yelling through the door, but it is loud in the cockpit and only on the second time did they hear me. If we had lost pressurization the masks in the back would have dropped and they would have felt it in their ears. The first time I denied his access to the cockpit door he should have known we were OK. I cannot just open the cockpit door without knowing who is behind it. My first priority is to fly the aircraft. I just didn't have enough time to respond to them the way they wanted me to.I tried to address all of their concerns and I did understand that they were upset. I wrote up the Public Address system as well as the Interphone system with their input to give the mechanics all they needed to fix the system. Maintenance came on board and reset the system. I tested the PA and both forward and aft intercoms with the Flight Attendants and in front of maintenance to make sure everything worked. Maintenance signed off the system and we than headed back. After our initial conversation about what had transpired I thought all Flight Attendants were OK just a little rattled but good enough to continue. If I had known they still had reservations about what had happened I would have immediately responded to them. My crew always comes first. During our descent on the arrival we heard a knock on the cockpit door. We turned around and saw a note that was slid under the door stating that the interphone was inoperative and there were lights flashing in the cabin. We heard the Flight Attendant said that he was trying to get a hold of us. We never heard him prior to that as this was a 30 minutes or so flight and we were busy from wheels up. The Captain told him we were landing soon. When we landed Maintenance was contacted. Upon arrival at the gate the Captain met with the flight attendants to discuss the event. I went to do the walkaround. The mechanic came and fixed the problem. The interphone and Public Address system was tested before we left the gate and they worked.
ASRS:1784981.s: During a turbulent descent and approach, the flight crew could not communicate with flight attendants due to an inoperative interphone and PA system. The crew denied unauthorized cockpit door access attempts while managing the arrival, later confirming the equipment failure with maintenance and resolving the issue after landing.

ASRS:1784984.n: My first attempt at writing this portion did not save so I will attempt it again. We had an A321 sharklet. Every portion of the beginning of the flight leg from gate departure, takeoff and climb up to the fume event was normal and routine. At sometime above 10,000 ft. we got a call from our #1 FA (Flight Attendant) telling us that the FAs in Economy Class more towards the rear of the aircraft were smelling a sweat odor and a more robust glue type odor. I believe from my prospective that the odor came from the back from the wings black wards because we did not smell anything in the flight deck and no one smelled anything in first class, #1 FA or forward section of the cabin behind 1st class section. Captain began trouble shooting the problem with the QRH guidelines and the FAs that was smelling the odors. One of the FAs was feeling ill from the fume which was strong in the area they were working. Passenger in that area smelled the odors as well. Captain asked if she can continue or do we need to get back to the gate in ZZZ so she can seek medical attention. She was not sure if she wanted to continue on toward ZZZZ1 or return. Captain asked the #1 FA to monitor the FA's condition and if she worsened we will return to ZZZ. While we were discussing the QRH fume trouble shooting pages and making plans to return to ZZZ or another airport that may be closer to our position if we continued to fly farther away from ZZZ, the #1 FA called and told us the FA that was feeling ill was on O2 and was not getting better. So we notified ATC that we will be returning to ZZZ which was the best option to land. We [were given priority handling] to expedite our return to ZZZ and so the FA can get the medical attention she needed. As we began to descend into ZZZ I remember it was below FL180 and through landing that the odors began to infiltrate the flight deck and the #1 FA and passengers began smelling it too. We donned our O2 masks. It was a sweaty smell and it also had an Elmer's glue order to us. The odors continued until we arrived to the gate. The FA that was really ill went to the hospital and the remaining flight crew continued with us to ZZZZ1 with a replacement FA.I don't know of any causal factors that would cause a fume event other than fixing the problem of the source that caused the fumes from escaping and preventing and future leaks from going into the cabin.The only thing that would prevent this from happening would be a complete redesign of the airplane systems that keeps the cabin ventilation isolated from any possible fume leaking into the cabin.
ASRS:1784984.s: During climb above 10,000 ft on an A321, a fume event caused a flight attendant to become ill and require oxygen, prompting a return to ZZZ. The odor later infiltrated the flight deck during descent, leading to the crew donning masks and the affected attendant being hospitalized.

ASRS:1784987.n: We were waiting to take off. The aircraft that took off ahead of us reported hitting birds on take off. The controller asked if they hit the birds directly over the runway, the crew confirmed it was. We were next for takeoff when the controller asked if we had heard the report from the aircraft ahead. We said we did. Tower then delivered a caution about possible FOD (Foreign Object Debris) and birds on the runway and cleared us for takeoff. We refused the clearance and asked that the runway be inspected. We were then informed that it would take a long time for an inspection, we said we will wait. This seemed to aggravate the controller. Tower continued to give takeoff clearances until eventually no one wanted to go until the runway was inspected. This seemed to expedite the runway getting inspected. Once it was deemed safe and free from FOD, takeoffs resumed.I then reached out to an airport authority and their ATC group. They informed me that they have an agreement between the ATC and the Airport Authority about such events. If at their airport that same report was made on takeoff they stated the runway would have been closed for an inspection. They also stated it takes less than 5 minutes At DFW I waited longer than that due to refusing the takeoff clearance.I then took the question to the APA National Safety Committee and asked what they knew about procedure when this happens. Coincidentally, on that call was another pilot that had the same thing happened to them at a different airport. As we have been researching this we are finding there is no standardization from airport to airport on this. Some airports have written agreements between ATC and Airport Authorities and others don't. Does this infer that certain airports take safety more seriously than another? It is factual that the Captain will always have final authority. But shouldn't ATC procedures across the system be uniform with regard to concerns with the runway condition? To give a takeoff clearance with no attempt to inspect the runway in order to keep traffic moving seems at odds with a culture of safety.
ASRS:1784987.s: The pilot refused a takeoff clearance at DFW after a preceding aircraft reported a bird strike, citing potential runway debris. The crew waited for an inspection, noting that inconsistent procedures between airports and ATC groups delayed the process compared to other locations.
