ASRS:1784993.n: During climbout from ZZZ, above approximately 2,000 feet AFL, an amber GPS-L enunciated. I continued to hand fly the jet as we climbed into IMC conditions in the pre-dawn darkness. The GPS-L caution distracted me from calling 'flaps-up' at the appropriate speed. The Captain called my attention to this as we approached 240 knots IAS. I called for flaps up and the captain retracted them normally. I engaged the autopilot after flap retraction. At no time did we exceed the 250 knot flap placard limit. Maximum speed I remember seeing was 244 knots IAS with flaps not up. The rest of the flight to ZZZ1 was uneventful. I believe my recency of experience was a factor, this being my first unsupervised flight since re-qualification. Also, night, IMC in low marine layer clouds while hand flying the initial portion of the RNAV departure. The GPS-L caution was a nuisance warning that served as the distraction. I was focused on hand flying smoothly and lost situational awareness of aircraft configuration.Earlier use of automation may have helped with my situational awareness during the nuisance GPS distraction. My habit is to hand fly the aircraft until clean.
ASRS:1784993.s: The First Officer, hand-flying a jet during climbout from ZZZ in IMC, missed the flaps-up call due to distraction from an amber GPS-L caution. The Captain intervened at 240 knots IAS to retract flaps, preventing a placard limit exceedance, which the reporter attributed to low recency and distraction.

ASRS:1785003.n: GPS jamming in vicinity of Iran and Oman at position about 20 miles west of waypoint SETSI (Airway P307) indicated by ADS-B FAIL and GNS 1, 2 FAIL. All systems returned to normal about 15 minutes later. Cause - External GPS jamming.
ASRS:1785003.s: The flight crew experienced GPS jamming approximately 20 miles west of waypoint SETSI on Airway P307, triggering ADS-B and GNS 1/2 failures. All systems recovered after 15 minutes due to external GPS jamming.

ASRS:1785020.n: Taxing from the device pad for departure we came very close to coming in contact with Aircraft Y. Aircraft Y had been given clearance to taxi to the runway while we were still finishing up de-ice and neither the Captain or myself as First Officer gave it much thought. When we finished the de-ice process I called for taxi and we were given clearance to taxi. The Runway Visual Range was being reported at the time of 1,000 ft. so the visibility was obviously a contributing factor in the described events. As we were on Taxiway A approaching an intersection, I began to notice some lights on the right hand side of the airplane. I assumed that I was seeing hangar lights as they did not appear to be moving. Looking back this was due to the fact that ourselves and Aircraft Y had roughly the same ground speed and therefore the lights were staying in the same position on my window.As we got closer the Captain and I both realized at about the same time that what we were seeing was Aircraft Y. Aircraft Y must have seen us about the same time because we both came to a stop. When we stopped on the slick taxiway we were probably no more then 20 or 30 ft. away from Aircraft Y. We began to taxi away and as we did I asked ground to verify that we were in fact cleared to taxi to the runway. They stated that we were. Aircraft Y then asked the same thing and ground replied that they as well were cleared to taxi to the same runway. Due to the 1,000 ft. Runway Visual Range I know that Tower could not see where either of us were. I think that the normal low visual procedures of reporting when passing certain points would have saved this from happening. I think that Ground thought that Aircraft Y was already at the end of the runway when we were cleared for taxi and for some reason Aircraft Y was delayed. We were departing. ATIS prevailing visibility was 1/4 mile in freezing fog. After start we went to device pad 1 and completed Type I and Type IV deicing. Ground gave us taxi instructions and to hold short the ILS critical area. Taxi was uneventful until reaching an intersection. Aircraft Y had been cleared to taxi to the same runway and we nearly met at the intersection. We both applied brakes. Aircraft Y told Ground they would 'give way to...' us. After starting to taxi we called Ground to confirm our taxi instructions. Aircraft Y did the same. We were both cleared all the way to Runway 12. Aircraft Y was cleared to taxi before us and either taxied slow or delayed their start. Ground could have confirmed their position before clearing us to taxi.
ASRS:1785020.s: Pilots of a departing aircraft nearly collided with Aircraft Y on a slick taxiway during low visibility (1,000 ft RVR) after both received conflicting clearances to the same runway. The incident occurred because Ground Control likely misjudged Aircraft Y's position, leading to a stop within 30 feet of the other aircraft.

ASRS:1785079.n: On private lesson I took off and went to practice area and went through all maneuvers with no problems. I then flew back to the airport and did two successful landings and one takeoff. On my last takeoff I was preparing to do a short field takeoff. I rolled onto [the] runway with the yoke all the way back once getting lined up with the center of the runway I put in full power and started my takeoff. As I was rolling down the runway I added right rudder to keep down the center line. The plane left the ground and instantly turned to the left. I tried adding more right rudder to get the plane going straight. The plane continued to go to the left as it gained altitude. After I felt the plane was not going to recover I tried to put the plane down as softly as possible in the field left of the runway. I touched down in the field and rolled to a stop. I then went through engine shutdown procedure to turn the plane off. After the plane was turned off I waited for help and got out of the plane.
ASRS:1785079.s: During a private lesson short field takeoff, the pilot reported the aircraft instantly turned left after liftoff despite applying right rudder. Unable to recover, the pilot executed a soft landing in a field left of the runway and shut down the engine.

ASRS:1785104.n: While enroute at FL280, I noticed the radio frequency was very quiet. Since COVID has impacted US aviation, frequency congestion has decreased significantly, which makes longer periods of radio silence a new sense of normalcy. My last handoff to ZZZ Center was eight minutes prior at which I made positive radio contact on frequency XYZ.AB. I was using COM 1 as primary radio and monitoring XYX.B on COM 2 with the proper audio panel selections to hear both radios simultaneously. After time passed by and I realized I was not hearing anyone, I transmitted my N number on COM 1 to ZZZ Center and did not receive a response. I selected microphone to COM 2 and reached out to ZZZ Center on XYX.B, no response. I switched the microphone back to COM 1 and tried XYZ.AB again, no response. I switched the microphone back to COM 2 and announced, 'All stations on guard, radio check.' After the second attempt, ZZZ1 Center answered and gave me a new frequency, XXC.DY. A Controller replied 'Aircraft X, possible pilot deviation, I have a number for you, advise when ready to copy.' I was extremely shocked at the situation as I was unaware the radio issue had escalated to that extent. I continued my flight to ZZZZ and called as soon as practical after landing. I spoke with a Controller. Controller said NORDO is a common issue but mine was excessive. I have no deviations on my record and strive to maintain a clean record. Going forward, I will be more diligent in recognizing radio silence and will reach out more frequently if I assume the silent period is excessive.
ASRS:1785104.s: A pilot enroute at FL280 experienced extended radio silence with ZZZ Center, leading to a NORDO status and a controller report of a possible pilot deviation. The pilot later learned the silence was excessive and committed to contacting ATC more frequently during future silent periods.

ASRS:1785106.n: On [Date], an in-flight [problem] occurred regarding a Gulfstream GIV-SP. The details are as follows:On [Date], [Aircraft X] was on a FAA Part 135 flight from ZZZZ to ZZZ1. There were a total of XX occupants on board of which included 3 crew members. The Pilot Flying (PF) was [Name], the Pilot Monitoring (PM) was [Name], and the third crew member, [Name], was the Cabin Server (CS).The aircraft departed ZZZZ at approximately XA:00 on an IFR flight plan. The aircraft climbed uneventfully to an initial altitude of FL430. After about 20 minutes at altitude, a passenger came to the flight deck and asked if we could cool down the cabin. The PM set the cabin temperature controller to a cooler temperature. After about 5 minutes, the R COOL TURBINE HOT CAS message displayed. The crew performed the appropriate checklist and after a minute the message went out.At this point, the cabin was at a higher temperature than before and the passengers complained again. The PF decided to go back into the cabin to verify that all the gasper vents were open and to check if there were any other indications of potential issues. It was apparent that there was a significant temperature difference from the forward portion of the cabin compared to the aft. The forward cabin was at least 10 degrees warmer than the aft. Additionally, the PF noticed some warm air coming out of the vents. After checking the upper cabin gasper vents, the PF returned to his seat. After a short discussion on possible issues, the crew elected to descend to FL390.When the aircraft leveled at FL390, the CS came up to the flight deck and asked the PF if he noticed any haze in the cabin. The PF looked back and saw no smoke or haze. The CS went about her duties.After a few more minutes, the PF noticed smoke coming from the PM's vent and the crew received another R COOL TURBINE HOT CAS message. The PF immediately donned his O2 mask and requested to the PM that we ask for an immediate descent and to pull out the checklist. At this time, the cabin started to fill up with visible smoke and the Cabin Server came up to the flight deck to respond. The Cabin Server donned her O2 mask. After O2 masks were on, the appropriate checklists were performed. The cabin started to depressurize immediately after the right pack was turned off (as required by the R COOL TURBINE HOT checklist). At this point, a rapid descent was performed and [ATC was advised]. During the descent, smoke remained in the cabin. Due to the smoke in the cabin and loss of pressurization, the crew elected for vectors to the nearest suitable airport ZZZ2. While the aircraft was descending, the passenger O2 masks deployed and the CS instructed the passenger to put their O2 masks on. At about 15,000 ft., the smoke started to dissipate. The crew continued their descent to 6,000 ft. and accepted vectors to the ILS XXR at ZZZ2. At this time, the cabin was completely free from smoke. The crew took off their O2 masks and completed all remainder checklists for landing. At XB:00 the aircraft landed uneventfully.On the landing roll out Fire and Rescue was approved on the runway to follow the aircraft to its parking spot. After shutting down the engines, the crew assessed the situation and verified that all passengers were OK and that no one was injured. At this point, the PM notified the airport that the crew and passengers will need to clear customs. After the crew and passengers were cleared from customs, the airplane was written up for multiple system failures including an abnormal cabin depressurization, the left pack unable to provide appropriate cabin pressurization under the above conditions, a malfunction within the right air cycle machine, and the aft [lavatory] O2 mask failing to deploy.
ASRS:1785106.s: A Gulfstream GIV-SP crew encountered an R COOL TURBINE HOT CAS message and cabin smoke during cruise, causing depressurization and passenger mask deployment. The aircraft descended to FL390 then 6,000 ft for an uneventful landing at ZZZ2, with post-flight reports citing air cycle machine and pack failures.

ASRS:1785107.n: Instructor and Student were landing on [Runway] XXL at ZZZ airport. The braking conditions were 3/3/3. ATC instructed the student to taxi off of the runway at [Intersection] X1. With the snow it was a harder left turn on the ground, almost a back taxi for theX1 intersection from the runway. The aircraft was turned onto A8 but had to come to a full stop and this allowed for a loss in steering authority on the ground. When going to straighten the nose out to go from back taxiing to X1 to exiting X1, the aircraft brakes became unusable and the aircraft slid to the side of X1 where there was a pile of compacted snow which [prevented] a quick recovery [of] control. An aircraft landed on the runway while [we were] almost exited off the runway at X1. Tower came on and asked if we needed to be towed off and informed everyone that there was a disabled aircraft on the runway. There was no damage to airport property or the aircraft itself. No needed assistance.
ASRS:1785107.s: An instructor and student lost steering and braking authority while turning off Runway XXL at ZZZ airport in snowy conditions, causing the aircraft to slide into a snow pile at Intersection X1. The aircraft was disabled but sustained no damage, and Tower coordinated the situation while another aircraft landed.

ASRS:1785122.n: Was working these two sectors combined. It needed a D side or to be split. Sector volume was high and complex. Two CPC's [Certified Professional Controller] had been held over on OT to supplement our 5 CPC count for the night shift. They were relieved to go home as they hit their limits. That left 5 CPC's working 5 sectors. No sector could be combined up to free up a controller to help on a D side. There was extensive military training aircraft working sector X at ZZZ1, ZZZ2, ZZZ3. I told the supervisor they needed to tell those aircraft to return to base so X and Y sectors could be recombined to free up a CPC. He got that process started and eventually sectors Z and A were able to combine as well. We have been working short staffed on our 5 day rotations for too long. I am beyond frustrated working combined R/D positions with busy traffic. I have lost my patience and work angry. These sessions are unsafe and on the cusp of causing a safety incident to occur (loss of separation, etc). Our traffic levels are, in my opinion, back to pre-COVID levels. We need to transition back to normal schedules. If not, management needs to place traffic restrictions on the military training flights that routinely come out of ZZZ4, ZZZ5, ZZZ6, ZZZ7, ZZZ8;and etc. I'd say no more than 3 total aircraft allowed to work practice approaches at the ZZZ1 area and no more than 1 at a time at the ZZZ9 area until we can get back to normal schedules and staffing levels.
ASRS:1785122.s: An air traffic controller reported unsafe conditions while working combined sectors with high military training traffic due to chronic understaffing. The controller requested traffic restrictions on military flights to prevent potential loss of separation until normal staffing levels are restored.

ASRS:1785146.n: On approach to IAH, just prior to FESTA on the Runway 27 ILS being flown in VFR conditions, we were notified by IAH Approach Control of VFR / no com traffic as we were receiving a TA and almost immediately an RA for that traffic at 400 feet below our path. As the controller was handing us off to the Tower, I advised him that we were responding to an RA. Another voice acknowledged this, and we were then switched to IAH Tower. The visual approach continued without further incident.
ASRS:1785146.s: The flight crew on an IAH Runway 27 ILS approach received a Traffic Advisory and Resolution Advisory for VFR traffic 400 feet below while being handed off from Approach to Tower. The crew responded to the RA, acknowledged by the controller, and completed the visual approach without further incident.

ASRS:1785167.n: Ground personnel are being asked to leave their work area, travel in their own vehicle to a random clinic. We are not opposed to being screened but believe the screener should come to us at our place of work. We feel it is unsafe to be placed in an environment that is filled with people who might have serious medical conditions during a pandemic.
ASRS:1785167.s: Ground personnel reported that being required to travel to a random clinic for screening during a pandemic is unsafe. They believe screeners should come to their work area to avoid exposing them to individuals with serious medical conditions.

ASRS:1785218.n: After takeoff at acceleration altitude I called for 'flaps 0, climb checks, pitch mode.' The PM (Pilot Monitoring) began the duties, however at the same time we were told to immediately turn right and level off at 3,000 feet as there was an aircraft that was not communicating with Tower headed straight for us. This diverted our attention from the task at hand. I suspect the PM omitted retracting the flaps accidentally and I failed to notice. Once we were clear of the traffic we were handed off to another frequency on which we were told to look for yet another aircraft in close proximity. By the time we were clear we were through 10,000 feet and due to the distractions we forgot to complete the climb check. I initially began accelerating and reached about 265 knots before I decided to slow to complete the second part of the ice test. Once the test was complete (at around 18,000 feet) I began accelerating and again reached about 265 knots before we realized the flaps were still set to 9. We slowed, retracted the flaps, contacted Maintenance and continued the flight without further incident.No real suggestions. It was human error on my part. I should have been more vigilant and will be in the future.
ASRS:1785218.s: The pilot and Pilot Monitoring omitted flap retraction and climb checks during climb due to distractions from ATC traffic avoidance instructions. The crew discovered flaps remained at 9 near 18,000 feet, retracted them, and continued the flight after contacting Maintenance.

ASRS:1785222.n: In our initial climb to 6,000 feet we were instructed by Departure to turn off course and given a fix to fly to. I confirmed the fix with the CA (Captain) and pressed Nav Mode on the FMS. I looked over to my PFD to set the new altitude assigned by Departure and the CA looked away at the same time. Shortly thereafter, Departure called and asked us if we were turning on course. We both looked up and realized that the Nav mode had not captured the course. I immediately turned the heading bug towards the course line on the display, while the CA notified the Controller that we were correcting and turning on course.While compensating for winds and flying via the heading bug, we started to analyze the problem. Shortly after changing the AP to the CA's side, we were able to correct the Nav issue, as the AP was functioning properly on the CA's side, I continued as the pilot flying. About 45 minutes out, the CA left the flight deck to use the LAV. As he returned, he noticed that we had about 8 status messages that popped up sometime after he had left the flight deck. I was engaged with a short conversation with the FA (Flight Attendant) and did not notice the display of messages until he returned. The status messages were flight control related, noting flight spoilers, rudder, etc. The CA referred to the QRH for landing data as a precautionary measure, in the event of a total system failure to those systems. The CA Then notified ATC of our potential systems status and requested deleting the LAHSO restrictions. ATC was unable to comply.Later, as we were given an intercept angle to intercept the final approach course, I selected the NAV button and was waiting for the intercept. We had a [heavy aircraft] on our left and we were paying close attention to that traffic, when we noticed that the aircraft had blown through the center line and was deviating right. The CA then asked me what was going on and while trying to process the information, I replied, 'I have no idea.' At that time Tower called to query our actions, It was as if the aircraft had a mind of its own and before I was able to kick off the autopilot, the CA then asked for the flight controls. We landed without incident and all flight control systems were operational throughout the landing phase, as all the spoilers had deployed. The AP had remained on the CA's side throughout the entire approach.Hindsight, I told the CA, that the one course of action we could have taken at the onset of discovering that the AP/Nav was not recognizing my side, we should have changed roles and allowed him to be the Pilot Flying. With the unexpected behavior of the FMS during the critical phase of flight, I was in total agreement with the CA's actions and decisions, I believe his actions were appropriate and timely while operating in the essence of safety for the passengers and crew.
ASRS:1785222.s: During climb and approach, the First Officer and Captain experienced FMS navigation failures and uncommanded flight control deviations while the autopilot was engaged on the Captain's side. The Captain took manual control to intercept the final approach course, and the aircraft landed safely with all systems operational despite earlier status messages.

ASRS:1785235.n: I checked in with the gate agent prior to my flight to ZZZZ. I don't recall if any passengers were boarded but there were no passengers that I remember waiting to check in because it was still pretty early. As I walked down the jet bridge I noticed a Flight Attendant walking the opposite direction. I had not met her prior as I had not been to the aircraft yet. She told me she was trying to get better cellular reception so she could complete her COVID-19 form which is required for entry into ZZZZ. When I boarded the aircraft, I met the other two FAs. At no time did I notice any passengers boarding or on our aircraft. After checking the aircraft maintenance log, flight documents, etc. I briefed the A FA. I only briefed the A FA as passengers were now being boarded. I assumed the other two flight attendants were on board. I was completely unaware that we didn't have minimum crew while boarding. Approximately 10-15 minutes prior to departure, the A1 FA informed me that she was informed that we had boarded without minimum crew. I think the COVID-19 online form (for ZZZZ) was the reason that caused this problem. I fly this trip nearly every week and it's generally always a bit of a scramble at the last minute to get the form completed by all crew members prior to departure. In addition it is a very difficult form to electronically fill out for the first time. I believe the FA was only trying her best to complete the form prior to boarding. Perhaps a reminder to both cockpit and cabin crew that a COVID-19 declaration form is required for entry into ZZZZ. And that the form takes a while to complete as it NOT intuitive and can take a few attempts to complete it and requires sufficient WiFi or cellular signal.
ASRS:1785235.s: The pilot reported that the aircraft began boarding without minimum crew because a flight attendant left the cabin to find cellular reception for a required ZZZZ entry form. This delay in completing the difficult electronic form caused the crew shortage, which was discovered approximately 10-15 minutes prior to departure.

ASRS:1785262.n: We had just taken off from ZZZ ferrying to ZZZ1 for a revenue flight. When after level off I went and turned the aft coffee maker on to brew some coffee. When not even 10 seconds after the power was turned on, I heard a loud pop come from behind the coffee makers. When I looked at the circuit breakers I noticed that they had popped. I immediately went to the cockpit and the pilots immediately asked what happened. Because they received multiple messages indicating a power surge coming from the galley equipment. After explaining what had happened, the pilots immediately disabled all power going back to the galley and cabin. They contacted [Company] Maintenance and were advised to divert to ZZZ2 for further maintenance with this occurrence. I have noticed on these particular coffee makers on the Gulfstreams that the coffee makers are on a slide out drawer to help put water in the brewer. When pulling out the drawer, the wires that connect to the coffee maker backing drag along with the drawer. So when the drawer is slid back in place it connects to a latch. The wires tend to get caught in the latch. This is where I believe the problem was with the above mentioned issue. Having those wires where they don't risk getting pinched in the latch would be a good idea to look into.
ASRS:1785262.s: A cabin crew member reported a galley power surge and circuit breaker trip on a Gulfstream shortly after takeoff caused by coffee maker wires pinching in a slide-out drawer latch. The pilots disabled galley power and diverted to ZZZ2 for maintenance.

ASRS:1785268.n: I work the #X position regularly on the aircraft. Personal observation of the close proximity in which #Z and #X [Flight Attendants] sit, facing each other, is of grave concern to me, due to COVID-19. While occupying the jump seats at XX, true social distancing isn't possible. Depending on height it can be a challenge to sit without our knees touching or without adjusting our feet under the jump seat. All a non-issue, pre-pandemic.The #X flight attendant does not have a door arming or disarming responsibility. There's no reason for the #X's preflight, inflight, or boarding duties to change. I'm suggesting for safety and health reasons the #X Flight Attendant is temporarily relocated to an unoccupied jump seat at door Y for takeoff and landing.
ASRS:1785268.s: A flight attendant reported that the close proximity of jump seats at XX prevents social distancing between crew members #X and #Z. The reporter requested relocating the #X flight attendant to an unoccupied seat at door Y for takeoff and landing to mitigate COVID-19 risks.

ASRS:1785278.n: On Date aircraft XXX had fumes/smoke in the cockpit smell noticed by the flight crew.The event occurred due to a razor blade that was left inside CBP1 possibly during a visit to ZZZ for the ADS-B modification in the middle of month of 2019 and I could have possibly left it there during the installation of breaker CBP1-XX during the mod. Due to the length of time between when possibly leaving a razor blade and when it was discovered I cannot recall whether or not I used a razor blade in the area. But, typically, when I do wiring work I don't use razor blades to cut tape or remove wiring insulation. As we usually have the equipment to remove fiberglass tape (a wire spoon and flush cutters or just peeling it off by hand;) and wiring insulation (standard wire strippers and the twisted pair stripping tool). Reflecting on the experience I would hope that even during the crunch time of the push to finish the ADS-B modifications on all our aircraft before the deadline that I would have continued to practice strict FOD control.My suggestion is to not use lose razor blades when doing work on wires unless absolutely necessary, and to practice strict FOD control and to perform detailed FOD inspections before every panel close-up. On date the crew of Aircraft X reported fumes in the cockpit. An AMT discovered a loose razor blade located behind circuit breaker panel 1. Records indicate that panel had work done inside on date. This event has been brought to my attention due to my participation in ADSB mod which the work was completed. Due to the length of time from when the work was accomplished until now, unfortunately I can not provide details on exact situation. I can say that I was the RII In the process and I understand the seriousness of the situation and would not have allowed a loose razor blade to be left in the circuit breaker panel. I did not see a razor blade in the panel when it was closed. AMT found razor blade after fumes noted in cockpit. The event was caused by a Razor blade left in CBP-1.
ASRS:1785278.s: Flight crew reported fumes in the cockpit of Aircraft XXX, prompting an AMT to discover a loose razor blade behind circuit breaker panel 1. The incident was caused by a blade likely left during a 2019 ADS-B modification, resulting in smoke generation.

ASRS:1785284.n: Upon closing the main cabin door to the aircraft, the Captain (other person) broke the loop end of the door handle from the main cabin door off. The door was still functional as it could be opened and closed, however as the part was broken, I argued that we were AOG (Aircraft On Ground) until it got fixed. The part is not in the MEL (Minimum Equipment List) / CDL (Configuration Deviation List). The Captain disagreed and stated that her conversation with the company said we were good to go. I had reservations about the broken part and made them known to both her and the company however the initial repositioning leg (empty) and two charter (Part 135) legs thereafter with passengers were flown. Only in a conversation today did I realize that the Captain did not actually report the problem in its entirety to our maintenance department for a full evaluation of the issue.The plane was fixed the following day.I have had a conversation with the company and may likely be resigning this position as this incident is indicative of a much larger, systemic problem within this company regarding maintenance culture. Operations will likely be making changes to the staff based on this event but I am not confident in this pilot position causing a future accident / incident / violation. I had been chastised about not following the chain of command in reporting maintenance issues in the past which is why I did not speak up further during this incident. I personally will never again put myself in a situation where an obvious maintenance issue such as this overrides common sense (and likely a few [CFR]'s) (Code of Federal Regulations).
ASRS:1785284.s: The Captain broke the main cabin door handle loop, but the aircraft flew three legs despite the reporter's AOG objection because the part was not in the MEL. The Captain failed to fully report the issue to maintenance, leading the reporter to consider resigning due to concerns over the company's maintenance culture.

ASRS:1785315.n: On DATE, Aircraft X was scheduled to depart on a two leg cross county trip from ZZZ to ZZZ1. The trip was slated to depart at XA:30 but was delayed approximately 50 minutes due to unforeseen complications dealing with one of the aircraft preflight checklist items. While checking the tire pressure of the landing gear tires, it was discovered that the left main landing gear tire valve stem was inaccessible due to the hub cap being installed incorrectly. There is a small access door that allows access to the valve stem through the hub cap and the hub cap was clocked in the wrong position rendering the valve stem inaccessible. A local A&P Service Center was contacted and on-site service was requested to remove the hubcap and re-clock. An A&P responded to the location and removed the hub cap. He asked to confirm the POH air pressure requirements, and continued to top off the air pressure per the POH. The hub cap was replaced in the correct position. All tire air pressures were serviced per the POH. This was the last remaining check list item to be completed, and Aircraft X departed ZZZ2 at XB:20 en route to ZZZ3 for the first leg of the trip. The taxi, take off, landing, and post landing taxi phases were normal. On DATE, Aircraft X departed ZZZ2 on the second leg of this cross country trip to ZZZ1. Taxi and takeoff were normal. The trip was uneventful. IMC conditions existed over ZZZ1 during our arrival time, with unknown tops and 4,400 ft. ceilings. VMC conditions existed below the ceiling with winds reported variable at 3 kts. The RNAV GPS approach was requested and granted into ZZZ1. Following the approach, the main landing gear touched down with the aircraft near center line just beyond the extended threshold. The aircraft responded as expected upon main gear touchdown. When the nose landing gear touched down the plane veered hard to the right. Left rudder pedal was used to counter the uncommanded right turn and the plane veered left and immediately began skidding to the left. The plane did not respond to input and skidded off the runway just short of taxiway F, into the landscaped area immediately adjacent to the runway. The nose wheel collapsed while the engine was still running and dropped the spinning prop to the ground. It was immediately obliterated. The turbine engine abruptly quit running. When the plane swerved to the right following the nose wheel touch down, the plane immediately felt unstable. It felt as if the runway was icy and without good traction. However, it was later determined there was no ice on the runway. I advised the tower when the plane came to a complete stop that I had just hit ice. This event duration happened extremely quick. There were no injuries. There was no known airport property damage observed. There is no other property damage. Emergency crews showed up quickly. The aircraft did not catch on fire. Emergency crews did not deploy any foam. The ELT activated. The airbag seat belts did not deploy. Environmental observation: Prior to decent, and while in cruise at FL270, I had been observing the OAT slowly creep down from around -45c to a max low of -51c. The minimum in-flight temperature limitation of this aircraft is -54c. When the temperature dropped to around -49c, I became acutely aware and concerned of the temperature as I knew I was approaching the maximum lower limit. I advised ATC I needed lower due to temperature limitations and they advised expect lower in three minutes. I was then instructed to descend to FL250. The temperature increased to above -49c. Shortly thereafter, the decent into the terminal area required a rapid descent of roughly 2,000 FPM.
ASRS:1785315.s: Aircraft X departed ZZZ2 for ZZZ1 after a preflight delay caused by an incorrectly installed hub cap blocking tire valve access. During landing in IMC, the aircraft veered right upon nose gear touchdown, skidded off the runway, and collapsed the nose wheel, destroying the propeller and stopping the engine without injuries.

ASRS:1785317.n: Took off from FPR approximately XA:40. Told to watch out for Aircraft Y. Had aircraft in sight. At about 1,000 feet, lost sight of Aircraft Y, he was below me at time of losing visual contact. I was closing on his aircraft. I took evasive action by turning right and climbing to 1,400 feet where I could see sky was clear of aircraft. At this time my radios started to have a lot of static, could not hear anything. We proceeded out of area to ZZZ, landed to see if radios could be fixed by changing headsets. Changing intercom helped a little.
ASRS:1785317.s: The pilot reported a near-miss with Aircraft Y shortly after takeoff from FPR, requiring a right turn and climb to 1,400 feet to avoid collision. Subsequent radio static prevented communication, and while changing the intercom headset at ZZZ provided slight improvement, the issue persisted.

ASRS:1785324.n: The issue is [the] extreme limit of CPC (Certified Professional Controllers). We were working with 3 CPC's on a shift that a year ago any less than 9 CPC's on a shift would have been unacceptable. The facility is combining 2 and 3 positions to one controller during very busy and complex traffic. All because a lack of CPC controllers due to COVID issues and minimum staffing due to the agency not hiring any more controllers for our facility. This whole COVID issue has caused all the rules and agreements to go out the window. It is unacceptable for the safety of the NAS! We are just treated like robots like we always have been. There is no empathy for the stresses in our lives outside of work. This year has created A LOT of stress due to all the COVID uncertainty and constantly changing ideas about how to deal with it. Also all the political stress that has gone on all year. As much as we try to push out personal issues and feelings when we work, we are still human. We are not robots. And some days all the crap going on in society added to an unacceptable over taxed work load just gets to a person. We need more controllers at ZZZ TOWER! Also the positions need to be de-combined when traffic is busy. Combining 3 positions to one controller puts that controller at risk of missing something. And that is not fair to that controller or the flying public. The flying public deserves better than this.
ASRS:1785324.s: An air traffic controller reported that severe staffing shortages at ZZZ Tower forced the combination of two to three positions into one during busy traffic. The controller attributed this unsafe workload to a lack of Certified Professional Controllers caused by COVID-19 and hiring freezes, increasing the risk of errors.

ASRS:1785329.n: Aircraft X was on an ILS Approach to Runway 16L. A VFR aircraft was skirting around AFW's Class D airspace, not in communication with AFW or D10. The VFR aircraft was eastbound then turned north and crossed over WIGZU the FAF for ILS RWY 16L at 2,600 FT MSL. Aircraft X was at the same altitude. The Local Controller called the traffic and Aircraft X reported the traffic in sight. Aircraft X reported that they had to turn off the ILS then turn back once they were clear of the traffic. The two aircraft were less than 1/2 mile apart at the same altitude head on to each other. This area is dangerous and this continues to be an issue. The airspace design is outdated. AFW airport has grown and is continuing to grow. The facility has recently been upgraded from a Level 5 Tower to a Level 6 Tower. In the last year three new air carriers have all started operating at AFW. A contractor for the US military has relocated their maintenance base to AFW. Aerospace company X has also begun construction at their new facility here as well. Both runways were extended from 9,000 feet to 11,000 feet in the last few years. Everything at this airport has been growing and expanding except the airspace. The Class Bravo airspace should be expanded to include WIGZU the FAF for RWY 16L. This would allow us the ability to talk to VFR aircraft that constantly cross this area around 2,500 feet. We have conducted pilot outreach at surrounding airports. It has not been successful. We just want the ability to talk to these VFR aircraft to provide traffic advisories. The airspace needs to be updated.
ASRS:1785329.s: Aircraft X on an ILS approach to Runway 16L encountered a VFR aircraft at 2,600 feet MSL near the WIGZU FAF, resulting in a head-on conflict less than 0.5 mile apart. The controller advised traffic, forcing Aircraft X to deviate from the ILS, which the reporter attributes to outdated airspace design preventing communication with the VFR pilot.

ASRS:1785337.n: Today was a very busy day and on top of that our area was short staffed. At the time of the event, all 5 people staffed for the day were working, we needed to have 6 sectors open but couldn't due to staffing issues. We were told that TMU (Traffic Management Unit) was to slow traffic to help alleviate some of the pressure on our area, and we were also told that they could not call for overtime because of the COVID situation at hand. Today was a completely unsafe and unhealthy situation to have been in without any support from management and TMU. What is more important to the NAS, safety or COVID? At the time of the event, I had been on position for just over an hour and it was after two other sessions that I had been working for well over 2 hours with a 20-30 minute break in between. I was definitely mentally fatigued at this time. Aircraft Y was a departure from ZZZ flying west bound direct to ZZZZZ slow climbing from FL260 to FL340. Aircraft X was a southbound ZZZ1 arrival initially on a heading to avoid other traffic and descending from FL350 to FL270. I had turned the Aircraft X back on course to ZZZZZ1 thinking they were clear of all other potential traffic. When Aircraft X established to ZZZZZ1 they 'flashed' with the Aircraft Y aircraft heading west bound near ZZZZZ1. I had already switched the Aircraft Y to [the adjacent ARTCC]. So I turned Aircraft X and called traffic. The turn helped but still didn't fix the situation. Ended with 4.5 miles and 300 feet. We need to have the support from not only our local management but also national level management. Volume needed to be slowed due to staffing. Regardless of what the airlines are pushing for or wanting from us. We have to be safe first.
ASRS:1785337.s: An air traffic controller, fatigued by understaffing and high volume, lost separation between a climbing departure and a descending arrival near ZZZZZ1. The controller issued a traffic call and turn, resulting in a minimum separation of 4.5 miles and 300 feet.

ASRS:1785342.n: A snow team had cleared snow from an intersecting runway and taxiway and had left snow on the runway. I asked the city vehicle about the snow on the runway and if it was safe for aircraft to depart. The city vehicle said the snow was 'just a dusting'. Two aircraft departed without incident. The snow team did another pass on the intersecting runway. After that, another aircraft started departure roll and then aborted the takeoff after hitting a snow bank. The pilot said it was about 2 feet deep and felt like hitting a herd of deer. The airport needs a vast improvement in their snow removal operation overall, and they need to be aware of snow that gets left on active runways.
ASRS:1785342.s: A pilot aborted takeoff after hitting a two-foot-deep snow bank left on an active runway by a snow team. The incident occurred after the team initially described the snow as a "dusting," leading the reporter to call for improved snow removal operations.

ASRS:1785369.n: After leveling at cruise for a few [minutes], got a Cabin Alt. caution msg. After getting some of the QRH done and starting down, got Cabin Alt. warning message. [Advised ATC] and diverted to ZZZ. The smell from the O2 canisters smelled like there may have been a fire. It took a few mins. to figure out it was just the O2 canisters making the smell. After landing had fire and rescue inspect aircraft. Taxied to the gate. Talked to [passengers] to let them know basically what happened. Asked if anyone needed help by paramedics on the airplane and all said no. So we let the [passengers] know that everyone would be [checked] out by paramedics in the gate area once they all deplaned. Everyone checked out ok is what I was told. Before leaving the gate in ZZZ1 had to get my O2 mask replaced because it would not test. Need to make sure every pilot knows how to pre-flight/check the O2 mask the correct way. Some [passengers] said they could not get their O2 mask to work. FA (Flight Attendant) tried to help and could not get O2 to come out [of] the [passenger's] mask. FWD FA O2 mask could not get O2 [to] come out. Even after being tested by [Maintenance] and the canisters got hot, it is not a sure way of telling that O2 came out of the mask or not. The auto 1st class PA did not work when the O2 mask deployed is what I was told by the FA's. [Cause of incident] appears [to be] the outflow valve opened.After an event there is way too many phone calls. Makes things way too confusing. Understand calling Dispatch and Maintenance. Had to answer so many question right off the bat from the company did not have time to finish the write ups and had to go back to finish. This brings another point to mind. If something comes out on [Company Document] lets say at midnight the pilot is responsible for the pages of info on their [flight], lets say at 6 am. This is not realistic and needs to addressed. Need to give a minimum of 5 days for a pilot, mechanic, and/or FA to be able to understand the info NOT just checking a box. The pilots are responsible if they get a line check to have [Company Document] up to date or pulled off line. This is NOT safe.Always check your O2 mask before leaving the gate. Need to make sure every pilot knows how to preflight/ check the O2 mask the correct way.
ASRS:1785369.s: The flight crew diverted to ZZZ during cruise after a cabin altitude warning caused by an outflow valve opening. Post-landing inspections revealed multiple oxygen mask failures and a non-functional first-class PA system, though passengers were cleared by paramedics.

ASRS:1785406.n: During the DINGO 5 arrival into TUS, after waypoint MAVVA, I continued on the charted 075 degree heading passing through the Runway 11L localizer course, not complying with the textual instruction to intercept the I-TUS localizer course. ATC gave me vectors back around to re-intercept the localizer course, and a normal landing was made.The cause of the event was a failure to cross-check the textual instructions with what is displayed on the chart. Contributing factors were as follows: 1) A 'Descend Via' clearance was not issued. ATC instructed to 'Descend and maintain 8,000 feet, and EXPECT a visual approach.' I misinterpreted that to mean he would provide vectors to the final approach course, or clear me for a visual approach passing MAVVA. 2) I found the verbiage on the chart confusing where it states 'Runway 11L EXPECT approach clearance'. I interpreted that to mean once established on the 075 heading from MAVVA, not upon intercepting the localizer, as normally you would not intercept a localizer without ATC clearance or prior to accepting a visual approach.To avoid a recurrence of this event, a thorough briefing covering all noted and textual information should be conducted and cross checked prior to every landing. While my briefing did cover all of the information on the plan-view of the arrival, I missed a crucial piece of information solely located in the textual description that was not well depicted nor defined on the plan-view. It would have been helpful if ATC had offered us a visual approach earlier, directed us to intercept the localized after MAVVA and THEN expect approach clearance, or have the instruction to Intercept I-TUS localizer clearly printed on the plan view. It is worthy to note, the ATC controller stated 'Yeah, you're not the first airliner to do this' both over the frequency and on the telephone while speaking with him after landing. This leads me to believe that this could be a common mistake that could be corrected easily with a revised, emphasized, note on the arrival chart.
ASRS:1785406.s: The pilot deviated from the DINGO 5 arrival into TUS by following the charted 075-degree heading instead of intercepting the I-TUS localizer due to misinterpreting textual instructions and ATC clearances. ATC vectored the aircraft back to the localizer for a normal landing, attributing the error to a failure to cross-check chart text with the plan view.

ASRS:1785418.n: I was First Officer and pilot monitoring for a reposition flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1. When I arrived to the airplane, the Captain was already there with multiple maintenance technicians working through a dual inoperative GPS situation. The consensus was to defer both GPS units, along with the associated MEL items. After processing our 9 MELs during our pre-flight discussion we waited approximately two hours for a flight plan to be filed due to the issue with ADS-B being inoperative.During the after-start checklist, the CONT CAB ZONE TEMP fault appeared on Master Caution recall. We complied with the QRH and MEL and contacted Maintenance Control for deferral under the 'flight crew placard' option. The Captain and I discussed the phrase in the QRH, 'if the light extinguishes when Master Caution System is reset, no further action is required' - and he noted that this does not alleviate us from the need to defer the item per the MEL XX-XXY. Along the same time, the Captain noted that the 'dispatch alert' box was unchecked, so after the deferral was complete we resumed normal operations.After takeoff we experienced two additional master recall lights - 'Anti-Skid Inop' and the 'Reverser' on the overhead panel.Shortly after we leveled off at cruise altitude the dispatcher asked if we had added a new deferred item after pushback. We responded that we had, that it was XX-XXY. He advised us to fill out a report, despite the 'dispatch alert' box not being checked.The reposition flights after long-term storage lend themselves to multiple maintenance related issues and could be planned ahead to be operated by Functional Check Flight pilots.The filing of our flight plan took nearly two hours. Not knowing the exact cause of the issue, it would be helpful for future flights to review the process for filing flights with inoperative GPS and ADS-B to minimize future delays. Aircraft X was a reposition flight for aircraft (tail) in storage several months. The aircraft was dispatched with multiple MELs. We waited over two hours for Dispatch to be able to get ATC to accept a flight plan into the system for a clearance.A Control Cab 'Zone Temp' light illuminated during Master Cation recall during the after-start checklist. QRH procedures were followed and Maintenance control was contacted for a crew MEL (XX-XXY) before departure despite the misleading 'No further action required' guidance in the QRH.Two more master caution lights were encountered after takeoff (Master caution 'anti-skid and reverser.')Dispatch sent an ACARs message after level off advising us to submit a report for not getting an amended release for XX-XXY before departure. We responded that a Dispatch alert is not required for XX-XXY. Dispatch responded 'They give us a heads up anyway.' We did not believe we violated any maintenance/dispatch procedures but were led to believe we had.Reposition flights from long term storage are a severely irregular operation and should be conducted by the Functional Check Flight department.
ASRS:1785418.s: The First Officer and Captain operated a reposition flight of an aircraft from long-term storage with multiple deferred items, including inoperative GPS and ADS-B. They experienced a two-hour flight plan delay and additional master caution lights after takeoff, while Dispatch later requested a report for a deferred item despite the crew following MEL procedures.

ASRS:1785430.n: During moderate turbulence and deviation around weather, airspeed became wildly erratic. Between maximum and minimum, the autopilot disconnected and several Level Two alerts displayed. I called, 'Airspeed unreliable;' disconnected AFS Override and Flight Director Switches, and established pitch for aircraft stabilized flight. The First Officer's airspeed was the closest to the Standby Instruments, and transfer of control was given to the FO (First Officer). Level Two 'SEL FADEC 1;2 3 ALTN', 'SEL FLAP LIM OVRD' and 'SEL ELV FEEL MAN' were displayed. The QRH procedures were completed and the flight continued without incident. Possible CADC #1 failure or pitot static malfunction. [Responded as] described above. Additionally, inspection of the logbook revealed that related malfunctions had occurred [previously on four separate dates]. This would suggest that the problem is ongoing and requires further action. [I suggest] maintenance troubleshooting of all related issues by reference to all previous write-ups. Airspeed unreliable event. Possible altitude deviation. I was deadheading on flight sitting in the observer seat. There were thunderstorms in vicinity and we were experiencing light to moderate rain and turbulence. CA (Captain) was PF (Pilot Flying) with autopilot engaged in climb to 14,000 MSL and also communicating to ATC on Com 1. FO (First Officer) was speaking to Operations on Com 2. I'm not sure exactly what altitude event occurred but happened around 14,000 MSL. There was a high speed warning and I noticed a large difference in airspeed between the CA and FO side. The CA-side airspeed was declining rapidly while FO-side was overspeeding slightly. The Captain recognized the issue and performed the memory items correctly and stabilized the aircraft. It was determined the FO-side was correct and the aircraft control was transferred to FO. The QRH was performed and CADC 2 was selected. There was no further incident. After the event we discussed the possibility of an altitude deviation during the recovery. There was a level off and delayed climb. I did not have a headset on and could not hear any altitude clearances or ATC communication. ATC did not inform the crew of any deviation. The crew handled the emergency well.[Responded by having an] in-depth discussion among the crew about the event and how to handle it better. Reports. Captain discussed event with Maintenance and entered it into logbook. In our event debrief it was discovered that this event has happened multiple times in this aircraft. The FO and another Deadheader both had separate airspeed unreliable events in the same aircraft in similar meteorological conditions. We read through the logbook to discover that this has happened multiple times recently and the aircraft has continued to be put back into service with no permanent resolution. The principle recommendation would be to correctly resolve the issue that is causing this. As for my part in this event, I realized I could have been more active in listening if I were using a headset. I could have verified the ATC clearance and assisted in communication.
ASRS:1785430.s: During a climb to 14,000 feet in turbulence, the Captain experienced unreliable airspeed and autopilot disconnect, likely due to CADC or pitot-static failure. Control transferred to the First Officer, QRH procedures were completed, and the flight continued, though logbooks revealed this recurring issue had occurred previously without permanent resolution.

ASRS:1785432.n: Outlet circuit breakers tripped overnight so the planes battery and engine was cold. I placed the heater duct under the RH cowling of the aircraft into the engine compartment to warm it up and left the engine cover over it to keep the heat in. Prior to departure, I decided that I was going to need an assisted start regardless so I moved the heater from the engine to the copilot door to heat the cabin (this is where I believe the latches were initially left unlatched). I left the engine cover on not noticing the latches and walked away. Prior to departure, I removed the engine cover from the pilot side and removed the tail stand and chocks and started up. There was no sign of anything wrong until I was on takeoff roll and the cowling caught wind and came up into my view. I immediately aborted the takeoff roll and taxi back to parking. I normally check the cowling during my preflight and ensure it is latched, but the heater event happened after I completed my preflight inspection. I think that many factors contributed, but the main reason for me was that I had never done what I did with the heater like that before so my preflight routine was off. I also failed to notice the latches on my walk around because the engine cover was on while I was on that side of the plane, which I normally take it off before I even go inside to get my final manifest. I will make sure that I stick to my routine when it comes to the pre-startup walk around and be very vigilant and aware when something non-routine happens. Having this event permanently in my brain will also help me never do this again.
ASRS:1785432.s: The pilot used a heater to warm the engine and cabin after circuit breakers tripped, leaving the engine cover on and cowling latches unlatched. During takeoff roll, the unlatched cowling lifted, forcing an aborted departure due to the pilot's deviation from standard preflight routines.

ASRS:1785447.n: Inadvertent Code 7500 message via Aircraft Communication Addressing and Reporting System (ACARS) message. During the flight the Captain was discussing with the First Officer about the data link pages in the Multi-Function Control Display Unit (MCDU). One of those pages is the covert declaration of aircraft hijacking or Code 7500. The Captain displayed the page and explained how to read the page and then exited out of the page without entering any information or sending the page. Shortly afterwards our flight received a query from ATC asking if the aircraft was squawking a special code to which the crew replied no and confirmed assigned transponder code. Upon parking, the flight crew was informed by dispatch that a message with the default information from the Code 7500 page had been received and asked if everything was ok. Airport Security Manager also confirmed with the crew of their status. Inadvertent Code 7500 message via Aircraft Communication Addressing and Reporting System (ACARS) message. During the flight the Captain was discussing with the First Officer about the data link pages in the Multifunction Control Display Unit (MCDU). One of those pages is the covert declaration of aircraft hijacking or Code 7500. The Captain displayed the page and explained how to read the page and then exited out of the page without entering any information or sending the page. Shortly afterwards the flight received a query from ATC asking if the aircraft was squawking a special code to which the crew replied no and confirmed assigned transponder code. Upon parking at the gate the flight crew was informed by dispatch that a message, with the default information from the Code 7500 page had been received and asked if everything was ok. Airport Security Manager also confirmed with the crew of their status.
ASRS:1785447.s: During flight, the Captain inadvertently triggered a Code 7500 ACARS message while demonstrating the hijack page on the MCDU to the First Officer. Although the crew denied squawking a special code to ATC, dispatch and airport security later confirmed receipt of the default message and verified the aircraft's status.

ASRS:1785459.n: ILS [Runway] 06 circle to land [Runway] 01 just after dark with gusty winds and windshear. Miscommunication in the cockpit dealing with 'programming' the airplane for the approach. Got distracted on the maneuver which got us close to the towers, then got a pull up prompt. Recovered and landed safely.[Cause was] Lack of cockpit communication.[Suggest] Training this approach with bad weather in simulator. Clearance by Approach Control - Intercept the Runway 06 approach course and expect the Runway 06 ILS, circle Runway 01. Clearance by Tower - Cleared for visual approach Runway 06, at TORBY cleared to circle to land Runway 01. During the circle we received TAWS Aural Warning - ''Obstacle, Obstacle, Pull Up'. The pilot flying began a climb from 820 ft. MSL to approximately 1,300 ft. MSL. Message cleared and the approach was continued to a full stop landing. The aircraft was flown too close to obstructions during the circling to land approach. 2 contributing factors: Unfamiliarity with the procedure at TEB and reliance on autopilot.With the frequency that [our company] operates in and out of TEB, it may be advisable to add some type of briefing to the pilot [group]. This is a common procedure at TEB, but it doesn't occur frequently enough to build pilot confidence in the circle to land maneuver.
ASRS:1785459.s: Pilots flying an ILS Runway 06 circle to land Runway 01 at night in gusty winds triggered a TAWS "Pull Up" warning at 820 ft due to proximity to towers. The reporter attributed the event to poor cockpit communication, unfamiliarity with the procedure, and over-reliance on the autopilot, though the aircraft recovered and landed safely.

ASRS:1785472.n: On rollout deployed reversers. Noticed left pull and used heavier braking on RH side. Aircraft tracked fine down centerline. Captain advised one reverser inop. Walk-around prior to flight revealed no indication that No. 2 reverser had been inadvertently locked out. On ground post-flight walk-around verified that reverser lockout pins on No. 2 engine were NOT extended showing red. Mechanic found hydraulics lockout in place after opening cowling. This would not be visible during an external walk-around inspection. This is a procedural issue. During maintenance there is probably a checklist for this and it was simply overlooked, perhaps due to fatigue.
ASRS:1785472.s: The crew experienced a left pull on rollout due to an inoperative No. 2 reverser caused by an overlooked hydraulic lockout pin installed during maintenance. The reporter attributed this procedural failure to a missed checklist item, possibly due to fatigue, as the defect was not visible during external inspections.

ASRS:1785482.n: Prior to crossing [Runway] XX at Yankee, we did the pre takeoff checklist flow. Held the takeoff checklist until crossing Runway XX. After crossing XX at Yankee, we ran the before takeoff checklist. After the Takeoff checklist was complete, I noticed a small twin taxing from FBO East to Yankee. I brought this up to my FO (First Officer), because Ground had told him to give way to Aircraft Y but I wasn't sure he saw us. He stopped short of taxiway Yankee and asked Ground if he was to give way to Aircraft Y. Ground advised him to give way to Aircraft Y. Both my FO and I agreed we had room to taxi by since he was not interfered with taxiway Yankee. As we taxied by the twin, he told ground our wing passed over his cockpit. It was really a surprise to both my FO and me as we had saw him, discussed him and thought we had plenty of room.[Cause was] the twin pilot's lack of situational awareness during taxingIf there is any question, I should have stopped the airplane and coordinated with ground.
ASRS:1785482.s: The pilot and First Officer taxied past a small twin aircraft at taxiway Yankee, resulting in their wing passing over the twin's cockpit. The reporter attributed the incident to the twin pilot's lack of situational awareness and admitted they should have stopped to coordinate with Ground.

ASRS:1785493.n: While on a left downwind for the visual approach (Runway 23) into CRW, we received a GPWS Pullup alert. The lowest noted AGL altitude was around 1,100 feet during the approach. We were aware of the mountainous terrain, the Captain selected the FAF attitude in the altitude sector once we were cleared for the visual. Sloping terrain set off the GPWS alert as we descended roughly 1,000 FPM.Perhaps a note in company pages would be a good way to remind crews who are on the visual.
ASRS:1785493.s: The flight crew received a GPWS Pullup alert while on a left downwind visual approach to Runway 23 at CRW. Sloping terrain triggered the alert during a 1,000 FPM descent to approximately 1,100 feet AGL, prompting a recommendation for company safety reminders.

ASRS:1785580.n: While working Aircraft X for a large issue with side-stay play and being the third documented discrepancy, it was requested to inspected and identify if the L/H (Left Hand) and R/H (Right Hand) side stays were still usable. It was found that they were also worn out and required replacement. Senior management refused to accept that fact and still was pressuring me for 8 hours to install the identified and documented unserviceable MLG (Main Landing Gear) side-stay assemblies and remained relentless to try any motive of pressure to have them installed with disregard with what was documented causing large amounts of stress and frustration and distraction on correctly repairing the aircraft referencing the corrected documents. Direct Supervisor and Direct Shift Manager were only relaying what was being directed and are not responsible for any pressure added.The reason for the distractions and pressure to install the side-stay assemblies that were found in poor condition for wear, was because the two side stays that were ordered could not be used until engineering had approved use and the two serviceable assemblies were the only two in the system. Senior Management was made aware that the repairs for this aircraft were going to be lengthy and to export the aircraft next door the heavy maintenance department, the discretion was ignored and they basically buried themselves into what did turn out to be a large repair on the aircraft after no side-stay assemblies were usable during the event, pressure was applied to try brush the issue out by installing the unserviceable side stays and accomplishing a visual inspection with no reference to do a visual for wear and play while installed on the aircraft. Engineering concurred the side-stay assemblies are inspected with the CMM (Component Maintenance Manual) while removed. The amount of stress and frustration with my senior management not wanting to accept the fact of what were honest documented finds after being requested to do so.The local senior management in ZZZ will not accept the reality of what large repairs are and refuse to listen and force pressure and manipulation tactics to try to get supervisors, shift managers and mechanics sign a document or stamp a block in any form possible to get what they want. It creates large safety risks and is why many of our aircraft have repeat write-ups. Senior Management relies on myself as one of the people who know how the A320F works to a detailed engineering level, until it is not the answer they want to hear. The only way to avoid the occurance would be to stop harassing people on the floor and realize that sometimes, it is what it is after poor managerial decisions were made.
ASRS:1785580.s: A mechanic reported that senior management pressured them to install unserviceable Main Landing Gear side-stay assemblies on Aircraft X due to a lack of approved replacements. This disregard for documented wear and engineering requirements created significant safety risks and stress, forcing the mechanic to resist installing the defective parts.

ASRS:1785581.n: I attended 737 Max class earlier in the week. This class has dwindled from an X-hour class to a Y-hour summary. There was virtually no discussions on the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS) other than it's non-deferrable. When I asked if there were any RIIs involved with MCAS maintenance, the instructor could only answer with, 'probably.' I feel the Y-hour Max class is insufficient for qualifications.
ASRS:1785581.s: A pilot reported that a reduced 737 Max training class lacked sufficient discussion on the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS) and maintenance RIIs. The pilot concluded the shortened course is insufficient for qualification due to the instructor's vague responses regarding system details.

ASRS:1785597.n: Aircraft Y was flying through established practice areas at 7,500 feet, flying various heading changes affecting other aircraft in the area. we adjusted course to avoid the traffic accordingly and the aircraft then turned around to a heading that would lead to a converging conflict. Our aircraft was to the right and proceeded with caution keeping an eye on the aircraft in case they made yet another heading change, they did not. we started to alter course to the right in order to maintain our general direction of flight but also resolve the converging conflict. The aircraft was not transmitting on the local frequency and not responding to radio queries. The aircraft never deviated course at any point. Had we not seen the aircraft and taken evasive action the conflict would not have been resolved.
ASRS:1785597.s: Our aircraft encountered Aircraft Y at 7,500 feet in practice areas, where Y made heading changes causing a converging conflict while remaining silent on the local frequency. We executed evasive action to the right to resolve the conflict, as Y did not respond to radio queries or alter course.

ASRS:1785616.n: During deplaning at ZZZ airport, a passenger advised the lead flight attendant that either she may have been or was exposed to COVID-19. The affected passenger advised she was transferring to an international destination. This passenger would have had to disclose at check-in if she was possibly exposed, but passengers lie because they want to get home or travel to their destination. Also, on this flight I observed at least 10 passengers walk off the plane without any mask on and about 20 passengers walk off the plane with their mask only around their mouth. I see this type of activity on EVERY flight EVERY week. This is even with numerous PA's telling the passengers they must wear the mask around their mouth and nose. Many customers just don't care. I've had passengers completely remove this mask right in front of me. I've even experienced passengers telling me, '[profanity] the mask' right in my face as they walk off the plane mask less. This is the type of activity I see on every flight.
ASRS:1785616.s: A lead flight attendant reported that during deplaning at ZZZ airport, a passenger admitted potential COVID-19 exposure while transferring internationally. The attendant also observed numerous passengers removing masks or wearing them incorrectly despite PA announcements, citing widespread non-compliance and passenger disregard for safety protocols.

ASRS:1785638.n: We were assigned and on the NAPAA4 Departure off Runway 19R at APC. During pre-flight and once again prior to departure we (as per SOP) confirmed the runway and SID was properly loaded into the Dual FMS. After takeoff, during the climb, I was 'heads down' as I was PNF and was just assigned a frequency change from the Tower to Departure Control while at the same time we encountered a TCAS for VFR traffic off the parallel runway (NOT DUE TO ANY NAVIGATIONAL ERROR IDENTIFIED IN THIS REPORT). During the scan for traffic and putting in the new frequency into the FMS, I noticed we were making a longer left turn than I anticipated. I said to the SIC (in left seat flying the aircraft) why is it turning so far and where are we going? We both looked at the SID displayed as well as the FMS and it was evident the FMS decided to sequence us to our next fix - SAC VOR and in doing so commenced a 'smart turn' in that direction.Upon contacting OAK departure, they verified our position/altitude and shortly thereafter contacted us and said 'Just so we are on the same page, you made a left turn after departing APC towards SAC and did not complete the SID.' I responded that yes, we were looking into the FMS turn as we had verified that the SID was loaded correctly in the FMS.Upon completing our day, we decided it was best to get both OAK and APC Tower on the phone to discuss. Both controllers appreciated us contacting them and mentioned that this was not the first time they have seen this happen with the NAPAA4 departure and they were going to look into it. Both controllers indicated since safety was not an issue, they were not interested in any action on us. In addition to the above discussion with ATC, I am also going to contact Collins and/or Jeppesen in regards to a possible issue with the database and/or SID for the NAPAA4 departure.
ASRS:1785638.s: The crew executing the NAPAA4 departure from APC experienced an unexpected left turn toward SAC VOR due to the FMS sequencing to the next fix during a frequency change and TCAS event. Controllers confirmed the SID was not completed but cited no safety issue, while the crew plans to investigate potential database errors with Collins and Jeppesen.

ASRS:1785644.n: In the traffic pattern at ZZZ, my CFI and I were on the right downwind for Runway XXR when we were told to Continue for Runway XXR. We then continued and a few moments later was told to turn right base for XXR. When turning right base we noted traffic, but I didn't think it was a factor at first because we assumed it was for the parallel because we still were told to turn right base. As we got established on base we saw the traffic was close and my CFI took controls to avoid a mid-air collison. We got no warning from the Tower and later found out that the tower told the other aircraft to continue for Runway XXR. Shortly after the Tower told them to continue for XXR that's when the tower said to turn base. I didn't think that traffic that was on final would be a factor for us and thought it was for Runway XXL. In the future, I think the Tower should be more clear and understand the traffic spacing better because if he did then he could've told us to extend a couple of miles so we could've passed behind the traffic instead of passing in front and coming within 1,000 feet horizontally of each other. I believe the talking between me and my CFI also contributed because maybe we would've heard the call for the other aircraft to continue and could've challenged that with the Tower but even then we still were told to turn base. I believe the tower should've noted the other aircraft and looked at the spacing, and told us this isn't going to work and this near-miss could've been avoided altogether instead we got turned directly into the path of another aircraft. I was flying with my student in the pattern at ZZZ. When we were downwind, Tower didn't clear us for a touch and go, but told us to continue. We continued downwind and waited for further instructions when Tower then told us to turn base.We turned base. There was some hesitation but then the Controller instructed us to turn directly towards the numbers. At this point, we were on right base unaware we were being turned onto an aircraft that was on final. Before my students turn for final, I always have them look on final to make sure it is clear of traffic. At this point, I noticed the traffic on the left hand side and saw it on my iPad. I took the controls from my student and climbed to offset to the right where we avoided a near miss collision of about 1,000 feet horizontal distance and 300 feet vertical distance over a densely packed neighborhood of City. We never were told to extend or follow this aircraft.Prior to the Controller telling us to turn base, he had spoken to the aircraft on the straight in final and told them to continue. He realized the aircraft was there, but did not communicate the location and told us to turn base onto him. This situation demonstrates that pilots must exercise extreme vigilance at airports where ATC is so busy to provide clear instructions.The term 'continue' can be vague in that…does it mean we're supposed to fly the pattern as regularly, or are we supposed to continue downwind? In that case, the term 'extend' would make more sense.When I talked to the Controller on the phone later, I was told that this situation occurred due to a late runway switch by the other aircraft. However, in examination of the track log, the aircraft was on a straight in approach. The pilot also called up that they were approaching a point on the approach for XXR. The Controller didn't acknowledge the mistake that had been made and the possible deadly consequences that could have occurred from this near miss.This is a serious near miss.
ASRS:1785644.s: A student pilot and CFI in a training aircraft at ZZZ were instructed to turn base for Runway XXR, placing them on a collision course with another aircraft on final. The CFI took control to avoid a near-miss caused by the controller's failure to manage spacing and provide clear instructions regarding the conflicting traffic.

ASRS:1785645.n: Aircraft X, was a training flight with a student performing a practice ILS Approach to FDK Runway 23, authorized and approved by FDK Tower. Aircraft X was 10 miles from Runway 23, approaching the NUMBE intersection on the 295-degree radial from the EMI VORTAC, the authorized feeder-route to the FDK ILS Runway 23 Approach.After receiving such approval, Aircraft Y, requested the same practice ILS Approach and self-announced they were 2 miles from NUMBE, but based on the ADS-B display in Aircraft X, Aircraft Y was approaching the inbound localizer course from the northwest, from which there is no authorized transition or feeder route.Aircraft Y told FDK Tower they would follow behind Aircraft X and slow down but at various points and times between NUMBE, the IAF (10 nm from Runway 23), and Runway 23, Aircraft Y was as close as 500 horizontal feet behind Aircraft X and was proceeding at a higher rate of speed than Aircraft X.Twice during the practice ILS Approach, the ADS-B-based Traffic Alerting System in Aircraft X (the leading aircraft) sounded an aural and visual caution (yellow), meaning Aircraft Y was closing in on the tail of Aircraft X.The flight student in Aircraft X was spooked by these warnings, as well as the radio calls from Aircraft Y saying they were 'too close', and had difficulty controlling the aircraft and/or experiencing productive learning.Because of this high risk, and the student's unease with the entire situation, Aircraft X aborted the practice ILS 23 Approach and took evasive action (executing the missed approach 1.5-miles from Runway 23 and side-stepping to the left), to get out of the way of the closing aircraft, Aircraft Y.Subsequently, while on the ground, Aircraft Y's Certificated Flight Instructor and co-pilot approached the crew of Aircraft X and laughed at Aircraft X for 'flying too slow.'The crew of Aircraft X felt this was an inappropriate and unsafe display of arrogance, especially in light of Aircraft Y's violation of FAR Section 91.113 (f).
ASRS:1785645.s: During a student training ILS approach to FDK Runway 23, Aircraft Y violated separation by closing to 500 feet behind Aircraft X, triggering traffic alerts and forcing a missed approach. The incident concluded with Aircraft Y's instructor mocking the crew on the ground for their speed despite the unsafe proximity.

ASRS:1785647.n: Training flight on IFR Tower enroute clearance from TOA to ZZZ. Clearance was fly runway heading to intercept LAX 170 radial to LIMBO, V64, SLI, Direct. On departure from TOA my student was flying under the view-limiting device and I was pilot monitoring and looking outside for traffic. We departed Runway 29R, shortly after there was a departure from a parallel 29L of a light aircraft that was faster than our aircraft. While switching to Departure Control frequency we were advised of proximity of the overtaking aircraft and its altitude being same as ours. I was looking outside and was able to spot the aircraft in about 20 seconds and student flying advised ATC of us having visual contact. Another 20 seconds later I lost visual contact and took over controls momentarily using 3 step process to raise the left wing to check on the overtaking aircraft that was turning south at that time. I gave the controls back to my student using 3 step process. When my student was saying 'my controls' he blocked end of Controller's transmission for me. The part that I heard was only 'turn left 150.' Then, student read back 'Turn left 150 Aircraft X' and initiated a left turn to 150. At that time I started to question myself if this instruction could really be intended to us since it would probably put us below the MVA in the area. I clearly heard my student's readback to ATC about left turn to 150 and since Controller didn't say anything about his read back being wrong, I thought I shouldn't probably even worry. Just a moment later, because of the oddness of the situation I decided to clarify the instruction with the ATC, but by the time I was able to key the mic, Controller already was getting back to us questioning our actions. Only then I realized that my student responded to a call intended to another aircraft and Controller didn't even hear his readback because the transmission was blocked by the radio call of the aircraft that really received that instruction.I think contributing factors to this little misunderstanding was our scratchy radio.
