Because of it the student misheard the call sign and I couldn't even hear it, due to intercom on that particular plane being clearer than the radio and student was talking at the same time.Good thing there was no conflicting traffic and VMC conditions let me see the terrain.
ASRS:1785647.s: During an IFR training departure from TOA, a student pilot misheard a clearance intended for another aircraft due to radio interference and blocked transmissions, initiating an unauthorized left turn. The instructor intervened after realizing the error, noting that poor audio quality and simultaneous intercom use caused the misunderstanding, though no conflict occurred.

ASRS:1785649.n: Taking off in ZZZ an incident occurred where we blew through altitude and we [were] slow to follow our heading assignment.I was PM on this flight, and it was the second flight of the day on this trip.Pre-flight was normal and we loaded up our passengers ahead of schedule with no pressure to rush.Upon receiving our takeoff clearance for Runway XX in ZZZ we were assigned a heading of 230 and an altitude of 2,000 feet. I performed the before takeoff checks and the PF armed the AT and the lateral mode (roll mode.) (SOP from manufacturer for takeoff with a heading assignment is either to activate heading mode and then spin the heading to the assigned heading at 400 feet, alternatively you can input the heading but leave it in roll mode until 400 feet upon which you can activate heading mode. Neither of which is particularly helpful during a high workload environment).Takeoff procedure was initially normal, we lined up on the runway and proceeded with a rolling start. The PF set takeoff thrust, and I made my first call at 40 kts. Sometime between 40 kts and 80 kts the AT Disconnect sounded. PF elected to continue. We rotated normally and after the call for 'Gear Up' and the '400 feet' call the pilot asked for me to engage the AT again. I hit the AT button, and continued with my climb sequence checklist. (Speed 180, FLC, Flaps to 0 and After Takeoff Checklist.)Around the time I hit FLC Tower called us to switch to departure. At approximately the same time the AT again disconnected (without an aural alert). I called AT disconnect and reminded the PF that he had to manually control the throttles for speed. As I swapped frequencies the PF attempted to rearm the AT's and blew through our initial altitude. The AT's again disconnected immediately after hitting the button and I called ATC informing them that we had blown through our ALT by 200 feet and were descending back to intercept as well and the late initial turn to a heading of 230.ATC acknowledged and asked us to IDENT and to turn to a heading of 260.At this point the PF had manual speed control, I finally armed the correct lateral mode. (Heading set to 230) PF and I had a quick discussion and decided now that the workload was lower we could troubleshoot. We armed the AT one last time however this time it did not disconnect, and we proceeded with the flight normally.There were a few contributing factors that caused this error.Firstly, we are both new on this equipment and are still learning the correct procedures and cadence of the flight.Secondly, due to COVID we have not been flying as much as we normally do further extend the period of settling into the new aircraft.Third, we believe manufacturer's procedure for setting the lateral mode during a very high workload stage of flight 400 feet during the climb sequence further exasperated the situation. The AP/FD should be programmed so that when you are in T/O mode that it will hold roll to 400 feet then will initiate the turn to a heading and revert to LNAV to HDG mode.Finally, the most critical error I believe was the PF's throttle technique. He would arm the AT and then bring the throttled straight to the stops whereas manufacturer procedure is to bring the throttle levers to around 40% TLA and then let the AT's set takeoff thrust. I hadn't noticed it in previous flight, but I noticed it on this takeoff because the throttle levers moved much to quickly to takeoff power. I believe that this movement overrode the AT logic and if he accidentally moved the throttles past the detent even momentarily it may have caused the AT's to disconnect. Then for the rest of the T/O roll the throttles were possibly still slightly past the detent not allowing engagement until they were finally moved to a lower power setting whereupon we could finally engage the AT's. We discussed this discrepancy during the cruise portion of the flight and the PF will use the correct throttle technique going forward.
ASRS:1785649.s: Two pilots on a ZZZ departure experienced repeated Autothrottle disconnects and an altitude overshoot due to improper throttle technique and high workload. The Pilot Flying's aggressive throttle movement likely overrode the Autothrottle logic, causing the aircraft to exceed the assigned 2,000-foot altitude before stabilizing.

ASRS:1785650.n: Our aircraft departed ZZZ at approximately XA:40Z on an IFR flight plan headed to ZZZ airport. Name was the pilot flying and I was the pilot monitoring. We climbed and cruised uneventfully at an initial altitude of FL430. After about 20 minutes at altitude, a passenger came to the flight deck and asked if we could cool down the cabin. As I set the cabin temperature controller to a cooler temperature. After about 5 minutes, the 'R COOL TURBINE HOT' CAS message came on. We performed the appropriate checklist and after a minute the CAS message went out.At this point, the cabin was at a hotter temperature than before and the passengers complained again. The PF decided to go back into the cabin to verify that all the gasper vents were open and to check if there were any other indications of potential issues. It was apparent that there was a significant temperature difference from the forward portion of the cabin compared to the aft. The forward cabin was at least 10 degrees warmer than the aft. Additionally, the PF noticed some warm air coming out of the vents. After checking the upper cabin gasper vents, the PF returned to his seat. After a short discussion on possible issues, we elected to descend to FL390.When the aircraft leveled at FL390, the Cabin Attendant came up to the flight deck and asked the PF if he noticed any haze in the cabin. The PF looked back and saw no smoke or haze. The Cabin Attendant went about her duties.After a few more minutes, the PF noticed smoke coming from my right-side vent and we received another 'R COOL TURBINE HOT' CAS message. The PF immediately donned his O2 mask and asked me to request an immediate descent and to pull out the checklist. At this time, the cabin started to fill up with visible smoke and the cabin attendant came up to the flight deck to respond. Now it has become our priority to get this airplane on the ground as soon and safely as possible. The cabin attendant donned her O2 mask. After O2 masks were on, the appropriate checklists were performed. The cabin started to depressurize immediately after the Right Pack was turned off (as required by the 'R COOL TURBINE HOT' checklist). I had to also switch the pressurization to manual and that increased my workload, as I had to control and visually monitor the opening of the safety valve. At this point, a rapid descent was performed. During the descent, smoke remained in the cabin. Due to the smoke in the cabin, a loss of pressurization, we requested for vectors to the nearest suitable airport which was ZZZ1. During the descent, the passenger O2 masks deployed, and the Cabin attendant instructed the passengers to put their O2 masks on. At about 15;000ft, the smoke started to dissipate. We continued our descent per ATC to 6,000 feet and continued with vectors for an ILS XX approach at ZZZ1. Now the cabin was completely clear of smoke. The crew took off their O2 masks and completed all remainder checklists for landing. The aircraft landed uneventfully on [Runway] XX.Upon the landing roll out, Fire and Rescue was approved on the runway to follow us to our parking spot on ramp. After shutting down engines and securing the aircraft, we assessed the situation and verified that all passengers were OK and there were no injuries.
ASRS:1785650.s: The flight crew experienced a right cool turbine overheat and cabin smoke during cruise at FL430, triggering an emergency descent to FL390 and a diversion to ZZZ1. The incident resulted in cabin depressurization and passenger oxygen deployment, but the aircraft landed safely with no injuries.

ASRS:1785655.n: Flying the NAPAA4.NAPAA departure out of APC airport we loaded the departure into the FMS and verified the routing was correct.As we departed the airport on Runway 19R with a clearance to climb to 3,000 feet we had the autopilot engaged in LNAV and vertical speed. Autothrottles where set at 200 kts.As we started our climb there was a piston single that had departed Runway 19L ahead of us. As we climbed out I had the other aircraft in sight but did get a traffic alert on the TCAS. I think at the time we received the TCAS alert he was already passing off our left wing and 400 feet below us. The autopilot made an initial slight right turn towards the VOR and then sequenced the next leg of our flight plan from the SGD VOR to SAC as was filed on our flight plan.Due to the tight turn that would be required to fly the leg from SGD to SAC I thought it had initiated the turn early in anticipation of our proximity to the VOR and that we were approaching our assigned altitude of 3,000 feet.Between the TCAS alert and seeing that the FMS was sequenced now to fly to the next fix on our flight plan I was focused on ensuring we maintained our separation from the other aircraft and after verifying that the FMS was sequenced to our cleared route I continued in the left turn and established the aircraft on the leg from SGD to SAC.Tower handed us off to Oakland [Center] and it was then that they inquired as to why we had made a left turn after takeoff rather than flying the departure as published. We had a brief exchange with the Controller about how the FMS had sequenced us on the next leg of the flight plan prior to reaching the VOR.Upon landing at our final destination later in the day I placed a call to Oakland Center as well as the Tower at APC. The Oakland Controller that I spoke with did not think there had been any issue with what happened since we had not been given a phone number to call from our Controller. When I called the Tower at APC, I was able to speak with the controller that cleared us for takeoff and handed us off to Oakland when we departed. He stated that they have had a few aircraft making the same left turn after takeoff while flying that same departure. He indicated that they needed to look into it and said that there had not been any conflict with other traffic. He thanked me for getting back to him and talking to him about it and that he would be following up the next day with his colleagues regarding this departure.Our filed and cleared route was APC NAPAA4 SGD SAC ZZZ ZZZ1.
ASRS:1785655.s: The pilot reported that while flying the NAPAA4 departure from APC, the FMS sequenced to the next leg early, causing an unauthorized left turn toward the SGD VOR. The controller confirmed this deviation had occurred with other aircraft and stated no traffic conflict existed.

ASRS:1785678.n: During a practice RNAV (GPS) [Runway] 35 approach to Colorado Air and Space Port (CFO), we had just crossed the Final Approach Fix (FAF) at ARRES at the charted altitude of 7,500 feet MSL. The student at the controls was 2-3 seconds late in beginning the glideslope intercept, and our glideslope indicated slightly high. Knowing that we had to descend 500 feet in order to be below the upcoming 7,000 feet MSL Class B shelf, I reduced power to increase our rate of descent. There was also an air carrier [Aircraft Y] at our 1 o'clock, approximately 1,000 feet above our altitude according to ADS-B, which was making a right turn from a southerly heading to a northwesterly as it make its approach to DEN. Denver Approach contacted us saying, 'I need you below the Bravo shelf at 7,000 feet.' I replied 'roger, we are increasing our rate of descent, currently indicating 6,800 feet.' The Aircraft Y crossed above and ahead of us, right to left, approximately 1,000 feet above and 200 feet ahead. I did not hear any of the communications between the Aircraft Y and Denver Approach, nor did I notice any maneuvering by the Aircraft Y indicating it was reacting to our presence. The complex airspace around DEN is extremely challenging, and this approach's FAF is approximately 1.4 NM from the 7,000 feet MSL Class B shelf. Descending 500 feet in less than 1.4 NM at small aircraft approach speeds does not require excessive rates of descent, but it does require a timely descent. Any delay, or crossing the FAF above the 7,500 feet MSL altitude, quickly makes it likely that an airplane may violate Class B airspace during the Final Approach Segment. In our case, the timing of the arriving Aircraft Y was coincidentally exactly the same time we were at this critical place. As a CFI-I, I am reluctant to use this approach for training ever again. One suggestion may be to cross ARRES at an altitude lower than the charted minimum of 7,500 feet MSL - if, and only if, it's a practice approach under VFR. The potential negative training this would cause would have to be weighed against the extra margin of separation from the Class B shelf. Additionally, in the future, if I use this approach for practice again, I will have the student execute a missed approach and turn away from the 7,000 feet MSL Class B shelf if the aircraft is high at ARRES, does not initiate a timely descent, or if I notice DEN traffic that could cross above us as happened on this flight.
ASRS:1785678.s: A flight instructor and student practicing an RNAV (GPS) approach to CFO crossed the FAF at 7,500 feet MSL but were late initiating descent, requiring increased power reduction to clear the 7,000-foot Class B shelf. An air carrier aircraft passed 1,000 feet above and 200 feet ahead, prompting the instructor to avoid future training on this approach due to the tight airspace constraints.

ASRS:1785690.n: We were doing approaches on an IFR flight plan because ATC currently won't allow practice approaches due to, we were told, coronavirus staffing levels. Being on an actual IFR flight plan increased the complexity of what should have been simple currency training in visual conditions to get instrument currency.The aircraft, an Aircraft X type, was newly purchased and had been flown VFR by my student (I trained him and signed him off for an instrument rating, he passed on the first attempt almost a year ago), but he had yet to take it IFR. It is nicely equipped with two Dynon combination PFD/MFD's and a Garmin GPS NAV/COM. I have 1000-2000 hours on Garmin products, both GPS and G1000 systems, but only about a dozen hours on an Aircraft Y type with similar Dynon systems and no prior hours on an Aircraft X type.We took off from ZZZ1 and shot two approaches into ZZZ2 (about 15 NM away) and were being vectored for a last approach into ZZZ1 to a full stop. I was simultaneously looking for traffic, explaining a point about GPS approach procedure, listening to another pilot on the radio report his position, and looking out for a scattered layer that was getting lower as the flight progressed and that we were just about to go into. The autopilot was on and I noticed the aircraft climbing through 2,800 feet. I thought I remembered that ZZZ approach had given us an altitude of 2,000 but I wasn't quite sure (my student was handling the radios), so I jumped on the radio and made an inquiry. Approach confirmed we had been given an altitude of 2,000. I immediately had my student hold the altitude we were at while I waited to jump in on the frequency as it was congested. I reported that we were inadvertently at 2,800 and asked what altitude they wanted us at. They replied 2,000. I said we would descend to 2,000 which we did immediately. ATC did not ask us to call a number when we got on the ground or make any other mention of it.The autopilot should have stopped the plane climbing at 2000. Neither of us could determine why it didn't as it worked fine leveling off at altitudes both before and after. I can only guess it was user input error on the part of my student. When he changed it to descend to 2,000 and hold that altitude it worked just fine.I believe the reason why I didn't notice the altitude deviation sooner than reaching 800 feet over our assigned altitude was a combination of sensory overload of having to teach, look for traffic, listen to radio chatter, look out for entering clouds (which should have been less of a consideration since we were on an actual IFR plan), combined with a lack of experience on the Dynon systems which limited my rapid acquisition of altitude information.I shall endeavor in the future to practice with the Dynon systems more in VFR conditions before venturing into IFR.
ASRS:1785690.s: During an IFR training flight in a newly purchased Aircraft X, the instructor and student inadvertently climbed to 2,800 feet instead of holding the assigned 2,000 feet. The instructor attributed the deviation to sensory overload and unfamiliarity with the Dynon autopilot, suspecting a student input error caused the system to fail leveling off.

ASRS:1785691.n: At approximately XA:45, I realized it seemed to have been sometime since I had heard from the Controller. This is not entirely unusual. Due to the pandemic, there are times of much less radio chatter. In fact, several times a week, there are periods where nothing is said by anyone on frequency for lengths of time as long as 20-40 minutes save the occasional 'You still there?' It seemed to have been a bit longer than normal, so we called on our last assigned frequency. We heard nothing so I tried Guard and heard nothing. Unbeknownst to me the volume of the radio receiving Guard was accidentally turned down. As I was trying Guard my copilot found a frequency on the chart, made radio contact and was given the proper frequency we should be on. We re-established communication with ZZZ Center. All seemed fine, until the hand-off came with a phone number for possible pilot deviation.Upon arrival at our destination I called the number I had been given. The Controller I spoke with asked if I knew why I was given the number to call. I told him I believed it was due to lost radio contact. He said it was. We then discussed how this might have happened and things to do to re-establish radio contact. He then said it seemed to him we had never been given a hand-off. He also said that sector was very busy at the time the incident occurred. I have no doubt they were. I suspect they were even a bit understaffed due to the pandemic. we concluded our conversation and thanked each other.My copilot and I spent considerable time discussing how this might have happened and how to prevent it in the future. But it must be noted there is no recourse for pilots that find themselves in this situation. There is also no sure way of completely preventing this type of situation. Pilots have no way of knowing when a hand-off should occur or when they have reached a specific time limit. Sometimes we check on, only to be immediately handed off with 'short stay, contact center on XYX.AB'. Other times we listen for long periods time listening to a completely silent radio. Those long periods of silence do not help at all. They only make the silence seem normal. Maybe controllers should be required to inform us, at check-on, how long or how many miles we can expect to be with them. They always seem to have an idea how long we will be in contact with them. At approximately XA:45 local, at FL360, in cruise, we noticed that we hadn't heard from Center in quite some time. During these times of COVID, it has become commonplace to go for long periods of time without hearing anything from Center or other traffic, especially in remote portions of the US. With the frequent occurrence that the only radio traffic heard is a pilot asking 'Still on?' just to make sure someone is still out there, it is impossible for a pilot to determine at what time/distance interval, he should be expecting contact, a hand-off, or any other instruction from ATC.This was the case on date. During a long cross-country flight, we went for what seemed a long time without hearing anything from Center. We acknowledged the fact and I keyed the mic to interrogate Center. There was no response. I tried again and even switched to the previous frequency, just in case. Still no joy. Pulled up the sectional to find the nearest Center and discovered ZZZ Center, Area X on frequency. Called out to this Controller who brusquely inquired who we were, where we were, and informed us that we were on the wrong frequency, providing us with the correct one. We immediately switched to the appropriate frequency, received a response and continued on our way. Shortly thereafter, we received a call from Center that we had a possible pilot deviation and they had a number for us. Number was copied, remainder of the flight continued without incident.Upon landing, we reached out to the Center phone number, who informed us that, after reviewing the recordings, we had not been handed off to the next sector, and it was no fault of ours. Easy enough. Controller called back a few minutes later, stating that the previous sector had filed a report on the incident, and needed pilot license number, etc., for the reports.This brings me to the point where I ask, what can be done in this situation? There is clearly no exact location where an aircraft is handed off to another sector/center/controller. There is no exact amount of time flying through a sector before a switch is made. What can we, as pilots, do to help with this situation? Obviously, I cannot do my job as a pilot AND do the job of the controllers on the ground, so where is the happy medium? Is there a guideline of the appropriate amount of time to go without hearing from ATC before inquiring? Should we set a timer after each hand-off, or create a GPS way-point a certain distance down the line?It can be argued that 'I have a number for you to call, advise when ready to copy' are the most stressful 13 words heard in a pilot's day. It generates fear, concern, trepidation and second guessing of the skills and abilities that we spend years honing and decades perfecting. When we make mistakes, that is a definite way to bring attention to the problems and help find a solution. What recourse do we have when a controller makes the mistake? We spent the remainder of the flight and, arguably, the next 24 plus hours, stressing over what we should have done, when we should have checked in, how were we supposed to know, etc.
ASRS:1785691.s: Pilots flying at FL360 in cruise lost radio contact with ZZZ Center due to an uncompleted hand-off by ATC. Although the pilots were initially notified of a possible deviation, the controller later confirmed the incident was not their fault.

ASRS:1785697.n: I had parked the plane and positioned my PowerTow to place the plane in the hangar. I noticed that my flaps were down and returned to the cockpit to raise the flaps. Forgetting that the PowerTow was in front of my plane, and not seeing it, I started the engine. The propeller tore into the PowerTow, damaging the propeller. I immediately shut the engine down.
ASRS:1785697.s: The pilot, while parking an aircraft, forgot a PowerTow was positioned in front of the plane and started the engine with flaps down. The propeller struck and damaged the PowerTow, causing propeller damage before the pilot immediately shut down the engine.

ASRS:1785705.n: On the 3rd touch and go landing after touch down on Runway 28 I could see a Aircraft Y approach our runway from left to right at Taxiway C. I commented to the student to keep an eye on him to make sure he stops. Aircraft Y proceeded to cross the runway in front of us without stopping. I immediately took control of the airplane and began a full brake application. We were getting close enough to Aircraft Y that I was considering turning the aircraft off the runway to avoid contact. We were able to avoid hitting the airplane and remain on the runway. We were slightly past Taxiway D when we came to a full stop, I do not recall hearing any radio transmission from the Aircraft Y announcing his intentions. I commented to Aircraft Y 'Thanks for crossing in front of a landing aircraft and you can buy us a new set of tires.' He commented that 'he did not see us.' This is just the latest of several incursions I have witnessed on this runway. Most are caused by pilots unfamiliar with our airport, this is the first from an what I would assume to be a highly experienced pilot and was told by the lineman that aircraft is here fairly often. I feel there is a need for more emphasis and training in making pilots aware of ground procedures and traffic pattern etiquette especially at uncontrolled airports with multiple runways. Having to cross a runway to get to the designated calm wind runway which also is the longest runway (10,000 ft.) presents a huge potential for an accident.
ASRS:1785705.s: During a touch-and-go landing on Runway 28, the pilot and student narrowly avoided a collision when Aircraft Y crossed the active runway without stopping or radio communication. The pilot attributed the incursion to the other pilot failing to see them, noting a need for better ground procedure training at this uncontrolled airport.

ASRS:1785717.n: It was snowing sideways on an early morning departure out of DTW. Ramp was mostly covered, making following taxi lines more difficult. We were cleared to taxi to the Central Deice Pad via [Taxiways] K, E2, and E3. Nowhere on our charts is E3 shown. E2 is shown going all the way to the deice pad. After searching unsuccessfully to find Taxiway E3, we queried Ground and they informed us to follow the routing shown as E2 on our charts to the deice pad (Spot 7). It would be nice if this were corrected (E3 shown) on our charts to avoid adding this additive condition every time any crew deices in the frozen tundra of Detroit.
ASRS:1785717.s: A flight crew departing DTW in snowy conditions could not locate the cleared Taxiway E3 to the deice pad because it was missing from their charts. Ground control instructed them to follow the charted Taxiway E2 routing instead, prompting a request to update the charts to reflect the correct taxiway designation.

ASRS:1785771.n: Late dangerous good. Load planner was not contacted to inform of 9 ballast bags added to secure dangerous goods.
ASRS:1785771.s: The load planner was not contacted regarding the late addition of nine ballast bags used to secure dangerous goods. This communication failure occurred during the loading phase, leaving the weight and balance plan unupdated.

ASRS:1785783.n: The parking area we have at ZZZ is not sufficient for the aircraft we have parked here. On a daily basis we are using a taxiway to position aircraft for storage and temporarily parking for live flights. This has now spilled over into unsafe parking of aircraft nightly in areas that are not officially parking spots for aircraft such as the XX Pad service road, parking aircraft behind other aircraft on the XY Pad and double stacking aircraft int the Hangar alley ways. This is being said by our management team that this needs to be done for parking because we don't have any more space here at the airport. We have been constantly fighting this space issue for years with no resolution in sight. These spaces we are currently using do not have stop marks, they do not have clearance zones and where they are parked the areas are used frequently by many vehicles from Maintenance to [Company] trucks. This leaves us open to having an accident. The planning of these mega storing of aircraft here needed to be better thought out. This is just extremely poor planning by not only local management but also the local operation center and the corporate operation and real estate divisions who believe that we can handle the amount of aircraft here without having an accident.
ASRS:1785783.s: Airport management and operations teams are parking aircraft on taxiways, service roads, and hangar alleys due to insufficient official space at ZZZ. This practice creates accident risks because these areas lack stop marks and clearance zones while being frequently used by maintenance and company vehicles.

ASRS:1785856.n: On descent to 6,000 feet with vectors to final for ILS 35 into AVL we received an obstacle warning caution message. The obstacle was a tower directly in front of us. I (FO) leveled off the descent at 6,200 feet and deviated from course to avoid the tower. ATC confirmed that they also received and obstacle warning cation. We proceeded 'with see and avoid' procedures and then returned to our original vector for final with no further incident.The deviation was caused during descent by a tower triggering an obstacle caution message with both the aircraft and ATC. We leveled off the aircraft above our assigned descent altitude of 6,000 feet and deviated from our assigned vector to avoid the tower. Though ATC also received an obstacle caution they claimed the tower's height was 5,100 feet and should not have triggered the caution message. The MSA of the area was 7,600 feet. Since we were in VMC conditions we felt safe descending to the assigned altitude. We had the tower insight and were in the process of requesting a different vector when the caution was triggered, and we deviated from course for safety.
ASRS:1785856.s: During descent to 6,000 feet for ILS 35 into AVL, the First Officer leveled off at 6,200 feet and deviated from course after an obstacle warning for a tower triggered in both the aircraft and ATC systems. The crew avoided the tower using see-and-avoid procedures before returning to the original vector.

ASRS:1785903.n: Problem with slide bustle and slide, no action or inspection by maintenance. Possible contact with COVID-19 passenger in which no actions were taken by company to protect passenger and crew from possible virus contact.Suggestion - New overhaul of employee management actions.Ill passenger sat on the slide bustle in front galley for more than 5 minutes. I asked if a mechanic could look at the slide and bustle to make sure that they were intact but was ignored. It was more important to get the flight out.
ASRS:1785903.s: Cabin crew reported an ill passenger sat on a front galley slide bustle for over five minutes, raising concerns about equipment damage and virus exposure. The crew's request for a mechanic to inspect the slide was ignored by the company to prioritize departure, with no maintenance action or health protection measures taken.

ASRS:1785939.n: I was conducting a discovery flight a requested flight following on the ground with a departure out to the southeast of the field near City X to fly over the house of the client. I was cleared to takeoff of Runway XX. On the climbout I was not sure if Tower wanted me to make a left or right turn towards the south east so I asked for clarification. He said 'you're going to the east right?' And I repeated stating we were going to the southeast. He replied back with instructions to make a right turn to head that way. Right as I turned onto the downwind, Tower switch me to Approach. I switched frequencies and began explaining something to the student as I started to cruise the plane out at 1,500 MSL. About 15 seconds after I switched frequencies to Approach, I gave them a call to check in telling them the altitude I was at and the direction I was headed, southeast. Immediately after I called in, I saw a King Air to my right that was supposedly on final for XX. They were on a track towards us but were in a climb. I saw they were climbing so I immediately started descending. After that is when Approach called in to tell me about the traffic saying that I was intercepting the final approach course for XX. When I looked at my ground track after the flight, I did drift slightly right when I was on the extended downwind, but I never intercepted the final approach course. I did not receive notice from the Tower about the King Air on final before being switched to Approach and it wasn't until after I checked in with Approach that they gave me the advisory. The King Air's TCAS system showed that we reached within 100 feet of each other but myself and the pilots in the King Air agreed that it was much more that 100 feet. I overall feel like there was a lack of communication from all parts that could have possibly prevented this occurrence. I personally could have been more specific with tower on where I was going. I could have been more watchful of my track to stay clear of final. The winds were from the northwest so that could have been a factor in why I was slightly drifting. That is why it is important to know where your winds are coming from to maintain a constant ground track along the ground and prevent drifting.
ASRS:1785939.s: During a discovery flight climbout, the pilot drifted right on downwind and encountered a King Air on final, resulting in a 100-foot TCAS alert. The pilot attributed the near-miss to wind drift, delayed traffic advisories from Approach, and unclear initial turn instructions from Tower.

ASRS:1785965.n: ZZZ1 ARTCC went ATC zero from XA-XB:X0p local. Sector X was required to get ZZZ [Airport] arrivals down to 9,000 feet at ZZZZZ [Intersection], near ZZZ [VOR].The reason for such an early descent was to get them below departures which were supposed to be at 10,000 feet southbound filed over ZZZ [VOR], which kept them out of ZZZ [ARTCC] XY airspace that was ATC zero. The arrivals were given certain routing which had them go through ZZZ1 [ARTCC] XY ATC zero airspace. We couldn't turn the arrivals to stay out of that airspace because the departures were sometimes coming out at altitudes other than 10,000 feet, and we couldn't see limited [Data Blocks] because radar coverage stopped. Plus, this was the coordinated routing so we weren't sure that we should take them off of it anyways. The paper that we were given that served as our 'briefing' on the event, had information to give the aircraft from Sector X to ZZZ Approach. This would have been fine, except ZZZ1 Approach was open and their airspace is between Sector X and ZZZ2 Approach.There needs to be better communication for the safety of the airplanes and controllers. Why were we allowed to fly through a portion of ZZZ1 [ARTCC] with the arrivals, but the departures had to wait. And, if we were supposed to turn the arrivals, or if we were allowed to climb the departure on contact, that needed to be better communicated to the Controller. also, when these route or procedures are being created, they need to have all facilities involved, so that the information we receive is actually pertinent and usable.
ASRS:1785965.s: Air traffic controllers in Sector X managed ZZZ arrivals through ZZZ1 ARTCC airspace during an ATC zero event. The reporter cited poor communication and inadequate briefing regarding conflicting departure altitudes and routing as the cause of the safety concern.

ASRS:1786021.n: Landed on a runway with snow removal equipment on it. While on rollout, the low visibility obscured runway activity until no other choice was available.Onboard equipment failed, distracting crew from making radio positions reporting to ZZZ traffic. Event occurred after Tower had closed for the night.Good accident prevention was conducted by all vehicles and aircraft involved, and no other problems occurred.This could have been a classic example of 'Chain of events causing a accident.' A late departure because of icing conditions at origin. Weather at arrival airport causing snow removal equipment to be on runway for extended periods of time. A minor problem during the approach to landing phase distracted the crew, and company procedures required crew to be playing the role of both flying and non-flying pilot at the same time. In this case, I believe, safety would have been better served if once the decision to hand off control was made, we didn't change back 600-400 feet above the ground. Once the decision was made our roles would have been clearer, and airplane radio communication would have been made at the critical trigger points. On approach to ZZZ Approach vectored my flight to join the ILS [Runway] XX. They cleared us for the approach and told us to contact ZZZ on the CTAF frequency. The vector brought us in at 2,000 feet MSL and outside of ZZZZZ final fix. We had tuned and identified the ILS frequency. I was flying the aircraft and had intercepted the localizer. The glide slope needle on the Captain's ADI flagged. The FO's instruments were still working so control of the aircraft was transferred just outside of the final approach fix. As we descended on the approach, I was monitoring the FO's progress. I had forgotten to make the needed radio call outs, (in the blind) on the CTAF frequency, to announce our presence on the approach and our intentions to land. On the landing roll, we saw the snow removal equipment clearing the runway at the far end.We were alerted to the presence of the snow removal operation upon our roll out on the runway. We also realized that the radio, although properly tuned into the stand-by position on the #1 radio, had not been switched over.The weather at ZZZ was a ceiling of 1,200 feet and visibility of 1 3/4 miles with blowing snow according to the ASOS. (There was nothing to advise us of snow removal activities in progress.) The instrumentation problem caused an unexpected transfer of control of the aircraft to a student pilot who was on his OE training. The transfer was completed successfully, but I was concerned about monitoring the progress of the student on the ILS approach. My attention was on the approach and I failed to make the needed callouts on the CTAF frequency to announce our arrival at ZZZ. The visibility prevented us from seeing the snow removal in progress as we approached the runway.We switched over to the proper frequency and proceeded to taxi in to the FBO.We could have used an alert from Approach control as to the presence of the snow removal equipment working on the surface at ZZZ or have that information broadcast on the ASOS.
ASRS:1786021.s: A crew flying an aircraft with a student pilot landed on a runway with snow removal equipment due to low visibility and a failed radio callout caused by an instrument malfunction and control transfer. The event resulted from a chain of factors including icing delays, weather, and procedural distractions, though no accident occurred.

ASRS:1786024.n: On the climb out from ZZZ on the SID we got direct ZZZZZ. On the climb in the clouds the ice protection came on normally. Within a couple minutes, the anti icing fail warning came on. There after the Bleed 2 Valve Fail also came on. We pulled out the QRH and ran the checklist for the events. Sometime above 15,000 ft. and while still running the QRH, the cabin pressure was being lost at around FL200, the oxygen masks deployed in the back. We also put our oxygen masks on in the cockpit. Notified ATC that moment [received priority handling] for the nearest airport due to loss of cabin pressure. ATC directed the flight to ZZZ1 being the closet. We diverted to ZZZ1. Ran all checklist for descent and landing to ZZZ1. Landed safe and taxied to the gate. Completed the after landing and parking checklist upon arrival. Passengers deplaned at the gate. EICAS alerted. Anti-icing, Bleed 2 Valve Fail and loss of cabin pressure.Diverted Due to the nature of the events, ZZZ might have been a better return option.
ASRS:1786024.s: The flight crew experienced anti-icing and Bleed 2 Valve failures followed by cabin pressure loss above FL200 during climb from ZZZ. They diverted to ZZZ1, landed safely, and noted ZZZ might have been a better return option.

ASRS:1786030.n: Climbing north on the SID we entered icing and turbulence. The anti icing turned on normally. After a couple minutes an EICAS massage, #2 Bleed Fail followed by a couple more anti ice failures. We started the QRH to deal with the bleed failure. I hoped we would soon climb out of icing conditions. By now we were approaching 10,000 ft. and cleared to FL230. Before finishing the bleed failure QRH, approximately 15,000 ft. we started loosing cabin pressure. We reached FL220 till we leveled off [received priority handling]. We used our crew O2 masks and the cabin oxygen deployed. Also started a decent and with ATCs suggestion and help we diverted to ZZZ1 and landed.Looking back it would have been better to return to ZZZ.
ASRS:1786030.s: The flight crew encountered icing and turbulence while climbing on the SID, triggering multiple anti-ice and bleed failures. Subsequent cabin pressure loss at 15,000 ft required oxygen use and a diversion to ZZZ1, though the pilot noted returning to ZZZ would have been preferable.

ASRS:1786039.n: We were on approach into CLT [Runway] 18C, level at 4,000 ft. We encountered wake turbulence which disconnected the auto pilot and caused us to take action to correct the aircraft from an upset state. Once corrected we contacted ATC and were able to continue the approach to landing with no other issues. Hard rolling action which disconnected auto pilot. Wake turbulence. Corrected the state of the aircraft and corrected back on course after deviation. As we did keep focused on the airplane and be ready for anything.
ASRS:1786039.s: The flight crew encountered wake turbulence while on approach to CLT Runway 18C at 4,000 ft, causing hard rolling that disconnected the autopilot and upset the aircraft. The crew manually corrected the deviation and continued the approach to a safe landing.

ASRS:1786068.n: I have two questions/concerns: 1) We could use some clarification regarding minimum altitudes to begin turns after departure from MIA. The problem seems to be centered upon the different altitudes in the Obstacle DP on the [Page] 10-9A and those on the SIDS. The differences are significant and need to be reconciled. 2) Can anyone shed light on the Note #5 in the header section of the 11-3 ILS or LOC RWY (Runway) 9 chart, 'Autopilot coupled approach not authorized'? As per the AIM and Company's FOM definitions, a coupled approach refers to any approach performed by the autopilot. This is obviously not the same definition as an auto landing. There are currently exist 2 NOTAMs concerning autopilot usage, one for ILS RWY 9 and one for the ILS RWY 26L. Neither refer to auto landings. If the FAA meant to restrict auto landings on Runway 9 it should be clearly stated in the header notes or in a NOTAM. The way it is currently written leads one to believe ILS or LOC approaches to Runway 9 must be hand flown.Poorly written Jeppesen notes.Clarify with succinct verbiage.
ASRS:1786068.s: A pilot reported confusion regarding conflicting minimum turn altitudes on MIA departure charts and ambiguous Jeppesen notes restricting autopilot use on Runway 9. The reporter requested clarification to reconcile chart discrepancies and correct the misleading definition of "coupled approach" to prevent unnecessary hand-flown approaches.

ASRS:1786082.n: After departure from ZZZZ [Airport], while enroute, ZZZ Center announced a closure from XA:Y0z-XC:Y0z. The NOTAM announcing the closure did provide routing through ZZZ Center during the closure. Flight AB approached the northern border of ZZZ Center at XB:Y0z and was placed into holding to allow 10 nm of separation between aircraft in a non-radar environment. Flight AB was informed to expect further clearance at XA:X0Z. Because the closure was not known at the time Dispatch prepared the release, the additional fuel needed was not planned. Flight AB was released with 17 min RPF fuel and no contingency fuel. The Captain called Dispatch on SATCOM at XB:Y5z and briefed the enroute delay. Captain was not comfortable delaying until XA:X0Z and diverted into ZZZ [Airport]. ATC Center COVID cleanings come with relatively short notice i.e., no more than 6 hours. For lengthy flights such as this one, additional contingency fuel even with excellent destination weather would have provided more options.
ASRS:1786082.s: Flight AB encountered an unexpected ZZZ Center closure enroute, forcing a hold and diversion to ZZZ Airport due to insufficient contingency fuel. The pilot attributed the fuel shortage to Dispatch's lack of closure awareness during release preparation.

ASRS:1786115.n: There are several concerns regarding the long term wearing of face coverings on an airplane. There is a reduced oxygen environment while in-flight. It is difficult to breathe normally with more layers and there are many studies that I am concerned that our company and the CDC do not take into account. The time of useful consciousness at 41,000 feet does not allow enough time for customers to get on supplemental oxygen and take off their face coverings at the same time. Time of useful consciousness is roughly 9-12 seconds. If a face shield is worn in addition to a face covering it takes even longer for non-trained customers to don O2 masks. In addition, the face covering takes away senses of smell to properly detect issues on board the airplane in the event of a biological mishap or a potential fire. Security concerns remain regarding covering a passenger's face along with flight attendants for cockpit entry and exit procedures to properly verify identities. Wearing a mask during critical phases of flight continue to be concerns when it comes to quickly communicating.
ASRS:1786115.s: A flight attendant reported concerns that face coverings reduce oxygen intake, delay donning supplemental oxygen during rapid decompression at 41,000 feet, and hinder fire detection, identity verification, and communication during critical flight phases.

ASRS:1786144.n: [Enroute] everything was normal, we had portable oxygen system which was engaged. I climbed to 17,000 feet and then climbed to 25,000 feet. I observed the passenger leaning forward as the oxygen line was not long enough to reach the rear seat. I moved the oxygen bottle from between the pilot and co-pilot seat. I assume my oxygen line kinked and the passenger's was working well. I subsequently lost consciousness and the passenger moved to the co-pilot seat.With help from Air Traffic Controllers the plane was brought back down to a lower altitude, I recovered and I landed at the nearest airport where emergency personnel checked both our vitals and oxygen and all was normal.
ASRS:1786144.s: During enroute flight, the pilot lost consciousness at 25,000 feet after moving a portable oxygen bottle, likely kinking their line while the passenger's remained functional. The passenger took control, and with ATC assistance, the aircraft descended to a lower altitude, allowing the pilot to recover and land safely.

ASRS:1786153.n: While on visual approach to COS [Runway] 35L, crew both identified a very large building under construction with crane offset between 1.7 to 2 miles from the runway threshold. At approximately 1.5 miles from threshold, received EGPWS (Electronic Ground Proximity Warning) 'Obstacle, Pull Up!' warning. Aircraft was stable and on visual glide path as verified by FMS 3 degree visual glide path indicator and also visually with Runway 35L PAPI. Sink rate at time of incident was 500 ft. per minute. As the building was either directly underneath or just behind aircraft, no other obstacles were noted and aircraft was stable and on glide path, PIC (Pilot-in-Command) decided this was an erroneous warning and elected to continue flight. Landing was uneventful. During debrief, both crew members agreed that the message was erroneous and must be an anomaly caused by the new construction and a go-around at that time would be futile. If the weather was not CAVU (Ceiling and Visibility Unlimited) an immediate go-around would have been performed. There is a current NOTAM (01/037) regarding a crane at this location but the crane was offset from the flight path and at 300 ft. AGL. An issue exists with the EGPWS system and this new building construction that will trigger false warnings and may cause aircraft to go-around unnecessarily.
ASRS:1786153.s: The flight crew received an erroneous EGPWS 'Obstacle, Pull Up!' warning during a visual approach to Runway 35L caused by a large building under construction. The Pilot-in-Command continued the stable approach and landed uneventfully, concluding the warning was a false anomaly unrelated to the NOTAMed crane.

ASRS:1786175.n: Aircraft X was originally going to land at ZZZ, however, 2 new NOTAMs entered the system just before starting an instrument approach regarding standing water and ice on Runway 20 and the taxiways. Due to the wind and previous icing encountered, he decided to not land at ZZZ. I put him into the published holding at JADGU at 120. We discussed his options for many other close by airports, but due to forecast and known icing and moderate to severe turbulence throughout the area we were having a hard time coming up with a good airport. Aircraft X was also not fuel critical, but did not have a lot of reserve fuel. During this, I was working departures and arrivals into/out of DEN with moderate turbulence. I advised Aircraft X that PUB was 60 miles northeast, and had VFR weather with no known icing. I advised him that he would have to climb to 160, but only for a few minutes and they could descend to 140. Aircraft X decided to go to PUB airport. I climbed Aircraft X to 160 and he asked if it was about a 050 heading. I concurred, but he needed to climb first due to terrain before I could turn him there. He accepted the climb and then asked again about the heading. I told him to remain in the published hold and climb to 160 and I would have the turn on course above 130. He advised me that he was already turning to a 050 heading but was climbing to 130. At this point the MSAW alert was going off, but he was through130 in the 130 MIA. I reiterated the climb to 160 and told him the terrain climbed rapidly and to expedite as much as he could. At this point, Aircraft X was climbing through 140 heading into the 160 MIA. I advised Aircraft X the minimum IFR altitude is 160 and to report reaching. I should have issued a heading south as soon as he advised me he was already turning to PUB. I know the highest mountains in that area are not above 140, but the terrain climbs so rapidly in that area I should have known he would not have topped the 160 MIA even though he did climb above the 130 MIA. He also reported turbulence and icing at this time.The pilot should not have exited the published holding without a clearance to do so. I should have issued a south heading as soon as he told me he was turning out of hold. It was poor service on my end. I know all of the moderate reports and constant transmitter changes did not help the situation.
ASRS:1786175.s: The pilot of Aircraft X diverted from ZZZ to PUB due to runway ice and turbulence, but exited the published hold at JADGU without clearance while climbing. The controller admitted poor service for not issuing a south heading immediately, though the aircraft climbed above the Minimum IFR Altitude despite MSAW alerts.

ASRS:1786187.n: At the gate we received a message that we needed to push early, or on time, due to ZZZ Center closure for COVID cleaning. We pushed back and taxied west route to Runway XL. Halfway down the taxi, by [Taxiway] 1F on [Taxiway] 1, we received a takeoff clearance for [Runway] XL. As I pulled out onto the runway, the FO advised me I entered the runway at [Taxiway] 1D and not [Taxiway] 1C full length. I started a back-taxi for full length and we received a clearance from Tower at [Taxiway] 1D for cleared for takeoff, and we had traffic on four-mile final. When we took off we were between [Taxiway] 1C and behind [Taxiway] 1D. Additive conditions were being off for three weeks. Takeoff at night on unfamiliar runway direction usually is [Runway] XXR. Getting takeoff clearance almost one minute prior to takeoff during taxi. ATC zero hour for destination COVID cleaning was a distraction trying to get off in time before ATC closure. While taxiing to [Runway] XL for a nighttime departure, we were cleared by the Tower to line up and wait well ahead of the runway end, roughly [Taxiway] 1F. As we had just completed the Before Takeoff Checklist after a single engine taxi and engine start, I was a bit behind in setting the Departure frequency. I went into the EFB to find the frequency, and when I looked up I realized we were turning onto the runway at [Taxiway] 1D. I alerted the Captain that we weren't at the end. At the same time, Tower advised us we were at [Taxiway] 1D, but cleared us for takeoff with traffic on four-mile final.The Captain had already started a bit of a back-taxi, and upon hearing the traffic report we discontinued the back-taxi, lined up and departed. We were not at the very end, rather somewhere between [Taxiway] 1C and [Taxiway] 1D, but behind [Taxiway] 1D. Upon reflection, we decided that our takeoff data may not have been valid since we were not sure of our start point. Additive conditions were an ATC zero hour at destination and the Captain admits his three weeks off prior to our day put him a little behind. I also didn't advise that my head would be down while taxiing out.Better verification of runway departure point and better awareness of taxi diagram.
ASRS:1786187.s: The flight crew, distracted by ATC closure and recent time off, entered Runway XL at Taxiway 1D instead of the full-length Taxiway 1C. They departed from an intermediate position between Taxiways 1C and 1D, raising concerns that their takeoff data was invalid due to the uncertain start point.

ASRS:1786222.n: Approximately 40 minutes prior to planned departure, we received a final Dangerous Goods summary after preliminary ACARS initialization. Although it indicated 'final Dangerous Goods summary' it contained the exact format and information as the planned Dangerous Goods summary see FOM. Specifically, it did not contain bullet point referenced in FOM (Hazmat loaded by section). I called Dispatch and in coordination with load planning they advised us to wait until closer to departure to see if a correct final summary was sent to the aircraft. Approximately 10 minutes prior to departure we again made contact and were advised to wait the final weights were sent. The final weights were sent, and the final summary as described in FOM did not come to the aircraft. After another contact, the correct 'final Dangerous Goods summary' was sent 4 minutes after scheduled departure. My concern is there were two 'final Dangerous Goods summary' notifications with different information sent to the aircraft. Please see [Report] for the same condition. Thanks
ASRS:1786222.s: The flight crew received two conflicting Dangerous Goods summaries via ACARS prior to departure, with the correct version arriving four minutes after the scheduled departure time. Dispatch and load planning advised waiting for the proper document, but the initial notification lacked required FOM details, causing a delay in receiving accurate cargo information.

ASRS:1786265.n: While turning into Spot XXX on the cargo apron in ZZZZ, the plane was unable to stop in a timely manner due to what I believe was contamination on the apron. Due to the lack of braking ability the CA (Captain) briefly deployed the thrust reversers and the plane was then able to slow and we regained braking ability. I was not aware that there was difficulty braking until the CA deployed the reversers. We then proceeded to finish the turn into [spot] without issue. The entrance to the ramp was well cleaned and mostly free of contaminants, and according to the Captain, the braking condition was very good. However, further into the ramp, the contamination became present, although it was not very visible, almost like it was black ice on top of the pavement. When we exited the plane after shutting down and securing, the ramp and parking area was covered in a transparent, very slippery layer of ice with slush scattered sporadically throughout. I believe that this ice existed on the apron just outside of the parking spot as well. There was no active precipitation and all of the airport surfaces we had been on up until that point had had good breaking conditions. Thankfully the CA was able to control the aircraft without causing damage to the plane or surroundings. I do not have an exact recollection of the ground speed when we had the difficulty breaking, but I would estimate it to be in the range of roughly 5-7 knots. We notified the ground crew of the difficulty braking and hopefully they took actions to decontaminate that area of the ramp for the next aircraft.I believe the transition from well-cleared, contaminant free areas, to the contaminated area caused the braking issue. It was also night and the light did not reflect off of the ice on the contaminated areas of the ramp, making it difficult to see the contamination. I thought the Captain was maintaining a safe speed for the conditions and was surprised when the reversers were deployed.I would suggest that the entirety of the ramp is cleared to the same standard in the future if able. Crews should also be extra vigilant of contamination that is not easily visible in low light, or poorly lit conditions. Normal arrival. While taxiing to Stand XXX we were following a company aircraft. Due to the light weight of our aircraft it kept accelerating while at idle thrust. When entering the cargo ramp, the pavement was bare and wet. The last 500 feet of taxi had thin frozen slush. The aircraft ahead slowed, and we were slowing to turn into our stand, when the Captain noted the aircraft was sliding. He applied full brakes to no effect, then deployed reverse thrust on both engines, slightly above idle. The aircraft slowed and stopped after sliding about 50 feet. The reversers were stowed and the aircraft turned into the stand and parked. As it approached the stop point it again slid about 5 feet in the attempt to stop. Reverse thrust was not used a second time. Less than 30% n1 in reverse.[The cause was] thin ice on the ramp. Taxi speed about 8-10 knots. Unnoticed change in braking effectiveness. Fatigue from a 15+ hour day.Reverse thrust was a last ditch effort to not scrape paint. Parking brake might have worked also. Even creeping to the stop point, the aircraft still slid about 2 feet past the stop point.
ASRS:1786265.s: Pilots reported that while taxiing at night to a cargo stand, the aircraft slid on invisible thin ice and slush, causing a loss of braking effectiveness at 5–10 knots. The Captain deployed reverse thrust to stop the aircraft safely without damage, attributing the incident to poor visibility of contaminants and inconsistent ramp de-icing.

ASRS:1786277.n: In cruise received notification from Dispatch that due to dry ice loaded with live animal in Forward Cargo divert recommended. Almost immediately after digesting message from Dispatch received call from a Flight Attendant indicating medical [situation]. Diverted to ZZZ2 without incident. Required overweight landing, followed QRH and landed without incident. Made required logbook entries and notifications. Maintenance accomplished requisite checks and entries proceeded to ZZZ1 without incident.The cause of the Hazmat violation [Cargo Illegal Load] was that flight crew received ACARS message to anticipate NOTOC (Notification to Captain) but did not receive NOTOC until departure time through window. Reviewed NOTOC indicating dry ice but did not trigger my mind for live animal loading in same compartment. Same during review of closeout. Captain suggest a normal procedure of receipt of NOTOC with normal inquiry of live animals boarded. Live animal notice of some kind to trigger mind about carriage restrictions. While enroute to ZZZ1 we received a message from Dispatch that we had dry ice loaded in the forward compartment bin with a live animal and recommended a divert to ZZZ3. The Captain and I discussed that we would be extremely overweight for ZZZ3 that was right under us so we were discussing ZZZ2 as a diversion airport. As we were discussing, we received a call from the #1 Flight Attendant that a passenger was having a medical [situation]. We diverted to ZZZ2, elected to land overweight, followed QRH, and landed without incident. Captain made the required logbook entries and notifications. Maintenance eventually accomplished the required inspections, dry ice was taken off airplane, and we then proceeded to ZZZ1 without incident. The cause was that we received a message to anticipate a NOTOC (Notification to Captain), but we did not receive the NOTOC until departure time through the Captain's window. Captain reviewed NOTOC and said we were good so I overlooked the fact that we had a live animal in the same bin. When I reviewed the load close out, I saw there was a live animal, but I did not know the restricted articles were dry ice so it did not trigger me that something was amiss. Flight crew suggests Crew Chief stating there is restricted articles, what it is, and if there are live animals. A more thorough review of the NOTOC on my part as First Officer.
ASRS:1786277.s: Flight crew diverted to ZZZ2 due to a medical emergency and a hazardous materials violation involving dry ice loaded with a live animal. The violation occurred because the crew received the NOTOC late and failed to recognize the incompatibility between the dry ice and the live animal during preflight review.

ASRS:1786293.n: Towards the end of the climb segment, I glanced down at the ACARS screen and noticed we had a message. The chime did not go off since we were still in the climb. When I checked the message, it said something to the effect of, 'There was an error in the loading of DG (Dangerous Goods) on the aircraft. I'm working to get the details. Standby by for further details.' Several minutes later, a message came in stating that a can had been loaded in Position 1L in error. It was slightly lighter than noted on out weight and balance (about 70 pounds, if I recall correctly), not a concern. Of note, it had some DG, and the concern was that it included some radioactive DG (0.8 TI). The Dispatcher stated that it was up to all of us to decide if we would continue or not. The Captain and I discussed our options and referenced the FOM. We noted that up to 50 TI (Transport Index) could be loaded in Position 3 without a waiver and that it seemed that would probably be a higher exposure than the 0.8 TI loaded in [Position] 1L, but that we did not have the expertise or information to determine that for sure. As we were getting ready to forward some of our questions to the [Dispatcher], he sent us a message stating that he was contacting the experts. After consultation with the Duty Officer, Safety representative, and DG experts, they determined that the exposure should be well within limits. This agreed with our hunch, and calmed any fears we had about continuing. We were also notified that the destination ramp would have a DG specialist meet us and take reading on the jet when we arrived, so we continued uneventfully to the destination. As promised, the DG specialist met us and took readings from both the supernumerary area and the cockpit. All were well below limits.The cause was either or combination of human error, inadequacy of training, or process breakdown. I can't say for sure as I'm not sure exactly how the error was made. During loading, I know the crew had problems loading a can. I believe they ended up off-loading the can and transferring the cargo to a new can. We were then delayed while the ramp agent and a manager had to confirm the loading of the can in order to get a final weight and balance. I'm not sure if this was the can in question, if that distraction led to the improper loading of this can, or if the two events were unrelated. Fortunately once someone realized the error, they brought it to attention even though we had already departed. The hub manager called after takeoff to inform [Dispatch] that the weight and balance manifest was incorrect and that the actual can in Position 1L was not the can on the manifest. The actual can had a different weight and also was carrying radioactive DG (Dangerous Goods). Radioactive material can only be loaded in Position 3 and aft. After conferring with the Captain, Duty Officer, Flight Safety Senior Manager, and DG Admin Safety Manager it was determined the flight could safely continue to ZZZ1. The can in [Position] 1L contained 0.8 TIs of Yellow 2.
ASRS:1786293.s: The flight crew received an ACARS alert after departure that a radioactive Dangerous Goods can (0.8 TI) was incorrectly loaded in Position 1L instead of the required Position 3. Following consultation with safety experts, the flight continued to the destination where ground specialists confirmed radiation levels were within limits.

ASRS:1786318.n: During approach to Runway 31L in visual conditions we became task saturated and failed to configure the aircraft by 1,000 AGL. We executed a go-around in response to the late configuration. During the visual go-around we leveled at 2,000 feet and ATC advised the minimum vectoring altitude was 3,000 feet so we initiated a climb to 3000 feet. Late configuration. Did not set altitude pre-select to the published missed approach altitude.Earlier configuration and reference the published missed approach altitude on the approach plate being used for the backup.
ASRS:1786318.s: The flight crew became task saturated during a visual approach to Runway 31L, failing to configure the aircraft by 1,000 feet AGL and executing a go-around. They initially leveled at 2,000 feet before climbing to 3,000 feet after ATC advised the minimum vectoring altitude, caused by late configuration and not setting the altitude pre-select.

ASRS:1786326.n: ATC changed our clearance via CPDLC (Controller Pilot Datalink Communications) before push to the Offshore2 [SID] McKey ZZZ as filed. Loaded SID in FMC Runway 1L. Observed a [disconnect] after SEPDY. We questioned Clearance Delivery what they wanted us to fly after SEPDY. I assumed a 203 degrees heading to intercept the PYE [VOR] 151. Noticed there were several points not programmed in the FMC..This clearance is confusing and the SID is very poorly written. What is expected after SEPDY? Will ATC give us vectors or are we to intercept the radial on our own?We questioned both Clearance Delivery and on initial contact with Departure so there was no deviation, but this needs to be better written on the SID procedures. Rewrite this SID to better explain what ATC expects the pilot to fly ie. radar vectors after SEPDY.
ASRS:1786326.s: The pilot reported a confusing Offshore2 SID clearance received via CPDLC before pushback, noting a disconnect after SEPDY and missing FMC waypoints. Although the crew questioned ATC to avoid deviation, they concluded the SID requires rewriting to clarify if radar vectors or self-interception are expected.

ASRS:1786330.n: I had been concerned with the aircraft even making it into ZZZ due to runway conditions and crosswinds at the time of landing. My focus then turned to being able to depart from ZZZ and making sure we had the fuel necessary for deice, and that braking conditions did not continue to deteriorate, as there were some reports of braking action being poor.The first alert I can find referencing a ZZZ Center closure was at XA:20L. There were several emails that followed, however due to the weather and runway conditions I was dealing with in ZZZ, and the multitude of messages coming through, it did not register that my flight would be affected by the ZZZ [Center] closure.Had we departed on time, and not been delayed for deicing, we would have entered the airspace in time to continue as normally scheduled. Our departure time was XA:50Z. The first fix into ZZZ [Center] airspace was ZZZZZ [Intersection], which is roughly 5 NM from the airspace border. To reach ZZZZZ [Intersection] based on my filed flight time took 1hr and 25 minutes, which would have put us into ZZZ [Center] at XC:15Z, with a 1 hour and 15 minutes buffer. At XB:54Z, I ACARSed the flight as they were close to their 1 hour Top of Descent Point, and I wanted to check in. At this time I was going through my email inbox, and we were receiving a lot, when I realized my flight would be affected by the closure. Once I realized this, I immediately called my coordinator, who verified that the NOTAM for the airspace closure did not allow us to even drop down once entering the airspace, and was only published for overflights, and at XC:00Z I ACARSed to return to gate, since even if they departed immediately, which they had just started the deice process, they would be pushing it to make it into the airspace in time (they were already filed fast). The flight returned to gate and was delayed several hours in order to allow for arrival to ZZZ [Center] after it opened at XF:30Z.I missed the original emails stating the closure which would have given myself, the crew, and the coordinator a heads up to be careful of our times deicing. It is hard to check every email. For ATC-0 events, I believe there should be other forms of notification to dispatchers to prevent this from happening. I do not believe ATC-0 NOTAMs attached for pilot paperwork, as the Captain said he did not see it, and reviewing the paperwork, I did not either.
ASRS:1786330.s: A dispatcher missed emails regarding a ZZZ Center closure while managing deicing delays, causing the flight to return to the gate after realizing it would enter the closed airspace too late. The aircraft was delayed several hours to depart after the center reopened, highlighting a need for better ATC-0 notification methods beyond email and pilot paperwork.

ASRS:1786391.n: In preparing for the flight, I could not determine the engine-out minimum cleanup altitude departing Runway 16R for an engine failure that occurs after D3.0 IRNO. The complex special EFP reads 'EO - Established on H325 and above 5,500 feet MSL' - a condition that will not be reached if climbing via IRNO LOC SOUTH COURSE per the EFP. After talking to the Chief Pilot on Call, who then made inquiries to other internal resources, it was determined that 5,500 feet MSL is the minimum cleanup altitude. In fact, at the minimum all-engine climb gradient of 440 ft./NM any departing aircraft will be above 5,500 feet MSL (1,085 ft. AAE) before D3.0 IRNO. However, with an all-engine minimum cleanup altitude of 7,400 feet MSL an engine failure can occur with the flaps extended. The EFP does not provide a minimum cleanup altitude for that case.Our departure was uneventful, and our light-weight [aircraft] reached 7,400 ft. MSL as we crossed D3.0 IRNO. Winds were out of the south at 45 kts. On a side note, the [Runway] 16L/R EFP for IRNO OTS (Out of Service) appears flawed. If IRNO and IAGY are both OTS the procedure specifies runway heading to 8,500 feet MSL. At max crosswind for a V2 of 131 KIAS of 70 kts., drift angle will be 32 degrees. With a ground track of 196 (degrees), the terrain at 7,862 feet is almost precisely on course from the FMG R-205 decision point. The crosswind limits appear to be for the early turn to H325, but may need to be more restrictive for a 164 heading climb to 8,500 feet MSL.
ASRS:1786391.s: The pilot identified a discrepancy in the Runway 16R engine-out EFP regarding minimum cleanup altitudes after D3.0 IRNO, noting the procedure lacks guidance for failures below 7,400 feet MSL. Although the flight departed uneventfully, the report also flagged potential terrain clearance issues in the Runway 16L/R EFP when both IRNO and IAGY are out of service.

ASRS:1786404.n: During cruse at FL400 mountain wave was encountered. The airspeed exceeded Vmo/Mmo with accompany EICAS alert, Master Caution Alert and audible alert. I was the pilot flying and the FO was Pilot monitoring. The FO extended the speed breaks to full extend and reduced the throttles immediately to idle. The aircraft descended 500 feet. The airspeed reduced below Vmo/Mmo, the warnings stopped. The FO retracted the speed breaks and the autothrottles increased to maintain VNAV programed speed. This all occurred within 10-20 seconds. I was attempting to determine what was happening as the FO accomplished the above items. ATC was notified of the mountain wave and altitude excursion.We briefed the mountain waive and actions which were taken. I reviewed the Flight Manual regarding high altitude overspeed situations. It was determined that the actions taken deviated from FM directed guidance. We reviewed CRM items on what went right, what went wrong and what we would do in the future. It was a great discussion.It became apparent to me that the 4 hour departure delay and all the associated tasks had taken a toll on my ability to process information in a timely manner. I was slow to react to the overspeed. As a result, the FO used CRM skill of leadership to deploy the speed break and reduce the throttles. We had a conversation about the FO acting too quickly and me not acting quickly enough. Maintenance Control was contact to determine what items needed to be included in the report regarding the overspeed. An electronic logbook write up was submitted.
ASRS:1786404.s: During cruise at FL400, a mountain wave caused an overspeed exceeding Vmo/Mmo, triggering alerts. The First Officer immediately deployed speed brakes and reduced thrust to idle, descending 500 feet to recover, while the Pilot Flying attributed their delayed reaction to fatigue from a four-hour departure delay.

ASRS:1786430.n: Departing RJAA. I was PF (Pilot Flying). Captain was PM (Pilot Monitoring). Relief FO (First Officer) was sitting in observer seat. We were within a close margin of max structural weight but within all limits. It was briefed that the best angle speed (258 kts.) and flaps up maneuver speed (254 kts.) would exceed the 250 [kts.] below 10,000 ft. restriction so we opted to keep Flaps 1 until passing 10,000 [ft.] so that we could maintain maneuverability. Once we cleaned up to Flaps 1, I opened the speed window and manually set speed to 240 kts. The overspeed margin was currently 250 kts. The underspeed margin was around 225 kts. Flaps 1 maneuver speed was about 235 kts. Upon reaching 10,000 ft., I put 245 kts. in the speed window to initiate an acceleration that would then continue past 254 kts. for the Flaps Up speed as the flaps transitioned. The transition was going as planned until we hit some moderate wake turbulence from crossing traffic. The speed started to shoot up dramatically towards the upper limit. I applied some back pressure while keeping the AP engaged to get the nose up and arrest the speed increase. I was able to arrest most of the speed increase but it still resulted in a 1 or 2 kt. overspeed. At this time, the turbulence became more intense and both the low and high speed regimes converged. I disengaged the AP/AT (Autopilot/Autothrottle) and hand flew to best maintain airspeed as I anticipated a drop in airspeed on the other side of the wake turbulence. The airspeed started to drop but was arrested with manual input. Once the high and low speed margins stabilized and the turbulence subsided, we re-automated the aircraft and continued our departure without incident.I did not anticipate the wake of crossing traffic to be such a factor in our tight tolerances. When so close to max structural weight on TO (takeoff), the transition from Flaps 1 to Flaps Up is always on a razor thin margin. Any significant wake, turbulence or even wind shift will put you into and undesired airspeed regime. I would suggest not loading the aircraft right up to max weights and this has always been an issue for flap transition on the 767.
ASRS:1786430.s: The Pilot Flying departed RJAA in a Boeing 767 near max structural weight and experienced a minor overspeed during the Flaps 1 to Flaps Up transition due to moderate wake turbulence. The crew manually disengaged automation to arrest airspeed fluctuations, stabilized the aircraft, and continued the departure without incident.

ASRS:1786435.n: During Climb we Leveled at 17,000 departure switched us to ZZZ Center on XYZ.AA. Upon check in with ZZZ Center we were given the clearance to climb and maintain flight level 290 and 270 knots. The Captain who was the pilot Monitor at the time read back those instructions and I set the altitude preset to FL290. During the climb coming through approximately 220/230 we were given traffic at our 2 to 3 o'clock which wasn't a factor. Then while climbing through FL250 ATC called us asking what our altitude was, he then told us that we were assigned FL190. He then cleared us to FL300. Flight continued without further issue.As pilots we take responsibility for any deviation of this nature and if there's questions it is our duty to ask and ask again to repeat if needed. I have however, noticed that since we've started flying more frequently since COVID that there are many more miscommunications on the radio than normal.I think we need to recognize that with what's been happening with COVID over the last year we as a group have lost a little proficiency especially with regards to radio calls and procedures. A lot of us have been out on the leaves that includes both pilots and controllers. The only way I can think of to mitigate this is that we're gonna have to slow it down, make sure that we have it right before we do anything. Maintain a vigilant watch, both on the aircraft and the radios. after copilot (pf) leved at 17000', dfw departure control handed us off to ft worth center (ftwc) on 127.000. upon checking in with 'aa461 level 17000'', i (ca-pm) heard ftwc say for us to climb to fl290 and maintain 270kts. I read back climb to fl290 and maintain 270kts. with the added narrative of 290 on the 'altitude' and 270 on the 'speed' to avoid any confusion between the two. the cp (pf) set 29000 in the altitude window and we both pointed at it confirming what we both heard. ftwc then additionally called traffic at our 2 o'clock, (do not recall distance and alt.), I replied, negative contact, looking. minutes later at 1917z and Passing through fl250, ftwc asked us to say alt, I replied FL250, climbing FL290. Fort Worth Center said, 'Say again?' and I repeated. Fort Worth Center then said, 'I assigned you FL190 for traffic'. I replied, 'roger'. Fort Worth Center then told us to climb and maintain FL300 (our final altitude) and contact center on the next frequency. following the read-back, I asked if there was any loss of separation from the previously called traffic. Fort Worth Center, replied, 'No, thank God.' we never received any TCAS alert nor did we ever see any traffic displayed on the nav display (ND).I read back the altitude and speed in two different ways. Maybe state 'FL290', 'twenty-nine on the altitude', in the future?
ASRS:1786435.s: During climb, the crew misinterpreted a clearance to FL290 as FL190 due to radio miscommunication, though no traffic conflict occurred. The controller corrected the error at FL250, cleared the aircraft to FL300, and attributed the confusion to reduced proficiency following the pandemic.

ASRS:1786484.n: On approach at night visual to Runway 26 in the Jacksonville. I was the pilot monitoring with the first officer as the flying pilot.
