We were given a visual approach and he [turned] off the auto pilot at approximately 1,000 feet. At the 500 feet call he was stable, I don't recall the exact altitude after 500 feet as I was heads up looking outside and I noticed three red and one white on the PAPI. I did observe he was getting low on the glideslope. We had the ILS backed up and when I looked up, I saw four red and instructed him ' four reds, level off' we also received the oral warning glideslope at the same time. He did respond and leveled off approximately two to three seconds later and I saw the three red one white again. Landing was uneventful.It is also worth noting that we were into a 13 hour duty day due to weather delays and rescheduling.Also, worth noting was both Approach Control and Tower stated that they were receiving PIREPs of 40 knot headwinds until a 4 mile final. In actuality the winds were gusting up to 40 all the way to about a 1 mile final.
ASRS:1786484.s: The pilot monitoring observed the first officer flying a night visual approach to Runway 26 in Jacksonville descend below the glideslope, indicated by four red PAPI lights and an oral warning. The pilot instructed a level-off, which was executed after a delay, resulting in an uneventful landing despite fatigue and stronger-than-reported headwinds.

ASRS:1786502.n: Due to the nature of wearing a mask due to COVID-19, it contributes to a couple safety concerns. It is a matter of time before there is a serious injury or damage due to the policy of wearing a mask the entire time while on airport property. I have been involved in a couple of close calls and have seen issues with my coworkers as well.First off, the communication issues. We already have issues with radio communication and I know there have been reports filed in the past for this. However, now there is another issue involving the wearing of masks and trying to understand what the person is trying to say. The voice is usually muffled or broken up and hard to understand. Most of the time requiring the person receiving the transmission to ask the other person to either repeat or in some cases just misunderstands the call. Throw in the inherent environmental noises from jet engines or air conditioning packs and other loud noise, communication becomes very difficult at times. As you can imagine, this can easily become a safety issue especially in times of urgency or clearing of flight control movement or other tests and engine runs. Second, visual impairment. The wearing of masks impairs your line of sight looking down. In order to actually see the ground in front of your feet, you need to actually bend your neck down to move your head to see and while you are looking down with your head down, then that is when you end up walking into something. You are unable to just look down. The obstruction has caused many trips due to the obstacles of power cords, tow bars, tools, steps on ladders, walking in cargo pits, and weather related issues, such as ice and snow. These are just a few of the most common items, but the list is endless.Also, when wearing safety glasses or prescription glasses or sunglasses, there is the issue of them constantly fogging up. Especially in colder weather. This just compounds the issue with not being able to see what is in front of your feet.The easiest and fastest way to fix this is to not require the wearing of masks. Maybe only wear a mask while stationary and unable to social distance as long as it doesn't affect your job. TSA does give an option to not have to wear a mask if it is a safety concern as stated in the TSA website for the Executive Order. So my suggestion is to make the determination that due to a safety risk, the safety guidelines need [to] be changed to make masks optional on the individuals choice, depending on the job he or she is involved in due to the reasons stated above.
ASRS:1786502.s: The reporter, an airport worker, states that mandatory mask policies cause safety risks by muffling radio communications and impairing vision through fogged glasses and restricted downward sight. These issues lead to misunderstood clearances and trips over obstacles like power cords and tow bars, prompting a request to make masks optional for safety reasons.

ASRS:1786518.n: I was doing an IFR XC for my instrument rating and descending to land almost at the DH altitude but still under the hood. MY safety pilot excitedly yelled for full power which startled me, so I looked up. I saw a twin-engine aircraft coming directly at us at about the same altitude. The other AC then banked left and climbed to avoid us. About the time they passed by and with my engine now at full power, the safety pilot banked left and climbed. I don't think he pushed the yoke to descend as we were already relatively close to the ground.Not sure if it was a turboprop or other twin as I only saw it a couple of seconds at most and was obviously trying to process things.I announced our position and that we were on the ILS5 approach at somewhere around 5-7 miles out and again at 1 mile or so out. I recall two other aircraft calling their position on the CTAF but never heard anyone say they were taxiing to, landing or taking off on [Runway] 23 so I'm not sure whether they were landing or taking off.With me being a student I was focused on flying the approach correctly under the hood so I'm not privy to what the safety pilot saw and really can't say how close we were to the other AC as I don't have radar.
ASRS:1786518.s: A student pilot conducting an IFR approach under the hood was startled by a safety pilot's call for full power, revealing a twin-engine aircraft on a collision course at similar altitude. The other aircraft banked left and climbed to avoid the student's plane, which also climbed and banked left after the safety pilot reacted.

ASRS:1786524.n: Due to COVID-19 and family issues there has been a considerable limited amount of flying. Flying practice flights to regain proficiency in all aspects.Assigned a heading and altitude of 2,500 feet on departure from ZZZ. If given a change to ATC I missed the call, but do not remember hearing it. I climbed to 4,500 feet which was my flight altitude.I was told by Tower to go to Departure. Departure stated I climbed to an unauthorized altitude as there was possible traffic. Was not allowed above 2,500 feet.Miss-communication and getting back into the system after the layoff. This is why I am practicing in VFR conditions with various phases of flight.
ASRS:1786524.s: A pilot practicing after a layoff climbed to 4,500 feet instead of the assigned 2,500 feet on departure from ZZZ, likely missing an ATC clearance change. Departure reported an unauthorized climb due to possible traffic, attributing the error to miscommunication and returning to the system.

ASRS:1786540.n: Flight originated in ZZZ with ZZZ1 as destination, original planned cruise was FL230.Upon reaching cruise level we were in IMC and light to moderate turbulence, a request was made for higher cruise level.After leveling off at FL270 we were on top of the layer and smoother air, a few minutes later we had an indication that #3 fuel computer had failed and proceeded to follow POH procedures to attempt a reset, that required bringing the affected engine to idle before cycling the fuel computer control switch. While we were in the process to reset the computer there was an advisory message on the FMS regarding an out of trim condition, before attempting to re-trim the aircraft I disengaged the auto pilot to ascertain the condition, while re-trimming we started to encounter that the tops of the clouds below were in fact rising to our current cruising fl and encountered a sudden but brief increase in turbulence from nil to moderate so the aircraft was pushed upwards about 500 feet before I could correct it without a violent maneuver as we had passengers, ATC requested a confirmation of our current flight level and we advised that we were returning to FL270.The flight proceeded to ZZZ1 without further complication or comment from Controller.As the turbulence encounter occurred while the autopilot was disengaged and the sudden change in flying conditions (from smooth to moderate turbulence) Except for the use of more aggressive maneuvering the altitude excursion was in my opinion almost unavoidable.
ASRS:1786540.s: The pilot reported that while resetting a failed #3 fuel computer at FL270, rising clouds caused moderate turbulence that pushed the aircraft up 500 feet after autopilot disengagement. The pilot corrected the altitude excursion without violent maneuvers and returned to FL270, attributing the event to unavoidable sudden weather changes.

ASRS:1786543.n: Due to COVID-19 and family issues there has been a considerable limited amount of flying. I am flying practice flights to regain proficiency in all aspects.Did not call in to Approach until 16 miles from ZZZ instead of the required 20 miles.It was a miss communication caused by time away and now getting back into the system after the layoff. This is why I am practicing in VFR conditions with various phases of flight.
ASRS:1786543.s: The pilot, returning to flying after a COVID-19 layoff, failed to contact Approach until 16 miles from ZZZ instead of the required 20 miles. This communication error was attributed to time away from the system and is being addressed through VFR practice flights to regain proficiency.

ASRS:1786572.n: While on an OE Refresher flight, I was the PM and my FO student was on his first PF leg in about 9 months due to being non-qualified during the COVID crisis.We were on a right down wind with a clearance to descend 2,000 feet. We were told to stop our descent and we leveled off at 2,600 feet. ATC alerted us to a helicopter crossing our path at 2,000 feet. We reported him in sight and ATC turned us for a right base. When we were clear of the traffic we were cleared to 2,000 feet and then for a visual approach with the airport in sight. The FO called for gear down just outside the marker and managed the speed at the marker. We were at 170 knots at the time. We had planned for a flaps 3 landing. With our encounter/interruption with the close traffic we didn't take into account that the marker was 3.4 miles from the runway and at 1,200 AGL. With the glide slope captured and a planned flaps 3 landing the airplane was having a hard time slowing down. I pulled the speed brakes to assist the aircraft and the FO was slowing the airplane down. I pulled them just inside the marker and stowed them a few seconds later when the airspeed was near Vref. What I didn't realize was I had left them extended below 1,000 feet. I think part of the issue is the approach seems a little nonstandard (standard: 5 NM, 1,500 feet AGL) and sneaks up on you with the marker at 3.4 NM from the runway at 1,200 feet.
ASRS:1786572.s: During an OE Refresher flight, the Pilot Monitoring left speed brakes extended below 1,000 feet after a traffic interruption caused a high-speed approach. The reporter attributed the error to a nonstandard marker location at 3.4 NM and 1,200 feet AGL, which made the approach difficult to manage.

ASRS:1786585.n: At approximately 100 kts, I noticed and called out a IAS Disagree warning indication on my PFD. I immediately looked at the First Officer and the STBY Airspeed indicators to compare speeds and saw the same warning on his. The difference in speed between both was about 5-7 knots (see FM, Airspeed Disagree Alert (amber) Indicates the Captain's and First Officer's airspeed indications disagree by more than 5 knots for 5 continuous seconds), and took about 5 to 10 seconds before the warning went away. My decision was to continue the takeoff since the IAS discrepancy was small and we were in the High-Speed regime. Following the disappearance of the warning indication, I closely monitored the speed differences which was reduced to 1-1.5 knots. Throughout the rest of the flight. An ELB write-up was made and local maintenance contacted to give a full description of the event after landing.Once we were at a safe climbing altitude, we discussed the situation further. I mentioned that if the difference in IAS had been larger I would have opted to reject. Interestingly, the First Officer expressed relief that we did not reject, and that we could have taken off even with the stick shaker going off, similarly as we experienced in a recent MAX training session (during climb), and that the company does not want us to reject other than for the exceptions stated in the FM. His honest answer left me to ponder and wonder if I made the right decision, and to take a closer look at our Normal and Non-Normal procedures, guidance, and its implications, and if any further clarification is needed or due. With that said, I would like to review on how would they apply in the following scenarios. For ease of page reference, I utilized FM dated XX-XX-XXX, however the manual date at the time of the event was [on] YY-YYY-YYYY. The information appears to be identical with the exception of a slight page numbering difference. As a point of reference to determine a reliable airspeed indicator, the checklist states 'An airspeed indication that differs by more than 20 kts or 0.03 Mach from the airspeed shown in the table should be considered unreliable.' Also, there is NO guidance for pitch attitude on takeoff for this situation other than an initial pitch to 15 degrees followed by the immediate actions, which would call for a pitch and thrust reduction just off the ground following gear retraction. The immediate above action items seems contradictory to safe and sound practice of flying away from the ground and executing an emergency procedure at a safe altitude. Should safer guidance be included?It seems very clear, as always, that excellent flying skills and judicious Captain's Emergency Authority will be needed.
ASRS:1786585.s: The Captain and First Officer experienced an IAS Disagree warning during takeoff at 100 kts due to a 5-7 knot speed difference. They continued the takeoff as the discrepancy was small, later questioning the lack of specific pitch guidance and the First Officer's comments on rejecting takeoffs.

ASRS:1786588.n: We encountered a significant unforecast mountain wave. Autothrottles were slow to react. I called out acceleration to Captain who was pilot flying. He acknowledged but did not react to the acceleration. We started to overspeed so I deployed the speed brakes and pulled back the throttles. Lost 500 feet in recovery. Reported altitude loss and wave to ATC. Debriefed event and discovered pulling throttles back was counter to FM guidance. During debrief we also discussed late departure and long taxi with complications on ramp due to weather on departure as contributing to our reaction to this event due to being fatigued. Good debrief.
ASRS:1786588.s: The crew encountered an unforecast mountain wave where slow autothrottle reaction caused an overspeed, resulting in a 500-foot altitude loss after speed brake deployment. A debrief identified counter-intuitive throttle inputs and fatigue from a delayed departure as contributing factors.

ASRS:1786624.n: Flight departing ELP. Flight crew input the flight data into FMS noticed that the RNAV and VOR approaches for Runway 26L was missing the last fix in the approach procedure (the runway), finding a discontinuity from MAF (waypoint in the RNAV) and the runway from WANUN and the Runway 26L, 0.7 DME. We were cleared for the Visual Approach into Runway 26L. We continued to use the RNAV Runway 26L data in the FMS as a reference to the final Approach Course in VMC conditions. All worked as predicted LNAV mode capture GP mode capture with coupled Auto Pilot. Prior to MAF the Autopilot was disconnected and a normal landing performed. No additional flags, or master caution alert nor altitude alert were observed. the flight proceeded normally to the gate. Upload database corrections to this software version.
ASRS:1786624.s: Flight crew departing ELP found missing runway fixes in FMS RNAV and VOR approaches for Runway 26L. They cleared for a visual approach, used the FMS as a reference in VMC, and landed normally after disconnecting the autopilot prior to MAF.

ASRS:1786675.n: We operated Aircraft X from ZZZ to MDW, and the majority of the flight was uneventful. Mr. Y was my Captain and PF, and we had setup well in advance for the RNAV RNP Y approach for Runway 22L at MDW according to their latest ATIS. Later we received an ATIS update showing that the ILS for Runway 31C was active, so we re-configured and briefed that, still with plenty of time. We had discussed the possible need of diverting to ZZZ1 rather than our filed ALT1 of ZZZ2 and ALT2 of ZZZ3, but the visibility at MDW stayed above the minimums we needed for either the RNAV or ILS approaches to 22L/31C respectively.Fast forward to our first approach attempt: we're established on the ILS to 31C, fully configured well before the FAF and I was thinking we've got it made. We broke out at around 1,700 MSL and inflight visibility was not an issue and better than reported. From around 2,000 feet and down we experienced constant light and moderate turbulence, but no icing or precipitation. Captain had turned the autopilot and autothrottles off to help deal with the winds that were gusting from 260 degrees at 21 to 39 knots. We were also landing with stall protection ice speeds, adding 10 knots to our Vref and Vapp speeds.Everything was going great until somewhere between 1/2 to 1 mile from the approach end of 31C we got multiple 'WINDSHEAR' automated call outs from the airplane. Captain elected to go-around which we did, re-configuring as needed and I let MDW Tower know at around 400 feet AGL per the SOP. They gave us a heading and altitude to fly, asked us the reason for the go-around and handed us back off to Chicago Approach. We cleaned up the airplane and got vectored in for another ILS approach to 31C behind an Air Carrier Y.The second ILS approach was almost identical to the first, albeit with slightly less wind and turbulence. This time, even though we were ready for the conditions and knew more of what to expect, we managed to catch a gust of wind right in the flare and didn't touch down on Runway 31C until between the first third and the midpoint of the runway. Captain did a great job of thinking quick and performed a rejected landing, setting and calling 'TOGA' almost immediately after touchdown and off we went. We reconfigured again, got vectored around and handed off to Chicago Approach again and came around for a third attempt at Runway 31C.The third time Captain was able to land normally and well within the touchdown zone, but when he applied the brakes we found out that the '5/5/5' runway condition codes advertised for 31C were optimistic at best with the airplane noticeably sliding and skidding as we rolled out. We also noticed that there was blowing snow obscuring at least 50 percent of the runway surface. Captain advised MDW Tower of the braking action we experienced, calling it 'poor' and, to their credit, they immediately directed the broom and plow teams out to clear Runway 31C again. The rest of the flight was normal as we taxied into our gate.If there's anything I learned tonight, it's that just because you're on short final that doesn't mean you're going to land. Also: just because the Air Carrier Y flight that landed ahead of you reported 'braking action good' doesn't mean you will. I remember being on short final during our first ILS approach to 31C feeling complacent that we 'had it made' being on the ILS rather than RNAV RNP approach with its higher minimums and having broken out early at 1,700 feet. My go-around call outs also could have been crisper and more prompt, but that was mostly due to the 'startle' factor which was my own fault.My one suggestion would be for the airport operations crews at MDW to conduct their own braking action tests more often and with a more pessimistic eye. When the ATIS states RCCs are '5/5/5' the Air Carrier Y flight that landed ahead of you reports 'braking action good' and yet you experience significant wheel slip/skid due to icy runway surface conditions upon landing, thatindicates someone is being either dishonest or overly optimistic on their own braking action reports. If we or our Dispatch had known that the 'real' RCCs for 31C at MDW were actually 3/3/3 or even 2/2/2, we most likely would not have had the required landing performance numbers that we needed to land at MDW's shorter runways and would've gone to ZZZ1.
ASRS:1786675.s: The crew of Aircraft X experienced windshear and poor braking action during three ILS approaches to Runway 31C at MDW due to gusty winds and inaccurate runway condition reports. They executed a go-around and a rejected landing before successfully landing on the third attempt, prompting the captain to report poor braking and request runway clearing.

ASRS:1786676.n: Descending via the NIIXX 2 arrival for the ILS Runway 35R in CAVOK conditions. Around the BSTON Intersection we were given a westerly to northwesterly radar vector and cleared to descend and maintain 10,000. As we got closer to the final approach course (somewhere between DEANE and DRUMM) we were cleared to descend and maintain 8,000 and cleared direct to the FRONZ Intersection (FAF for the ILS). The Controller asked if we had 35R in sight, after a pause, we had the runway in sight and advised ATC. We were then cleared for the visual approach to 35R. The FAF altitude at FRONZ is 7,000 so that is what we set in the MCP while descending through approximately 8,800 in FLCH. We had just gotten the '2,500' call from the Radio Altimeter and made our call outs. As we descended through 8,000 I noticed the Radio Altitude around 1,800 and descending. A quick look at JeppFD PRO showed our aircraft position just south and east of the DRUMM Intersection. I called out the altitude and the fact that we need to go back up to 8,000 (our last cleared altitude prior to the approach clearance) until we are north of DRUMM. I reset the MCP to 8,000 and verbalized that we need to climb back up. The Captain selected a V/S climb back to 8,000. We joined the approach course and followed the G/S and landed without incident.ATC never mentioned anything to us about violating airspace or going below the DEN Class B. Though it is nice to get directs, etc. However, I believe the direct to FRONZ clearance, if not really familiar with the DEN Class B, can set crews up to possibly violate airspace and even lead to an unstable approach.Once parked at the gate with all checklists complete, we debriefed and there certainly was some confusion as to exactly where we were when we descended below 8,000. We had a jump seat observer who thought we might have been a little low as he has a lot of General Aviation experience in the DEN area.
ASRS:1786676.s: The flight crew descended below their cleared 8,000-foot altitude while on a direct to FRONZ for a visual approach to Runway 35R. The First Officer identified the deviation via radio altimeter and JeppFD PRO, initiating a climb back to 8,000 feet before joining the glide slope for a safe landing.

ASRS:1786680.n: As an LCA I was in the right seat and training a new B787 type aircraft Captain in the left seat. We had landed from on Runway XXR in ZZZ and taxied to gate. Upon approaching the gate there was a marshaller and a wing walker on both sides. They were all giving us the all clear signal and marshalling us in to the gate. Gate X is a challenging gate because close proximity to other aircraft. We noticed tractors, baggage carts, containers, and container trailers all parked in the transgression zone on both sides of the entry path. We stopped the aircraft and attempted to contact Operations. As we waited the wing walker, especially on aircraft right, seemed to be frustrated and continued to try to get us to move forward. I witnessed a baggage tractor drive up and just push some of the baggage carts, not even taking time to hook up and pull them. Operations radioed back and told us they would call the ramp. A pickup truck showed up, presumably with a ramp supervisor. The person got out and started directing the removal of the equipment from the path of the aircraft. It was extremely hard for us to see the lines marking the transgression zone and we wanted to be able to rely on the ramp team, but it was more than obvious due to our experience with our aircraft, taxi training, and taxi experience, that we weren't safe to proceed. Finally they cleared all of the obstructions except for one container cart. Once that was cleared and could confirm that the transgression area was clear, we taxied in. What was most disturbing about this whole situation was the continued all clear signal from the wing walkers and the signal to continue the taxi from the marshaller.
ASRS:1786680.s: An LCA training a B787 Captain stopped during gate entry due to ground equipment blocking the transgression zone, despite marshalling signals to proceed. The crew refused to move until a ramp supervisor cleared the obstructions, citing poor visibility of zone markings and unsafe conditions.

ASRS:1786698.n: Landed without incident. Took taxiway D. At a slow pace got 2/3 of the way up the taxiway and left brake froze up. Slid off to the left and stopped the aircraft. Throttled up a little to try to get centered again to no avail. Stopped engines. Airport personnel came and attempted to clear out the snow. Started engines and tried again to get centered. Slid even more to the left and stopped aircraft again. Left main ended up off the pavement. Called for maintenance to tug me in. Kept engines running for passenger comfort, heater, until tug showed up. Stopped engines and was tugged in. The cause was primarily due to 5 to 6 inches of snow on the ground, below freezing temps.
ASRS:1786698.s: The pilot reported that after landing and taxiing on a snow-covered taxiway, the left brake froze, causing the aircraft to slide off the pavement with the left main gear. The incident was attributed to 5 to 6 inches of snow and below-freezing temperatures, requiring a maintenance tug to recover the aircraft.

ASRS:1786704.n: I do not believe jamming was a factor. I believe there was a failure of the HF antenna. If I am correct, there is only one antenna for the two HF radios. The observer pilot was at rest during the initial stages of the event and was not involved in the decision making process. An example of how [to] deal with dual HF failure and a reference to where the Chief Pilot was able to coordinate our continuation would be helpful in either the [Jeppesen] notes or some other searchable publication. I felt the Captain did a thorough job of putting safety and regulatory compliance first and operational reliability second. In the future, I will start to check the HF radios to ensure that they will tune prior to departure.
ASRS:1786704.s: The reporter, likely a pilot, described a dual HF radio failure caused by a single antenna malfunction during flight. The Captain prioritized safety and regulatory compliance over operational reliability, prompting the reporter to plan pre-departure HF checks in the future.

ASRS:1786726.n: Multiple Center Hydraulic EICAS messages resulting in a total loss of quantity and pressure in the in the Center Hydraulic System. [Reported situation] with ZZZ Center, complied with QRH procedures, alternately lowered the flaps and landing gear, landed Flaps 20 on ZZZ [Runway] XXC. Towed to gate.Center Hydraulic System failure. Upon landing, Maintenance found a hydraulic leak on right spoiler.
ASRS:1786726.s: The crew experienced a total loss of Center Hydraulic System quantity and pressure, triggering multiple EICAS messages. They followed QRH procedures to land safely on Flaps 20, after which maintenance identified a hydraulic leak on the right spoiler.

ASRS:1786740.n: Coming in to ROA we were cleared for the visual approach for Runway 34, I was PM and Captain was PF. We were set up for a left base and kept our descent coming down to 4,000 feet. On the descent down we received a GPWS warning for terrain and Captain took immediate action and we climbed out of the terrain we were near. Captain and I both had our terrain mode on, but it was not showing up on the MFD for both sides. ATC also reported to us if we saw the terrain ahead before we received the GPWS.I believe this started from the beginning of our trip both Captain and I were deadheading from ZZZ to ZZZ1 and the aircraft had a hydraulic issue which made our flight delayed. Which got rid of 2 of our 3 flights that we were supposed to operate and made this flight our first flight of the day together. This was also my first time at ROA and Captain told me that he has been there a couple times before so I was unfamiliar with the airport and the surrounding terrain. With it also being a moonless night it was very hard to see the terrain in front of us and with terrain mode on but it wasn't showing us anything made it very difficult to determine exactly where we were at on the ILS approach plate when we were in VFR conditions. I also should have spoken up when I was looking on the approach plate that the highest terrain was 3,508 and Captain was setting the altitude bug to 4,000 feet. I believe our vertical speed was also a factor but I don't remember exactly what Captain had it set to. Captain and I also debriefed together to figure out what we did wrong and what we did right and learn from our mistakes.Add terrain photos or jepp plates on the 10-7 pages to help with situational awareness. Cleared for ILS 34 on an extended left base and received the ground proximity warning for terrain on decent to the final approach fix altitude. Initially cleared to altitude on our route to 9,000 feet crossing Pulaski (PSK) [VOR]. After PSK on rout to ROA we were then given a decent down to 6,000 feet. Clear night we called airport in sight for the sight of the rotating beacon we set up for ILS 34. On an extended left base approach control gave us heading 090 and we were cleared for the visual to 34. After our clearance I gave a further turn to heading 100 and tried to widen out the base for Runway 34. With our clearance I descended down to 4,000 initially keeping in mind we had a tailwind until turning on final for Runway 34. On our descent to 4,000 we both switched to terrain mode on the PFD and saw nothing. Initially I was still on my legs page on my IPAD and my First Officer on the approach plate. We got a call from Approach asking us if we know the terrain around us and while he asked leveling at 4,000 we got a a TERRAIN TERRAIN PULL UP WARNING. We exercised the escape maneuver and leveled at 6,000. We replied to the approach that we exercised the escape maneuver and discussed that we thought we were south of the terrain further back. At night it is hard to distinguish that but exercised extreme caution until back on final.Cause - No initial knowledge of the area of terrain at night even in terrain mode on PFD. Cross reference with iPad to select altitude until final. Suggestion - I will hold the last cleared altitude at 6,000 feet and go further out towards the IAF before turning for final and descending to final altitude before glide slope capture.
ASRS:1786740.s: During a night visual approach to Runway 34 at ROA, the crew received a GPWS terrain warning while descending to 4,000 feet due to unfamiliarity with local terrain and a non-displaying terrain mode. The Captain executed an escape maneuver to 6,000 feet, attributing the event to poor situational awareness and the decision to descend below the highest terrain of 3,508 feet.

ASRS:1786767.n: The FO was on the very first leg of OE. The flight proceeded perfectly until arriving in the ZZZ1 [airport] terminal area. ZZZ Center descended us and never handed us over to the local [ZZZ] TRACON. Instead, we were told to expect holding instructions. It was clear the Center Controller was very busy (he was doing an exceptionally good job). Instead of issuing holding instructions we were asked where we wanted to hold. We told him we wanted to hold at ZZZZZ [Intersection], the initial approach fix for the ILS Runway XX to ZZZ [airport]. He issued instructions to hold south. We asked if we could hold north inbound, right hand turns. He issued instructions 'cleared as requested' with no EFC. He asked how much fuel we had onboard and we replied 2 hours. I didn't push the EFC because it was clear he was saturated and we were holding at 11,000 feet above a lower layer in VFR conditions. ATC explained to other aircraft that ZZZ [TRACON] was ATC Zero and he was the only Controller handling all aircraft going into and out of 4 controlled fields. It was difficult to simply get a break on the frequency so I decided to just be patient.We had been sending ACARS messages to the company enroute and didn't get any responses, this is not that unusual, usually Dispatch will reply with 'OK' but not always. When we were issued holding instructions we sent Dispatch an ACARS message 'Holding at OM for Runway YY ZZZ, no reason given' and once again, we did not receive a reply. Incidentally, I instruct all my OE pilots, as I did in this instance, to look for the 'VHF IN PROGRESS' display after selecting SEND on an ACARS message to be certain the unit actually sent the message. In all cases it did.The airport pages indicated that ZZZ2 [airport] was just XX miles away and we knew they were not affected by this situation. The weather at ZZZ2 was also good. Our FMC fuel reserve was 4.0 since we had no alternate. At first I wanted to use 7.0 as a decision point on fuel. My thought it would probably take 20 minutes to get to ZZZ2 if needed and I wanted a cushion so I added 3.0 to the FMC fuel reserve to make my decision. If we hit 7.0 on the fuel it would be time to contact Dispatch and go to ZZZ2. While we were doing all this ATC was relying on us to contact aircraft going into and out of the airports below to issue instructions. Needless to say we were a bit busy. We were told to descend first to 8,000 feet in the hold, then to 6,000 feet. On several occasions VFR aircraft popped up on our TCAS (no alerts were issued) as we were holding in Class E airspace above the ZZZ Class D and the ZZZ1 Class C. We were keeping a keen eye outside. At one point ATC issued instructions to climb to 8,000 feet in the hold for traffic. Again, the Center Controller was doing an exceptionally good job. We were told on several occasions what our sequence was going into ZZZ, third, then second, then next. Our intent, of course, was to get into ZZZ safely.ATC was issuing phone numbers for aircraft to call when on the ground. I was a bit confused as to why, I thought the towers were open, but paid it no mind. We heard the Controller mention COVID as the reason to another aircraft. Unfortunately, the aircraft landing ZZZ in front of us, Aircraft Y failed to call the phone number. This haunted ALL landings into all 4 airports. The Controller explained to another aircraft that his procedures precluded him from clearing any other aircraft for approaches into any of the four fields until had had a cancellation from the Aircraft Y. In fact, ATC had us attempt to call him on the frequency.I considered whether we could get in VFR but we could not get down into the class D with ZZZ Center and there was a layer between us and the field (I've forgotten where it was but probably about 3,000 feet). I then considered our fuel considerations, rather than using the 4.0 FMC fuel reserve I decided to use the actual FAR fuel reserve of roughly 3.6. The FO stayed on top of duties not only contacting other aircraft but complying with my requests as the flying pilot very well. Finally, when we reached 6,600 pounds of fuel remaining I asked the FO to contact Dispatch via ARINC phone patch. We had already looked at the ARINC Services page in the Jepps early on and determined that ARINC had a surface on ground frequency of XYX.XZ at ZZZ1, and we would be able to get a hold of them down low. I asked FO to come up with a diversion plan. FO worked with Dispatch who recommended ZZZ2 (of course) and said the fuel required would be 1,100 pounds at 10,000 feet. This seemed too low, I didn't see how we could climb to 10,000 feet, fly XY miles, and shoot an approach and landing on 1,100 pounds (and change) of fuel, so we declared minimum fuel and requested an immediate direct vector to ZZZ2. At no point did we use the words 'Mayday' or 'Emergency'. We were instructed to fly a heading (I believe it was 045 degrees) and issued climb instructions to 10,000 feet. We immediately complied and began to set up for an approach into ZZZ2.The FO did a great job juggling responsibilities, getting ATIS and setting up for the approach, contacting ZZZ1 local, etc. At one point ATC queried our fuel status and the FO initially used the word Emergency but then quickly corrected and said we had declared Minimum Fuel. We landed on ZZZ2 Runway XXL with 3.7 on the fuel. We pulled off the runway and asked ATC for a position where we could sit and call the company.We called Dispatch on the cell phone and were instructed to go to the 'Maintenance Ramp.' We complied and were met with a follow me car where we parked, right next to an aircraft with a full load of passengers (obviously there for the same reason, we were later joined by another aircraft). We were immediately met with a set of stairs and a representative who asked what we needed. Dispatch immediately gave us a field load and we ordered thirteen thousand pounds of fuel. We arranged for the proper fuel load. It took some time for the fuel truck to arrive.We then had to coordinate getting paperwork to the aircraft. While Dispatch and the team did a great job of getting that all set up, the young lady driving back and forth had to go quite a ways to get our paperwork which took a great deal of time.Once we had our paperwork we were able to depart for the short flight to ZZZ. We completed the legs without further incident.I am uncertain what drove ZZZ TRACON to close, whether it was a scheduled cleaning due to COVID or some type of emergency. We reviewed the ATC and FIR NOTAMs and did not have anything mentioning the closure. Clearly this was the beginning of the delay. Then, it was further exacerbated by the crew of Aircraft Y jet failing to call the phone number after landing. Had they called we were next to be cleared to land and we would not have diverted.Several suggestions: We need clear and concise ACARs policies in the FOM. Each and every time Dispatch receives a message from a crew inflight they should ALWAYS reply. Perhaps this is a policy with Dispatch, but since it is not in the FOM and once in a while we do not hear from them we have no idea and I was not concerned about not getting replies, until we mentioned holding to them and I got no reply. That's when we hopped on the ACARS Services chart and noted that ZZZ1 had a ground based frequency and we could reach them from our holding position (incidentally, many of our pilots don't even know that table exists). Second, It is not unusual for ACARs not to work. This needs to be cleaned up. We are constantly writing up aircraft for 'NO COMM' and ACARs failures and they don't work. Honestly, I'd say ACARS works correctly about 2/3 of the time, certainly not the spirit of FAR 121.99. Granted we have ARINC, but crews will rely on ACARS just to find out after the fact that dispatch never got anything from us. Next, if this was a scheduled COVID cleaning we should have known they were going ATC Zero before we arrived in the terminal area. Dispatch was even caught off guard about it. ATC must develop a means of communicating this so we don't find out so late in the game. They should also consider issuing a TFR. Perhaps the FAA should consider a new type of TFR for COVID. Frankly, I am a small aircraft owner and use it frequently. I don't want to be told I can't fly over class D airspace while in Class E airspace simply because they are cleaning TRACON. On a beautiful sunny day there are going to be aircraft all over. If I were flying GA in the area and knew the TRACON was down I'd probably stay away just because I don't want to get run over by a transport. Finally, the company should consider what paperwork we REALLY need at the aircraft. For instance, we can already get performance via ACARS. We can pull up our NOTAMS on our tablet. That would leave signing fit for duty and the release. Perhaps we could give Dispatch all the pertinent info (they already had the ZFW weight and balance) so all they needed was fuel onboard and they could simply give us the necessary numbers for departure. Next, send us an ACARS message for signatures - we could print 2 of them and leave one with the rep on the ramp. Had we been able to do that we would have been out about an hour earlier and would NOT have taken another delay. Incidentally, we obtained our PDC via ACARS in ZZZ2 correctly and it worked properly all the way back, including the summary page.
ASRS:1786767.s: The First Officer and Captain held at ZZZZZ while ZZZ TRACON was closed due to COVID, causing a delay when a preceding aircraft failed to call a required phone number. The crew declared minimum fuel, diverted to ZZZ2, and landed safely after refueling, attributing the incident to the ATC closure and the other aircraft's non-compliance.

ASRS:1786774.n: We were flying into GUC in a non RNP aircraft. Winds were 250/11, SKC, elected to fly [Runway] 06 approach per ops pages, then enter downwind via Plato to GU24D. Used RNAV for SA (Situational Awareness), but did not Nav due to UNABLE RNAV RNP. When level at 9200 feet in valley on down wind, received 3 separate GPWS 'terrain, terrain' erroneous indications. There was no terrain and we were not descending. Additionally, there was no red GPWS indications on ND, just the aural cue one time with red warning light. I was the PF (Pilot Flying), and we both were perplexed by the indication. We continued the approach, as there was no reason to react to this partial warning. This event did make us question our flight path, but we also agreed that all was performed correctly. We didn't see any warnings about erroneous GPWS, and the Aircraft appeared to have no issues. We both also agreed that flying a Basic airplane that is not RNP capable into Gunnison was unsatisfactory. Are we to land with a 10 kt. tailwind to avoid indications such as this when performing the pattern as prescribed by the company?Flying a Basic, non-RNP AC into a challenging mountainous terrain airportOur original aircraft was swapped out for some reason. Non RNP airplanes should go to basic destinations.
ASRS:1786774.s: Pilots flying a non-RNP aircraft into Gunnison received three erroneous GPWS "terrain" aural warnings at 9,200 feet while level on downwind. The crew continued the approach but concluded that operating non-RNP aircraft in this mountainous terrain is unsatisfactory.

ASRS:1786792.n: I am submitting this copy of a fumes report submitted following a SOF event that occurred following deicing at the gate at ZZZ as a report. The only thing I might add pertaining to legalities is that after the event when we elected to attempt to fly the leg a second time before Maintenance took the plane out of service, that decision was made after conferring with the Duty Chief at Maintenance Control who had consulted with Maintenance following the SOF event. We had been running the packs with the APU for a long period of time after the passengers deplaned, and then did an engine run on top of that to blow out the entire air conditioning system and had no further issue with deicing fumes. The plane was only subsequently removed from service because it came to light that there might be an IOD claim from one or more of the flight attendants (3 of whom elected to deadhead home on the very same airplane they'd been working on when we had the fumes event) 'This is a report of a fume event that occurred post-deicing at the gate at ZZZ. A separate Fume Event form was also submitted. This is the third such occurrence I have encountered following ZZZ deicing in the past 2 years. In the previous 2 occurrences the effects were much less pronounced and not deemed a hazard because their duration was brief and the cause obvious. In those two cases when the aircraft was reconfigured post-deicing, when the packs were reinstated there was an immediate introduction of visible deicing fluid fumes entering the flight deck, with a much less pronounced but slightly noticeable effect in the cabin that did not warrant any action or alarm. In both cases the packs were turned off and cockpit windows opened followed by an eventual attempt to turn the packs back in one at a time with no further issues. In this case the same thing happened only to a much greater and somewhat alarming degree. When we ran the reconfiguration checklist using the HOT app in this event, turning the APU bleed on reinstated the packs which caused an immediate introduction of thick deicing fluid smoke into the flight deck. My memory of the next couple minutes is a blur because it felt like there were several things demanding my attention and not a lot of information to triage their importance and make a proper best decision given all the variables present. The cockpit smoke was so thick that I could barely see the First Officer and had to feel for my oxygen mask to find it. At some point the packs were turned off, oxygen masks used and the cockpit windows opened. At that point my primary concern was how bad did it get in the cabin? Based on past experience and the current magnitude of the problem, I suspected not nearly as bad as the flight deck but probably getting everyone concerned. Almost immediately the flight attendants called and said the cabin was hazy and what was going on? I said it was deicing fluid and tried to ascertain their assessment which while alarmed didn't suggest it was dire. (The QRH was never considered as the smoke/removal procedures are inflight procedures and rely on using the packs). At this point I was weighing the possibility of evacuating into frigid, arctic conditions with high winds onto a glycol-covered ramp (including 2 wheelchair passengers) vs getting the jetbridge up to the aircraft ASAP (as soon as possible) in case an [immediate] deplaning was deemed advisable. I asked the First Officer to contact ramp control to get the jetbridge attached immediately and tried to think of a way to provide some relief to the cabin air situation. I called the flight attendants back and instructed them to disarm all their doors and to the extent possible crack them open a couple inches to get fresh air into the cabin. That turned out to be unsuccessful because a tailwind was blowing the APU fumes from back to front so that idea was abandoned pretty quickly. Based on my previous two experiences I began wondering if enough time had gone by and perhaps turning the packs on might actually help to bring fresh air into the cabin so I experimentally flipped on the left pack only, but the smoke returned and I immediately turned it off again. It felt like a Catch-22 situation. I knew the only way we could clean out the air was to run the packs but I didn't dare turn on the packs again with the passengers on board. The jetbridge was eventually attached during which time I had assessed the cabin personally and there was a faint lingering odor but nothing I considered alarming. After the passengers were off I asked the flight attendants to self-assess whether they were okay to continue or did they want some medical evaluation and they all said yes they could continue. At some point I contacted the Duty Chief Pilot and after he consulted with Maintenance they suggested doing an engine run. It was at this point that the gate agent informed me that the flight attendants, who had also deplaned, that the flight attendants 'did not want to take this airplane'. We eventually did run both engines at the gate, using both APU and engine bleeds to blow out the pack air until we were satisfied that there were no further issues with fumes. At some point 4 standby flight attendants were assigned and we reboarded the aircraft and departed. My strategy this time was to take the APU completely out of the equation and we requested and received permission to deice at the CDF instead. Halfway into this deicing I was notified something to the effect that the previous flight attendant crew was claiming an injury on duty and because of that Maintenance was therefore taking that plane out of service. We eventually returned to the gate and deplaned to a different aircraft. As I reached the new gate boarding area I saw an off duty [Company] pilot [Name] waiting to board and I asked him for a candid assessment of his impression of what the cabin situation seemed like, and he confirmed my initial suppositions, namely that it was noticeable but not alarming. He likened it to the kind of haze that might be initially experienced when turning on the packs in very humid conditions, but nothing like the thick smoke we encountered in the cockpit. Once again we had to deice but the CDF was closed by then, so I modified our post-deicing procedure to turning the pack switches off prior to reinstating the APU bleed, and leaving them off through both engine starts and then turning them on after the APU bleed was off at the conclusion of starting the engines. We finally departed uneventfully.' I believe the cause of the fume event was 'inadvertent introduction of Type 1 deicing fluid into the APU intake'. I have one recommendation that I will personally use from now on, namely what I mentioned earlier which is not running the packs until they are set for engine bleed as the air source following deicing. I also have to wonder why this has happened 3 times now (all at ZZZ). Clearly there needs to be more emphasis on protecting the APU inlet door when spraying Type 1 fluid. I don't know their procedures, but maybe spraying in brief spurts above the inlet door from back-to-front might help, or just avoiding the area altogether and clearing it by hand in the worst case scenario, but I'm picturing the usual visual of Type 1 fluid cascading down the cockpit windows like a car wash, and if that is going on in the back of the fuselage that can't be a good thing.
ASRS:1786792.s: The flight crew experienced thick deicing fluid fumes in the flight deck and haze in the cabin at ZZZ after turning on the APU bleed post-deicing. The pilot attributed the cause to Type 1 fluid entering the APU intake, leading to an aircraft removal from service due to a potential injury claim before a replacement aircraft departed.

ASRS:1786794.n: Captain was pilot monitoring. FO (First Officer) was pilot flying. Passing through 4,000 feet MSL on climbout from ZZZ we noticed a fuel imbalance developing - right wing main tank fuel indication already 400 pounds lower than left wing. Right wing main tank fuel appeared to be feeding at approximately twice the rate of the left and it appeared that the center tank fuel was not feeding at all. Engine fuel flow readings appeared normal and equal. By 10,000 feet MSL the imbalance had increased to the point that the IMBAL alert was activated. We coordinated with ATC to level off at 12,000 feet MSL in order to reduce fuel flow and begin taking appropriate action. Upon leveling at 12,000 feet MSL we observed the right fuel tank quantity feed rate appear to normalize and then observed a 50 pound increase in right main tank fuel quantity. Fuel imbalance at that point was 1,100 pounds. We initiated the IMBAL checklist in the QRH. Observing what then appeared to be normal tank quantity indications for a crossfeed operation, we coordinated with ATC to continue our climb and proceed on course to the destination knowing we would also coordinate with Dispatch and maintenance promptly to determine if proceeding to ZZZ1 was advisable. As soon as we established climb fuel flow settings and pitch attitude, the right main tank quantity began to decrease again at what appeared to be the same abnormal rate observed during the initial climb. We then requested priority handling initiated the return to ZZZ (nearest airport) and started the APU as a precaution. I advised Dispatch, the cabin crew, and the passengers of the situation using SOP. As soon as we stopped the climb to initiate the return to ZZZ the right main fuel tank indication again stopped decreasing at an abnormal rate. We concluded the IMBAL checklist and for the remainder of the flight we observed no further indications of abnormal rate of decrease in right main wing tank fuel. During the descent, I spoke with the flight attendants and they confirmed that there were no visible indications of fuel leaks on either wing or engine. We landed uneventfully at ZZZ with a total imbalance of 1,220 pounds with 8,370 pounds in the left wing, 7,150 pounds in the right wing and 13,470 pounds in the center tank - 29,000 points total. The aircraft was below max landing weight at touchdown. ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) personnel were standing by as requested. After landing and before further taxi, ARFF personnel inspected the aircraft closely and reported no leaks, no visible damage, and no abnormalities. We shut down the number 2 engine as an additional precaution and requested that the ARFF vehicles follow us to our gate. Maintenance personnel were debriefed in person at the gate upon arrival.Captain suspects suspect faulty fuel crossfeed valve.Reporter recommends company consider revisiting the IMBAL checklist in light of this particular malfunction.
ASRS:1786794.s: The flight crew experienced a developing fuel imbalance during climbout from ZZZ, suspecting a faulty crossfeed valve caused the right main tank to feed abnormally fast. They returned to ZZZ, landed safely with a 1,220-pound imbalance, and ground inspections revealed no leaks or damage.

ASRS:1786796.n: After pushing off gate and starting 1 engine, we received an Elevator Servo Fault ECAM message. We went through all QRH procedures to resolve the problem to no avail. After calling ZZZ Operations to coordinate a return to the gate, we were informed that we were not allowed to return to the gate for a maintenance problem without Maintenance Control authorization. This seems to be in conflict with 14 CFR 121.533, 14 CFR 121.535 regarding Captain's Pilot in Command authority, as well as the MEL preamble which states that Maintenance Control's role is that of technical consultation (Not Command and Control). In any event, we eventually reached Maintenance Control via personal cellphone, and, eventually, Maintenance Control concurred that we should return to the gate. We returned to the gate, maintenance personnel troubleshot the problem to no avail, and the aircraft was taken out of service. My concern is that, in this scenario, the flight crew was forced to go through a Maintenance Control process that has 3 possible outcomes. First, Maintenance Control directs some off book procedure over the phone that 'fixes' the problem. Second, Maintenance Control directs us to flight crew placard the malfunction (which is not allowed by the MEL in any event). Neither one of those outcomes are acceptable with a primary flight control malfunction. The last possible outcome, and the only realistic outcome, is to return the aircraft to the gate, which we were frustrated from doing by this Maintenance Control permission regimen. I am concerned we are being pushed into possibly unsafe operation as our judgment is automatically questioned by a corporate policy that directly conflicts with Federal law.[Reporter stated the need for a revision of] company policy regarding maintenance troubleshooting.We [flight crews] need clearer understanding of the roles and responsibilities of Maintenance Control versus the PIC.
ASRS:1786796.s: Flight crew received an Elevator Servo Fault ECAM message after engine start and were initially denied permission to return to the gate by Operations without Maintenance Control authorization. The aircraft was eventually returned to the gate and taken out of service, prompting the reporter to cite a conflict between company policy and Federal law regarding Pilot in Command authority.

ASRS:1786797.n: During offload a ground air cart blew a radiator hose into the intake and contaminated the packs. Maintenance tried clearing it and thought they had it clear. When ready to leave we started one in the chocks and cross bleed number 1. After both were started, we reconfigured the bleeds and packs and started to taxi. Once power was added we got an aft smoke then mid smoke then forward smoke warning. The odor was of the antifreeze that contaminated earlier. Shut off all air and the warnings went away. Coordinated with ground and taxied in to the chocks and turned it back over to maintenance. They changed the pack filters and signed off the aircraft.The cause was [air cart] equipment malfunction.
ASRS:1786797.s: During offload, a ground air cart malfunction blew a radiator hose into the engine intake, contaminating the packs. After starting and taxiing, smoke warnings and antifreeze odor occurred, requiring the crew to shut off air, return to the chocks, and have maintenance replace the pack filters.

ASRS:1786826.n: We were working on Aircraft X. The task was to accomplish work order XX. We were told the new oxygen generators are in a box, in stores. After looking inside the box, I saw none of the paperwork was filled out. When I questioned the supervisor about this, he went to check on my issue. He came back and said he called inspection and they made one sheet to cover all these generators and we were good to go for install. After further review by the techs on my crew, none of these units in the box were usable for the Work Order and would have been expired prior to the run-out date listed on order XX. I did not ever see any blanket sheet for the box of oxygen generators. I have no idea how many of these were installed on the aircraft by the prior 2 shifts. We are working Aircraft X performing the oxygen generator date check. We have conflicting dates on the oxygen generator service life. Work Order XX states the service life of the generators is XX years and makes no mention of the YY year units mentioned in MM XX. All oxygen generators we changed are the required type.
ASRS:1786826.s: Mechanics working on Aircraft X found oxygen generators in stores lacked proper paperwork and had conflicting service life dates compared to Work Order XX. The crew determined the units were unusable and expired, noting uncertainty about how many were previously installed by other shifts.

ASRS:1786845.n: C172 was established in the left hand traffic pattern [at] TRM, RWY (Runway) 35, performing touch and go training. Position reports were made in middle of left downwind and left base. CE560 entering a wide downwind circumnavigated [us] on its base leg. Upon noticing being circumnavigated, CE560 was inquired by [us] to confirm having the preceding traffic in sight. Visual contact was confirmed. Whilst established on a 2 mile final [we] were overtaken on the right side by CE560 having offset its final approach track to the right, subsequently cutting in front of [us]. Seconds later at a height of approximately 150 feet. [we] were caught in the jet's wake and a temporary low altitude loss of control was perceived (bank angles of 45 degrees were noticed without control authority in roll). A go-around was initiated and control over the aircraft regained. Subsequent calls addressed to CE560 to address the issue remained ignored.
ASRS:1786845.s: A C172 performing touch-and-go training at TRM was overtaken and cut off by a CE560 on final approach. The C172 entered the jet's wake at 150 feet, experiencing a temporary loss of control with 45-degree bank angles, forcing a go-around while the CE560 ignored subsequent calls.
